A more efficient nonlinear observer and nonlinear error feedback strategy will be considered in our future research.

In the present study, the interaction of NO2 gas with ice surface was investigated by preparing a thick ice film that could be maintained under UHV up to ~170 K, which is close to the stratospheric temperature ( > 180 K). The use of a thick ice film eliminated the possibility that the reaction on the sample surface is affected by the metal substrate or a roughening transition of the ice film; these effects could interfere with the measurement of the reaction on a thin ( ~ 4 BL) ice film in the previous work. Also, TPRIS and TPLES measurements were performed under the conditions of low NO2 coverage to investigate the reaction mechanism more closely. The following deductions about the reaction of NO2 on the ice surface could thus be drawn.

(i) Adsorption of NO2 gas on the ice surface produces various surface species, including NO2 δ-, HONO, NO3 -, H3O+, and N2O4. Among these, NO2 δ- is the major species present on the surface at low temperature ( < 110 K), and it may be present as an NO2 moiety with partial negative charge character in the hydrogen-bonded adsorption structures. Upon heating the sample at 110-130 K, the NO2 δ- species are either desorbed as NO2 gas or react with the ice surface to form HONO, NO3 -, and H3O+. Nitrous acid gas is desorbed from the surface at 140-160 K. Interestingly, many of these species are formed on the surface even at ~100 K, albeit in low populations.

(ii) The formation of nitrous acid shows no correlation with the presence of N2O4 on the ice surface. The conversion efficiency of NO2 to nitrous acid gas increases with a decrease in the NO2 coverage. These observations favor the mechanistic interpretation that hydrolysis of NO2 occurs via the interaction between an isolated NO2 molecule and water rather than through the formation of N2O4 species. However, NO2 molecules can diffuse on the ice surface and form clusters at ≥120 K. For this reason, the possibility that NO2 clusters play a role in the hydrolysis of NO2 cannot be ruled out completely.

(iii) The efficiency of conversion of NO2 to surface nitrous acid is about 40%, and the efficiency for conversion to nitrous acid gas is about 7%. The efficiency of the reaction of NO2 on the ice surface is higher than the mass accommodation coefficient of NO2 gas at the gas/liquid water interface.

(iv) The observed hydrolysis of NO2 on the ice surface at low temperature indicates that the reaction has a low energy barrier. This observation suggests that the heterogeneous reaction of NO2 may be efficient on ice particles in cold atmospheric environment.

In conclusion, a new small-molecule acceptor FDNCTF with an A-D-A structure and incorporating NINCN as the new extended end group was designed and synthesized. FDNCTF exhibited red-shifted optical absorption, little changed LUMO energy level, higher charge carrier mobility, and more ordered molecular packing. Non-fullerene OSCs using FDNCTF as the acceptor and a wide band gap polymer PBDB-T as the donor demonstrated a high PCE of 11.2% with a V oc of 0.93 V, a J sc of 16.5 mA cm-2, and an FF of 72.7%, which is much higher than the PCE of 10.06% for the corresponding FDICTF-based device. The higher J sc and nearly maintained V oc are benefited from the better complementary absorption and suitable LUMO energy level. The significantly improved FF should be ascribed to the higher charge separation efficiency and efficient hole transfer from FDNCTF to PBDB-T, confirmed by the transient absorption study. These should be due to the appropriately enhanced intermolecular interaction between the donor and the acceptor because of the extended conjugation of the end groups. These results indicate that employing larger conjugation end groups to the small-molecule acceptors is an effective way to enhance both the absorption and the molecular interaction of the NF acceptor while keeping the LUMO level. This should offer a good strategy to manage the difficult balance and trade-off of J sc and V oc in many cases and achieve higher J sc and FF while keeping the V oc relatively unchanged, simultaneously. A similar strategy might be applied for the donor design.

In summary, atomistic MD simulations of dimers of several fluorobenzenes indicate that the formation of contact pairs is within a small energy dispersion of 0.7 kJ mol-1, with the highest for 1,4-difluorobenzene (3.5 kJ mol-1) and the lowest for 1,3,5-trifluorobenzene (2.8 kJ mol-1). In all cases, entropy favors the solute-pair association in the π-stacked configuration. The sampling of the π-stacked structure by partially fluorinated benzene is also endorsed by enthalpy, especially in 1,4-difluorobenzene. The absence of the π-stacked configuration in benzene and hexafluorobenzene is due to the destabilizing effect caused by enthalpy. Although the well depth of the potential of mean force is characterized by entropic contribution, enthalpy governs the dimer configuration at contact-pair minima. The normalized water density distribution functions suggest that the accumulation of water in the first solvent shell gradually decreases from benzene to hexafluorobenzene, with the increase in the number of fluorine atoms, which implies progressive hydrophobicity of fluorobenzenes. The progressive hydrophobicity in fluorobenzenes can be attributed to the diminishing negative electrostatic potential with the increase in the number of fluorine atoms.

It is shown that ceria oxidation rates are not only dependent on temperature and CO2 concentration but also strongly dependent on reduction extent and surface morphology of the sample. For sintered ceria pellets reduced with H2 to extreme nonstoichiometries (δ > 0.2), a transition toward very slow oxidation rates is observed. Specifically, as nonstoichiometry increased, the oxidation rate for a fixed oxygen concentration (constant δ) decreased. The nonstoichiometry where the transition occurs slightly increases with temperature and agrees well with a near-order phase change reported in literature. Results are further supported with Raman spectroscopy results that indicate an active compression of the oxygen anion-cation near order and ceria lattice in this region. For nonstoichiometries < 0.06, achieved during higher-temperature thermal reduction with low oxygen partial pressure, the opposite behavior is observed, and oxidation rates increase almost linearly with increasing nonstoichiometry for pure ceria. We attribute this trend to one of two phenomena: (1) the formation of defect clusters that affect bulk transport, primarily because such behavior is not observed for 10 mol % Gd doped ceria where defect interactions are known to be less prevalent or (2) slight changes in morphology due to chemical expansion. While these results shed new light on oxidation rates of ceria under a broad range of operating conditions, further work is required to obtain more quantitative information about the rates and their relationship to nonstoichiometry so that they may ultimately be applied in system models to improve overall performance. For example, it will be important to decouple intrinsic reaction rates from any changes in subtle morphology during reduction (i.e.. expansion, crack propagation). Already, extensive data exists describing the chemical and thermal expansion behavior of these materials, ,,,, but it will also be important to quantify how cracks propagate as a function of grain size and nonstoichiometry.

High-energy X-ray measurements were performed on beamline 6-ID-D at the Advanced Photon Source, Argonne National Laboratory. The setup and correction procedures have been described in detail by Skinner et al. This experiment was performed using a monochromatic X-ray beam, where E = 100.305 keV and λ = 0.123607 Å-1, which was collimated to a 0.5 mm2 cross section and the scattered radiation was detected using an amorphous silicon PerkinElmer (XRD 1621) area detector. NIST CeO2 powder was used for sample-detector distance calibration, which was set to 383 mm to balance the resolution and Q-range. Reduction of two-dimensional images to one-dimensional scattering data was performed using the software FIT2D. Pair distribution functions were extracted from total scattering data using the PDFgetX2 software by correcting for background, Compton scattering, and oblique incidence effects. The data were normalized to the average electron density given by the weighted sum of the independent-atom X-ray form factors to yield X-ray structure factor S(Q).

Surface imprinting was employed to synthesize magnetic imprinted polymers in this study. It was found that a polymer layer with template molecules was successfully imprinted on the Fe3O4. The batch adsorption experiments demonstrated that the increase of temperature can improve the adsorption capacities of polymer. The adsorption isotherms and kinetics studies showed that the adsorption of dichlorophen complied with monolayer adsorption and was subject to pseudo-second-order kinetics. Selectivity experiments showed that MMIPs had significantly higher adsorption capacity for dichlorophen than MNIPs. In addition, MMIPs had higher adsorption capacity for chlorophene than 2,4-DCP and 2,6-DCP due to similar chemical structure of chlorophene with dichlorophen. Moreover, the regeneration experiments indicated that MMIPs had good stability. Upon the basis of the results of this study, MMIPs is a promising material to remove trace levels of dichlorophen in aqueous environment.

In large light harvesting systems, not all pigments are coupled strongly, and therefore, the situation is well-described by the formation of delocalized states in certain domains of strongly coupled pigments. The excitation energy transfer between the different exciton domains is described by the generalized Forster theory. The threshold value for assigning pigments to domains is usually defined, and pigment pairs in which the electronic coupling is greater than a threshold value are included in the same domain to describe the dynamic localization effect implicitly. However, domain assignment by a single threshold value may make it difficult to include the possible localization of exciton states induced by the temperature and energy gap between pigments.

In this study, we performed domain assignment by the variational polaron approach to include the possible localization of exciton states by the temperature and energy gap in addition to the reorganization energy. We explored the behavior of the renormalized factor B introduced by the variational transformation over a wide range of parameter regimes. We demonstrated that B can potentially be a criterion for domain assignment, which includes the possible localization of exciton states by the temperature, energy gap, and reorganization energy. We defined the criterion for domain assignment based on the property of B. To demonstrate the validity of domain assignment by the variational polaron approach, we applied our domain assignment approach to pigments in the photosystem II (PSII) core complex and compared the domain model determined by domain assignment based on a single threshold value. We demonstrated that domain assignment by the variational polaron approach could be used to determine the valid domain model in PSII at T = 77 K without using the empirical threshold value; however, it may overestimate the localization of the exciton states by the temperature at T = 300 K. The combined generalized Forster-Redfield approach was successfully applied to study large light harvesting systems, although the best threshold value for domain assignment needs to be determined empirically. We believe that domain assignment by the variational polaron approach is the first step in systematically determining the best threshold value, and it needs to be improved for determining the valid domain model at high temperature.

The ESIPT mechanisms of alizarin in ethanol solvent and binary solvent of ethanol and water with different proportion have been investigated based on DFT and TDDFT methods. The ground- and excited-state geometric structures, IR vibrational spectra, electronic spectra, frontier MOs, NBO, and the potential energy curves are examined to explore the ESIPT mechanism. The results show that the hydrogen bond is strengthened in the first excited state due to the decrease in hydrogen bond length and the red shift of IR vibrational spectra of group involved in the formation of hydrogen bond, which would facilitate the excited-state intramolecular proton transfer. The calculations of frontier MOs and NBO analysis reveal that the intramolecular hydrogen bond reinforcement is ascribed to the characteristics of intramolecular charge transfer in the excited state. Therefore, the excited-state intramolecular charge transfer is the underlying mechanism of ESIPT, and the ESIPT is the primary isomerization pathway from ALR-E to ALR-K.

The effects of water on the ESIPT mechanism of ALR are examined in detail by considering more water molecules to be linked to the ALR-E molecule via intermolecular hydrated hydrogen bonds. The molecular structure, potential energy curves, frontier MOs and NBO analysis are calculated for the several complexes. It can be concluded that the formation of a hydrated hydrogen bond between the carbonyl oxygen and a water molecule weakens the intramolecular hydrogen bond associated with proton transfer, increases the barrier height of ESIPT, and thus hinders the transition of ALR-E to ALR-K in the excited state. What's more, the intramolecular hydrogen bond attenuates with the increase in water molecules, which can explain the experimental reduction of emission intensity as the water proportion in binary solvent increases.

All calculations were performed with dispersion-corrected density functional theory (DFT-D), by employing the Becke-Perdew exchange-correlation functional (BP86) , and Grimmes D3 dispersion correction with Becke-Johnson damping functions, D3 (BJ). - The BP86-D3/TZ2P scheme was shown to be successful to reproduce the experimental data in our previous work with the same heterocalixarene class of compounds. It also provides very good results when compared with high level DFT functionals as well as with RI-MP2 calculations. All host-guest complexes were verified as a minimum in the potential energy surface through the absence of negative eigenvalues in the Hessian matrix.

The bonding mechanism of the host-guest systems were studied through the qualitative Kohn-Sham molecular orbitals (KS-MO) in conjunction with an energy decomposition analysis (EDA). - The EDA scheme decomposes the total interaction energy (ΔE int) between two interacting fragments into chemically meaningful contributions: Pauli repulsion (ΔE Pauli), electrostatic (ΔV elstat), orbital interaction (ΔE oi), and dispersion (ΔE disp) energy terms 1 Δ E int = Δ V elstat + Δ E Pauli + Δ E oi + Δ E disp The ΔV elstat term accounts for the classical electrostatic interactions between the interacting fragments, ΔE Pauli describes the Pauli repulsive interactions between the occupied orbitals of the fragments, and ΔE oi corresponds to both the interactions between occupied molecular orbitals of one fragment with the unoccupied orbitals of the other fragments and the inner-fragment polarization. The ΔE disp term is Grimmes empirical dispersion correction and accounts for the long-range dispersion effects between the interacting fragments. The preparation energy, ΔE prep, is associated with the geometrical deformation of the individual fragments. The ΔE int and the preparation energy are related to bond dissociation energy, BDE, a physical observable, according to 2 - BDE = Δ E int + Δ E prep Further details about the EDA methodology are found elsewhere. ,,

To give more insight about the electrostatic nature of the interaction, the ion-dipole (i-d) contribution to the ΔV elstat term (besides the higher-order terms, such as, dipole-dipole, dipole-quadrupole, etc.) was computed according Ponce-Vargas and Mun ~ oz-Castro - 3 i-d = [ 1 - ( Δ V elstat N Δ V elstat ) ] × 100 % where ΔV elstat N is the electrostatic energy computed changing the anion (Cl-) by its isoelectronic neutral analogue (Ar).

Geometry optimization, analytical vibrational frequencies, - the EDA analysis with the Hirshfeld charge analysis, , and the NBO (natural bond orbital) method - with its NPA charges were performed with the ADF software package, - by employing the relativistic optimized triple-ζ quality plus polarization and diffuse functions, TZ2P basis set in conjunction to the zeroth order regular approximation, ZORA. -

The use of oxides is a promising alternative to replace precious metals as cost-effective and highly active electrocatalysts. Although oxides exhibit a wide range of physical, chemical, and electrochemical properties, there are still many issues associated with their electrochemical activity and stability. Substituted cations with different oxidation states can modify the catalysts' electrochemical activity, but the change in oxide composition during electrochemical reactions may result in cation segregation and enrichment that could cause stability issues. By reviewing efforts on understanding cation distribution in different oxides using various surface techniques, it is realized that proper control or engineering of the surface segregation could lead to improved activity and stability, as perhaps shown in the case of (La1-y Sr y )2CoO4±δ/La1-x Sr x CoO3-δ and (La1-y Sr y )2CoO4±δ/La1-x Sr x Co0.2Fe0.8O3-δ heterostructures. With assistance from DFT, oxygen p-band theory is found to describe electrocatalytic activity for perovskites. Following the guidance from this descriptor for perovskites, it is optimal to design oxide electrocatalysts with an electronic structure such that the O p-band can approach as close as possible to the Fermi level while maintaining stability, thus improving electrocatalyst activity and perhaps even leading to bifunctionality for both the ORR and OER.

Although this Account mainly discusses Sr related migration, other cations such as Ca2+ and Ba2+ are also used for substitution. It is possible to use other cations to tune the oxidation states, vacancy concentration, and oxygen p-band center position with novel electrocatalytic activity and stability. It is also suggested that future work should focus on understanding the mechanism and the functionality of electrocatalysts under reaction conditions. In situ surface techniques are preferred to probe how electrocatalysts work or fail during operational conditions. A combination of studies on atomic and electronic structures can better reveal the underlying structure-property relationships. As mentioned in this Account, there are changes that can be either structurally coherent or incoherent with respect to the catalyst supports. Therefore, complementary methods are needed for achieving comprehensive understanding. The application of in situ surface X-ray diffraction and COBRA for understanding the coherent atomic and chemical changes will be essential for future electrocatalysis studies. These structural probes, together with in situ APXPS for surface chemistry and electronic structure and density functional theory, are providing key insights into electrocatalytic properties and helping to identify suitable activity and stability descriptors for the design of highly efficient oxide electrocatalysts for electrochemical and photoelectrochemical applications.

Here we have shown that electronic and nuclear quantum fluctuations in the active-site tyrosine triad in KSI D40N give rise to small changes in the residues' partial ionizations and ΔΔpK a in response to perturbations such as unnatural amino acid mutagenesis, by shifting the proton positions and redistributing the electron density to buffer the perturbation effects. In the extended hydrogen-bond network upon binding an intermediate analogue, we showed that the quantum mechanical treatment of the electrons results in a large electric field in the enzyme's active site, in excellent agreement with recent experiments. We have demonstrated how this flexibility and the large electric fields arise from the fact that the short O-O distances lower the potential energy barrier for transferring protons along the hydrogen-bond network and that NQEs further flood the potential energy well, thus allowing the electrons and protons to move over a wide range of distances. This work further highlights how AI-PIMD simulations of biological systems can be powerful tools that can reproduce and explain experimental observables such as isotope effects and electric fields. ,,,,,

Finally, it is worth commenting on how the flexibility of the hydrogen-bond network might impact the enzyme's function. For example, our observation of the small change in the ionization of the residues upon chlorination is consistent with the recent experimental observation that replacement of Tyr16 with a chloro- or fluoro-tyrosine leads to very little change to KSI's catalytic activity. In addition, the ability to form an extended hydrogen-bond network with enhanced proton flexibility, rather than a single hydrogen bond, may also be of importance. In particular, a single Tyr57Phe or Asp103Leu mutation, both of which retain an extended network where the substrate can dock, leads to modest 6 or 100 fold decrease in KSI's catalytic activity, respectively. , However, the combined Tyr57Phe/Asp103Leu mutation, which leaves Tyr16 as the only hydrogen bond donor to the substrate with no extended network and might be expected to yield a 600-fold decrease if the effects of these mutations were independent, reduces the activity by over 15 800 fold. This suggests that Tyr57 can partially compensate for the impact of mutating Asp103 since the substrate can still be incorporated in an extended hydrogen-bond network, which possesses electronic and nuclear flexibility. This robustness of the network thus might protect the enzyme from losing its function unless multiple mutations occur concurrently.

In this study, the first instants of an ultrashort laser excited 316L stainless steel are modeled in the framework of the density functional theory. The thermal nonequilibrium properties have been calculated assuming a thermalization of the electronic subsystem and disregarding ionic temperature effects. The structure of the stainless steel has been rounded to its main constituents and generated according to the special quasirandom structure method in order to get a representative solid solution. Results have been compared to γ-Fe, as it is the main constituent of 316L stainless steel, that has an austenite structure, i.e.. a FCC atomic arrangement.

Within the electronic density of states, the d block is found to enlarge and to shift toward higher energies due to the excitation process. This is in agreement with an increase of the electronic screening corresponding to a change of the electronic distribution from spatially delocalized states to more localized ones, as already observed for the pure metals W and Ti. According to the unbalance of occupied electronic states and unoccupied ones from both side of the Fermi energy, the electronic chemical potential is found to shift toward higher energies to accommodate the excess of electrons for both metals.

The electronic heat capacities, electronic pressure, free electron numbers, effective electron-phonon coupling, and optical and thermal conductivities have been computed with a dependence on the electronic temperature. Electronic heat capacities are in agreement with the number of valence electrons per atom showing a clear asymptotic behavior for stainless steel. Electronic pressures increase significantly with T e , as expected for intense laser irradiation conditions. However, at the difference of most of pure metals, the electron-phonon coupling is very high at low temperature, decreasing by a factor two at intermediate temperatures, and reaching an asymptotic behavior at high temperature. The interband signal for optical conductivities is weakened while the thermal conductivity significantly increases with the electronic temperature.

These nonequilibrium thermodynamic or transport properties are quite similar between 316L stainless steel and γ-Fe, with some deviations at high temperature, especially concerning the number of free electrons and the electron-phonon coupling. This similar behavior tends to show that these results concerning both 316L stainless steels and γ-Fe can be extended to a set of similar austenitic steels. Accordingly, the dynamics of femtosecond laser ablation of a stainless steel target was studied based on a hydrodynamic simulation, relying on nonequilibrium DFT calculated data for electron temperature range commonly reached in materials processing.

In conclusion, we showed that the formation of a type II heterojunction between TiO2 and TaO x N y in an IO structure led to improved PEC performance compared to their standalone counterparts. The uniformity of the heterojunction throughout the IO film is crucial to its PEC performance, and the deposition temperature of TaO x N y plays an important role in achieving this. As a result of this heterostructure formation, the photon absorption of TiO2 is extended into the visible spectrum; an onset potential reduction and improved stability in alkaline electrolytes were achieved for TaO x N y . The appropriate band alignment between TiO2 and TaO x N y creates a large built-in electric field for minority carriers that inhibits electron-hole recombination, extends photogenerated carrier lifetimes, and promotes charge transport, as corroborated by LSV and EIS analyses. Reduction in photogenerated hole accumulation at the SEI and longer photogenerated carrier lifetimes suppress self-oxidation during photo-irradiation, thus improving stability in an alkaline electrolyte.

In this paper, a variety of control structures are implemented to improve the dynamic performance of EA-PSD processes for separating pressure-insensitive minimum-boiling azeotrope methanol/toluene and maximum-boiling azeotrope phenol/cyclohexanone. The crucial influence of the control mode of the recycling or connecting stream on the controllability of EA-PSD is investigated. The strategy that sets the recycling or connecting stream as flow controlled or level controlled is able to work better than the strategy that sets the recycling or connecting stream flow rate as directly proportional to the feed flow rate. In addition, high-selectors can be applied to the deliberately selected control loops of the reflux flow rate or reboiler duty to further improve the dynamic performance. The input of the ratio multiplier is the output of a high-selector, whose input is deliberately selected to be one of the two product flow rates instead of the feed flow rate, because the selected product flow rate can serve as the indicator for both the feed flow rate and composition changes. The high-selector is used to implement excess control to maintain good results by avoiding decreasing output when the indicator decreases. When manipulating the reboiler duty to control the temperature near the top, the high-selector can also be used to avoid fluctuations when the indicator decreases by maintaining the reflux flow rate unchanged. Overall comparisons and analyses are made for these control structures. Generally, A-CS3-HSC and B-CS3-HSC are the best control structures of EA-PSD for separating the methanol/toluene mixture, and A-CS2-HSC1, A-CS4-HSC2, B-CS2-HSC1, and B-CS4-HSC2 are all the good control structures of EA-PSD for separating the phenol/cyclohexanone mixture. These effective control structures are valuable in practice for the control of EA-PSD for separating both minimum-boiling and maximum-boiling azeotropes. Meanwhile, the analyses on the application of high-selectors are good reference for the control of other distillation processes.

Spot urine samples from NHANES 2015-2016 were analyzed for urinary IPM3 using ultrahigh-performance liquid chromatography (UPLC; I-Classic Acquity, Waters Inc.. Milford, MA) coupled with electrospray ionization tandem mass spectrometry (ESI-MS/MS; Sciex 5500 Triple quad, Sciex, Framingham, MA). A chromatographic separation was achieved using an Acquity UPLC HSS T3, 100 Å, 1.8 μm, 2.1 mm × 150 mm column (Waters Inc.. Milford, MA) with a Waters HSS T3 VanGuard precolumn (Waters Corporation, Milford, MA). The solvents consisted of a gradient of 15 mM ammonium acetate, pH 6.8 (mobile phase A), and acetonitrile (mobile phase B). Column and sample manager temperatures were set to 40 and 25 °C, respectively. The injection volume was 2 μL using a full-loop injection mode. The mass spectrometer was operated in a negative ion ESI-scheduled multiple reaction monitoring mode. The optimized ion source parameters were as follows: ESI voltage, -4000 V (negative mode); CAD gas, 7 psi; curtain gas flow, 45 psi; nebulizing gas (GS1) flow, 55 psi; heating gas (GS2) flow, 65 psi; and heater temperature, 650 °C. UPLC-MS/MS data were acquired using Analyst software (Sciex, Framingham, MA), and the data were processed in MultiQuant 3.0.3 (Sciex, Framingham, MA). Urine specimens were prepared on a robotic liquid handler by diluting urine 1:10 in 15 mM ammonium acetate (pH 6.8) with a deuterated internal standard, IPM3-d3. Sample concentrations were determined based on their relative response ratio (ratio of native analyte to stable isotope-labeled internal standard) against a calibration curve with known standard concentrations. IPM3 was monitored for transitions m/z 246 → 117 (quantitation ion), m/z 246 → 87 (confirmation ion), and m/z 249 → 117 (internal standard). The limit of detection (LOD) was 1.20 ng/mL.

Developing bioinspired hydrogel lubrication materials with extraordinary lubrication, load-bearing, and antiwear property is necessary for the preparation of functional lubricious implants or devices. Despite the extensive study focusing on lubrication investigation of hydrogel materials, achieving the balance between lubrication and load-bearing for the current system is commonly difficult because of their poor mechanical property. Inspired by the biochemistry structure of the natural cartilage, herein we report a simple method to prepare a layered hydrogel material by employing a NaOH treatment-induced network dissociation strategy. The top layer of the layered hydrogels is soft and porous, which can adsorb much water for swelling to act as an extraordinary lubrication phase. The bottom layer of the layered hydrogels is robust and antiswelling in water, which can work as a good load-bearing phase. The hard steel balls with a high elastic modulus of ~200 GPa are used as slide pairs against the layered hydrogels under a typical ball-on-disk contact mode to evaluate the lubrication property. Meanwhile, the synergy between the top soft and porous layer, which provides excellent aqueous lubrication, and a high bottom-strength robust layer, which gives a high load-bearing function, is shown to be capable of attaining an ultralow COF of ~0.009 under a 3 N load, a low COF of ~0.016 under a 5 N load, and a COF of ~0.035 even under heavily loaded condition of 20 N (P ave: 3.03 MPa), only by employing low viscosity water as a lubricant. Very surprised, the layered hydrogels with a 5 min NaOH treatment can maintain a low friction state (COF < 0.05) after being subjected to 50 000 reciprocating cycles, indicating their good antiwear property. Especially, our simple method can be used to develop a layered hydrogel lubrication catheter, for which both of its inner and outer surfaces exhibit a slippery feature. The extraordinary lubricious performance of the layered hydrogels and the resulted lubrication tube implies their important potential application in the field of tissue engineering and medical devices.

The reactor parameters used in the simulations were taken from the experimental setup by Wheeler et al. Monoliths coated with catalyst had a diameter and length of 17 and 10 mm, respectively, and a porosity of 0.8. The inlet flow rate was 3 SLPM (standard liters per minute), with a molar composition of the reactant inlet stream of 22.9% H2, 11.4% CO, 45.7% H2O, diluted in N2. The temperatures and gas mixture composition were measured at the reactor exit.

Steady state PFR simulations utilizing the full detailed mechanism in Table were performed in order to validate the kinetic model. Low-temperature variations along the reactor length were reported by Wheeler et al. ; thus an isothermal profile was assumed for the PFR simulations. Additionally, coverage dependency of the enthalpy of adsorbed species was taken into account using the coefficients shown in Table . The only adjustable reactor parameter used in the simulations was the active catalytic area, which was set to 1.75 × 104 m-1. This corresponds to a ratio of active catalytic area to reactor geometric area of approximately 66, which is within the typical range for supported monolithic reactors such as the one employed by Wheeler et al. The equilibrium curve was calculated using Cantera's kinetic libraries. Figure shows results for the CO conversion as a function of temperature. The predicted results show good agreement with the experiments, especially in kinetic regime, between approximately 350 and 500 °C. Measurements around 500 °C are expected to be affected by mass transfer effects and, therefore, the simulations tend to overpredict values around this region. Results above 500 °C are considered to be at thermodynamic equilibrium. Neglecting the fact that there is uncertainty in the active catalyst surface area, which can shift the conversion curve along the temperature axis, the ability of match the slope of conversion vs temperature indicates that the model is capturing the kinetics appropriately.

Further validation of the full 19-step mechanism is performed by computing kinetic parameters such as global reaction orders and the apparent activation energy. Assuming that the overall rate constant follows Arrhenius law, the reaction order with respect to species i (a i ) and the apparent activation energy (E a,app) are calculated from 19 a i = ( ln r ln Y i ) T , p 20 E a , app = R g T 2 ( ln r ln T ) p , Y i where r is the reaction rate. Thus, the reaction orders and apparent activation energy can be obtained by performing a number of simulations varying the inlet composition and temperature. Table shows a comparison between the kinetic parameters predicted using the microkinetic mechanism and experimental data on Ni/Al2O3. On Al2O3-supported catalysts, Grenoble et al.. reported an order of approximately zero with respect to CO and 0.5 for H2O for various transition metals. Exceptions are Au and Fe with zero order for H2O and 0.6-0.7 order for CO. The effect of cofeeding H2 and CO2 on the WGS kinetics was also studied. The reaction order with respect to CO2 is zero. Negative first-order H2 kinetics and negative half-order CO2 kinetics were reported for WGS on Pd/CeO2 and for Cu-based catalysts.

Because of the novel applications of ILs in biochemistry and biomedical technology, the search for biocompatible ILs has recently gained increasing attention. In this study, we present two novel biocompatible ILs, TMGAla and TMGAsp, and characterize their effects in dilute aqueous solutions on the structure and stability of the widely used RFP mCherry. Our temperature-dependent spectroscopy data show that while TMGAsp have effects similar to previously studied conventional ILs (BMIBF4, EMIAc, and TMGAc), TMGAla has a much stronger destabilization effect and lower the mCherry unfolding temperature from 80 to 60 °C. At 25 °C, the chromophore is modulated by TMGAla but not TMGAsp or the other conventional ILs, leading to a blueshift in absorbance and fluorescence peaks and an increased Stokes shift. Whereas the blueshift in absorbance and fluorescence indicates an increase of the viscosity of the chromophore local environment, the redshift to the Stokes shift implies an increase of polarity of the chromophore environment. Our MD data at 25 °C show that the chromophore conformation and its interaction with the protein are slightly changed relative to the conformation exhibited in the absence of ILs or TMGAsp. While the key interactions with Lys70, Arg95, and Trp93 are maintained, a hydrogen bond between the chromophore and Gln163 present more pronouncedly in mCherry with TMGAla than TMGAsp or no ILs. These changes might explain the increase of the local polarity and viscosity of the chromophore that cause the spectra shifts. In addition, the conversion of a short fragment 142-144 of the β-strand 7 into coiled conformation was observed in mCherry with TMGAla and TMGAsp. This loss of an interstrand hydrogen bond might partially explain the destabilization effects of ILs. Ala by itself has minimal effect on mCherry at the same concentration. The MD simulations predict that the mCherry-Asp interactions are hydrophilic and the mCherry-Ala interactions are more hydrophobic. Therefore, we speculate that the hydrophilicity/hydrophobicity of the amino acid anion modulates the destabilizing TMG-mCherry interaction, and with TMGAla causes a slight conformational change in the β-strand structure and destabilizes the protein structure.

In this study, we report photoluminescence from the lowest energy LMCT states of the [NpO2Cl4]2- dianion to either the ground or first electronically excited states. We assign weakly emitting transitions at 13 265, and 15 402 cm-1 to the IV → 0 and V → 0 origins based upon comparison with excitation spectra, but are unable to detect the IV → I and V → I origins. Assignments of vibronic structure assignments are consistent with the energies of the ungerade vibrational modes ν2, ν3, ν6, ν8, ν9, and ν10, and the gerade mode ν1. We also investigated the population decay kinetics of the LMCT states. Time-resolved photoluminescence decay waveforms were recorded while monitoring emission from both states IV and V. Emission from V can be described by a single exponential decay after either direct excitation of this state or excitation of IX, in the visible region. However, the presence of a delayed emission on-set in the temporal waveform measured while monitoring emission from state IV following excitation of states IX or V suggests that V decays to IV. A qualitative analysis of the energy of the vibrational frequencies of the symmetric stretch associated with the ground state and excited states I, II, and III suggests that in I and II, the unpaired electron resides in a 5fϕ type orbital, while the unpaired electron resides in a 5fδ orbital in 0 and III.

All solutions and thin films were prepared in a glovebox to prevent from oxygen and moisture influence on the sample. A small microreactor with integrated sensor AC1.W2.R2 supplied by BVT Technologies, Inc. (Pt working electrode, Ag/AgCl reference electrode, Pt auxiliary electrode) was used for the electrochemical analysis of ~10-3 M P3HT solution prepared in benzonitrile (99%, for spectroscopy) with 0.1 M TBAPF6 (for electrochemical analysis, ≥99.0%), PTFE membrane filtered (200 nm pore size), and sonicated for 60 min.

Thin films were deposited on ITO substrates in the glovebox with spin-coating from 1 wt % solution of P3HT in dichlorobenzene with the spinning rate of 30 rps. Samples were subsequently annealed at 110 °C for 5 min. Some of the prepared samples were exposed to air for 3 days to study the influence of the air on the thin film properties. The 3 days long exposition was chosen to reach reproducible and detectable changes in DOS due to the introduced defects. Electrochemical microcells were formed on the P3HT-modified ITO substrates bounding disc working electrode areas of 12 mm2. The solution of 0.1 M TBAPF6 in acetonitrile was used as the supporting electrolyte. The potential of the working electrode with respect to the reference Ag/AgCl electrode was controlled via the potentiostat. Pt wire was used as the counter electrode. The potential recorded with respect to the reference Ag/AgCl electrode was recalculated to the local vacuum level assuming the Ag/AgCl energy vs vacuum value of 4.66 eV. In order to generate excitons in P3HT, the red Lasiris laser emitting light with the wavelength at the absorption edge of P3HT (670 nm, power density of 100 mW/cm2) was used for the sample illumination.

Some irreversible degradation processes can occur at higher positive or negative potentials. Examples include irreversible anodic overoxidation depending on temperature, solvent, and electrolyte at the site of the radical cation of the polymer backbone, anodic overoxidation of polythiophenes in wet acetonitrile electrolytes, or electrolytes containing chloride. Anodic overoxidation proceeds beyond the positive limit, as cathodic overreduction is observed at negative potentials. Therefore, the electrochemical measurements of HOMO and LUMO levels were split in two separate sweeps. Each measurement started from the zero potential and was performed with a virgin microcell or microreactor. The whole-energy range scans from ~-2.4 eV vs vacuum to ~-5.9 eV vs vacuum enabled us not only the estimation of HOMO and LUMO level positions vs vacuum but also the detection of a low-level sample contamination with defect states within the band gap.

In this report, we have scrutinized the effect of ethanol-water binary solvent mixtures on the structural response of papain by various bulk- and single-molecular level spectroscopy measurements and compared the result with the GnHCl-induced structural change of papain. From the spectroscopy studies, we can conclude that GnHCl denaturates papain, whereas ethanol induces its aggregation. A strong correlation between the structural change at single molecular-level measurement and secondary structural change from the CD measurement has been found. Chemical denaturation of papain by GnHCl is associated with the loss of helicity with a concomitant increase of the random coil and a small increase of the β-sheet, whereas, ethanol-induced aggregation of papain is associated with the formation of a high percentage of the β-sheet. The findings are supported by the steady-state experiment, solvation dynamics, and rotational anisotropy of the protein in ethanol-water mixtures and in GnHCl. The visual conformation of aggregation formation of papain in the presence of ethanol comes from the AFM experiments. Our result suggests that two chemical constituents can interact with a protein in a very different way, reminding us of the tremendous degree of complexity involved in the biological system. Another surprising highlight of the report is that papain was found to form aggregates in ethanol-water mixtures at concentrations as low as 50 nM. As a whole, the global and local structural change of papain in ethanol-water binary solvent mixtures and also in the presence of GnHCl has been summarized, quantified, and explained. Papain, being tremendously important in industry, is required to be protected against aggregation. In this paper, we showed that papain is very much prone to aggregation in the presence of ethanol. In our upcoming projects, we will come up with some strategies to prevent this aggregation.

A modular coextrusion die was optimized via simulation software and machined to fit a commercially available capillary rheometer. Simulation allowed screening of unacceptable designs and yielded a final design that produced coextruded bilayers with fewer than 50 g of material and less than 10% edge distortions. Nonreactive miPP/mLLDPE, miPP/mHDPE, and ziPP/zHDPE pairs showed excellent agreement over 2 orders of magnitude in G IC between the CapCoEx device developed in this research and typical laboratory scale continuous coextrusion technology. Results from CapCoEx were obtained using ~90% less material and matched the results of continuous coextrusion much more closely than samples prepared by hand lamination in a compression press.

Finally, the ability to control interfacial coupling reactions between MA functionalized HDPE and PET was demonstrated using the CapCoEx device. Adhesion for PET/HDPE1.5 (MA grafting density 1.5 wt % in HDPE layer) increased 15-fold over PET/HDPE0 after only 4.4 s of melt contact time. Adhesion doubled and appeared to saturate after 10 s. Reducing MA graft density to 0.8 wt % reduced the number of interfacial reactions that occurred, and G IC increased more slowly before complete saturation after 22 s. This development represents a valuable new screening technology for assessing interfacial chemistry using small material quantities.

In summary, we have demonstrated an extensive application of 1H NMR relaxation to examine the 1:1 host-guest inclusion complex of β-CD with two orally active drugs in aqueous media, and reported their stoichiometry and binding constant. In the 1:1 drug-β-CD complex, both paracetamol and aspirin behave similarly, exhibiting an intermediate motional dynamics and giving rise to R 1 ns/R 1 se very close to the theoretically expected value of 1.05. To emphasize the use of NMR relaxation measurements for supramolecular inclusion complexes the following points might be highlighted: NMR relaxation measurement allows the assessment of intermolecular interactions between a drug and supramolecule present in solution. Measurement of nonselective and selective relaxation rate ratio for the free drugs indicates activation of any other relaxation mechanism other than IDD and XDD dipolar interactions for the free drugs. The molecular rotational correlation time of the free drug can be evaluated from the selective relaxation rate by considering the extreme narrowing limit (ωH 2τc 2 ≪ 1). Significant change in the molecular rotational correlation time (τc) extracted from the nonselective and selective relaxation rate ratio in the case of the drug in the presence of β-CD confirms encapsulation. Measurement of bi-selective relaxation rates employing modulated shaped inversion pulses for the simultaneous inversion of a drug proton and a β-CD proton allows extraction of the cross-relaxation rate of the drug proton. The cross-relaxation rate thus measured represents the contribution toward overall drug proton relaxation due to dipolar interaction with the β-CD proton after encapsulation. The cross-relaxation rates can further be converted into intermolecular proton distances between the drug and β-CD to estimate a mode of insertion of the test molecule. However, it should be mentioned here that experimental cross-relaxation rates can be directly converted into internuclear distances provided there is no internal motion. Hence, in the present case, limited internal motion of the drug molecules within the cavity has been assumed. Further, it would be advisable to measure the internuclear distances of these intermediate-sized inclusion complexes at a lower external magnetic field strength, ca. 200 MHz. Results of the DFT calculations performed further reinforce our predictions of the host-guest geometry presented here. Paracetamol enters the cavity through vertical insertion whereas aspirin chooses a horizontal mode, which is in agreement with the order of polarity of the different functional groups present as substituents, for example, amide > acid > alcohol > carbonyl. Finally, it may be concluded that 1D 1H NMR relaxation experiments offer a much faster and cost-effective method compared to that of 2D ROESY experiments to analyze drug-supramolecule complexes.

In-cell spectroscopy has gained considerable momentum in the past decade driven by the need to study biomolecules in their native environment. Whereas in vitro experiments have been indispensable to our understanding of biomolecule structure and function, a large part of the interactome relies on weak interactions that are disrupted in vitro unless a native-like solvation environment can be painstakingly reproduced. In this section, we discuss the two main methods to characterize sticking in vivo: (1) fluorescence microscopy and (2) in-cell NMR.

Fluorescence microscopy is a time-honored technique to study biomolecule dynamics in vivo. The ease of availability of fluorescent labels as well as robust and flexible tagging methods have made fluorescence microscopy the method of choice for studying many different processes in vivo. These include but are not limited to the diffusion, ,, binding, , and stability ,,, of biomolecules. Moreover, the availability of different fluorescence techniques such as FRET, fluorescence lifetime imaging (FLIM), FCS, , or FRAP can identify different aspects of the tagged biomolecule dynamics. An important outcome of the stickiness of the cytoplasm is the slowdown of biomolecules as they diffuse through the cytoplasm. This can be easily visualized by fluorescently labeling biomolecules and then tracking them as they diffuse through the cytoplasm. Gruebele and Guo measured the diffusion of a GFP-labeled protein, phosphoglycerate kinase (PGK), in both the folded and unfolded states inside cells and saw anomalous diffusion. They also observed that unfolded PGK diffused slower than folded PGK in the cell. It was concluded that this slowdown could not be explained by the larger hydrodynamic radius of the unfolded protein chain alone but required sticking of exposed hydrophobic patches to other cellular constituents.

Whereas fluorescence techniques have been extensively diversified for in-cell applications, they are somewhat limited when the conformational dynamics of biomolecules needs to be monitored. Most of these techniques also involve using fluorescent proteins that are bulky and could perturb the tagged biomolecule. In the past decade, in-cell NMR has been developed to complement fluorescence microscopy. ,- Isotopically labeled proteins for in-cell NMR can be both overexpressed and microinjected directly in the cell. In general, NMR line broadening is a signature of the interaction between biomolecules and can be used as such in-cell to characterize both functional and nonspecific interactions. Nonspecific interactions are easy to visualize when exclusively eukaryotic proteins are studied in prokaryotic organisms such as E. coli. In this case, most functional partners for the protein of interest are absent, and only nonspecific interactions occur. In-cell NMR and mutagenesis have been used to predict the role of specific surface charges in nonspecific electrostatic interactions, as explained in section . - , Gierasch, Wang, and Zhuravleva showed that these nonspecific interactions are not modulated by a single variable but are a function of several factors like the overall charge, distribution of hydrophobic patches, and conformational flexibility.

In most cases, sticking has a negative consequence for the protein stability or function. For example, ProtL, SOD1, and GB1-D40K are destabilized in-cell as compared with buffer. This is evidence that entropic stabilization from crowding can be overcome by destabilization due to sticking. Furthermore, there is also evidence that sticking can lead to the disruption of functional interactions. Oliveberg and coworkers showed that two mammalian proteins, HAH1 and SOD1, diffused freely in mammalian cells but seemed to get stuck in the bacterial cytoplasm (Figure ). A freely diffusing protein can form functional interactions with its partners. A slowdown such as the one observed for SOD1 and HAH1 in E. coli can reduce the sampling of such interactions.

In-cell measurements are just starting to scratch the surface of the widespread nonspecific interactions that are abundant in the cell. The usability of in-cell NMR is somewhat limited to studying eukaryote-specific proteins in prokaryotes. Eukaryotic proteins that are conserved in prokaryotes pose a challenge because very strong functional interactions can broaden lines beyond detection. However, in-cell NMR has been successful in eukaryotic systems by mutating out residues in the binding pocket to reduce broadening due to strong interactions. For example, Shirakawa and coworkers were able to record the in-cell NMR spectra of a ubiquitin derivative (Ub-3A), whose affinity to cytosolic proteins was reduced by making three point mutations in the binding interface. Whereas wild-type ubiquitin showed peak broadening due to interactions with endogenous proteins in vivo, Ub-3A showed well-resolved peaks. Hydrogen exchange in combination with NMR also showed that binding to proteins in the cell destabilizes wild-type ubiquitin in vivo compared with in vitro. Interestingly, even though Ub-3A has a lower binding affinity, it is still destabilized in vivo due to sticking.

This study involved a multifaceted experimental and theoretical approach to explain variations in the crystallization inhibition properties of a series of polysaccharide derivatives. Small changes in the chemical structure of the polymer strongly influenced its ability to inhibit crystallization. The determination of radial distribution functions and estimated free energies of interaction between a nucleus of drug molecules and a polymer chain, using computational modeling, were useful to predict possible intermolecular interactions in solution. The tendency of the polysaccharides to interact at the amorphous drug-water interface was verified by AFM measurements, whereby computational predictions showed good agreement with experimental data. These approaches lend support to the hypothesis that polysaccharides that are effective crystallization inhibitors have a balance of hydrophobic and hydrophilic groups. Thus, effective polysaccharides interact with drug aggregates via hydrophobic interactions with backbone functionalities such as ethyl groups, while carboxylate groups associated with tethered substituents lead to an extended polymer conformation that in turn minimizes the tendency for intramolecular interactions. These results not only provide fundamental insight into mechanisms by which polymers modify nucleation rates, but also pave the way for the rational design of new materials for crystallization inhibition.

In the present study the performance of a series of star-like branched polyacrylamides (SB-PAMs) was investigated in oil recovery simulations. The rheological measurements of the SB-PAMs showed unique properties compared with their linear analogues. Although a linear reference polyacrylamide (PAM) represented the highest solution viscosity, it is instantly prone to shear thinning, while in contrast SB-polymers exhibit robustness under shear which in turn is advantageous under the harsh conditions (high shear) during injection into oil fields. The observations from the viscoelasticity measurements, displayed that higher branching density in the core corresponds to more elastic behavior of the polymer at equal viscosity. The flow-cell experiments showed that SB-PAMs perform approximately 3-5 times more efficient (at comperable polymer concentration) than a linear analogue with a slightly higher molecular weight in recovering residual oil out of dead ends. Highest recoveries were 33-35% of the OOIP respectively. This effect is more relevant for larger arm length values due to stretching (entanglement) of the arms. In consequence of pronounced entanglement of the arms, more oil is recovered as the polymeric arms pull the oil out of dead ends (pulling effect). Finally, SB-PAM is more resilient to harsh reservoir conditions, which gives SB-PAMs a competitive advantage for EOR at the applied concentrations.

Non-food and waste fatty acid/triglyceride feedstocks and by bio-Fischer-Tropsch wax (produced from biomass based synthesis gas) were converted to produce alkanes on different catalysts. We studied the hydrodeoxygenation/decarboxylation/decarbonylation of various fatty acid/triglyceride feedstocks over commercial NiMoP/Al2O3 catalyst to get liquid mixtures rich in n-alkanes. Heterogeneous catalytic hydroisomerization over Pt/SAPO-11 catalysts produced according to a traditional method and a new production method were applied to convert the n-alkanes produced from fatty acid/triglyceride feedstocks and the FT wax to isoalkanes. Results suggest that structural and catalytic properties of a Pt/SAPO-11 catalyst depend on the synthesis method applied to obtain the SAPO-11 catalyst component. The studied SAPO-11 catalyst components were prepared either by the conventional method applying aluminum isopropylate as aluminum source or by a new method that applies aluminum acetate or basic aluminum acetate as aluminum source in the synthesis mixture. Results suggest that a more efficient hydroisomerization Pt catalyst can be obtained from the SAPO-11 prepared by a new synthesis method.

On the catalyst synthesized by the new method in the obtained products, the proportion of the hydrocarbon chains with one branch was significantly higher than those with multiple branches. The formation of multiple branched isomers is limited because of the higher proportion of sites with smaller acid strengths. The above reasons all lead to the formation of isoparaffin mixtures of better quality (more favorable flow properties).

The liquid hydrocarbon products of the studied catalytic processes are excellent quality renewable diesel fuel or base oil components having high hydrogen content. Results showed that reactions can be directed to get mainly either monobranched or multibranched alkanes by selecting appropriate process parameters. The properties and, thereby, the quality of the products could be controlled in a wide range to satisfy the demands for biobased diesel fuels and lubricating base oils. Positive results were gained using very different feedstocks and either microscale or large-scale laboratory reactor systems.

The silicalite-1 catalyst support has been prepared by the sonication approach, and the effect of sonication time on the textural properties and HDS catalytic activity has been extensively studied. The SILC-1 support prepared by 1 h of sonication of the precursor solutions yields a largely microporous surface area support, and the SILC-4 support prepared by 4 h of sonication lost its mesoporosity after loading the Ni and Mo active metals. The 2 h sonication support, SILC-2, retained a large percent of its mesoporosity even after loading of the active metals. In addition, the crystallinity of the silicalite-1 support has been retained in SILC-2-NM, and traces of bulk crystalline MoO3 were not observed from the XRD pattern. The H2-TPR results also show lower reduction temperature for the SILC-2-NM catalyst, which signaled better active phase dispersion. The NH3-TPD and XPS analysis showed an increasing number of acidic sites and active MoS2 phase, respectively, with increasing sonication time of the supports. The catalyst activity test reveals that the SILC-2-NM catalyst with relatively good textural properties and active-phase acidity and dispersion performs better than the other catalysts. The observed activity of the SILC-2-NM catalyst implies that the sonication time of 2 h is the optimum for the loading of 3 and 10 wt % Ni and Mo active metals, respectively, via the wetness impregnation method. The experimental and modeled kinetic parameters reveal that the HDS reaction over the studied catalysts occurs largely via the DDS pathway.

Applying Fourier transformation (FT) to time-dependent internal coordinates (C-O and C-N bond lengths and C-N-H angles of each amide group in LM7-2) converts the time domain into the frequency domain and provides their vibrational frequencies. To that end, we used the Octave package for fast FT (FFT). As we explain in the Results and Discussion section, LM7-2 experienced helical and helix-hinge-helix conformations. Hence, we applied FFT on C-O and C-N bond lengths and C-N-H angle of all amide groups of LM7-2 for four selected 200 ps time periods in which LM7-2 has either a helical or a helix-hinge-helix conformation. Wavenumbers computed from FFT spanned n/[cNδt] = 0.167-33,400 cm-1 for n = 1 to N = 2 × 105 steps, and c indicates the speed of light. These calculated vibrational spectra over the more narrow range 1100-1800 cm-1 enable us to compare amide band vibrations among these states of LM7-2.

The excited states of tolane have been investigated using the ab initio algebraic-diagrammatic construction scheme for the polarization propagator of second order to explain the differences in fluorescence and phophorescence spectra of planar and twisted tolane derivatives. The optical properties of tolane and its derivatives are strongly influenced by the central twisting angle, which determines the relative orientation of the phenyl rings and the degree of π-electron delocalization. Relaxed scans of the lowest excited states have been calculated along this twisting mode but also along the trans-bent motion, which leads to the lowest-energy minimum on the S1 potential energy surface. The trans-bent configuration of tolane is isoelectronic to the azobenzene dication, and the lowest S1 state corresponds to a πn* excitation.

In Figure , the photochemistry of twisted and planar tolane derivatives is summarized. Upon photoexcitation, tolanes planarize in the excited S1 state, and therefore, twisted as well as planar tolane derivatives exhibit very similar fluorescence spectra independent of the twisting angle in the ground-state equilibrium structure. The presence of an energy barrier leading from the planar S1 minimum to the trans-bent minimum was confirmed, which nicely explains the temperature dependence and excitation wavelength dependence of its population. In other words, planar tolanes do not possess sufficient excess energy to overcome the barrier and show normal fluorescence from the planar S1p minimum, which corresponds to the 11B2u state at the planar D 2h symmetric ground-state structure. However, when twisted tolanes are excited, sufficient excess energy is present to overcome the barrier and to also populate the trans-bent minimum of the 11Au state. At low temperature in glassy medium, the lifetime of this population is long enough to allow for ISC into the 13B2u state. This supports the previous suggestion that the 11Au state may act as a precursor for ISC of tolane. In summary, this paper clarifies why only twisted tolane derivatives exhibit phosphorescence while planar ones do not.

Twelve unique spectroscopic constants were determined from the rotational spectra of C5F8 between 6 and 16 GHz. Isotopic substitution allowed for an experimentally derived carbon ring structure. The ring-puckering potential function was also fit, and both were explored in detail and compared to cyclopentene.

We have developed a FRET-based depolarization model to describe the excited-state rotational dynamics as measured using time-resolved anisotropy, which allowed us to quantify the energy-transfer efficiencies in selected mCerulean3-linker-mCitrine constructs. To test this model, we investigated the excited-state rotational dynamics of hetero-FRET probes as a function of both the linker (lengths and flexibilities) and the excitation and detection wavelengths in heterogeneous (crowded) and homogenous (viscous) environments. The rotational dynamics on the nanosecond time scale indicate that the fluorophores are rotating much faster than expected for a 56-64 kDa protein, which we attribute to the flexibility of the linker. Under 425 nm excitation and 531/40 nm detection, we observed a slow and fast component of the anisotropy decay that we attribute to the overall rotation (tumbling) of the probes and energy-transfer rate between the donors and acceptors, respectively. These energy-transfer efficiencies are in general agreement with previously reported results using steady-state spectroscopy approach. ,

An assessment of the FRET efficiencies in buffer reveals that the G12 probe, which has the shortest and most flexible linker, has the greatest FRET efficiency (36 ± 1%) compared to the GE probe (14 ± 1%) that has the longest, most rigid linker. In solutions of homogenous viscosity (glycerol-enriched buffer), the FRET efficiencies of all five proteins decrease due to increases in the average donor-acceptor distances (Figure ). This decrease can be explained by the lack of rotational mobility of the fluorophore in highly viscous environments, thereby reducing the potential dipole orientations and possibly stabilizing the extended conformation. In contrast, crowded, heterogeneous environments of similar viscosities (i.e.. Ficoll-70-enriched buffer) led to increased FRET efficiencies for all five probes and corresponding decreases in the donor-acceptor distance (Figure ). This increase in FRET can only be attributed to the excluded volume effects of Ficoll-70, not viscosity, thus supporting the use of these hetero-FRET probes as a sensitive macromolecular crowding sensor.

Macromolecular crowding in vivo has been proposed by a combination of both excluded volume and electrostatic interactions. , Future experiments using these hetero-FRET probes in biomimetic, protein-crowded environments (e.g.. bovine serum albumin and ovalbumin solutions) would help elucidate the roles of weak intermolecular interactions. , The proposed time-resolved anisotropy approach for FRET analysis can also be applied to different donor-acceptor pairs for both in vitro and intracellular, location-specific in vivo studies.

Elemental analyses (C, H, and N) were performed using a EuroEA 3000 CHNS elemental analyzer. IR spectra were recorded on a Thermo Nicolet 6700 FT-IR spectrophotometer with a KBr pellet in the frequency range of 4000-400 cm-1. 1H NMR (400 MHz) and 13C NMR (100 MHz) spectra were recorded on a Varian Mercury plus spectrometer in DMSO-d 6, and TMS was used as an internal standard.

The chitin fibers with the nanofibril structure were fabricated successfully from the chitin solution via a "bottom-up" approach on a lab-scale wet-spinning machine. In our findings, the chitin molecular chains dissolved in NaOH/urea aqueous solution could self-aggregate easily in a parallel manner to form nanofibers in the phytic acid/Na2SO4 coagulant bath. The dried chitin fibers were composed of nanofibers and displayed excellent tensile strength. With an increase of the draw ratio from 1.0 to 1.8, the crystal index and the degree of orientation increased slightly, whereas the tensile strength and Young's modulus of the chitin fibers enhanced significantly. The strong self-aggregation force between chitin chains and bundles driven by numerous hydrogen bonds sustained the nanofibers and densely aligned structure. Furthermore, the chitin fibers retained the intrinsic characteristics of native α-chitin and displayed good biocompatibility toward NRVA cells by promoting their adhesion and growth. Biodegradation tests demonstrated that the chitin fibers can be completely biodegraded in soil and in vitro. This work provided a new avenue to construct strong chitin fibers with biocompatibility and biodegradability, which is beneficial to both avoiding secondary surgery in clinical use and protecting the environment.

Since environmental conditions are often not linearly related to k att, Spearman rank correlations (ρ) were applied to determine the correlation of k att with solar radiation and water temperature. Kruskal-Wallis tests in combination with Conover tests (posthoc pairwise test for multiple comparisons of mean rank sums) including two-stage linear step-up p-value correction as described by Benjamini et al. were implemented to identify significant differences in distributions of k att between sampling situations (SI Table S2). This ranked nonparametric test was used, because according to Shapiro-Wilk tests normality was not given in all distributions (SI Table S2). The significance levels (p) for the correlations and the comparisons were set to 5%.

We explored some of the aspects of the complexation of diglycolamides with varying alkyl chain length with lanthanide and actinide ions in different oxidation states. Two-phase solvent extraction studies showed that increasing the length of the alkyl group from n-pentyl to n-dodecyl in the DGAs adversely affects the extraction efficiency of the ligand. This was also corroborated from single-phase complexation studies in methanol medium using UV-vis spectrophotometric titrations, which indicated a decrease in the complexation constant values with Nd3+. However, the complexation constant values increased going from TMDGA (Figure , R = Me) to TPDGA (Figure , R = n-pentyl). Similar observation of increasing complexation efficiency with increasing alkyl chain length from TMDGA to TPrDGA was also noticed in the literature, which could nicely be explained from the ΔG values calculated with the help of DFT-based calculations showing more negative ΔG value with increasing alkyl chain length from TMDGA to TBDGA. DFT studies also indicated the effect of branching on the steric hindrance in the Nd3+ complex, which ultimately results in increasing of the metal-ligand bond lengths and unfavorable ΔG value for the Nd3+ complexation with branched alkyl DGA derivative, T2MPrDGA. Luminescence studies on the two phase extracted complex of Eu3+ for different DGA derivatives showed the absence of water molecules in the inner coordination sphere of the Eu3+ ion forming the EuL3 3+ type of extracted complex in n-dodecane medium as also reported in the literature. Further structural and EXAFS studies are required to address issues like the extraordinary high extraction efficiency toward trivalent actinides and lanthanides.

Since the publication of the previous articles published in this journal on this subject in 2004, , significant further advances have been made in our understanding of the nature of copper-oxygen complexes relevant to catalytic intermediates. New motifs have been discovered, including heterbimetallic bis (μ-oxo), [CuOH]2+, (cis-1,2-peroxo) dicopper, and mixed-valent (μ-hydroxo) dicopper (II,III) cores. In addition, as described above, new examples of previously known cores have been characterized with variable supporting ligands, including simple ones like imidazoles, which more closely mimic biological donors. Moreover, new insights into the reactivity of a variety of copper-oxygen species have been obtained that have changed the way we think about their role in catalytic oxidations.

No doubt, the field has matured and the questions being addressed are ever more focused on details of spectroscopy and mechanism. Many important challenges remain, however, that continue to stimulate research. For example, while identified in the gas phase and evaluated by theory, complexes with the [CuO]+ core have yet to be isolated and characterized. Postulates of novel copper-containing structures as active species in important oxidations, such as the hydroxylation of methane or the oxidative cleavage of DNA (by the ATCUN motif, for example), await unequivocal verification. Indeed, the nature of the oxidant in LPMO and pMMO remains a mystery, and efforts continue to be made to synthesize and characterize relevant compounds that are capable of attacking strong C-H bonds at rapid rates, such as those with oxo/hydroxo bridges between copper ions at various oxidation levels. New catalytic oxidations using copper compounds as catalysts continue to be discovered, but firm identification of intermediates and mechanisms often is lacking. Examples span oxidations of water , and hydrocarbons, reactions of particularly keen interest, because of their relevance to energy transformations. The need to understand how such reactions proceed provides ample impetus for further study using approaches like those described herein that involve the clever use of supporting ligands to enable the detailed characterization of novel copper-oxygen compounds.

We first describe the force fields employed. The hydrocarbon part of the ligands was described by the polymer consistent force field (PCFF). The Au-S-C interfacial interactions were described using FF parameters from previous literature. The cis/trans and anti/gauche conformation searches were done by first rotating the corresponding Au-S or S-C or C-C bonds by 120° (or -120°), then followed with geometry minimization using the conjugate-gradient method as implemented in the LAMMPS code. Convergence criteria for the minimization were that all partial forces on each atom were less than 0.02 eV/Å. For all the FF-based geometry optimization, only the R- groups were allowed to move, while all the Au and S atoms were fixed to their experimental positions.

Validation of FF by DFT was done by using the Vienna Ab Initio Simulation (VASP) code. The projector augmented wave was used for the core-valence electronic interaction, Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof (PBE) functional for electron exchange-correlation, plane wave for the basis set, and DFT-D3 method for the vdW interactions. A box of 35 × 35 × 35 Å was used to minimize interaction among periodic images. Γ-point only was used to sample the Brillouin zone. Conjugate-gradient algorithm was employed for geometry optimization with force convergence criterion of 0.03 eV/Å. Only the C and H atoms were allowed to move, and the structure relaxation was done in Cartesian coordinates, to ensure that the DFT minimization was restricted to the same conformations from the FF minimization.

To confirm the most stable FF-found structures, DFT calculations were performed using the Turbomole program (V6.5). We used the Turbomole code for the confirmation because the structure relaxation can be done in internal coordinates and periodic image interaction can be avoided. The DFT-D3 method was used to account for the vdW interactions, with the def2-TZVP basis sets and the TPSS functional for electron exchange-correlation. All atoms were allowed to move in Turbomole DFT geometry optimization. The rational for our choice of PBE and TPSS functionals to study thiolate-protected gold nanoclusters has been elaborated in ref .

We have reported the preparation of a series of green inexpensive cellulose nanocomposites containing organic modified montmorillonite. For the first time, significant inhibition against the quorum-sensing regulated pigment production of the bacteria C. violaceum CV026 was achieved by using only the cellulose nanocomposites without any small molecular agents. At the same time, the bacterial growth was not significantly influenced by the RC/ODA-MMT nanocomposites. Although the exact mechanism for the observed strong anti-QS effect is still to be unraveled, we believe that the exfoliated ODA-MMT nanofillers dispersed in the cellulose matrix are the key factor for the peculiar observation. Because the autoinducer for the pigment production of C. violaceum CV026 (i.e.. N-hexanoyl-l-homoserine lactone) also regulates many other important physiological processes of bacteria, it is expected that our new cellulose nanocomposites can be potentially used to inhibit other important physiological processes such as biofilm formation. Furthermore, we have demonstrated that the nanocomposites have better thermal stability compared with regenerated cellulose, which can greatly facilitate the processing and application of those new green nanocomposites as packaging materials, medical textile, or various biomedical devices. Besides those applications, such sustainable nanocomposites may also have potential in the development of new antivirulence drugs or additives. Explorations on the processing of these cellulose nanocomposites are currently being investigated.

The forces F(d) needed to calculate the PMF can be obtained from a series of simulations with two parallel tubes at varying distance d, where F(d) is the ensemble average of the sum of the forces (parallel to d) acting on all the carbon atoms on one of the tubes. Due to the high symmetry of the nanotubes one would obtain the same force per tube length for each of the periodic rings of carbon atoms (Figure ) as for the entire tube, although sampling would have to be increased proportional to the reduction in tube length considered.

The general idea of the corresponding distances method is to create a system where all tube/tube distances are present at the same time. The simplest way to achieve this is to use two tubes that cross at a small angle (bottom panel of Figure ). The forces on the horizontal tube are calculated in the same way as for the parallel tubes but for each ring of carbon atoms separately. The distance to the other tube that is associated with each of the rings is determined as shown in Figure , that is, it is given by the distance to the first solvent layer added to the (shortest) distance from the first solvent layer to the other tube.
The CDM is clearly an approximation; however, it performs very well for coarse-grain models, and below we demonstrate its excellent performance for an atomistic model.

The transient optical and X-ray measurements reported here demonstrate that the protein (CarH) controls reactivity of AdoCbl by stabilizing the excited electronic state and preventing the expansion of the axial bonds. This harnesses photon energy in the AdoCbl excited state to enable slow reactions including triplet formation and a reaction to form the stable 4′,5′anhydroadenosine product rather than bond homolysis and the reactive 5′-deoxyadenosyl radical.

The influence of glycerol on the phase transformation time and α-HH crystal morphology was explored systematically, aiming at the preparation of α-HH tuned by succinic acid and NaCl in glycerol-water mixtures. With an increase in glycerol content from 55% to 85%, the average length and diameter of α-HH decreased from 60.97 to 7.21 μm and from 15.21 to 5.17 μm, respectively, which resulted in a decrease in average aspect ratio from 4.06 to 1.41. The phase transformation time was reduced dramatically from 30 to 3 h.

As glycerol increased from 55% to 85% in glycerol-water mixtures, the maximal relative supersaturation for α-HH precipitation enhanced significantly from 0.06 to 0.30. Meanwhile, as the glycerol content increased, the dissociation constants of succinic acid generally rose, which resulted in the decrease of carboxylate ions in the solution and a corresponding reduction of Ca2+ ions chelated by carboxylate ions. This further improved the maximal relative supersaturation of α-HH in the mixtures with higher glycerol content. At the same time, the enhancement of glycerol increased the kinematic viscosity and density of the mixed solutions, which led to the reduction of ion diffusion rate. Therefore, the increase of α-HH maximal relative supersaturation and decrease of ion diffusion rate, which were superior to the adsorption of the crystal modifier, were hypothesized as explanations for the change of α-HH crystal morphology in the mixtures with high glycerol.
The enhancement of α-HH maximal relative supersaturation was the explanation for the reduction of phase transformation time with the increase of glycerol in glycerol-water mixtures.

As we continue to translate new MOF discoveries into robust CO2-capture and other clean energy technologies, the materials requirements to do so demand that we also lay the foundations for expedient and scalable MOF production. Our focus here on the fundamental materials chemistry governing expedient M2(dobpdc) formation from metal oxide precursors via dissolution-crystallization identified MO etching as rate-limiting.
