The success of a TMMC simulation depends on proper sampling of the entire domain of the phase space. Multicanonical sampling allows the acceptance ratio to be biased using weighting functions such that all regions of phase space are sampled properly. It has been observed that having an approximate idea of the weighting function before a simulation run reduces time required for convergence of the probability distribution in the GC-TMMC run. WL simulations provide an alternative technique for calculation of the probability distributions at different macrostates. In WL simulations, the acceptance probabilities of moves that change from one macrostate to the other are such that all macrostates are visited with equal probability. However, these acceptance probabilities are unknown and have to be determined by updating a weighting function while the simulation is in progress. The weighting function corresponding to a particular macrostate is updated by a constant factor every time the system exists in that particular macrostate, S 14 ln Π ( S ) = ln Π ( S ) + ln f where f is an arbitrary predefined constant, fixed during the simulation. We also update a histogram, H(S), containing information about the number of steps for which the system has been in a particular macrostate when the system occurs in the particular macrostate 15 H ( S ) = H ( S ) + 1

After the above histogram has achieved a degree of flatness, which is defined to be the difference between the maximum and the minimum values of the histogram being equal to 40% of the minimum value, the value of f is reduced (f = √f, f > 1) and the simulation restarted with the reduced value of f. This is continued until f reaches the prescribed minimum value depending on the time taken for simulations. The weighting functions required for input to GC-TMMC simulations are given by Π (S).

It is noted here that the above formulation of the WL+GC-TMMC technique for calculation of the vapor-liquid coexistence properties has not been used previously, to the best of our knowledge, for computation of phase equilibria properties of molecular mixtures.

Modeling heterogeneous chemical reaction systems that comprise instantaneous equilibria has always been a difficult task. The presence of fast reactions-which can be modeled via instantaneous equilibria in the time scale of interest-affects the numbers of moles of other species, that is, also the other rate processes such as the kinetically controlled reactions and the mass transfers. Conventional modeling using the simultaneous approach requires modeling the effect of equilibria in addition to the other rate processes. In contrast, the incremental extent-based model identification technique simplifies the modeling by generating a single extent for each rate process. As a consequence, a kinetically controlled reaction can be modeled independently of the instantaneous equilibria.

This paper has investigated the use of incremental extent-based identification for two-phase reaction systems with instantaneous equilibria. Different alternatives for decoupling the reaction system based on the nature and the number of available measurements have been discussed. It has been shown that statistically correct estimation of the extents of reaction and mass transfer is possible from (1) measurements of all species, (2) measurements of kinetic species and equilibrium components only, and (3) measurement of a mix of kinetic species, equilibrium components, and equilibrium species. Case 1 allows estimating the equilibrium constants, whereas both cases 2 and 3 require the knowledge of equilibrium constants, case 2 for the identification step and case 3 already for the transformation to extents. All these different cases have been illustrated via the simulated example of the oxidation of benzyl alcohol using hypochlorite in a batch reactor.

To develop a meaningful preference rule based on π-electron energetics only, we should select the compounds whose energy gaps are not much affected by additional side effects such as hydrogen bonds, steric hindrance, hyperconjugation, and solvent effects. For example, the enol form of acetylacetone is stabilized by intramolecular hydrogen bonds to a large extent. , The enol preference of phloroglucinol is due to the keto instability caused by the hyperconjugation of the three methylene groups. The stabilities of polar molecules with low symmetries are probably affected by solvation energies to a large extent. Thus, we focused only on nearly planar compounds, in which the degree of such side effects can be neglected or canceled out if any exist between the most stable one and the next most stable one.

We carefully selected 16 compounds for the analysis of amino-imino tautomerism (Figure ), and 13 compounds for analyzing hydroxyl-oxo/amino-imino hybridized tautomerism (Figure ). In the former case, the protons transfer from an amino group to an imino group, and vice versa. In the latter case, the active hydrogen atoms transfer from hydroxyl groups to imino groups, or conversely, from amino groups to carbonyl groups. As a result, some tautomers have biradicaloid-zwitterionic resonance structures. Both types of tautomerism approximately conserve the planarity of the systems. It has been pointed out by many workers that semiempirical and ab initio Hartree-Fock (HF) methods are not sufficient for the estimation of energy gaps in protomeric tautomerism. - However, geometry optimization under configuration interactions (CI) or perturbation methods, e.g.. the Møller-Plesset perturbation level of theory, is not realistic even today. Nowadays, DFT is probably the most suitable method to estimate the energetics without using highly complicated calculations. Thus, in the present study, the computations were performed under the B3LYP/6-311+G (d,p)//B3LYP/6-311+G (d,p) level of theory - by using the GAMESS program. The polarization functions on the s and p atomic orbitals are essential to describe subtle energy gaps.

In this study, the geometries of 229 structures of β-hydroxy- α,β-unsaturated aliphatic ketones, aldehydes, acids, halides, amides and esters with intramolecular hydrogen bond(s) forming the six-membered rings were built and optimized as previously at the DFT B3LYP/6-311++G (d,p) level of theory using the Gaussian 09 program package. All structures were checked by the vibrational analysis at this level and were found to represent true energy minima. The calculated νOH and νC-O frequencies were identified with the GaussView 5.0.9 package, without correction for the zero-point energies and without scaling the force constants to produce experimental vibrational frequencies. At the same level, the absolute proton shielding for each structure and TMS (standard tetramethylsilane) were obtained using the gauge-including-atomic-orbital (GIAO) method. The SCF GIAO magnetic isotropic shielding tensors of H-bonded hydrogen atoms were used with the consequent calculation of the chemical shifts δH [ppm] by subtraction of the averaged shielding of the TMS hydrogen atoms.

Afterward, the electron correlation was included via the Møller-Plesset treatment of the second order (MP2) in which each structure was finally optimized at MP2 (FC)/6-311++G (2d,2p), and its energy was specified at MP2 (full)/6-311++G (2d,2p) calculations.

The topological properties of the electron density at the bond critical points (BCPs) were characterized using the atoms in molecules methodology (AIM) with the AIM2000 and AIMAll program packages for every fully optimized compound. As in previous paper, to describe the nature of the hydrogen bonding we chose the electron density ρBCP at the (3, -1) bond critical point, its Laplacian ∇2ρBCP for the BCP between the donor OH hydrogen atom and the O-C oxygen atom of the acceptor, and the electron density ρRCP at the ring critical point in the center of the six-membered ring of the HB.

The geometry of each intramolecular hydrogen bond was provided by the length of the O-H covalent bond (d OH), the length of the HB as H O (r HB), the angle of the HB as O-H O (φHB) and the distance between both of the oxygen atoms as O O (dO O). This information, together with calculated frequency of O-H and C-O stretching and the hydrogen chemical shift is collected in Table S2, along with the AIM characteristics of the analyzed structures.

For the estimation of the O-H O-C intramolecular hydrogen bond energy, a systematic fragmentation of each optimized molecule was performed using the same methodology as previously. Equation is based on an earlier version of the 1bAA potential by Bereau and co-workers. , It is constructed in a form that is more amenable to preserving common repulsions in molecular dynamics simulations, and it was used here for compatibility with prior and future work.

Equation was evaluated using Mayer sampling with overlap sampling (MSOS) to provide B 22 relative to the value of B 22 if only steric interactions were present (denoted B 22,steric). MSOS is a type of importantance sampling (umbrella sampling) that favors those configurations having larger contributions to the integrand of eq . According to the MSOS method, a series of configurations are created using Monte Carlo moves (i.e.. iterations). Each move can be either a rotation or translation for one of the antibodies, with the other antibody held fixed at the origin. The new configuration can be either rejected or accepted for the system based on a probability distribution defined using the ratio of the absolute value of the integrand in eq . First a pre-equilibration simulation with 105 steps at constant temperature (300 K) was employed to find the maximum displacement and rotation for each Monte Carlo (MC) iteration to obtain a 50% acceptance rate, for use during the averaging phase of Mayer sampling. B 22 was calculated based on the averaging phase of 106-107 configurations created by either a random translation or rotation of one antibody while the other is fixed at the origin. More attractive B 22 values required more Monte Carlo steps to converge. As discussed above, there are two adjustable parameters in the model, εSR and ψ. Prior experimental static light scattering results were used to fix those parameter values to best reproduce the experimental behavior for each MAb.

In summary, the charge storage process of WO3 film electrode in aqueous electrolyte is quantitatively analyzed in detail. The charge storage mechanism of WO3 film is thickness-dependent and the 100 nm-thick product shows excellent capacitive charge storage property in terms of capacity density. The 100 nm-thick WO3 film stores charges mainly by capacitive effects (including both electric double layer capacitance and pseudocapacitance). For example, at a scan rate of 5 mV s-1, more than 78% of stored charge is attributed to capacitive effects. In addition, pseudocapacitance contribution is accountable for around 70% of the total capacitance, therefore it plays a very important role in the capacitive charge storage. These analysis approaches and results should be able to provide insightful information and valuable guidance to design and apply metal oxide-based electrodes for electrochemical energy storage system applications.

This study reports the first measurements of the kinetics of electron transfer quenching by a neat ionic liquid. Its main purpose was to provide a comparison to similar experiments in conventional dipolar solvents and to explore whether the slower and more distributed solvent/solvation dynamics of ionic liquid solvents gives rise to any distinctive behavior in ionic liquids. It was hoped that such measurements would provide a new window on ionic liquid dynamics.

It was shown that a range of 7-aminocoumarin dyes is rapidly quenched in the ionic liquid 1-butylpyridinium bis (trifluoromethylsulfonyl) imide ([Py4] [Tf2N]). The quenching mechanism entails electron transfer from an excited coumarin to the Py4 + cation, as confirmed by its strong dependence on ΔG ET. The direction of electron transfer is opposite to the well-studied case of electron transfer quenching of coumarin dyes in aromatic amine solvents. - Nevertheless, the range of quenching rates observed (.01 ≤ k 1e ≤ 3) × 1012 s-1 is quite similar to the range previously in these dipolar quenching solvents. The reorganization energy required for the ionic liquid reaction is, however, considerably larger ( ~ 1 eV) due in part to the greater polarity of the ionic liquid compared to solvents like dimethylaniline. Solvatochromic analyses indicate that solvation energies of coumarins in [Py4] [Tf2N] are very close to those in acetonitrile solution, as was anticipated from prior work. Bimolecular rate constants for oxidative quenching of coumarins by Py4 + in dilute acetonitrile solution are also close to those for reductive quenching by anilines over the same range of driving force. Thus, at least superficially, the present system shares much in common with the coumarin dye + substitute aniline systems. Preliminary experiments on the related ionic liquid [Py4] [BF4] suggest that corresponding measurements should be possible in a range of pyridinium ionic liquids, potentially enabling both the driving force and solvent/solvation dynamics to be systematically varied. Dilution with a non-reactive ionic liquid such as [Im41] [Tf2N] would also enable study of the dilution effect without significantly changing the solvent dynamics.

In the case of the most rapidly quenched coumarins, there is little to distinguish between the aniline and ionic liquid reactions. In both cases, reaction is faster than most of the solvation response and it occurs over time scales similar to the fastest solvation components. In contrast, quenching of slowly reacting coumarins spans a much larger range of times than are observed in the aromatic amine solvents. It seems reasonable to associate the more dispersive kinetics of these reactions with the slow and broadly distributed solvation response characteristic of ionic liquids. Whether this association results from solvation dynamics controlling electron transfer, as in a number of intramolecular electron transfer reactions, ,, or whether the primary effect of the slower motion in ionic liquids is to slow the small-amplitude motions modulating the electronic coupling is unclear at this point. More computational and theoretical work will be required in order to determine which is the primary effect.

Coalescence in the FTIR spectra of this family of mixed valence dimers has been studied extensively. We expect that the high variability in the IR lineshapes is related to electronic dynamics; however, our 2D-IR results indicate that full charge transfer between the two metal sites is not the origin of coalescence observed in the mixed valence systems. Ultrafast electron site exchange slower than 15 ps may still occur but should have negligible effects on the IR line shape. In general, if an exchange reaction is too slow to affect the line shape, a quantitative Bloch equation analysis is no longer applicable. On the picosecond time scale, it can be very difficult to distinguish equilibrium fluctuations from reactions involving a barrier crossing with FTIR spectra alone. For a known rate, the Bloch equations can predict the associated changes to an IR spectrum. However, for a given spectrum, it is not generally possible to separate the contributions due to exchange from other contributions to the overall line shape. For this reason, the quantitative application of the optical Bloch equations to vibrational spectra is not generally reliable and should be avoided in cases where the extent of exchange-based contributions to spectral changes is not fully known.

The full nature of electron dynamics in these mixed valence dimers remains uncertain. The presence of such highly tunable IR peak coalescence in the absence of electron site exchange on the sub-15 ps time scale suggests that a fluctuation-based mechanism may be a more accurate description of dynamics. Intrawell charge redistribution that is highly coupled to the vibrational frequency of the carbonyl spectator ligands may be able to explain the diversity of lineshapes observed in these systems. The torsional bridge fluctuation model is consistent with much of the previous work on these systems - as well as the lack of exchange observed in the 2D-IR experiments presented here. Whether or not the peak coalescence and charge redistribution can be definitively connected to a specific mechanism will require further investigation. This will be addressed in ongoing synthetic, theoretical, and experimental studies of these complexes. Future work will seek to establish the equilibrium geometry (or geometries) of these mixed valence compounds as well as elucidate the role of geometric fluctuations in the charge distributions. Two-dimensional peak shape analysis with Fourier-transform 2D-IR may reveal insights into spectral diffusion dynamics related to ground-state fluctuations. Further computational work can examine the role of ligand substitution and oxidation state on the charge distribution and its sensitivity to bridging ligand torsional motion in solution.

Perovskite structured SrTiO3 was synthesized by a hydrothermal method and then modified via a second hydrothermal treatment with H2O or NaOH (STO-H2O or STO-NaOH) for the photocatalytic mineralization of gaseous toluene. The second hydrothermal treatment, especially with NaOH solution, enriched surface hydroxyl groups; induced a negative shift of conduction band edge; and promoted more O2 -, HOO , OH, and hole generation. Moreover, the modified STO exhibited enhanced light absorption and improved photocarrier separation. Finally, greatly enhanced photocatalytic mineralization of toluene over STO-NaOH was obtained. Toluene was completely oxidized into CO2 after UV light illumination for 6 h at ambient temperature, demonstrating better performance than STO and commercial P25 catalyst. In short, the development of effective photocatalysts by a facile surface hydroxylation method and their potential environmental application are demonstrated.

Crystals of the compounds Cu-1-Cu-6 were obtained from the reaction of the lacunary precursor Na9 [B-α-BiW9 O33] 19.5H2O with CuSO4 in deionized water. Generally, a solution of CuSO4 was added dropwise to a stirred solution of the precursor at room temperature. After complete addition of the CuSO4 solution, the countercation was added as an aqueous solution. A detailed description of all synthetic procedures, including further information on the isolation of Na9 [B-α-BiW9 O33] 19.5H2O and of the applied analytical instrumentation, can be found in the Supporting Information (S7).

Single crystals of each compound were selected from the reaction mixture, mounted on a glass fiber loop with the help of Infineum oil and placed in a N2 stream. Data sets were collected at 183 K on an Oxford Xcalibur Ruby CCD single-crystal diffractometer. Structure solution and data treatment procedures are described in the Supporting Information, along with detailed crystallographic discussions of the disorder observed in the title compounds (S2). Details on the crystal structures as well as the crystallographic information files (CIF) may be obtained from the Fachinformationszentrum Karlsruhe, D-76344 Eggenstein-Leopoldshafen, Germany (Fax: +49 7247 808 666; email crysdata@fiz-karlsruhe.de), by citing the depository numbers CSD-431217 (Cu-1), CSD-431215 (Cu-2), CSD-431213 (Cu-3), CSD-431218 (Cu-4), CSD-431216 (Cu-5), and CSD-431214 (Cu-6).

Cu-5 was tested for photocatalytic oxygen and hydrogen evolution with standard [Ru (bpy)3]2+/S2O8 2- and [Ru (bpy)3]2+/ascorbic acid assays in buffer solutions, respectively. A blue LED (470 nm and 4600 Lux) was used as light source. All reactions were monitored with O2 or H2 sensitive gas sensors, and the amounts of O2 or H2 were quantified by gas chromatography. All experimental details are summarized in the Supporting Information (S5).

In the present research, the experimental results clearly evidence that the nature of active sites of a Ziegler-Natta catalyst, which is synthesized using Mg (OC2H5)2 as a precursor of MgCl2, is profoundly affected by the feed rate of TiCl4 used in the catalyst synthesis. Octahedral and trigonal-bipyramidal moieties of titanium were identified as two groups of active sites. In fact, the characterization data from UV-DRS evidence the participation of the ethoxide group as a ligand of the titanium in octahedral moieties only. Indeed, titanium moieties containing ethoxide groups were also identified by FTIR, which were coordinated to Mg and Ti. Trigonal-bipyramidal titanium moieties have preferentially chlorine as ligands according to the UV-DRS results.

A reaction kinetic for the chlorination reaction of Mg (OC2H5)2 by TiCl4 was proposed to explain the formation of ethoxide-based titanium sites considering the feed rate of TiCl4. Taking into account such a proposal, the increase of TiCl4 favors the formation TiCl3(OC2H5), which is a byproduct, resulting in a higher probability of forming titanium moieties presenting one ethoxide as a ligand in not dangly position. In fact, the increase of the feed rate of TiCl4 favors the formation of titanium sites presenting structure (I) but it does not mean the other structures do not exist. It is supposed a distribution of nature of active sites to exist.

The increase in the average molecular weight indicated by the reduction of MFI is also due to the increase of octahedral titanium having ethoxide as a ligand. This experimental conclusion is corroborated by some previous studies.

The results and conclusions obtained in the present research serve as guidelines for the optimization of the catalyst synthesis. In addition, the experimental results of this study validate theoretical studies that pointed out about the performance of Ziegler-Natta active sites having ethoxide as a ligand of the titanium.

We performed extensive ReaxFF MD simulations to investigate the detailed water-mediated proton conduction mechanism along the surface of GO sheets. We found that both epoxide and hydroxyl functional groups can effectively attract water molecules onto the surface of GO sheets and form a hydrogen-bonding network. Twenty weight percent of oxygen functional groups are enough to induce a relatively homogeneous distribution of adsorbed water molecules. Instead of bonding with adsorbed water molecules to form hydronium ions, protons prefer to bond with oxygen functional groups on the surface of GO sheets. Proton conduction on the surface of GO sheets covered by pure epoxide functional groups can barely occur for the relatively high energy barriers. On the other hand, proton hopping between adjacent hydroxyl functional groups is almost barrierless. The energy barrier for water-mediated proton conduction between nonadjacent hydroxyl functional groups is estimated to be 0.119-0.138 eV, which is also feasible at room temperature. The adsorbed water molecules provide bridges for proton conduction between nonadjacent hydroxyl functional groups and can contribute to a good proton conductivity. Our work clarified the water-mediated proton conduction mechanism of GO sheets and shed light on the future design of GO-based proton conductors.

Dissolution of UO2(s) in the presence of T. denitrificans and dissolved nitrate (± nitrite) was compared to abiotic rate experiments. Replicate experiments always included an abiotic control column run simultaneously with the same influent solution as the biotic columns (Table S2). In most experiments, columns with T. denitrificans showed rates of UO2(s) dissolution of about one order-of-magnitude faster than those of the simultaneous abiotic control experiments (Figure , Table S2). However, in a few simultaneous replicate columns, UO2(s) dissolution rates were lower and closer to those of abiotic controls (e.g.. B1-R2, B2-R3, and B4-R1, Table S2). In addition, nitrite concentrations (Figure S4) were below the detection limit (B1-R2), slightly lower (B2-R3) than the biotic replicates, or followed the same trend as the control experiment (B4-R1), which could indicate low or no enzymatic oxidation. Overall, UO2(s) dissolution rates were more variable in experiments with T. denitrificans than in abiotic experiments, and a relatively constant effluent U concentration was sometimes not observed until near the end of the experiment. Nitrite concentrations measured in the effluent solutions of experiments involving T. denitrificans with nitrate (but no added nitrite) were higher ( ~ 20-160 μM) than those in abiotic nitrate control experiments ( ~ 5-10 μM), demonstrating microbially accelerated conversion of nitrate to nitrite (Figure S4). Furthermore, in two control column experiments with T. denitrificans and quartz but no UO2(s), solutions with influent nitrate concentrations of 1 or 10 mM produced effluent nitrite concentrations near the limit of detection (0.42 μM) (data not shown). Overall, abiotic dissolution rates measured in experiments with added nitrite were similar to rates observed in experiments with T. denitrificans and added nitrate (Table ).

Column experiments were performed with a mutant strain of T. denitrificans that was previously shown to be ~ 50% defective in U (IV) oxidation. Results showed a decrease of 44% in the average UO2(s) dissolution rate compared to that of experiments with the wild-type strain. The decrease in the dissolution rate was smaller (34% rather than 44%) if effluent U concentrations were compared with those of simultaneous abiotic control columns with the same influent nitrate concentration (10 mM) (e.g.. controls B3b-CT6 and B5-CT8 in Figure c,e, respectively) (Table , Figure ). The differences in rate exceeded the estimated propagated error for these experiments (Table ). This result supports the role of enzymatic mediation by T. denitrificans in the U (IV) oxidation process (Figure ).

In this paper, neural network potential models are proposed to describe the interaction between zinc ion and water. With NN models, the atomic charges, potential energy, and atomic forces of molecular clusters containing one Zn2+ and 1-9 water molecules can be predicted with high accuracy compared with DFT calculations. By combination with the classical force field for bulk waters, the NN potential can be used to perform an MD simulation for the hydration of Zn2+. The experimental RDF and XANES spectrum which reflect the local water structure around Zn2+ can be accurately reproduced.

Compared to classical force fields, these neural network potentials are not limited by the form of the potential function and the complicated parametrization process. They are flexible and unbiased and effectively include all local quantum effects, especially polarization and charge transfer, which are crucial for molecular systems that have strong quantum effects such as the hydration of metal ions and metalloproteins. In addition, the efficiency of the NN potential could be orders of magnitude faster than that of the QM and QM/MM methods. For the Zn2+-water system, both the NN/MM-RESP and NN/MM-TIP3P models take about 0.02 s for a single step of MD simulation on a normal Linux cluster with 16 CPU cores and one NVIDIA GTX1080Ti GPU card. Thus, they offer the possibility to perform large scale MD simulations to study many important processes such as water dynamics in concentrated ionic solution.

However, while summarizing the successes, we also find some shortcomings in the current version of the NN model. First, the long-range polarization effect of the bulk water environment is not considered properly. In the NN/MM-RESP model, only the short-range polarization effects between Zn2+ and water molecules within 2.6 Å of it are included. Second, a buffer region was defined in this work to deal with the exchange of water molecules between the NN region and the MM region. Although such an approach is reasonable to some extent, more rigorous methods and more in-depth testing are needed. Finally, the neural network in this study is trained with reference to DFT, which may have some accuracy problems in describing water systems. Therefore, higher-level ab initio methods should be used to prepare the reference set in future studies.

Despite these shortcomings, the neural network models proposed in this study can be used to construct molecular potentials for the hydration of other metal ions. The algorithms used in this study can also shed light on the development of molecular potentials for metals in other environments such as biomolecules.

Intramolecular H bonding in PRODAN derivatives affects the excited-state behavior in several ways. The most prominent effect is that it leads to greater fluorescence in apolar (and aprotic) solvents by inhibiting ISC. It also leads to slight quenching in the presence of low concentrations of alcohol due to a doubly intramolecular, intermolecular H-bonded excited state. The results corroborate the importance of carbonyl-twisting in quenching by alcohols. They also corroborate the necessity of more than one H-bonding interaction for efficient quenching.

Spectral graph theory, which has been used to describe properties of a graph by analyzing eigenvalues and eigenvectors of various matrices representing the graph, is shown to be useful for identifying differences in morphological structures of osmolyte aggregates as well as water H-bond structures in highly concentrated osmolyte solutions. The protecting renal osmolytes, e.g.. sorbitol and TMG, form large-scale network-like aggregates at high concentrations, whereas the destabilizing osmolyte urea fits into water's tetrahedral H-bonding structure and forms cluster-like aggregates in high urea solutions. Despite prolonged efforts to understand osmolyte effects on water structure, we believe that the present work is the first attempt showing an interesting interplay between morphological structure of osmolyte aggregate and water H-bonding network structure in high osmolyte solutions. A speculative but far-reaching implication of this result is that the intrinsic propensity of an osmolyte to form large-scale aggregate structures determines the thermodynamic stability of the protein in such high osmolyte solutions found in mammalian kidneys. Currently, this is under investigation by using the time-resolved vibrational spectroscopic measurement method.

When treatment systems were effective on 50% of trips, exchange plus treatment was more effective than treatment alone for trips arriving to freshwater ports, more than doubling the mean number of trips until ≥ 1 species establishes from 585 (effective treatment on 50% trips) to 1442 (exchange plus treatment, with effective treatment on 50% of trips; Figure a). A similar, but smaller, positive effect was found for brackish water recipient ports, with the mean number of trips until ≥1 species establishes increasing from 2007 to 2948 (Figure b). In contrast, there was no apparent benefit to using exchange plus treatment versus treatment alone for marine recipient ports (1169 vs 1287 trips until ≥1 species establishes, respectively; Figure c). These results indicate that exchange may serve as an important backup strategy most protective of fresh or brackish recipient ports, at least until treatment can be applied successfully across all ship trips.

Fully effective treatment extended the time frame required until ≥ 1 nonindigenous zooplankton species establishes compared to partially effective treatment for all recipient ports (all salinities; Figure ). Still, even with fully effective treatment, exchange plus treatment was more effective at preventing nonindigenous zooplankton establishments than treatment alone in freshwater ports, increasing the mean number of trips until ≥ 1 species establishes from 11 338 to 58 140, respectively (Figure a). On the other hand, exchange plus treatment provided no additional benefit compared to treatment alone in recipient ports that were brackish (141 443 trips until ≥1 species establishes for both scenarios; Figure b) or marine (42 553 vs 58 824 trips until ≥1 species establishes, respectively; Figure c). Summarily, exchange plus treatment was most effective at mitigating establishment risk in freshwater ports, regardless of whether treatment was successful on 50% or 100% of ship trips.

These results highlight the importance of considering environmental context when designing and implementing management plans and demonstrate that additional benefit (reduced establishment rate) can be achieved with a multidimensional management approach. Since the combined approach of exchange plus treatment entails additional costs (in terms of crew effort and operational costs), this study can inform a more targeted management approach that maximizes the cost-benefit ratio.

The DFT calculations were performed using the Gaussian 09 suite of programs. We employed the def2-SVP basis set (hereafter called DZ) since it provides the accuracy of calculated adsorption energies within 1 kcal/mol to those obtained with a broader def2-TZVPP basis set at a considerable smaller computational cost. The point defects were modeled by removing one C, N, or B atom from a rectangular unit cell containing 48 atoms arranged in the perfect honeycomb structure (see Figure S1 of the Supporting Information). The periodic boundary conditions were applied in the planes of graphene and the h-BN. The graphene surface Brillouin zone was sampled by 24 special Monkhorst-Pack k-points. For the wide band gap insulator h-BN, we used 4 k-points since our tests show that further increase in the number of k-points changes adsorption energies less than 0.05 eV. The adsorption energy E ads(X) of an adsorbate X was calculated according to the standard formula E ads ( X ) = E ( X / S ) - ( E ( X ) + E ( S ) ) 1

where the E(X/S), E(X), and E(S) represent total energies of the adsorbate X at the substrate S, free adsorbate X, and pristine substrate S, respectively. A rectangular 10×10×10 Å3 box and a single k-point are used in the calculations of free adsorbates.

The electronic exchange and correlation effects were described employing the screened hybrid HSE06 exchange-correlation functional. The geometry optimization was performed using the Berny algorithm and the synchronous transit-guided quasi-Newton (STQN) method, which was applied to locate the transition states. Due to limited post-processing features of the Gaussian 09 package when used in the mode with applied periodic boundary conditions, the analysis of specific electronic properties of studied systems was performed with GPAW code, , based on real-space grid implementation of the projector augmented wave (PAW) method. , The calculations were carried out with a grid spacing of 0.15 Å and the same number of Monkhorst-Pack k-points as in the Gaussian calculations. GPAW calculations were performed using the GGA-PBE exchange-correlation functional and serve only to provide a qualitative analysis of the electronic properties of SACs that we were not able to accomplish with the Gaussian 09 package. However, all adsorption geometries, the energies, and band gap values reported in the paper were obtained from the Gaussian calculations with a more accurate hybrid functional.

The repair mechanisms and kinetics on dGuo radicals by ROH and RO- forms of trans-resveratrol in polar and nonpolar solvents have been studied using DFT, and HT/PCET and SET mechanisms have been considered.

It was found that trans-resveratrol could repair base radicals of dGuo rather than 2′-deoxyribose radicals regardless of the polarity of the environment. The repair activity of RO- toward dGuo-radicals is better than that of ROH. The overall rate constants for repairing dGuo-radicals by trans-resveratrol are 9.94 × 108 and 2.01 × 109 dm3 mol-1 s-1 in polar and nonpolar solvents, respectively. When the molar fractions of ROH and RO- are considered in a polar solvent, the total rate constants for repairing dGuo + by ROH and by RO- via the SET mechanism are 7.17 × 109 and 9.35 × 105 dm3 mol-1 s-1, respectively. The repair activity of ROH toward dGuo + is better than that of RO-. The overall rate constant of repairing dGuo + by trans-resveratrol is 7.17 × 109 dm3 mol-1 s-1. Therefore, trans-resveratrol is an effective antioxidant to repair the base radicals of dGuo and dGuo +.

The work presented in this paper was the first theoretical study on repairing DNA radicals with polyphenol. In particular, it provides information on the repairing pathways of two forms of trans-resveratrol under biological conditions, and this study can help us understand the repair activity of trans-resveratrol toward DNA radicals.

We have employed Raman spectroscopy to investigate the temperature dependence of the E2g phonon mode of single-layer (1L), FL (11L), and bulk (120L, 400L, and 1400L) hBN sheets supported on a Si/SiO2 (90 nm), in the range of 183 K up to 473 K. The recorded temperature dependence exhibits two distinct regimes below and above a specific temperature, at a value that differs from sample to sample depending on the characteristics of the substrate and the transferring procedure. In the low-temperature region, the monolayer and FL samples exhibited significantly higher slopes compared to the thicker ones. In the high-temperature region, all the examined samples show almost the same temperature slope. This behavior indicates slippage of the hBN sheets and unveils that the slopes of monolayer, FL, and bulk hBN are quite similar of about -0.020 cm-1/K.

Using a FE method, we have determined the TEC of the underlying Si/SiO2 (90 nm) substrate, and by careful evaluation of the thermal strain mismatch effect, we have extracted the intrinsic frequency shift of the E2g mode. The obtained fwhm of the samples and the observed similarities of the TEC of 1-3L and bulk hBN reveal a comparable level of anharmonicity of the E2g mode from the monolayer up to bulk hBN, justifying the similar, aforementioned, E2g-T response. Moreover, for the case of bulk hBN, we have shown that the contribution in the frequency shift and fwhm from three-phonon processes is an order of magnitude higher than that from four-phonon processes.

Also, we have provided strong evidence, based on our experimental data, that interlayer friction of multilayer hBN is higher compared to that of multilayer graphene. The intrinsic temperature dependence of 11L hBN has been determined by applying a simple theoretical model.

By means of MD simulations, using the Tersoff-2012 potential and employing the kVACS method that explicitly accounts for anharmonic effects, we have determined the temperature dependence of phonon dispersion curves and, in more detail, the E2g vibrational modes of monolayer hBN. Theory overestimates the rate of the E2g dependence on T, most likely because of deficiencies of the used classical potential.

Finally, it should be stressed that the accurate determination of the thermomechanical response of 2D materials deposited on top of engineering substrates such as Si/SiO2 is crucial for designing the next generation of optoelectronic devices.

In this work, the thermodynamics and kinetics of cross-linking reaction between PAHs possessing different reactive edge types have been studied by means of density functional theory calculations. Computations of the bond energies and barrier heights generally affirmed that cross-linking reactions that resulted in the formation of strong bonds generally had low barriers. This was primarily the case for reactions involving PAHs with edge type A or aryl-type σ-radicals. One noticeable exception was for reactions between localized π-radicals, or edge type B, and acene diradicaloids, or edge type D1. These reactions were seen to have very low barriers despite forming weak bonds. Additionally, reactions involving two PAH radicals were broadly barrierless, namely, reactions between two PAHs of types A (aryl σ-radicals), B (localized π-radicals), and C (delocalized π-radicals).

The computation of the forward rate constants confirmed that reactions involving edge type A are faster than others. It was noted that generally having the σ-radical on the five-member ring resulted in faster kinetics than when the σ-radical was on the six-member ring. At flame temperatures of 1400-2000 K, the forward rate constants were generally of the order of 108 to 1012 cm3mol-1 s-1. Notably, the rate constants between PAHs with edge type A and edge type D and edge type A and edge type B were seen to be as large or even larger than for that between two of edge type A. It was also seen that the rate constant for the reaction between A1 and A2 was substantially faster than that between A1 and A1 or A2 and A2. The reaction between two localized π-radicals on rim five-member rings was seen to be notably faster at temperatures below 1000 K but then declines and is one of the slowest reactions at 2000 K. Reactions involving combinations of edge types B, C, D, and E were generally seen to be slower in comparison. Generally, all computed rate constants are unlikely to be high enough to result in substantial enough fluxes for processes such as soot formation on their own, as the higher rate constants involve reactions between two radical PAHs that are expected to be in lower concentrations. This is also true for suggestions involving cross-links on five-member rings and delocalized π-radical PAHs.

Analysis of the equilibrium constants showed that most of these cross-linking reactions have substantial equilibrium constants and stability at flame temperatures, provided that they involved one PAH of edge type A or two PAHs with radical edge types A, B, or C. The localized π-radicals were seen to have large equilibrium constants for reactions with edge types A, B, and C and were seen to be more reactive than all edge types aside from type A. It was also noted that despite having large forward rate constants in some cases, reactions of PAHs with diradicaloid edge type D were seen to have lower equilibrium constants than those involving edge types A, B, and C, highlighting their relative reversibility. It was also noted that the reduced equilibrium constants and fraction of cross-linked dimers formed for cross-links between two radical PAHs of edge types A, B, and C will be lower due to their expected lower concentrations. However, the equilibrium constants for reactions between PAHs of edge type A and a PAH of edge type A or B are still substantial enough such that cross-links are expected to form under flame conditions.

Computations of the equilibrium constants for larger PAHs that are able to bond and stack in rim-bonds showed that there is a substantial enhancement in the equilibrium constant that is dependent on the PAH edge types. It was observed that a larger enhancement was present for reactions between two localized π-radical PAHs of edge type B than for other edge types that could bond and stack, which highlights the difference in dispersion interactions between different edge types. This suggests that these dispersion effects could potentially promote reactions of larger localized π-radicals. These effects could be further enhanced by considering the role of dynamics such as internal rotors and multiple localized π-radical sites on the same aromatic species. It was also noted that this enhancement effect is dependent on having sufficient concentration of larger PAHs. Further work is necessary to study the dynamics of reactions and combined physical and chemical interactions involving these localized π-radicals as well as determine the concentrations of these larger localized π-radical species to determine if such reactions are able to provide the nucleation flux required to explain soot formation.

We investigated the mechanism of the conversion of B and SiH4 to a structure with two H atoms bridged between the units (Si (μ-H2) BH2, IM4) using DFT and high-level ab initio methods. The relative energies of the thermal reaction calculated using the PBE0/aug-cc-pVTZ are in good agreement with those obtained using CCSD (T)/aug-cc-pVQZ//PBE0/aug-cc-pVTZ. The vibrational frequencies calculated using PBE0 and CCSD (T) are in good agreement with the experimental values. Therefore, PBE0 describes the molecular structures, vibrational frequencies, and relative energies well. Thermal conversion of IM2 to IM4 is not feasible because two high energetic barriers must be overcome. In contrast, the reverse thermal reaction from IM4 to IM2 is feasible as effectively only one barrier must be overcome. On the basis of the vertical excitation energies calculated by MS-CASPT2, the D2 state of IM2 (H2B-SiH2) is an optically available state as shown by its large oscillator strength. In addition, the excitation energy of the D2 state (3.69 eV and 336 nm) falls within the energy range (300-350 nm) used for photoconversion in the recent experimental study, and the D2 state would be populated from this irradiation. The MEP calculations show that two successive CIs are involved in the photochemical reaction from IM2. The reaction proceeds to IM4 through lifting the degeneracy of CI2 by the activated BSiH4 bending mode. All calculated results in this work reasonably well describe the recent experimental observations. We hope that this work will stimulate further theoretical and experimental investigations of reaction mechanisms involving B- and Si-containing compounds.

Figure gives the transition among different products (aggregated into five categories) and losses of the location of Cr and Ni under alternative scrap sorting scenarios across 100 years (results with a more detailed classification of products are given in the SI). The results for Fe were similar to our previous results, and are shown in the SI (Figure S4).

The top panel in Figure refers to the default (current) scrap sorting and shows that of the amounts of Cr embodied in the initial endowments of products, 40% is lost after 50 years, and 70% is lost after 100 years, with the refinery losses (slag) occupying the dominant share, followed by collection losses, scrap losses, and manufacturing losses. Smaller losses are observed for Ni, with 20% of the initial endowments lost after 50 years, 45% lost after 100 years, and the collection losses of EOL products occupying the largest share, followed by scrap losses, and manufacturing losses, with no slag losses occurring thanks to its thermodynamic properties (Ni is nobler than Fe).

Another remarkable feature is the change over time in the location of the metals among different products. Whereas cars and machinery constituted their major applications initially (84% for Cr and 75% for Ni), their shares decline to around 50% after 100 years, with the rest occupied by buildings and civil engineering.

The "maximum sorting" scenario (the panel in the middle of Figure ) results in a significant reduction in metal losses for Cr, which is mostly attributed to the sizable reduction in refinery losses. In contrast to Cr, a slight increase in the material losses was observed for Ni: alloy-based scrap sorting did not appear to contribute to reducing the material losses for Ni. Common to both Cr and Ni is that their applications to products preserve their initial patterns, mostly consisting of cars and machinery, with the shares of buildings and civil engineering remaining below 20%, and that the recovery losses of EOL products occupy the largest share of losses, followed by scrap losses, and manufacturing losses.

The "minimum sorting" scenario (the bottom panel of Figure ) results in a significant increase in the material losses of Cr because of drastic increases in refinery losses, with the losses reaching around 90% after 100 years, whereas a slight decline in the losses is observed for Ni. Common to both Cr and Ni is the rapid shift in their applications from cars and machinery to buildings and civil engineering, with the shares of the former declining to around 30% for Cr and 50% for Ni, after 40 years.

Another way of tracing the fate of metals, which is made possible by the MaTrace-alloy model, is to look at the transition in their alloy locations (Figure ). The panel in the middle shows that, under the "maximum sorting" scenario, Cr and Ni remain in their initial applications, nc-alloy steels, whereas under the default sorting (the top panel), their increasing fractions are dissipated into carbon steels. Under the "minimum sorting" scenario (the bottom panel), their initial applications to nc-alloy steels are almost entirely replaced with those to carbon steels. For Cr, this results in sizable refinery (slag) losses because it is less noble than Fe. For Ni, it results in sizable functional losses because of its dissipation into carbon steels, where its function is not required.

Besides causing functional losses, the elevation in the level of Cr and Ni in carbon steels can turn the metals into undesirable contaminants that compromise the quality of recycled carbon steels (Figure ). The result obtained for the default scenario of the concentration of Cr, where it reaching around 0.17%, is in good agreement with Oda et al.. who found the concentration of 0.15-0.19% for samples taken from Japanese electric arc furnace (EAF) facilities. Under the "minimum sorting" scenario, the concentration of Cr in carbon steel can reach a level well above 0.3% exceeding the maximum admissible concentration, whereas the level remains well below that under the default sorting scenario. The concentration of Ni in carbon steel remains at a level lower than that of Cr, in most cases, because of its higher recovery rate as austenitic scrap or Ni scrap. In contrast to Cr, however, once it is dissipated into carbon steel, its concentration remains kept at that level, or even tends to rise, because of its conservation in refinery processes. Under the "minimum sorting" scenario, this feature of Ni renders its concentration non-negligible over time when the same cohort is repeatedly recycled without any dilution; it could exceed 0.2% after 30 years. Whereas this level of Ni concentration is regarded as unproblematic when considered in isolation, simultaneous occurrence with Cr can make it problematic because of their mutually reinforcing effects as contaminants. We will return to this point at the end of this section.

The "maximum sorting" scenario appeared to reduce the material losses of Ni, if only by a small margin. This is attributed to the shift under the "minimum sorting" scenario of the applications of Ni from the initial one mostly consisting of cars and machinery, high-function applications, to those dominated by construction and civil engineering items. The longer product lives of the latter items induce a smaller number of products cycles over a given period, and, hence, smaller amounts of associated losses. This results in a trade-off relationship between high-function applications and material losses, as pointed out by Pauliuk et al.

The above observation, however, was made based on the losses in terms of mass only, without any consideration of function losses. The cumulative service index () with the weights w referring to the function of metals occurring in different alloys in terms of embodied energy enables one to consider function losses of metals. The results in Figure show that under the "minimum sorting" scenario the dissipation of high functional metals into applications, where their functions are not needed, results in sizable function losses. This is in particular the case for Ni. Hidden behind the seemingly slight reduction in material losses of Ni under minimum sorting, in terms of mass, is thus a drastic increase in the losses in terms of embodied energy with μ(100) falling from 0.76 under "maximum sorting" scenario to 0.3. Depending on the level of scrap sorting, μ (T) can differ by more than 40 points in terms of embodied energy for both Cr and Ni. Noteworthy for Ni is that, in terms of mass, the difference in μ(100) among the sortring levels is negligible, or even slightly reversed. Reliance solely on mass criteria can greatly underestimate the effects of improving the level of scrap sorting. Under the "maximum sorting" scenario, the average energy losses could be kept at well below 30% of the initial level for both Cr and Ni, whereas they could exceed 70% under the "minimum scrap sorting". This demonstrates the inadequacy of considering the efficiency of recycling in terms of mass only, neglecting its functional aspects.

The above results on μ (T) were obtained by allocating zero function values to Cr and Ni for applications other than nc-alloy steels: applied to carbon steel, they were evaluated with zero values, just as the case they were no longer used in any product. This can be regarded as an extreme case. As an alternative, we considered the case where the energy value was set equal to that of Fe when applied to carbon steel, but to zero when no longer used in any product. It turned out that whereas the extent of reduction in μ (T) under the "minimum sorting" scenario decreased, the results remained unaltered qualitatively (see Figure S5 in the SI).

The ratio by which Cr is distributed between molten metal and slag in an EAF is known to be subject to wide variations. , The above results were obtained for a particular value of the ratio, a representative one taken from the literature. , To assess the effects of the ratio on the cumulative service index and the concentration of Cr in carbon steel, a sensitivity analysis was conducted by altering it in the range of 30-95%. As for scrap sorting, the default case was assumed. It is obvious that the mass-based cumulative service index increases with the ratio of Cr ending up in metal. Less obvious is its effects on the energy-based cumulative service index. It turned out that the energy-based cumulative service index was hardly affected by the increase in the ratio (Figure S7 in the SI). Another noticeable effect of the increase in the ratio is the increase in the concentration of Cr in secondary steels toward, or even surpassing, the tolerated levels (Figure S6 in the SI).

Dissipation of Cr and Ni in carbon steel represents their function losses, but would not cause any harm to carbon steel provided their concentrations remain within the admissible levels. If the admissible levels were exceeded, however, their presence could compromise the functionality of carbon steel, and needs to be taken care of by adding Fe from primary or clean EoL sources to dilute their concentration. This amount of Fe for dilution can be regarded as a loss. For the cases where this was found relevant, we estimated the amount of Fe required for dilution, and obtained the cumulative service index μ (T) of Fe that incorporates this loss. It was found that whereas the required rate of dilution could reach as high as 30%, its effect on the cumulative service index of Fe was negligible. See SI, Figures 8 and 9, for further details.

In conclusion, we developed a new method for growth of organic crystals on substrate. The method, which we called microspacing in-air sublimation, most characterized by the microspacing distance between the source and the growth position, represents an advance on both growth mechanism and implementation techniques. The synergy effect between the microspacing and the temperature distribution induced an unprecedented vapor transport regime and crystallization mechanism. A vapor-to-melt-to-crystal process was revealed via in situ observation. The method, by employing 10 kinds of organic crystals, including different semiconductors and a pharmaceutical crystal, that were successfully grown with high crystallinity proved a broad generality to various materials. The method, totally being implemented at ambient conditions, requiring neither vacuum systems, nor inert gases, nor even a growth chamber, possesses advantages in many aspects such as growth time, materials utilization ratio, applicability for real time observation, etc. (Table S2 in Supporting Information presents a detailed list of comparison of our method to traditional PVT.) FET devices based on the rubrene crystals grown on the Si/SiO2 substrate exhibited higher mobilities than the best record ever reported. Thus, the new method on one side serves as an effective organic crystal growth technique that can be affordable and handled for almost every lab and, on the other hand, provides a platform to probe the realistic mechanism of organic crystal formation. In future work we will tackle other technologically relevant challenges on location and orientation of the grown single crystals, via substrate patterning or other strategies to control the distribution and solidification of the melt droplets and on issues when scaling to larger areas. We hope the new method will open a new era for the future research and application of organic crystals.

Hybrid nanopapers of CNF and chitosan were prepared and physically cross-linked to significantly improve their wet tensile properties by reducing hydration of chitosan inside the films with a base-treatment. Already a small increase in chitosan content from 0 to 5% caused dramatic improvements in wet tensile properties when the film was base-treated with 100 mM NaOH solution. The base-treated CNF/chitosan 80/20 w/w film reached the highest wet tensile strength measured, 100 MPa. A maximum strain of at least 18% was recorded for all base-treated compositions with chitosan and many strained up to 25% without breaking. Tensile moduli increased with plastic strain from 4 and 14 GPa at low (0.5%) and large (16%) strains. Increasing the chitosan content to 75% increased the maximum strain further, but negatively affected tensile strength. A clear increase in wet strength was observed as the pH increased from 5.7 to 6.8, that is, from below to above the pK a of chitosan. The wet strength of the base-treated CNF/chitosan was interpreted to result from cross-linking whereby chitosan tightly binds onto cellulose surfaces, probably via multivalent physical interactions. The physical cross-linking did not reduce the remarkable toughness of more dry hybrid nanopapers: a tensile strength of 200 MPa (with maximum strain of 8%) was measured at 50% air relative humidity for base-treated CNF/chitosan 80/20 w/w film. In addition, high transparency ( ~ 70-90% in the range of 400-800 nm) resulted from homogeneous mixtures, nanoscale dimensions of CNF fibrils and suppressed component aggregation leading to reduced diffraction of visible light. The presented new and simple approach of physical cross-linking expands the high mechanical properties of transparent CNF-based materials to the wet-state, as demanded in advanced applications.

We have shown how a variety of models, ranging from empirical ones to those grounded in fundamental physics, can be used to design new functional glass compositions producible on an industrial scale. Such model-driven development of industrial glass compositions has already shown successful. For example, Corning Gorilla Glass 3, an ion-exchanged aluminosilicate glass, was designed to have maximum compressive stress by adjusting the glass composition under the subjection of certain constraints (e.g.. liquidus viscosity, zircon breakdown viscosity, ion exchange time, damage resistance, etc.). Using the approach presented herein, the modeled composition was indeed confirmed to be the optimal one out of more than 50 compositions subsequently melted. These and other prominent advances in understanding the dependence of composition and processing on glass manufacturability, mechanics, and other properties have provided a solid foundation for designing new compositions. This is line with the Materials Genome Initiative, which aims to accelerate the development of new advanced materials through modeling. As such, our "glass genome" approach presented herein can be used to accelerate the design of new functional glasses for use in various applications.

Nonetheless, the challenge of improving the mechanical properties of industrial glasses remains, and some of the more pressing open questions are (i) How can we control flaw chemistry and stress fields? (ii) Can we induce brittle-to-ductile transition in oxide glasses through variation of Poisson's ratio? (iii) What is the relation between crack propagation, fracture toughness, scratching behavior, and frangibility? (iv) What are the fundamental mechanics controlling crack tip formation and propagation at the nanoscale? (v) What is the ultimate achievable strength and toughness that can be attained by using microstructured glasses, glass-ceramics, and composites? A fundamental understanding of these issues will be essential in the design and development of mechanically reliable oxide glasses capable of withstanding harsh chemo-mechanical environments.

Our study demonstrates that the electrochemical reversibility of Li2CuO2 can be improved by substitution with 50% Ni2+. We have investigated the role Ni plays in improving the performance at both the structural and electrochemical level. In situ XAS and gas evolution measurements indicate that both nickel and oxygen are redox active during delithiation of Li2Cu0.5Ni0.5O2. A reversible Ni2+/3+ couple contributes approximately 125 mAh/g to the capacity. XAS does not show any evidence for the formation of Cu3+, suggesting that oxygen participation in the redox chemistry is responsible for much of the additional capacity (250 mAh/g) during the first charge. Li2Cu0.5Ni0.5O2 is stable against oxygen release up to extraction of one lithium per formula unit. During the first charge, though, the structure changes irreversibly before the extraction of even one lithium. In situ Raman spectroscopy indicates the orthorhombic phase transforms to a close-packed layered structure. Redox reactions at voltages >3 V only occur in subsequent cycles if the system is driven past the point of stability and oxygen is released during the initial cycle. If the voltage window is limited to avoid structural transformations and the associated oxygen evolution, only a low voltage Cu1+/2+ redox couple contributes significantly to the capacity. Efforts are underway to limit the participation of oxygen in the redox process and stabilize Cu3+ through anionic substitution.

SFVS was used here to quantify the kinetics and thermodynamics of DSPG flip-flop in a range of DSPG + DSPC bilayer compositions. The data presented here show that the activation energetics are directly dependent on the amount of DSPG present in the bilayer. Selective deuteration was used to independently probe lipid flip-flop of the DSPG and DSPC components in these mixed bilayers. The data revealed that the measured activation energies for flip-flop were identical for both lipid components.

When DSPG is present in small quantities in bilayers composed of 10%, 14.3%, and 25% DSPG, only minor changes in the energetics are observed. The significant increase in the ΔG ⧧ and corresponding ΔH ⧧ and TΔS ⧧ observed in bilayers composed of 50% and 75% DSPG is the result of charge repulsion between PG headgroups. This was experimentally confirmed by altering the buffer conditions such that neighboring PG lipids in bilayers composed of 25% and 75% DSPG experienced the same relative electrostatic potential. The identical ΔG ⧧s measured for DSPG flip-flop under these conditions confirm that the charge repulsion between neighboring PG headgroups is the driving force behind the energetics of lipid flip-flop in the DSPC + DSPG bilayers examined here. For biological membranes, where the concentration of PG is relatively low, the neighboring PG lipids are spaced far enough apart that their anionic charges are effectively shielded, suggesting that under physiological conditions the charged nature of the headgroup does little to modulate its lipid flip-flop energetics and corresponding rate of translocation.

The complexation behavior of EGMP molecule and poly (EGMP) chains anchored on a rigid graphene oxide platform toward UO2 2+ and Pu4+ ions was found to be quite different from that in a pure polymeric form (cross-linked poly (EGMP) gel) having several ligating groups in close proximity. It was unusual to observe that the nonselective EGMP exhibited a remarkable selectivity toward Pu4+ ion when interacted as a single unit. The poly (EGMP) chains on GO (GO-poly (EGMP)) have a 2 times higher distribution coefficient for Pu4+ ions as compared to GO-EGMP and cross-linked poly (EGMP) gel under similar conditions. The DFT computation modeling has attributed high selectivity of GO-EGMP toward Pu4+ ion to higher stability of Pu (NO3)4EGMP complex with respect to UO2(NO3)2EGMP complex in the presence of an excess of nitrate ions. The findings of the present work suggest a new possibility of developing the ion-selective functionalized GO by appropriately preorganizing the functional groups.

In this paper, the transient absorption spectra of pure water and variable concentration of UMP solutions excited at 320 and 260 nm have been measured. The eaq - signal is obtained and the variation of the eaq - signal with the change of UMP concentration is discussed. It is found that the initial yield of eaq - decreases with the increase of UMP concentration under 260 nm excitation. This is due to the fact that UMP absorbs 260 nm pulse and the attachment of epre - to UMP would result in a decrease in the yield of eaq -. However, under 320 nm excitation, the initial yield of eaq - increases with the increase of UMP concentration. The analysis reveals that UMP itself releases electrons after excitation at 320 nm. The higher the concentration of UMP, the higher is the initial yield of eaq -. In summary, the use of femtosecond pulse pump-probe transient absorption spectroscopy to study the properties of eaq -, especially epre -, must take into account both the solute and solvent effects. The rate constant of the epre - attachment to UMP cannot be simply obtained from the initial yield of eaq -. We believe that the results of this paper are helpful for people to study the properties of epre - by pump-probe transient absorption spectroscopy.

Na3V2(PO4)2F3-y O y (0 ≤ y ≤ 0.5) compositions are isostructural and crystallize in the orthorhombic space group Amam, with an increasing disorder in the Na+ ions distribution and a continuous oxidation of vanadium resulting in the formation of vanadyl-type bonds. The electrochemical signature obtained for the sodium cells Na//Na3V2(PO4)2F3-y O y evolves from a complex phase diagram with two voltage plateaus for y = 0 to solid solution type reactions with an "S-shape" for the two voltage domains for y = 0.5. The influence of the oxygen substitution for fluorine on the structural and transport properties of Na3V2(PO4)2F3-y O y (0 ≤ y ≤ 0.5) has been investigated as a function of temperature. Changes in the crystal structure have been identified using high resolution Synchrotron powder X-ray diffraction, whereas the electronic and ionic conductivities have been determined for powders and single crystals and separated using electrochemical impedance spectroscopy in AC/DC configuration. The order-disorder transition occurs at 125 °C for Na3V2(PO4)2F3, with the formation of a more symmetrical tetragonal structure (space group I4/mmm) and a full disorder on the Na+ sites. The temperature of this transition increases slightly with the content in oxygen. This transition affects only the ionic transport properties, with a significant decrease of the activation energy associated with a break of slope in the evolution of a and b cell parameters with the temperature. The oxygen substitution allows one to improve the electronic transport properties (higher electronic conductivity and lower activation energy), which can explain the better electrochemical performances of the mixed valence Na3V2(PO4)2F3-y O y materials (with y > 0).

We have characterized the structure of the Aβ1-42 dimer and its disulfide-bond-locked double mutant (S8C) using extensive REMD simulations at pH 7. Our goal was not to understand why the intermolecular disulfide bond prevents Aβ oligomerization upon S8C mutation. REMD simulations in explicit solvent are computationally demanding, and only CG simulations of the Aβ1-42 S8C tetramers could provide physical insights explaining this fact. - Instead, in this study, we reveal that the intermolecular disulfide bond at position 8 significantly impacts the equilibrium structures and propose one possible structural scenario for preserving the toxicity of the S8C mutant that cannot form large aggregates. This study, in concert with recent simulations and experiments on new variants, - may help design new inhibitors for early-stage Alzheimer disease. -

In this study, the mode shape and the internal flow pattern for different modes (2, 4, 6, and 8) of a deionized water droplet placed on a hydrophobic surface were identified when a forced vibration was applied to the hydrophobic surface. The hydrophobic surface used in this study had a high contact angle of 115°, and we obtained the actual resonant frequency values for each mode and compared them to each other in terms of the size of the lobes. As a result, the actual value of the resonance frequency was lower than the theoretical value of the resonance frequency, and it was confirmed that as the mode number increased, the measurement uncertainty increased. In addition, the size of each lobe at the resonance frequency was relatively greater than that at the neighboring frequencies, and the internal flow of the nth order mode was observed through the flow visualization. Subsequently, a central bottom region of the droplet was chosen for the PIV measurements, and the velocity values were compared to each other. In all of the modes, a bisymmetrical flow pattern was generated about the central axis of the water droplet. In modes 2 and 4, a Y-shaped flow to the node point was observed, and in modes 6 and 8, a big elliptical vortex was confirmed. In addition, a small vortex was generated inside the lobe generated in each mode. Furthermore, it could be observed from the inner lobe that a small vortex is generated in each mode. In the case of the velocity field at the lower center of the water droplet, mode 4 exhibited higher velocity than mode 2, and the velocities of modes 6 and 8 were almost similar, but the velocity of mode 6 was approximately 7.2% higher than that of mode 8. Further research taking into account diversified variables affecting the water droplet pattern, such as forced vibration, temperature change, particle density inside water droplets, viscosity, and surface tension of water droplets, would be required for a better understanding of the behavior of water droplets.

In conclusion, we demonstrated a facile solvothermal method for efficient diffusion doping in 2D Mn:CsPbCl3 NPLs and even the formation of a new CsMnCl3 phase by spinodal decomposition without significantly altering the morphology and size of host perovskite NCs. ICP-OES, EPR, XAFS, and luminescence lifetime data confirm that the Mn doping efficiency was continuously improved during solvothermal treatment, while phase separation by spinodal decomposition can occur at later stage of diffusion doping, leading to the coexistence of Mn:CsPbCl3 and CsMnCl3 phases. The Mn doping efficiency and phase transition are strongly depending on the solvothermal reaction temperature and time, which further affects the optical properties of 2D Mn:CsPbCl3 NPLs. The CsMnCl3 inclusions by spinodal decomposition in Mn-doped CsPbCl3 NPLs are the first reported example of a nanoinclusion in isovalent doped NCs to the best of our knowledge. The ability to incorporate a new phase by spinodal decomposition provides a new understanding of doping inside quantum-confined NCs and a promising approach to study the interactions between the impurity and the host under moderate temperature and pressure.

The systems examined are illustrated schematically in Figure . The Lewis acid was taken as SMe3 + for several of these systems, as the sulfonium group plays a crucial role in a number of methyl transferase enzymes wherein the interaction between its transferring methyl group and a nucleophile is a prime issue of current inquiry. ,- This cation is paired first with NH3 as a model of the N-nucleophile to which this methyl transfers in some of these enzymes, ,, and second with HOH, which models not only a water molecule itself but other hydroxyl-containing groups. OCH3 - was chosen as a representative anion so as to determine how the strong cation-anion interaction might change the spectroscopic parameters. Both OH- and HCOO- were chosen as anions that might interact with a neutral thioether SMe2. The former is present in basic solution, and the latter serves as a model of glutamate and aspartate residues. So as to broaden the scope to methyl groups attached to atoms other than S, NMe4 + was taken as an alternate methyl donor, pairing it with the peptide group model HCONH2. Indeed, a methyl group bonded to a N atom is a common tetrel-bonding unit as, for example, in the M3 muscarinic acetylcholine receptor bound to tiotropium.

As indicated in Figure , R represents the distance separating the methyl C atom from the approaching nucleophilic atom, whether N or O. The θ angle is equal to 180° when the nucleophile lines up directly along the S/N-C axis, as would occur in a purely tetrel bond. A smaller value of θ, ~110° but varying a bit from one system to the next, corresponds to a linear CH O/N H-bonding arrangement. To establish the manner in which the spectroscopic parameters might be used to distinguish between a tetrel versus H bond, θ was set to a series of values varying between 180° and the precise angle that would present a linear CH O/N angle ( ~ 110°) in 20° increments. For each such angle, the remainder of the molecular geometry was fully optimized, including the R distance separating the two monomers.

Calculations were performed within the context of Gaussian-09, with the MP2 treatment of electron correlation, in concert with an aug-cc-pVDZ basis set. This level of theory has demonstrated its accuracy for H bonds as well as other noncovalent bonds of the sort examined here. ,- The presence of several methyl groups on the Lewis acid leads to strong coupling between the normal vibrational modes of the CH3 of interest and those of the others, which complicates any interpretation. To focus on the methyl vibrations of interest, and to decouple its modes from those of the others, the H atoms of the other methyl groups were replaced by D. Vibrational frequencies were calculated with the harmonic approximation. NMR chemical shielding was computed at the M06-2X/aug-cc-pVDZ level.

The photochemical experiments were conducted in a 750 mL, magnetically stirred, cylindrical, borosilicate glass reactor with a quartz tube in the center, in which a low-pressure mercury lamp (Heraeus GPH 212T5L/4, 10 W) was placed. The temperature was maintained at 25 ± 0.2 °C. The UV photon flux (I 0) entering the solution was determined to be 0.477 μE L-1 s-1 using iodide/iodate chemical actinometry. The effective path length (L) was determined to be 2.43 cm by measuring the photolysis kinetics of dilute H2O2 (Figure S1). The corresponding average UV fluence rate (Ep0) was estimated to be 0.78 mW cm-2.

A 750 mL test solution containing 1 μg L-1 of each PPCP and 2 mM phosphate buffer was dosed with the NaOCl stock solution and simultaneously exposed to UV irradiation. The chlorine dosages were 10 μM and 20 μM. Samples were collected at different time intervals and quenched with ascorbic acid at a molar ratio of ascorbic acid to chlorine of 1.5:1. Control tests of PPCP degradation by direct UV photolysis and dark chlorination were carried out in a similar manner but in the absence of chlorine and UV light, respectively. All tests were conducted at least twice. All data plots represent the average of the experimental data of the duplicated test results.

A total of seven nonphase-separated Lo or Ld phase lipid bilayer systems were studied, namely, symmetric Lo, symmetric Ld, and five asymmetric Lo/Ld systems. Both Lo and Ld phases are composed of the high T m lipid DSPC, the low T m lipid POPC, and CHL. The compositions are summarized in Table , with the Lo phase containing DSPC/POPC/CHL in a ratio of 0.49:026:0.25 and the Ld phase in a ratio of 0.09:0.79:0.12, consistent with experimental studies. - The two symmetric Lo and Ld bilayer systems, denoted as LoLo and LdLd, respectively, were built using the CHARMM-GUI web server. The numbers of lipids and water molecules for both systems are listed in Table .

When constructing asymmetric bilayers, it is important that both bilayer leaflets contain the correct number of lipids so that the surface tension within each leaflet is zero (i.e.. a tensionless bilayer). Following the approach of Perlmutter et al.. we first built an asymmetric Lo/Ld system based on simulations of symmetric Lo and Ld bilayers. With the number of lipids fixed at 400 in the Lo leaflet, the requisite number of lipids in the Ld leaflet was calculated from the APL ratio between the LoLo and LdLd systems. If the phase behavior in the two leaflets is not coupled, the Lo and Ld leaflets in the asymmetric bilayer should have the same lateral area, and the bilayer is thus tensionless (denoted as LoLd(0)). However, it is not obvious that this assumption is valid. To investigate the possibility of interleaflet coupling effects, we built four additional asymmetric LoLd bilayers in which the number of Ld lipids was systematically varied by adding/removing 5 or 10 lipids. These bilayers are referred to as LoLd(0), LoLd(-5), LoLd(5), LoLd(-10), and LoLd(10) (Table ).

Simulations were carried out using the GROMACS 5.0.1 program. The CHARMM c36 force field was used for the lipids, and the TIP3P model was used for water. All systems were simulated under constant pressure (1 bar) and constant temperature (303 K) (NPT) with periodic boundary conditions. The Nose-Hoover thermostat was used for temperature control with a 1.0 ps coupling constant, , and the Parrinello-Rahman extended ensemble coupling was used for pressure control with a coupling constant of 5.0 ps. Pressure coupling was applied semi-isotropically, with the z dimension (i.e.. perpendicular to the plane of the bilayer) allowed to fluctuate independently of the x and y dimensions. Long-range electrostatic interactions were treated using the particle-mesh Ewald method. The van der Waals interactions were treated using a switching function to reduce the force to zero, from 0.8 to 1.2 nm, according to Piggot et al. 's work. All bond interactions involving hydrogen atoms were constrained using SETTLE and LINCS to allow for a 2 fs integration time step. The LoLo, LdLd, and LoLd(0) systems were each simulated for 700 ns, while the LoLd(-10), LoLd(-5), LoLd(5), and LoLd(10) systems were each simulated for 500 ns. A total of 4.1 μs of simulations was performed, and analysis was done for each of the trajectories, excluding the first 100 ns, unless otherwise stated.

Interfacial (surface) tension is an important characteristic of a lipid bilayer as it determines its rigidity and stability and is thus directly relevant for interpreting the various physical phenomena taking place in the lipid bilayer. The surface tension (γ) in each bilayer leaflet may not always be zero as it can be compensated by membrane deformations.
