Separation regions on the plane of key ratios of net liquid flow rate through the separation zone illustrate improved separation performances over the basic SMB cases. While we cannot guarantee our approach to find a global optimum, we are able to achieve notable improvements; some additional grid searches have confirmed that the operating points we find are close to the global optimum. We compare the separation performance in terms of different purity and recovery regions, and combine with the Pareto plots for the operational modes to provide the performance results for two conflicting indices.

Figures summarizes the results of the operational mode improvement with varying m-values in terms of productivity and recovery for both cases. These two figures reveal that the addition of the operational modes improves the productivity over that of the basic 4-zone or 5-zone SMB (1.38, 1.53, and 1.57 g/L/h for the binary separation, and 0.08, 0.14, and 0.18 g/L/h for the ternary separation at three recovery regions ≥99%, 95%-99%, and 90%-95%). Each bar result represents the highest productivity result we can get in that specific average product recovery range. We can get higher productivity improvement if we drop the recovery criterion. We conclude from the separation region plots and the Pareto plots that applying operational modes does improve the performance much for the models with changing m-values, although it barely improves the basic SMB model with the chosen m-values. Therefore, it is possible to improve the performance of both the basic 4-zone and 5-zone SMBs significantly by applying various operational modes and their combinations.

Through the simulation and improvement, we find some similar trends between the two cases: (1) Varicol provides only small improvements over the basic 4-zone or 5-zone SMB. Varicol is limited by its ability to fully improve all the component purities in both cases. However, it improves the base case in some of performance indices, while only slightly sacrificing other performance indices. We consider this operational mode when we need high purity in one component, but the other is considered as waste. (2) PowerFeed in both systems performs better with a rear feed loading scheme. PowerFeed is highly sensitive to the m 2 ratio. We should be cautious when operating a PowerFeed unit to keep the flow rate in zone 2 constant. (3) ModiCon is the best single operational mode for both product purity and recovery, and is the first choice for a single operational mode. ModiCon gives the largest improvement in the feasible separation region, and it is able to achieve both the highest productivity and lowest solvent consumption of the single operational modes we investigated. (4) PF&MC expands the separation region over the ModiCon operation, and is the best choice of the combined operational modes we investigated for both cases. (5) Significantly, the qualitative rankings of the different operational mode improvement mostly remains identical across the different performance indices between our heuristic improvement methods and Pareto optimization.

We also find some different trends between the binary and ternary cases. (1) For the 4-zone SMB, PowerFeed gives only small improvement over the base case. However, PowerFeed performs quite well in the 5-zone system, nearly as well as ModiCon. In the future work, we need to study more separation systems to see whether PowerFeed works better for the systems with multicomponents and multizones. (2) For the 4-zone case, the combined operational mode V&PF&MC only has small improvement over the PF&MC. However, for the 5-zone case, adding Varicol to PF&MC has no benefit at all compared to other operational modes. It is not recommended over others because of its increased complexity.

The ability of cyclic peptides to target protein surfaces and protein-protein interaction interfaces makes them an attractive drug modality. Capturing the solution structure of a cyclic peptide is a crucial step toward any quantitative understanding of its properties. However, cyclic peptides tend to adopt multiple conformations in solution and such a feature makes it difficult to characterize their solution structures using traditional means such as NMR spectroscopy. This review shows that MD simulations with enhanced sampling techniques are capable of characterizing the solution structures of cyclic peptides and providing a rationale for their sequence-structure-activity relationships.

As simulation performance is an important aspect when applying enhanced sampling methods to studying cyclic peptides, Table provides a summary focused on the computational performance of the cyclic peptide simulations discussed in this review. These enhanced sampling methods often take advantage of using multiple replicas, and some cyclic peptide systems could require ≤100 ns per replica to achieve convergence. We hope to encourage computational chemists to take on simulating this challenging class of molecules and also to consistently apply measures to verify simulation convergence. As computational tools tailored to simulations of cyclic peptides become more readily available, the utility of MD simulations in solving this problem continues to increase. Already, targeting cyclic peptides' essential transitional motions using BE-META has enabled studies of dozens of sequences at a reasonable time scale. , Further improvements on this front will be critical in enabling MD simulation to be used for systematic studies of large cyclic peptides to establish sequence-structure relationships and for computational screening for therapeutic designs.

Cyclic peptides typically have fewer than 20 residues and a small modification in sequence oftentimes leads to a big change in structure and activity. The small sizes of cyclic peptides require high force field accuracy for each amino acid and residue-specific force fields provide more flexibility to achieve this goal. , Further improvement of force fields to simulate cyclic peptides with N-methylated amino acids and artificial amino acids, along with the ability to predict cis/trans isomers, will enable MD simulation to model cyclic peptides with even more therapeutic relevance.

In addition to being used to explain known experimental results, we have recently seen MD simulation take a leading role in making predictions followed by experimental verification. , Providing easy-to-follow, streamlined protocols will further enable researchers other than computational chemists to apply MD simulation with enhanced sampling as a routine method for studying cyclic peptides. MD simulation with enhanced sampling has proven to be a powerful tool to elucidate the elusive solution structures of cyclic peptides and we expect that its use will soon become a trend in cyclic peptide designs.

As mentioned above, we have chosen a hematite surface as the model for the pipeline surface, because our hypothesis is that the ILs interact with α-Fe2O3; this is supported by the work of McMahon, Ramachandran, and Obot. Alternately, there are no quantum mechanics results concerning corrosion inhibitors on iron oxide. The most common form of corrosion in the oil industry occurs when steel comes into contact with an aqueous environment. When metal is exposed to a corrosive solution (the electrolyte), the metal atoms at the anode site lose electrons, and these electrons are then absorbed by other metal atoms at the cathode site. Oxidation occurs by the closed circuit constituted through the Fe0 anodic region, the α-Fe2O3 cathodic and the electrolyte Figure , our hypothesis is that the cation having positive charge covers the cathode which has negative charge, protecting it and stopping the electron flow from anode to cathode, so passivation occurs.

It is known that the most probable exposed hematite surface is the (112) plane; then, we computationally built a surface whose faces are along this plane by cutting a slab from the bulk crystalline cell included in the database of the Materials Studio (MS) software. Previously to the cutting process, we have assigned spin values to the iron atoms in the hematite primitive cell, according to the spin ordering that leads to the lowest total energy, - which we have confirmed among three different orderings Figure .

We enclosed within a cell with periodic boundary conditions a hematite surface possessing a width of three oxygen slabs and left a 20 Å-width vacuum space; this resulted in an unit cell with dimensions of a = 5.43, b = 5.04, and c = 22.26 Å. Moreover, to calculate the adsorption energy of the ILs on the hematite surface, we have built a simulation cell (SC) whose dimensions were a SC = 32.61, b SC = 30.23, and c SC = 22.26 Å, obtained as a 6 × 6 × 1 supercell from the hematite-surface-containing unit cell, whereas the ILs models were computer drawn based on methylimidazole, Figure . These SC dimensions were sufficient to fully allocate the IL with the maximum length chain.

The geometry of the clean hematite slab, single ILs molecules inside in-vacuum SC and ILs molecules interacting with the hematite slab were fully optimized, keeping fixed the SC dimensions, through Density Functional Theory (DFT) energy minimizations by using the MS DMol3 code. , LDA/VWN functional, the DN basis set and the OBS method for DFT dispersion corrections were employed. A detailed electronic structure for each fully isolated IL was calculated by using the GGA/PBE functional, the DNP basis set, and the TS method for DFT dispersion corrections. For in-SC calculations, the run parameters were set at coarse accuracy; that is, the systems were relaxed until either two of the energy, force, and displacements differences between consecutive optimization steps were below 1 × 10-4 Ha, 0.02 Ha/Å, and 0.05 Å, respectively. In the second calculations, fine-accuracy run parameters were used; that is, the energy-, force-, and displacement-difference thresholds were 1 × 10-5 Ha, 0.002 Ha/Å, and 0.05 Å, respectively. The isosurface of the frontier molecular orbitals was set at the isovalue of 0.03 (in arbitrary units).

We have used the Conductor-like Screening Model for Real Solvents (COSMO-RS) quantum chemical theory , to compute the natural logarithm of the octanol-water partition coefficient by means of a statistical thermodynamics treatment of interacting surface charges of the single molecules. First, by using the TURBOMOLE software through TMoleX interface, version 3.1 (2011), a DFT-based geometry optimization of each molecule is performed under the COSMO continuum solvation model; that is, as if embedded in a dielectric medium via a molecular surface or cavity that is constructed around the molecule. Each segment of this surface is characterized by a screening charge density (SCD), which takes into account the electrostatic screening of the molecule by its surrounding and the back-polarization of the molecule. Afterward, by using the COSMOthermX software, version C30_1301, a liquid mixture is considered under the COSMO-RS model; that is, as an ensemble of closely packed ideally screened molecules in which an electrostatic interaction arises from the contact of the different SCDs calculated by TURBOMOLE using a dielectric constant of infinite value. Finally, the calculation of the octanol-water partition coefficient is toggled in the COSMOthermX run.
The energy band gap, E gap, is defined as 5 E gap ≡ E LUMO - E HOMO a large gap indicates low chemical reactivity and a small gap indicates high chemical reactivity. ,-

The Fukui indices allow identifying those specific atoms at the IL molecules that could favor the linkage on the hematite surface since they are a measure of the capacity to exchange electrons. The Fukui index f k + for an atom k measures changes in the atomic-centered charge when the molecule gains electrons and, hence, corresponds to reactivity with respect to a nucleophilic attack. Conversely, f k - corresponds to reactivity with respect to an electrophilic attack (i.e.. when there is a loss of electrons). Fukui indices are defined as 6 f k - = q k ( N ) - q k ( N - 1 ) 7 f k + = q k ( N + 1 ) - q k ( N ) where N is the number of electrons, and q k is the electronic charge in the IL molecule at the atomic site k, respectively. ,,,, Atomic charges were calculated in the Mulliken ,- approximation.

Adsorption energy calculations were performed in order to study the IL ability to form a protective film on the α-Fe2O3 surface, allowing covering of latter and therefore protecting the Fe anodes avoiding the electron flow. The adsorption energy ΔE , of an IL molecule on the hematite surface was calculated by means of the equation 8 Δ E = E IL , surface - ( E IL + E surface ) where E IL, E surface, and E IL,surface are the total quantum energy of the isolated IL, the total quantum energy of the pristine hematite surface, and the total quantum energy of the interacting IL-hematite surface system, respectively. However, the optimized IL undergoes deformation with respect to the isolated IL. Therefore, the adsorption energy (ΔE) contains deformation energy (E def) of the IL molecules. E def was estimated as the energy difference between the energy of the optimized IL and the energy of the IL structure in each adsorption system. All total quantum energies were obtained at the end of molecular geometry optimizations. Negative values of the adsorption energy indicate that there exists an attraction between corrosion inhibitor molecules and the hematite surface. Generally, the high absolute value of the adsorption energy denotes a strong attraction between corrosion inhibitor molecule and the hematite. The inhibitor can be adsorbed tightly onto the oxide surface (cathode) ILs strongly interacting with the oxide surface and stopping the electronic flow from the anode to the cathode; that is, the circuit is opened and then the corrosion decreases.

The total electronic charge transfer Δq from hematite surface toward the adsorbed IL molecule was calculated as 9 Δ q = ∑ k ( q k , after adsorption - q k , before adsorption ) The octanol/water partition coefficient of an IL allows us to have insights on the IL transport feasibility through two flows that allow the IL to arrive onto the pipeline surface. The octanol/water partition coefficient (P OW) is defined as 10 P OW = [ X ] octanol [ X ] water where [X] s is the concentration of the solute X in the solvents (octanol or water) when both solvents are in contact at equilibrium. Because of the wide range values that P OW can have, usually it is reported as its logarithm instead, log10 P OW.

The BOCS toolkit provides software tools for parametrizing the potential, U(R,V), for a CG model based upon information from an AA trajectory. Table summarizes the primary input and output for these tools. Figure outlines the workflow for determining the interaction potential, U R , while Figure outlines the workflow for determining the volume-dependent potential, U V .

The cgmap tool generates a mapped ensemble as the CG representation of an AA ensemble. The cgmap tool requires an AA trajectory file that contains atomically detailed configurations and, optionally, the corresponding velocities and forces. The cgmap tool also requires (1) a plain text file that determines the mapping coefficients, {c Ii }, by specifying the CG representation for each type of molecule in the system; and (2) a CG topology file that specifies the type and connectivity of the sites in the CG model. Based upon the specified mapping coefficients, the cgmap tool determines the CG representation of each AA configuration according to eq . If the AA trajectory file includes velocity and force information, the cgmap tool determines the mapped velocities and forces according to eqs and . The cgmap tool then provides a mapped CG trajectory file that can be analyzed using standard GROMACS tools.

The cgff tool calculates the parameters for U R from the mapped CG trajectory file. The cgff tool requires a plain text input file to specify the types of potentials, U ζ, included in U R and also the basis functions, f ζd , employed to represent each U ζ. The cgff tool also requires a CG topology file to specify the instances, λ, of each interaction. Assuming that the mapped CG trajectory contains explicit force information, the cgff tool calculates the force correlation function, b D , and structural correlation function, G DD′, according to eqs and , respectively, for each pair of basis functions D = ζd and D′ = ζ′d′. If forces are not present in the mapped trajectory, the cgff tool calculates b D directly from structural information according to eq . Although force-based calculations (i.e.. via eq ) require less sampling to accurately determine b D , structure-based calculations (i.e.. via eq ) yield equivalent results for sufficiently well sampled systems ,, and have proven quite useful for several applications. , The cgff tool then solves the normal system of linear equations, eq , for the potential parameters, ϕ D . Finally, the cgff tool outputs these parameters, as well as, b D , G DD′, and additional supplemental files that characterize the system and provide diagnostic information about the calculation.

The cgff tool treats a fairly wide range of CG potentials that can be represented according to eq , i.e.. bond-stretch potentials, bond-angle potentials, dihedral potentials, and short-ranged pair potentials. The cgff tool can represent each of these potentials with either piecewise constant functions, piecewise linear functions, or B-spline functions. The cgff tool also implements several standard analytic functional forms, including harmonic bond-stretch or bond-angle potentials, Fourier-series dihedral potentials, and Lennard-Jones-type pair potentials. Additionally, the cgff tool allows for fixed "reference potentials," U R ref, that are specified by the user and can be of arbitrary complexity. , In this case, the user must supply an additional trajectory file specifying the resulting reference force, F I ref, on each CG site in each mapped AA configuration. The cgff tool computes a corresponding contribution to each force projection, b D ref, from the reference potential, i.e.. using F I ref in the place of f I in eq . The cgff tool then optimizes the remaining terms in U R to match the remainder of each force projection, δb D = b D - b D ref. In particular, if Coulombic or other long-ranged potentials are defined as reference potentials, then the cgff tool will determine the short-ranged potentials that, when combined with the specified long-ranged potentials, provide an optimal approximation to the many-body PMF.

The cgff tool provides several additional options for the calculation of ϕ D and the resulting output. The cgff tool can precondition the normal equations, eq , by normalizing the G DD′ matrix according to the norm of each column, the max of each row, the total variance in each column, or the variance in b D . The cgff tool can solve these normal equations via single value, Cholesky, UU, or LU decomposition. The cgff tool can regularize these methods according to Bayesian inference or a simpler uncertainty estimation. The cgff tool also provides several options for specialized diagnostic output, including error estimates, eigendecomposition of G DD′, and also decomposition of b D into contributions from different interactions according to the g-YBG theory, i.e.. eq .

Because it quantifies many-body structural correlations, the calculation of G DD′ can be quite time-consuming for large systems with many interacting CG sites. As indicated by eq , the cgff tool calculates the correlation between the forces generated on each site, I, from each pair, λ and λ′, of nonbonded interactions. The cgff tool performs this calculation by looping over all triples of interacting particles. For a CG model with N sites, this calculation scales as O(N 3). We have expedited this calculation by exploiting the symmetry of this loop and by employing the OpenMPI framework to distribute the frames of the mapped trajectory over multiple processors. This parallelization scales perfectly because each frame is treated independently in calculating G DD′ and because this nested triple loop typically dominates the time required for calculating ϕ D .

We note that the MSCGFM code implements the normal equations, eq , as well as several other numerical methods for minimizing χ1 2 to determine the MS-CG force field. Lu et al. have provided an excellent discussion of various numerical methods for minimizing χ1 2, including methods for solving an overdetermined system of linear equations with a block-averaging approximation. In comparison to this block-averaging approach, the normal system of equations is more time-consuming, due to the nested triple loop discussed above, and also requires the numerical inversion of a matrix with a relatively high condition number. Nevertheless, we find that, with proper choices of solution method, preconditioning, and regularization, our implementation performs well and, in test cases that we can rigorously test, accurately determines the MS-CG potential. Additionally, because they correspond to a g-YBG integral equation that is explicitly expressed in terms of equilibrium ensemble averages, the normal equations facilitate molecular insight into the system and the resulting CG potentials. , Moreover, the normal equations allow for the calculation of these potentials directly from structural information. ,,,

The cgff tool separates the calculated potential parameters, {ϕ D }, into files corresponding to different interactions. For interactions represented with simple functional forms, such as bond-stretch interactions represented with harmonic potentials, the resulting parameters can be immediately employed as input for CG simulations. However, for potentials represented with more flexible functional forms, such as nonbonded interactions represented with spline functions, the calculated parameters may require additional processing. The tables tool performs the necessary smoothing, extrapolation, and interpolation to generate input files for use in GROMACS simulations. , The lammps_tables.py script converts these files for use in LAMMPS simulations.

The cgff tool also implements the extended ensemble framework to determine transferable potentials that provide an optimal approximation to the many-body PMF's for multiple mapped ensembles, Γ, that correspond to distinct chemical systems or distinct thermodynamic state points. In this case, the cgff tool requires a mapped CG trajectory file for each AA ensemble, as well as plain text and CG topology files that specify the contributions to the interaction potential, U Γ, for modeling each Γ. The cgff tool also requires the user specify the weight, p γ, for each AA ensemble, γ, included in the extended ensemble. Given this input, the cgff tool calculates b D and G DD′ as extended ensemble averages and determines the optimal potential parameters, ϕ D , from eq , as in the case of a single system.

The cgmap and cgff tools have been historically developed for use with GROMACS and currently employ several functions and data structures from the GROMACS libraries. , In particular, we currently employ GROMACS functionality to read and write GROMACS trajectory and topology files, as well as for some aspects of the user interface employed by the cgmap tool. In order to buffer these tools from the GROMACS source code and in order to facilitate future compatibility, we developed an interface that wraps all references to GROMACS functions and addresses changes to relevant GROMACS libraries and files. The BOCS toolkit is currently natively compatible with GROMACS 4.5.×, 4.6.×, 5.0.×, and 5.1.×.

The BOCS toolkit also provides tools for determining U V in order to simulate CG models that sample isotropic volume fluctuations under constant external pressure. The first step in this process is to estimate U V via pressure-matching. , This calculation requires a fixed CG interaction potential, U R , and a mapped CG trajectory file containing the mapped configuration, M(r t ), mapped momentum, M P (p t ), and volume, V t , for each time t. We then evaluate, for each t, the pressure, P int 0, that is defined by eq and accounts for the kinetic and interaction contributions to the instantaneous pressure of the CG model. In practice, this can be done by postprocessing the mapped CG trajectory file using the "-rerun" option with the standard GROMACS mdrun tool. (Note that, if the CG potential includes table files, then these files must be specified in the topology files for this postprocessing calculation and for subsequent CG simulations with GROMACS, as indicated by * in Figure .) Given the resulting set of CG pressures, {P int 0(t)}, as well as the corresponding AA pressures and volumes, {p int(t), V t }, the pmatch tool then determines U V to minimize χ2 2.

The resulting CG potential, U(R,V) = U R (R) + U V (V), can then be simulated with lmp_pmatch, which is a modification of the LAMMPS distribution from 17 June 2013 that includes the contributions from U V in the barostat equation of motion. These simulations determine an estimate for the pressure-volume equation of state, P int(V), for the CG model. In practice, this CG model does not perfectly reproduce the pressure equation of state, p int(V), of the AA model. ,, This discrepancy presumably arises due to differences between the mapped and simulated configurational distributions at each V. Consequently, if necessary, we perform iterative self-consistent pressure-matching in order to refine U V . , The CG and AA pressure equations of state are provided as input to the pmatch tool, which then estimates the necessary correction for U V (V). This process can be iterated until the CG model adequately reproduces the AA pressure equation of state. In practice, this usually requires fewer than 10 iterations. ,

There is no special workflow for determining U V for transferable potentials obtained via the extended ensemble approach. In practice, we perform self-consistent pressure-matching to determine a separate potential U VΓ for each mapped ensemble, Γ. In principle, it may be possible to generalize the extended ensemble approach to determine a transferable pressure correction for modeling multiple state points or chemically distinct systems with similar interaction potentials. However, we have not yet tested this possibility.

A dual-reflectron time-of-flight mass spectrometer combined with a pulsed cluster source has been utilized to investigate the photofragmentation of cationic cobalt oxide clusters, Co n O m + (n = 5-9 and m = 4-13). Oxygen-deficient, oxygen-equivalent, and oxygen-rich species are produced, mass-selected, and photofragmented. The loss of an oxygen molecules is the main dissociation channel of oxygen-rich and oxygen-equivalent clusters (m ≥ n). While Co n O n-2 + clusters tend to decay via the evaporation of a Co atom, the photofragmentation behavior of Co n O n-1 + species interestingly can be divided into two regimes: for n ≤ 6 the loss of an oxygen atom is the most prominent, while for n > 6 the clusters' most intense decay channel is the loss of a cobalt atom. The observed size-dependent fragmentation could be related to the predicted 2D-to-3D structural transition of cobalt oxide clusters. In combination with available experimental and computed results, the lowest-energy fragmentation channels of m = n - 1 and m ≥ n, which could not be achieved in previous work, are identified in this study. DFT computations have been carried out for selected m = n - 2 clusters. The comparison between the computed dissociation energies for different dissociation channels and photofragmentation spectra provides a clear picture of the dissociation behavior of oxygen-poor clusters. These results are important for understanding relative stabilities and dissociation pathways of cobalt oxide clusters. They also provide input for computational studies that deal with their growth mechanism.

The present work provides convincing evidence that the phenomena, earlier shown to occur in water, are general for fluids of very varied nature, both as for theory and for experiment, and therefore do not reflect any water anomaly.

So, as postulated earlier for water, , at its T 0 a liquid becomes altogether inert in many aspects. Owing to the interaction of its molecules in the liquid, if T < T 0 none of them can escape, and also they do not allow transport of any kind. These behaviors suggest that kT 0 can be identified as the multimolecular potential of the liquid, that itself would be related to the interaction of pairs of molecules. Such a relationship indeed exists and appears to be a proportionality on plotting T 0 versus the Lennard-Jones potential parameter ε/k.

The paper dealt with the risk-based process safety management for a GTU of a GOSP through the implementation of a process simulation into a general QRA procedure using the concept of static inventory. The proposed integration methodology could connect two different natures of simulation in a reliable manner: the static nature of a QRA simulation based on the storage conditions of a fluid, and the dynamic nature of a process simulation dealing with the fluids flowing through a pipe or separated by the phase equilibrium.

The QRA results were utilized to concretely determine the risk reduction targets through the total risk integral ranking of all the accidental scenarios and major outcomes that had a dominant impact on the risk. Consequently, a small leak (10 mm hole diameter) scenario at the hydrocarbon liquid stream from the three-phase separator in case of an isolation failure and the associated flash fire and pool fire effects from that scenario were targeted to be managed.

The risk reduction approach was applied in two different ways according to the risk target. First, in order to reduce the risk by mitigating the flash fire and pool fire probabilities under the selected leak scenario, modification of the process design by altering the operating pressure of the three-phase separator from 12.0 barg to 0.52 barg was proposed. Modification resulted in a 27% decrease in the total societal risk from 1.41 × 10-3/year to 1.02 × 10-3/year with an additional capital cost of around $50,000, which dragged down the risk to the tolerable ALARP region. Second, a sensitivity analysis of the total societal risk to the isolation success probabilities was performed. As a result, the improvement of the success probability up to 40% drastically reduced the risk from 1.02 × 10-3 to 5.82 × 10-4/year.

Through these two risk reduction methods, the risk of the GTU process could be practically managed, and a much safer process design was suggested in the early design stage. Even though this study dealt with the simple GTU process for conveying the methodology effectively, it is surely extendable to a more complicated chemical process with more complicated unit operations as the process and risk simulation are integrated with each other. Further study will be performed for the remainder of the GOSP processes, and generalization of this risk management methodology will be studied to verify its applicability to all chemical processes.

The polyelectrolytes DNA and CPE PEDOT-S were assembled together for organic opto/bioelectronics. In this study, the major findings are as follows: (1) The blends self-organize into phase-separated insulator/metal micro and nanostructures. (2) Both polyelectrolytes, DNA and PEDOT-S, show similar heat absorption around 100 °C because of the water residue in the sample. (3) DNA fibers are aligned perpendicular to the brushing direction. (4) DNA:PEDOT-S biocomposite films show a conductivity of 10-6-10-5 S/cm. (5) We studied full complexes of [DNA:CTMA]:[PEDOT-S:CTMA] as a function of composition. The supramolecular ordering of DNA is to a degree retained in the hybrid material, offering pathways for designing electronic properties. DNA:PEDOT-S-based films may be relevant for the design of selective electron and hole transport layer in organic optoelectronic devices.

By combining complementary analysis techniques such as scanning probe microscopy (STM and AFM) with reflection absorption infrared spectroscopy (RAIRS) and X-ray diffraction (XRD), we analyzed the structural evolution of TiOPc films on Au(111). Growth at room temperature shows various (metastable) phases with short-range order that hampers the formation of well-ordered multilayer films. By contrast, growth at 450 K yields very long-range ordered crystalline films which exclusively adopt the phase I polymorph. In such films, the TiOPc molecules adopt a bilayer-wise growth mode with alternating up/down orientation of their titanyl units in consecutive single layers. This is also found for the initial bilayer, which comprises an exclusive upright orientation of the first monolayer. This stabilization leads to the formation of macroscopically smooth films largely immune to dewetting and thus parallels the growth scenario observed earlier for TiOPc/Ag(111). While the molecular contrast in the STM micrographs of bilayer films depends critically on the tip conditions which hamper a precise assessment of the tilting, an exclusive recumbent molecular orientation is derived from the RAIRS measurements (even for films grown at room temperature).

The present study emphasizes the importance of using complementary analysis techniques to derive an accurate structural characterization of molecular films, especially beyond the seed layers, while advising caution in the extraction of microscopic structural parameters solely based on STM data. This is crucial to a fundamental understanding of the microscopic mechanisms and principles that govern the growth of highly ordered crystalline organic semiconductor films.

In summary, a simple Pdots-based PEC sensor capable of broad-range pH measurement was developed. Due to the presence of -COOH groups in these Pdots, the configuration of the Pdots and the production of carriers after photoexcitation can be easily regulated by pH value, leading to the sensitive response of photocurrents. Compared with other pH sensors, this Pdots-based pH sensor was very simple and exhibited good stability, reversibility, and sensitivity. This work extended the applicability of the PEC sensor. Besides, on the basis of various functional conjugated polymer nanomaterials, it offered a new prospect for the future development of an advanced PEC pH sensor.

In summary, 2-mercaptobenzimidazole was successfully loaded onto the nanoparticles through thiol-ene reaction between KH570-modified TiO2 and MB to yield TiO2-KH570-MB, and the MB loading amount was 5.19 wt %. TiO2-KH570-MB was applied in the anti-UV/O3 modification of thermoplastic vulcanizates. SEM images showed that TiO2-KH570-MB was uniformly distributed in TPV due to the good compatibility between TiO2-KH570-MB and the TPV matrix. The effects of TiO2-KH570-MB on the aging resistant behavior of TPV were evaluated on the basis of the surface morphology, mechanical properties, gel content, and carbonyl index of TPV upon UV/ozone exposure. The results demonstrated that TiO2-KH570-MB exhibited aging resistance to UV/O3 exposure that was much better in comparison with those of TiO2-KH570, MB, and their physical mixtures. Among all of the TPV samples, the TPV/TiO2-KH570-MB nanocomposites had the fewest surface cracks, the highest retention ratios of mechanical properties, the highest gel content, and the lowest carbonyl index after UV/O3 exposure for 1000 h. The superior anti-aging performance of TiO2-KH570-MB could be attributed to the better compatibility with the TPV matrix as well as the much lower level of migration and volatility of chemically bonded MB. In conclusion, this nano-TiO2-loaded MB exhibits a high efficiency in anti-aging performance against UV/O3 and achieves a meaningful increase in the service life of polymer products with good prospects.

This work shows that even the act of exposing a weak polyacrylamide hydrogel to osmotic swelling generates hydrogen peroxide by mechanochemical bond breakage. First, an assay was developed to monitor H2O2 levels based on the peroxidase-mediated conversion of colorless Amplex Ultrared to pink resorufin. Next, the effect of osmotic swelling on hydrogel structure was determined. When weaker, disulfide-containing crosslinkers were used, >10 μM H2O2 was produced. Addition of stronger, PEG-based crosslinkers reduced but did not eliminate H2O2 generation. However, constrained swelling of hydrogels with PEG-based crosslinkers increased H2O2 levels. Finally, this effect was found to be generated mostly after the gel reached its full extension and did not depend on dissolved oxygen. This work has considerable implications for those utilizing hydrogels for cell culture, particularly with stem cells.

The single-phase water flow experiment was carried out in the homogeneous micromodel to better understand the effect of w/o emulsion flow on pressure drop responses. Figure shows pressure drop as a function of injected pore volume at different flow rates of 10, 7, and 5 cc/h. The flow rate is decreased in each step after the system reached the steady state condition at each specific flow rate. This explains the step function decrease observed in this figure.

As can be seen from Figure , as the flow rate decreases from 10 cc/h to 7 cc/h and then 5 cc/h, the pressure drop decreases accordingly which is expected from Darcy's equation of flow in porous media with constant permeability. This figure also shows that there is no significant pressure fluctuations during the single phase flow of water at different injection rates, and the pressure drop responses in this experiment are qualitatively different to the pressure drop responses during w/o emulsion flow provided in Figure . This issue reveals that the possible syringe pump injection pulse or the accuracy of pressure transmitter in recording the pressure drop data does not have a considerable effect on the pressure drop behavior or its fluctuations. Therefore, pressure fluctuations in Figure during waterflooding of emulsions with different brine salinities are not affected by accuracy of the syringe pump or pressure transmitter (DP), and they are related to droplet capturing of w/o emulsions during their flow in the micromodel porous media.

In this work, a hybrid process with a mixed solvent was proposed to separate PM and water. The optimization was carried out to obtain the minimal TAC, and the relationship between different compositions of mixed solvent and the reboiler heat duties was studied. The optimum results showed that when the solvent is 70 mol % chloroform and 30 mol % 2-EA, the TAC and energy consumption are minimal. Compared with the single solvent (2-EA), the TAC of the optimal process with mixed solvent decreased by 26.7%, and the reboiler heat duty was reduced 27.45%. Furthermore, we calculated the CO2 emissions index and the thermodynamic efficiency in the hybrid process with mixed solvent to evaluate their performance. CO2 emissions were reduced 27.5%, and the thermodynamic efficiency improved from 8.55% to 10.15%. The feed-effluent heat exchanger saves the TAC 17.73% and the CO2 emissions 17.11%, and the thermodynamic efficiency improved from 9.71% to 10.67% compared with the feed-effluent heat exchanger in the single solvent process.
Therefore, the hybrid process using a mixed solvent has greater advantages than the hybrid process using a single solvent in terms of both economics and environmental benefits.

In this paper, we present a combined anion photoelectron spectroscopic and relativistic coupled-cluster study of the electronic structure of the UN2 molecule. UN2 is much less characterized than its isoelectronic counterpart UO2 2+. Energy levels of the UN2 excited states are well characterized via the close interplay between the experiment and theory. We find that both electron attachment and electronic excitation significantly bend the UN2 molecule and elongate its U-N bond. This suggests that the morphology, coordination, and reactivity of UN2 and the related uranium nitride compounds may be tuned using optical or electrochemical approaches. Knowledge of the electronic structure of uranium nitride may also be valuable in better understanding the behavior of uranium nitrides in nuclear reactors, where excited-state uranium nitrides may be prevalent.

A novel simultaneous electrochemical phenol detoxification and heavy metal recovery from multicomponent acidic media is successfully developed in this study. Because of the enhanced mass transfer, 50 ppm refractory phenol is efficiently degraded at the anode, while the dilute copper is also completely electrodeposited at the cathode with 90.3% current efficiency. It has been demonstrated that the simultaneous utilization of anode and cathode can alleviate the side reactions and facilitate the target reactions. And there is also good performance toward the industrial phenol-containing heavy metal wastewater containing copper, zinc, lead, and cadmium ions, offering a sustainable method for the efficient resource recycling and wastewater purifications.

In this research, we developed the photocombustion method to reduce the temperature of VO2 crystallization down to 250 °C and investigated the crystallization kinetics of VO2 films prepared under various conditions using in situ and ex situ electron microscopy techniques. This is the lowest temperature reported to date for sol-gel derived crystalline VO2 film formation. All the comprehensive film analyses reveal that ammonium nitrate is a key additive which effectively promotes not only the combustion synthesis but also the DUV photoactivation, leading to the promoted crystallization at low temperatures. Furthermore, the reliable and robust VO2 phase transition behaviors on flexible substrates were reported for the first time, which suggests that sol-gel derived crystalline VO2 formed by photocombustion can be applied to large-area and/or flexible applications (e.g.. smart windows , ). Finally, we expect that the low-temperature metal oxide crystallization via DUV photocombustion in combination with AN incorporation can be employed for other crystalline metal oxide films prepared via sol-gel chemistry.

Summing up, the study yielded the following results: The process of coacervation can be used for the production of concentrated hand dishwashing liquids. The coacervate phase contains practically all surfactants (active ingredients) present in the composition of the starting formulation, though the coacervates should preferably be formulated using electrolytes with monovalent cations. The type of electrolyte used affects the process of coacervate formation. Selecting a salt with monovalent cations results in an increase in electrolyte weight which is necessary for inducing the coacervation process. The emulsifying properties of coacervates decrease in line with increasing valency of the cation contained in the salt. The tendency can be a consequence of a lower concentration of surface active agents in the product obtained using compounds of this type. The resultant hand dishwashing liquids exhibit very high washing and foaming abilities, though better parameters were achieved for products formulated using salts with cations having a single electric charge. The type of electrolyte used has a decisive influence on the zein value which is a measure of the skin irritating potential of products. The study confirmed existing literature reports on a considerable reduction of the studied parameter in the presence of cations carrying a double electric charge such as Mg2+ or Ca2+. All dishwashing liquids in the coacervate form were found to exhibit an increased viscosity in contact with water. The type of electrolyte used in the formulation affects the susceptibility of coacervates to thickening after the addition of water. Electrolytes with cations carrying a double charge were found to be associated with lower maximum values of dynamic viscosity (ηmax) which can be obtained for coacervates after the addition of water. These products required the addition of a smaller weight of water to achieve ηmax values.

It is highly important to investigate the recycle stability of the catalysts for esterification of the LA when it comes to the practical applications. The catalysts were easily separated from the production mixture, because the solid catalyst settled at the bottom of the reactor. The catalysts were filtered when they are hot at the end of the reaction, and then washed with n-hexane and dried at 65 °C in a vacuum oven. It can be seen that the catalysts show excellent stability without significant decrease of catalytic activity after at least 5 runs (Figure ). Moreover, XPS measurements of both catalysts after reuse for five times show the same W 4f7/2 and W 4f5/2 at 35.8 and 37.9 eV for compound 3; and 35.7 and 37.9 eV for compound 4. Such results indicate that the structures for both catalysts remain no change during catalytic reaction.

With an increase in the volume of esterification of LA to 100 mL, esterification could be completed in 180 min. Compound 3 exhibits high esterification efficiency with almost 97% methyl laurate yield and 99% selectively.

To confirm compounds 3 and 4 are truly heterogeneous, the dehydration of fructose has been carried out using compound 3 as an example. As shown in Figure , when the reaction time reaches 20 min, compound 3 can be removed simply from the reaction mixture by filtration and the reaction is allowed to proceed with the filtrate under the same experimental conditions. It can be seen that no additional 5-HMF can be obtained with time increasing. After 30 min, compound 3 is added back to the reaction mixture. The dehydration of fructose to 5-HMF continues with time increasing. The results clearly indicate that compound 3 is a heterogeneous catalyst. Moreover, ICP measurement of the filtrate by removing of compound 3 cannot detect the W content, suggesting that compound 3 does not leach during the catalytic reaction. Similar catalytic results can be achieved with compound 4 as the catalyst. Therefore, compound 3 is truly heterogeneous.

Through the use of octahedral Au cores, Cu nanocubes and octahedra have been synthesized in aqueous solution with tunable sizes. The synthetic condition is simple and particle growth is complete in 45 min to 1.5 h. The added hexadecylamine increases the solution pH and acts as a coordinating ligand to the Cu ions. Due to the large lattice mismatch between Au and Cu, nonuniform Cu shell growth yields cubes and octahedra with noncentrally located Au cores. The Au-Cu octahedra are ultrasmall and show little change in plasmonic band position with increasing particle size. For nanocubes, progressively smaller spectral red-shifts were recorded with increasing cube dimensions. Au-Cu nanocubes have shown moderate catalytic activity toward the 4-nitrophenol reduction reaction. The Cu nanocubes and octahedra can be explored for organocatalysis application.

This rapid assay for creatinine detection by point-of-care testing (POCT) was able to produce consistent signal levels that accurately detected the creatinine concentrations from clinical blood samples. The creatinine sensor covered the desired clinical range for detecting allograft dysfunction (0 mg/dL to 11.3 mg/dL). Signal levels that were detected electrochemically correlated closely with the creatinine blood concentrations reported by the Ronal Reagan UCLA Medical Center traditional clinical laboratory assay (R 2 = 0.94). With the development of an accessory that could consistently deliver 40 μL of blood to the sensor, this device could become a prominent clinical diagnostic tool for measuring allograft dysfunction in renal transplantation.

The DFT method was used to study distinct inclusion and adsorption complex structures formed between cisplatin and carbon nanotube molecules. The theoretical results reported here using the B3LYP/6-31G (d,p)/LanL2DZ level indicate that for the two types of carbon nanotubes employed (capped and open nanotubes) the structure in which cisplatin is adsorbed outside of the tube is more favorable energetically. However, M06-2x/6-31G (d,p)/LanL2DZ single-point calculations indicate better stability results for the complexes formed with the cisplatin inside the nanotube. The energetic difference becomes around 90% more favorable to the complex in which the cisplatin is closer to the capped nanotube in complex III. In this molecular configuration of inclusion complexes, the cisplatin can be carried out through the biological media without strongly interacting with other reactive molecules, which would disable its action, and reach in an efficient way the final molecular target inside the DNA structure. According to the reported results, the experimental detection of the formation of the inclusion compound can be attained through the analysis of the 1H (NH3 protons) and 15N NMR spectra. The B3LYP/6-31G (d,p)/LanL2DZ 1H and 15N NMR results showed a variation of about 20-21 ppm for the inclusion complex VI, which is expected to be easily observed in NMR experiments, leading to identification of the cis-DDP@OCNT compound. Thus, with this study we showed again that the DFT method with the 6-31G (d,p) basis set is sufficiently valid for the NMR spectra calculation of the class of compounds formed between cisplatin and carbon nanostructures.

Using biomimetic design principles, a series of new PTDMs was reported. Both hydrophobic phenyl and cationic guanidinium groups play important roles in PTDM activity. Increasing the hydrophobic content led to more efficient transporters. The ability to efficiently deliver functional proteins into cells has been conclusively demonstrated. These novel PTDMs are more efficient than noncovalent complexes of Pep-1 and TAT-fusion proteins. Two functional proteins were delivered including a transcription factor into primary murine splenocytes. The synthetic flexibility of this platform allows numerous other PTDMs to be envisaged, and this work is currently underway.

Acetylene black (AB, Denka Black) and Na3PS4 glass-ceramic as electronic and ionic conductive pathways were added to the sulfur electrode because sulfur active material is an insulator. , If close contacts of sulfur active materials with AB and Na3PS4 solid electrolytes are prepared, utilization of the full discharge reaction of sulfur active material, unlike the NAS batteries with capacity restriction, is also expected in the all-solid-state Na/S batteries. The sulfur mixture was mechanically milled to prepare ionic and electronic conducting pathways and to increase these contact areas where redox reactions occur. Thus, two kinds of sulfur composite electrodes were prepared using sulfur (Aldrich, 99.98%), acetylene black, and Na3PS4 glass-ceramic powders with a weight ratio of 25:25:50 (S:AB:Na3PS4). One was prepared by hand mixing of these three powders (S + AB + Na3PS4). The other was prepared by mechanical milling using a planetary ball mill apparatus (Fritsch, Pulverisette 7). Sulfur and AB were placed into a 45 mL ZrO2 pot with 250 ZrO2 balls (4 mm in diameter) and milled at 510 rpm for 10 h. The milled mixture was mixed with Na3PS4 glass-ceramic powder and milled at 300 rpm for 15 min (S-AB-Na3PS4). X-ray diffraction (XRD) measurements of the sulfur electrodes were conducted using a diffractometer (SmartLab, Rigaku) with Cu Kα radiation (1.54 nm, 40 kV, 200 mA). Structural units in the electrodes were investigated by Raman microscopy (LabRAM HR-800, Horiba-Jobin Yvon) with a 532 nm laser. The laser power and spot size were ~1 mW and ~2 μm, respectively. The element distribution in the sulfur electrodes was investigated using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) (JSM-6610A, JEOL) coupled with an energy dispersive X-ray spectrometer (EDX) (JED-2300, JEOL) at an acceleration voltage of 15 kV. In the all-solid-state cells, the sulfur composite electrodes and Na3PS4 glass-ceramics were used as the working electrode and solid electrolyte separator, respectively. A mixture of Na15Sn4 alloy and AB (Na-Sn) was used as the counter electrode. All the peaks in the XRD pattern of the mixture (Figure S1) could be attributed to Na15Sn4. The Na15Sn4 phase has a potential of 0.11 V versus Na+/Na with the two-phase reaction between Na15Sn4 and Na9Sn4. Bulk-type all-solid-state cells were fabricated by stacking these powders and pressed at 360 MPa with stainless steel disks as a current collector. The electrochemical performance of the cells was examined at constant current densities of 0.013-0.38 mA cm-2 at room temperature using a charge-discharge measuring device (VMP3, Bio-Logic Co.). Electronic structures in the S-AB-Na3PS4 composite electrodes after the discharge tests were analyzed by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) (K-Alpha, Thermo Fisher Scientific) with a monochromatic Al Kα source (1486.6 eV). XPS spectra of Na2S ( > 99.1%; Nagao Co.), Na2S2 ( > 90.0%; DOJINDO), Na2S3 ( > 90.0%; DOJINDO), Na2S4 ( > 90.0%; DOJINDO), and the Na3PS4 glass-ceramic electrode, all reference materials, were also measured. The observed binding energies were calibrated with the adventitious C1s peak to 284.7 eV or the AB peak to 283.8 eV.

The influence of the addition of the nonionic surfactants C12DMPO, C14DMPO, C10OH, and C10EO5 at concentrations between 10-5 and 10-1 mmol/L to BCS and BLG solutions, respectively, at a fixed concentration of 10-5 mmol/L on the dilational surface rheology is studied. It is shown that a significant change of the viscoelasticity modulus occurs, and a maximum at very low surfactant concentration (10-4 to 10-3 mmol/L) appears for BCS mixtures with C12DMPO and C14DMPO, while for all other studied mixtures the increase of the modulus is not so pronounced. For BCS mixtures with C10EO5 only a slight increase of the modulus with increasing concentration was observed, while for BLG mixtures with C10EO5 this increase is essentially higher. As can be seen, the rheological behavior of mixtures of proteins with surfactants is affected by the protein structure and the type of the polar group of surfactants. BLG is a typical globular protein, and BCS is a typical flexible protein. To understand the mechanism of the surfactants' effect, we require more research on the structure of the complexes. The viscoelasticity modulus was calculated using the theoretical model developed in ref , which takes into account the surfactant influence on the adsorption activity of proteins. The model assumes that the increase of the equilibrium adsorption activity of a protein is proportional to the surfactant concentration in the solution. The values of the viscoelasticity modulus calculated using this model, with the additional assumption that the presence of surfactant affects the minimum molar area of adsorbed protein molecules, are in a satisfactory agreement with the experimental data for all systems studied.

It is shown that a linear dependence exists between the ratio of the maximum E value for the mixture to that of the individual protein solution and the value of the coefficient k that expresses the impact of surfactant molecules on the adsorption activity of proteins. A linear dependence exists also between this ratio and the difference between the surface tension calculated disregarding the influence of the surfactant on the protein adsorption activity and its original value. A maximum value of the modulus (twice as large as that for the individual protein solution) was found for BCS mixtures with C14DMPO, for which k = 2.7, while the surface tension decrease amounts to 6 mN/m.
All of the reagents were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich Inc. (St. Louis, MO, USA) except where noted otherwise.

Five typical MOFs derived from four metal centers and two organic ligands, that is, MOF-5, HKUST-1, MIL-53 (Fe), MIL-53 (Cr), and MIL-101 (Cr), were employed for investigation. Their adsorption capacities for three representive aromatic sulfur compounds (i.e.. thiophene, BT, and DMDBT) were systematically studied using a fixed-bed adsorption system. The factors including the adsorbate-adsorbent interaction, window diameter, and porosity were considered to correlate with the adsorption performance of MOFs. It is demonstrated for the first time that the adsorbate-adsorbent interaction plays a major role in adsorptive desulfurization. Metal sites and structure of MOFs as well as types of aromatic sulfur compounds is responsible for the adsorbate-adsorbent interaction. The effect of window diameter becomes apparent when the molecular size of aromatic sulfur compounds is comparable or smaller than the window diameter of MOFs. The present study may provide some clues to the selection and synthesis of efficient MOFs for adsorptive desulfurization.

We have thoroughly analyzed the influence of surface trap states on the electrical transport properties of intrinsic Ge NW. Controlling the trap population by electrostatic gating, we demonstrated the potential of effective surface doping to cause a transition of charge transport from hole- to electron-driven, enabling NDR in intrinsic Ge. Importantly, the electrostatic control of surface states may enable to avoid the charge trapping related hysteresis effect that is commonly considered parasitic for nanoelectronics and even introduces new functionalities based on polarity control. Consequently, our investigations provide a framework for utilizing surface trapping related transport phenomena in Ge nanostructures, which could be a significant step towards the development of future device concepts for post-Si nanoelectronic and nanophotonic devices.

We start by showing the effect of the weights and multipliers for one specific AFV. Figure illustrates how the inclusion of GHG AFV incentives results in increased emission rates for a Chevrolet Volt. The black line shows the annual GHG emissions standards with which the manufacturer needs to comply. If one vehicle has emissions lower than the standard, a second "balancing vehicle" can be sold with higher emissions such that the average emission rate of the two vehicles is equal to the standard. This is an illustrative case with a single balancing vehicle model, equal sales volume for the AFV and its balancing vehicle, and no change in sales volume induced by the AFV incentives. Without AFV incentives, the average of the Volt emission rate (solid blue) and the balancing vehicle emission rate (solid red) is equal to the standard with which the manufacturer would need to comply in each year. The Volt emissions appear to increase over time only because the EPA uses AFV upstream emission estimates relative to the upstream emissions of an average conventional internal combustion vehicle (as described earlier), which decrease over time as the standards become more stringent (see p 62822 of ref ). With the AFV incentives, the adjusted emission rate for the Volt used in GHG accounting calculations is artificially lowered using a weighting factor (dotted blue). The balancing vehicle (dotted red) produces higher emissions for two reasons; between 2012 and 2016, the weighting factor allows the balancing vehicle to be a higher-emitting vehicle, and after 2016, the inclusion of a multiplier, m, greater than one compounds this effect. The net increase in the average emission rate resulting from the AFV incentives is the difference between the red lines (shaded area in Figure ). For the Volt, this increase ranges from ~40 gCO2/mi (25 g/km) in 2012-2016 to 140 gCO2/mi (87 g/km) in 2017. We perform a similar assessment for the AFVs listed in Table S3 in the Supporting Information and find that the increase in emissions ranges between 10 and 400 gCO2/mi (6 to 250 g/km)-a range comparable to the emissions that would have been created if an extra conventional light-duty vehicle's emissions were added to the fleet's emissions each time an AFV is sold in place of a conventional vehicle (a Toyota Camry is 330 gCO2/mi (200 g/km)).

The net lifetime increase in fleet GHG emissions and gasoline consumption for several AFVs is shown in Figure (again for the case of no change to the manufacturer's GHG target induced by the incentives). The greatest increase occurs for battery electric vehicles (BEVs), such as the Nissan Leaf and the Ford Focus BEV, because AFV incentives for these vehicles have weighting factors of w = 0 and multipliers as high as m = 2. The Chevrolet Volt and Toyota Prius PHEV follow a similar pattern at lower magnitude. Flex fuel vehicles benefit from a 0.15 weighting factor and assumed 50% of VMT propelled by ethanol, both of which expire in 2016.

We also estimate the cumulative increase in GHG emissions resulting from AFV incentives from 2012 to 2025. We use the AEO vehicle sales projections made in 2012, 2013, 2014, and 2015 reports, as explained in the Data and Methods section. - The results are shown in Figure S3 in the Supporting Information. The largest source of emissions difference between vehicle technologies is caused by the difference in projected sales from the AEO reports. The FFVs have the highest sales in both cases and as a result produce the highest cumulative increase in emissions, although the emissions from FFVs peak earlier, as their AFV incentives expire first. Despite relatively large differences in projected sales of plug-in electric vehicles, we find that the cumulative emissions effect is comparable across technologies from sales in 2012 through 2025, ranging between 2 and 11 million metric tons of increase in CO2 emissions for each technology using 2013 projections. The net effect of the AFV incentives is an increase of 30 to 70 million metric tons of CO2 emitted over the lifetime of the vehicles sold during this period. This is the equivalent of relaxing the GHG standard by about 0.8-1.5% (assuming no change in total sales). The effect of AFV incentives on gasoline consumption depends on the change in AFV sales induced by the incentives. Assuming no change in sales, the incentives result in 3-8 billion gallons (11-30 billion liters) of gasoline consumed over the lifetime of the vehicles sold during this period.

Primarily, the proposed DIPCA method consists of two steps. In the first step, we perform an iterative PCA on the matrix of lagged measurements (for an appropriately chosen L) and determine the process order η from the identified number of constraints. This step of determining the correct process order constitutes a key novel contribution of this work. An important byproduct of the first step is the estimate of the noise covariance matrix. Subsequently, in the second step we reconfigure the data matrix as per the estimated order and scale it with Σ e -1/2. A PCA of this scaled matrix is used to obtain the desired regression model. Estimation of delay is implicit in the model identification step.

For the special case when error variances are known, we provide a theoretical proof (attached in Supporting Information) that the process order and consequently the model parameters are consistently estimated by applying DPCA on the lagged scaled data matrix. However, we are unable to provide a theoretical proof for joint consistency of the estimates of error variances, model order, and model parameters using DIPCA. Instead, Monte Carlo simulations are used to estimate a confidence interval (CI) for the parameter estimates. The CI obtained through simulations seems to indicate that DIPCA can provide consistent estimates of all model parameters.

We briefly reviewed the recent progress of HIPEs and foams. We also discussed several issues addressed by researchers already in this field who often encounter four categories of subjects: Synthesis methods, choice of stabilizer, flow behavior control, and polymeric foams for various applications. To address the challenges for each subject, we say the following: (1) for synthesis, it will be beneficial to have a new technique to synthesize monodispersed droplets and bubbles in a large scale without a large energy input, (2) designer polymers, colloids, and surfactants that efficiently stabilize HIPEs and foams without a complicated fabrication process for the HIPEs/foams would allow huge progress in this field, (3) a better understanding of flow behavior will make it possible to process the materials more diversely in controlled circumstances, and (4) finally for polymeric foam synthesis via a HIPE/foam template, it would be extremely useful if uniform and size-controlled droplets and bubbles with well-defined surfaces could be controlled spatially and temporally at the same time.

Although many researchers have made significant progress on this subject, there still exist many challenges to overcome in both basic research and industrial applications. New chemistry and techniques are needed to successfully address the issues. We mainly focus on the material perspective and present a few future directions. (1) Nanosized droplets and bubbles Nanosized droplets and bubbles themselves are interesting subjects to study since the interfacial/surface area rapidly increases as their size decreases, so larger interfaces can be utilized. Each of them is independently being studied as a nanoemulsion ,,,- and nanobubbles - (more accurately bulk nanobubbles, differentiating them from surface nanobubbles). For now, it is difficult to increase the concentration of nanoemulsions and nanobubbles even up to moderate concentrations, , although it is not clear why this is so. Smaller droplets could also improve the mechanical properties as G′ ~ σ/a, if their stability is guaranteed. When nanosized HIPEs and foams are turned into the porous materials after polymerization, they could exhibit improved mechanical strength since nanopores compared to larger pores provide a better mechanical stability. , More importantly, nano-HIPEs and nanofoams can reach pore sizes from 20 to 200 nm in which other techniques cannot easily be achieved. (2) Uniform size distribution without using a microfluidic technique In addition to the nanosized droplets/bubbles, the size uniformity may be important as well. Although microfluidic techniques can create monodispersed droplets, they are potentially limited to the larger droplets (typically >10 μm). Other synthesis techniques for high size uniformity with smaller sizes would be advantageous for many applications, although only a few examples can form the uniform size. ,,,,- Once the nanosized uniform droplets and bubbles can be formed, then various optical applications such as photonic crystals would also be possible. - (3) Adhesive emulsion gels The lower volume fraction gel is another interesting system that has not been fully developed from the emulsions and foams. Surfactants, lipids, and particles have been used to make a gel that exhibits flow behavior similar to that of HIPEs and foams, using only a very small volume fraction of dispersed fluids. - Instead of a high volume fraction of the dispersed phase, achieving similar rheological properties with a smaller fraction of the dispersed phase would make additional opportunities for other new materials. To achieve it, appropriate attractive interaction between droplets is introduced to make a gel. If it is too strong, a very low fraction gel can be formed, but it is likely to be unstable. Meanwhile, if the attraction is too weak, a considerable amount of the dispersed phase is needed to span the gel network. Maintaining a similar flow behavior using different volume fractions would be promising for applications, considering different polymeric foam structures from the templates. Creating porous materials from a low volume fraction of emulsion/foam could provide another design of porous materials. Lastly, it would be interesting whether the adhesive emulsions can be transformed to bicontinuous interfacially jammed emulsion gels (BIJELs), - because they share structural similarity (Figure ). (4) Volume fraction maximization As the volume fraction of the internal phase, ϕ, increases, the stability naturally becomes worse as the stress at the interface, τ ~ σ/r where r is the radius of curvature at the edge, gets bigger as described in Figure c. , The curvature r becomes smaller as ϕ increases. Another challenge to address is up to what volume fraction a HIPE or foam can be made with considerable stability. Once the gaps between droplets become smaller as the volume fraction increases, one can save materials significantly while maintaining the transport properties, such as the electrical property, thermal conductivity, and permeability. How small of a volume fraction of the continuous phase is required to impart the transport properties is another challenge to be solved. Another important feature of both HIPEs and foams with extremely high volume fraction is that the thickness of the continuous phase will become easily nanosized as the volume fraction increases, and then the confinement effect can be realized relatively easily. (5) Under extreme conditions for practical applications Many practical applications require stable HIPEs and foams under extreme conditions such as low temperature or high pressure accompanied by phase transition and under constant perturbations by external stress. The stability, and thus applicability, is naturally limited to a narrow temperature range since typical HIPEs have water as one of the two phases. A lower temperature than the freezing temperature of water solidifies the water phase, but in the process of melting, we do not understand what will occur, especially for stability. Another problem that is poorly understood is how the external pressure and high temperature affects the foam stability, so these will be great questions to answer.
By addressing these questions/challenges, fluid composites as HIPEs and foams could be used for much broader applications, beyond our current main usages such as personal care products and foods.

To augment or replace oil, reduce CO2 emissions, and minimize the flaring of associated gas, a lower-cost, lower-emissions process for converting methane to products that are liquids at standard atmospheric temperatures and pressures is urgently needed. Importantly, only large volume products such as fuels or large volume commodity chemicals will have any significant impact in meeting these goals. This is one of the remaining "grand challenges" in chemistry today. The challenges are substantial as the primary methods currently utilized for methane conversion to fuels or chemicals are based on high temperature ( > 800 °C), energy and capital intensive syngas-based chemistry that has been exhaustively optimized to over 70% C-yields based on natural gas over the past many decades. Given the enormous investment in capital required for large scale fuel or commodity chemical processes, any next generation process must have substantial economic advantages to warrant the risk of development by the petrochemical industry. Unfortunately, given the economic realities of the world, economic advantage is likely more important than, or at least as important as, reductions in energy and emissions. Developing new chemistry that can convert methane directly (without the need to generate syngas) to useful products at temperatures substantially below 800 °C has the potential to address the grand challenge. This review focused on the use of homogeneous (gas/liquid) systems for direct, nonsyngas, methane functionalization.

As highlighted in this review, substantial progress has been made, through years of dedicated research by many groups, toward developing a process for lower temperature, direct conversion of methane to liquid products with high selectivity. Despite this effort, a process has yet to be developed that can economically outcompete the currently employed, temperature and energy intensive, syngas-based process. Consequently, it is necessary that the development of new chemistry with methane continues. To meet the "grand challenge" of replacing or augmenting oil, the ideal products are either large volume oxygenates (such as methanol, dimethyl ether, acetic acid, etc. ), olefins, or higher hydrocarbons (such as long chain alkanes or aromatics). Other smaller scale, specialty or fine chemicals, such as methanesulfonic acid, methyl chloride, etc.. may play an important role in replacing existing chemical processes but would not address the spirit of the "grand challenge" to substantially augment or replace oil. It could be possible, but less ideal, to use such materials as precursors to liquid fuels or large scale commodity chemicals.

Given the current low cost of natural gas in the United States, which is being driven by the influx of shale natural gas production, industrial companies are increasingly moving into natural gas conversion businesses. As most of these new processes are all based on improving traditional energy and capital intensive syngas chemistry, there remains the opportunity for a next generation direct conversion process. A particularly interesting new, nonsyngas, advance is the development by Siluria Technologies of a new gas-phase, heterogeneous catalyzed process for the "oxidative coupling" of methane to ethylene. - This approach is not covered in this review as it does not involve homogeneous systems. The central challenge in "oxidative coupling" continues to be obtaining high selectivity given the intrinsically high reactivity of olefins relative to alkanes. However, according to the company this process is now being developed in a small-scale plant. This is an important advance as this would be the first, new direct functionalization process for methane. Eventual successful, large scale commercialization of this chemistry could renew interest in the possibility for other new, direct, selective methane conversion chemistry.

Given the central requirement for the use of O2 as the only coreactant to meet the "grand challenge", we have categorized the broad range of homogeneous, metal-mediated methane functionalization systems as O2-regenerable or non-O2-regenerable, based on whether or not O2 has the thermodynamic potential to regenerate the oxidant (or if, as in some cases, O2 is the terminal oxidant in the system). To aid in connecting these practical considerations to more fundamental insights, we have made an effort to further classify all reports based on reaction mechanism. Importantly, these mechanistic classifications were based only on the species undergoing the elementary reactions with methane. We found that the various systems reported fell into two broad, fundamentally different classes of chain and nonchain reactions with methane. The nonchain reactions were further classified into two subclasses, CH activation (CHA) and CH oxidation (CHO), to emphasize their fundamental differences. Given the interchangeable use of these terms in the literature and the stark differences in the chemistries, a method of quantitatively identifying reactions in these categories is presented and discussed. Thus, the CHA reaction is defined as elementary reaction between a hypothetical species, LMX2, and a CH bond of methane that generates an, e.g.. L (X) M-C-IVH3 intermediate with a characteristic M-C bond where, importantly, the formal oxidation state (FOS) remains unchanged relative to methane at -IV. In contrast, CHO reactions are defined as elementary reactions with methane that generate a C-species that is oxidized relative to methane, i.e.. where the FOS is less negative than -IV. These CHA and CHO nonchain reactions are further classified as stoichiometric (where the stoichiometric reagent undergoes the elementary reactions with methane) and catalytic (where the catalyst is the species undergoing the elementary reactions with methane in the presence of a stoichiometric oxidant). While these are related, this distinction highlighted the differences.

Given the economic importance of the use of O2, either directly or indirectly, it was encouraging to see that a significant number of reports fell under the category of O2-regenerable (which includes direct use of O2). There were several reported systems that directly utilized O2. Many systems utilized O2 indirectly through the use of stoichiometric oxidants whereby the reduced form of the oxidant could be reoxidized by O2. The reader should be reminded that such indirect systems are based only on the thermodynamic potential for this reoxidation. In most of these indirect, O2-regenerable systems the reoxidations were not actually demonstrated since these reactions are generally known. Introducing this regeneration step would undoubtedly add complexity but is not inherently impractical given the possibility to integrate the chemistry into a two-step, continuous process analogous to the well-established, commercial Wacker process where Cu (II) is used as a stoichiometric oxidant that is regenerated with O2 in a separate step. As discussed, there are potential advantages of a two-stage, Wacker-type process over a process that involves direct use of O2 mixed with methane.

However, many of these indirect, O2-regenerable systems reported are based on H2SO4/SO3 as the oxidant. As discussed, we believe there are inherent challenges with the use of this O2-regenerable system that could prevent practical use. Use of 98% H2SO4 (without SO3), while overcoming some of these issues, would still suffer from the disadvantage related to the high costs of removing methanol from a strong acid. If this O2-regenerable, SO3 system is eliminated, relatively few reported indirect systems would meet the requirement for an integration into a practical, two-stage Wacker-type system. One of these is the use of stoichiometric HgII in 98% H2SO4. However, this suffers from the need for strong acid solvents and toxicity associated with Hg. Given the advantages of a two-stage Wacker-type systems, the identification of nontoxic systems that do not require strong acids and utilize stoichiometric, O2-regenerable oxidants should be a priority.

There are also many reports on the use of oxidants that cannot be regenerated with O2, e.g.. those based on hydrogen peroxide or persulfate. It is likely that these non-O2-regeneralbe oxidants provide both greater driving force and lower barriers for reaction. While these non-O2-regenerable systems can provide important insight and the systems can be directed at lower volume chemicals, it would be ideal if there was greater emphasis on O2-regenerable systems in new lines of research.

It is not clear that any conclusion can be drawn from the reports to direct emphasis to a particular approach. However, it is the opinion of the authors, given the challenges with direct reactions of methane with O2 (related to the inherent low reactivity, explosivity, possible need and associated costs to separate O2 from air, and generation of radicals that can lower selectivity), that an indirect system based on a modified, two-stage, Wacker-type process is preferred as this avoids direct methane/O2 reactions while allowing use of O2 (as air) as the overall oxidant. It is also worth considering whether this review and classification suggests a preference for a particular reaction mechanism to develop improved systems. In this regard, it is interesting to note that this classification scheme shows that there are no reports of systems that fall under the category of nonchain, O2-regenerable, stoichiometric, CH oxidation (CHO).
