This is likely related to higher limits on oxidation potential for oxidants that can be regenerated by O2 and the need for strongly oxidizing species to carry out elementary reactions with methane that generate oxidized intermediates or products. This highlights a possible advantage of approaches based on CH activation (CHA), which can be considered an acid-base reaction, since it proceeds by elementary reactions with methane that generate methyl intermediates that are not formally oxidized at the carbon. It is possible that CHA reactions, as is generally the case with acid-base reactions, can be inherently more facile than CH oxidation (CHO) reactions which require significantly more electronic reorganization in the transition state for CH cleavage. However, it is by no means clear that any strong recommendation can be made regarding the merits of a particular mechanism or approach. What is clear is that, while significant progress has been made, sustained research is still needed to address the "grand challenge" of developing a new, lower temperature, nonsyngas, direct methane conversion process.

A series of Mn-Ce-Ti-O catalysts was synthesized by a modified sol-gel method. The test of NH3-SCR activity shows that the MCT-15/1 catalyst has prominent deNO x activity, and the MCT-15/20 catalyst has 80% deNO x activity when a small quantity of SO2 is introduced. XRD shows the catalyst has two phases coexisting of rutile and anatase, and the MnO x and CeO x are well distributed and strongly interact on the surface of the two phases. H2-TPR, O2-TPD, and XPS show that there were a lot of oxygen defects produced by Mn3+ + Ti4+ ↔ Mn4+ + Ti3+ and Ce4+ + Mn3+ ↔ Ce3+ + Mn4+, which was in favor of improvement of deNO x . NH3-TPD illustrated that catalysts have a great deal of acid quantity at 100-450 °C, which widened the reaction temperature window. The mechanism was speculated by in situ IR, and the conclusion as follows: (1) B acid sites were the main active sites in the low temperature section, and L acid sites worked in the high temperature section. (2) In the low temperature section, the L-H mechanism and E-R mechanism both occurred, and the E-R mechanism dominated in the high temperature section. (3) The additional Mn atom was in favor of adsorption of NH3, but the oxygen defects, generated by MnO x and the transition layer between anatase and rutile, were exposed on the surface of catalysts which was propitious to the oxidation of NO to NO2.

We have presented a comprehensive characterization of blade-coated N2200 for TFT applications, including significant detail in the measurement of in-plane orientation and alignment from multiple structural data sources. N2200 displays the expected power-law dependence of film thickness on blade speed in both the evaporative and LLD regimes. However, bulk polymer alignment flips from perpendicular to the coating direction to parallel as blade speed increases. The anisotropy of top-gate TFT mobility did not agree with the bulk backbone orientation; rather, mobility anisotropy was strongly correlated with the in-plane alignment of the fibrillar morphology at the surface, quantified through AFM image analysis. We also observed a striking periodic, wavelike packing of N2200 fibrils at the air interface for low blade speeds and quantified this morphology with a custom orientation correlation algorithm that extends the functionality of GTFiber image analysis software. The high-angle grain boundaries present in this structure appeared to impede charge transport despite an overall high degree of fibril alignment.

Through the analysis of a nanogroove-aligned thin film in conjunction with high-resolution in-plane GIWAXS pole figures, we developed a model of crystal orientation for N2200 thin films. While the bulk crystal population for high-speed-coated films was aligned in agreement with optical and AFM results, the crystal population in low-speed films was aligned perpendicular to the coating direction but with a bimodal character suggesting conflicting surface and bulk populations. We used the model of crystal anisotropy to analyze simultaneous in situ GIWAXS and UV-vis reflectance data from N2200 thin films coated at 5 mm/s. The data suggest that a small population of crystals that orient early in the drying process template bulk alignment that occurs very late in the drying process and, furthermore, that the majority of aligned material in N2200 thin films is not crystalline at these conditions. Bulk alignment was likely established through a lyotropic liquid crystalline phase.

Importantly, we have demonstrated the utility of S 2D as a general and quantitative metric to describe and compare in-plane orientation distributions of structural features and electrical properties for oriented thin films of conjugated polymers. This metric can be easily approximated from ratio-based representations of anisotropy, while mitigating the inherent sensitivity and nonlinearity of such ratio-based approaches. These results should further the rational design of aligned semiconducting polymer thin films for high-performance TFT applications.

The role of surfaces in modulating protein conformation was examined by investigating the folding of the GB1 hairpin near the air-water, ice-water, and silica-water interfaces. GB1 was destabilized at the air-water and ice-water interfaces but stabilized at the silica surface. In the case of the air-water interface, destabilization was caused by direct interaction of the hairpin turn and of the hydrophobic pair formed by residues 43W-54V with the vacuum. This strong interaction promoted a large exposure of nonpolar surface area and a resulting loss of structure. In the case of the ice-water surface, the interaction of residues 43W-54V with the surface promoted a partial loss of structure; however, the turn structure was retained, and complete unfolding was not observed. By contrast, the GB1 hairpin was stabilized at the silica surface because of confinement effects and absence of strong protein-surface interactions.

Surfactants are commonly used in experiments to stabilize proteins in the event of surface-induced denaturation. We investigated the mechanism of surfactant action using the polysorbate Tween 80 as a model surfactant. We found that the surfactants stabilize the protein when the denaturing air-water and ice-water surfaces are present but slightly destabilize the protein in the bulk and at the otherwise stabilizing silica interface. We observed that the surfactant molecules bind to the surface in the presence of air and silica, while they preferentially cluster around the protein in the case of ice. At the silica surface, the surfactant molecules coating the interface also directly interact with the protein, leading to mild destabilization. We identified an orientation-dependent mechanism of the surfactants, in which the protein was stabilized when the hydrophilic heads of the surfactant were oriented toward the protein and destabilized when the hydrophobic tails pointed toward the protein. The latter orientation stabilized partially unfolded states of the protein, characterized by a larger nonpolar surface area. We found that the tails-toward-the-protein configuration is favored in a hydrophilic environment, explaining the mild destabilization observed in the bulk solution, and, even more strongly, at the silica-water interface. A hydrophobic environment, on the other hand, promotes the heads-toward-the-protein arrangement, which is particularly efficient in stabilizing the protein native structure. Finally, in the case of the air-water surface, the coating of the interface by the surfactant molecules, and the resulting inhibition of protein adsorption, account for the observed stabilization of the protein native structure. In this case, the amphipathic nature of Tween 80 plays a major role, with the favorable interaction between the hydrophobic tails and the vacuum leading to the coating of the surface by the surfactants.

Overall, our simulations suggest that the action of surfactants is complex, as it can either stabilize or mildly destabilize the protein. The amphiphilic nature of the surfactant and its relative affinity for the protein and the surface eventually determine the effect on the protein structure.

The study of kinks is more easily understood from a differential representation of the protein main chain. Indeed, the angle θ i is directly related to the local curvature κ i (κ = π - θ) of the protein main chain, whereas the angle γ i is the local torsion of the main chain (see Figure and Methods). Assuming constant virtual bond distances between the Cα atoms, the free energy of the polymer can be written in terms of (κ,γ) internal coordinates using a Landau-Ginzburg-Wilson free-energy model - [eq ]. Minimizing this free-energy relative to κ and γ leads to a nonlinear equation of motion for the curvature similar to a generalized DNLS that admits kinks as particular solutions.

In earlier studies, - the modular building blocks of folded proteins, that is, supersecondary structure such as a helix-loop-helix or strand-loop-strand motif, have been described in terms of the kink of a generalized version of the DNLS equation. It was found that the formation of a kink is initiated by an abrupt change in the orientation of a pair of consecutive side chains in the loop region. It has been shown that, in order to obtain a clear picture of kink formation, it is necessary to start MD simulations from the full α-helical or β-strand structure and investigate the dynamics of the formation of loops; otherwise, it would be blurred by α-helix or β-strand formation. Moreover, kink analysis enabled us to realize the importance of local interactions, specifically the bimodal character of the potential of mean force in virtual-bond angles κ, as the driving force of folding. It is notable that the only long-range interaction present in the Landau-Ginzburg-Wilson Hamiltonian - is a stepwise Pauli exclusion that introduces self-avoidance and prevents chain crossing. The effects of the long-range Coulomb and van der Waals interactions are accounted for by the global multikink profile resulting from the minimization of free energy. The multikink structure describes both local and collective motions. Previously, it has been shown that, using kink parameters that are derived from the experimental folded protein structure, its folding can be simulated. ,,,,, Moreover, a phase diagram of protein with temperature (T) and acidity (pH) as the thermodynamic variables can be constructed as well. Therefore, it is of interest to investigate whether a kink analysis of the experimental structures , can uncover the mechanisms, which govern L26D and especially L26W to fold through downhill folding.

In summary, we report herein for the first time the environmental-friendly and efficient synthesis of 2-amino-4H-chromenes 1, exhibiting interesting biological properties, catalyzed by 1-butyl-3-methyl imidazolium trifluoro methane sulfonate (5). Our preliminary studies demonstrated that the nature of the counterpart sulfonate affects the reaction, with IL-5 being the most efficient catalyst. The main advantage of using IL-5 for the synthesis of chromenes 1 relies on its easy separation of the reaction mixture and recycling, exhibiting high activities and selectivities, and operating under mild reaction conditions.

Although the acid-base properties in ILs are often not immediately visible, our theoretical study has suggested that both the imidazolium core and the anion are involved in the reaction course, acting as a hydrogen bond donor and acceptor, respectively. Contrarily to the most widely accepted mechanism through Knoevenagel condensation, the most favorable reaction pathway consists of aldolic condensation followed by heterocyclization, subsequent dehydration, and, finally, a Michael addition to form the chromenes 1. Moreover, the different catalytic activity of these imidazolium-based ILs has been justified in the Kamlet-Taft framework.

By the functionalization of CNCs with surface-grafted thermoresponsive copolymer molecules, we developed a new building block for the generation of temperature-responsive nanofibrillar gels for cell encapsulation and culture. The temperature-responsive nature of these building blocks enabled on demand hydrogel formation and dissociation under physiological conditions. The mCNC hydrogels exhibited controllable variation in structure and mechanical properties and were stronger and had a larger pore size than the hydrogels formed by the corresponding copolymer. The temperature-responsive hydrogels used for the encapsulation and culture of fibroblasts and T cells exhibited low cytotoxicity toward both cell lines and significantly promoted the proliferation of T cells (suspension cells) with a proliferation index of 2-4.5 after 1 day of cell culture.

Due to the low cytotoxicity, biocompatibility, and tunable properties, the temperature-responsive hydrogels formed by copolymer-modified CNC can be used as injectable gels and as an artificial extracellular matrix for three-dimensional culture. The mCNCs represent a new family of nanofibrillar materials that can be used for the preparation of environments for cell culture, followed by cell release for their detailed and precise characterization or re-encapsulation in a new environment to create more complex biological structures. In comparison with other man-made nanofibrillar hydrogels, mCNC hydrogels with tunable biophysical properties can be prepared in a robust, cost-efficient, and easily scalable manner. Furthermore, the biofunctionalization of the copolymer with peptides promoting cell adhesion can be used to improve the culture of adherent cells such as fibroblasts and endothelial cells.

In conclusion, the addition of fluoride or sulfate to silver-containing phosphate glass has different effects on glass structure, leading to distinct optical and luminescence trends with composition. The Tauc plot of absorption spectra showed that the optical energy gap E opt decreases with increasing fluorine content and increases with higher sulfate content. Under an excitation of 265 nm, the maximum of the Ag+ emission band was found at ~380 nm in Ag-doped fluorophosphate (PF) glasses and at approximately 400 nm in sulfophosphate (PS) glasses. In addition, the main peak position of the emission spectra shifts to longer wavelengths (redshifts), with increasing fluoride or sulfate content. The optical basicity theory appears to be less applicable to the optical property trends for the very mobile Ag+ ions; only the emission peak in the PS glasses followed the expected trend from optical basicity and simple [O]/[P] calculations. Instead, Ag+ ions exhibit complex optical property-composition trends, with the absorption and emission wavelengths having the opposite dependence on composition, very clearly in the PS series.

The solid-state NMR results confirmed that when AlF3 replaces NaPO3, P-O-P and P-O Na+ bonds are replaced by Al-O-P and Al-F Na+ bonds in PF glasses. With increasing amount of NaSO4, an obvious conversion of Q2 species to Q1 species was observed and the glass network connectivity decreased, as no SO4 2- species were found to link to phosphate groups. Meanwhile, the higher sodium content led to a decrease in the average aluminum coordination number. From the 31P NMR spectra of compositions with additional 10 mol % Ag2O or Na2O and valence unit theory, we found that in these mixed-anion aluminophosphate glasses, silver has a bonding preference in the order of Q1 Al ≈ Q0 > Q1 > > Q2. This observation is in agreement with the trends in optical properties, where the absorption and emission peak energies are correlated with the quantity of ionic Qn species (Q0 and Q1 mAl) and network connectivity. For example, the higher amounts of Q0 and Q1 mAl units (lower network connectivity) with Na2SO4 addition compared to AlF3 addition led to larger blueshifts of the absorption wavelength in PS glasses. This trend was not reflected in the optical basicity values, emphasizing that the optical basicity is a global metric of a glass, not necessarily of the local environment of the dopant. Additionally, the association of Ag+ with ionic Qn species (Q0 and Q1 mAl), as demonstrated by the reduction of those ionic Qn species in the NMR, provides a possible pathway for the formation of intermediate Ag2O and subsequent silver reduction in oxide glasses.

Density functional theory (DFT) calculations suggested that the Ag+ O-S bonds have a less ionic character than Ag+ O-P bonds; the bonding between the Ag atoms and the phosphate matrix is purely ionic. Given that the PF optical trends consistently countered those predicted from optical basicity theory, the theory may only be applicable to more covalent interactions between dopant ions and a glass matrix, such as the Bi3+, Pb2+, and Tl+ ions upon which the scale was founded. The calculated electronic band structures also revealed that with the addition of more Ag+, more covalent bonding between Ag and the phosphate matrix occurs. The large Stokes shift of the emission wavelength of the Ag+ may be due to the absorption of a photon by a more ionically bonded Ag+ -O-P and a transfer of the excitation to the surrounding atoms in a more covalently bonded Ag2O-like cluster.

The results presented herein offer new views of the delicate interplay between polymer conformational and packing ordering and obtainable doping efficiencies. Most notably, current doping models have not explicitly considered the roles of these delicate structural factors on determining polymer-dopant and polaron interactions. However, the integer charge transfer doping model put forth recently by Pingel and Neher provides a basis for explaining observed trends in Figures -. For example, if the injected polymer hole polaron can escape the Coulombic attraction with the ionized dopant, increased free carrier levels and conductivities are observed. Based on our present and previously reported findings, polymer chains with high intrachain order promote exciton and polaron intrachain delocalization which is essential for producing mobile charges and increasing conductivity. Otherwise, conformational and packing disorder (i.e.. torsional distortions, packing defects, and ordered-disordered domain boundaries) localizes injected holes leading to bound charge transfer complexes that do not contribute to increased conductivity. These disorder effects are minimized in J-type nanofibers due to molecular weight fractionation during aggregate assembly, resulting in aggregates of greater purity and crystallinity. Injected holes are then able to escape Coulombic attraction with ionized dopants leading to free charge carriers. Conversely, an appreciable amorphous fraction leads to underdeveloped aggregates (i.e.. H-aggregates) with lower intrachain order that limits charge mobility and suitable dopant interaction sites.

Overall, we have shown that self-assembly approaches can be effectively utilized to tune doping efficiencies by controlling aggregate order and morphology. These nanofiber platforms also help bridge the gap in understanding polymer-dopant and polaron interactions that are usually obscured in conventional doping studies due to the evolution of complex morphological features during film deposition (e.g.. spin-casting) following addition of dopants in solution. We have further demonstrated that the formation of spinless bipolaron-like states observed in highly doped J-aggregate nanofibers via interchain antiferromagnetic coupling is the limiting factor for further maximizing doping efficiencies in these systems. Lastly, the larger doping efficiencies found in J-aggregates may have implications for achieving efficient, long-range charge transport with minimal losses due to preservation of their structures over a large doping range. ,

On the basis of explicitly correlated DFT+U electronic-structure calculations, we have analyzed the electronic structures of MnO and MnNCN and their chemical bonding as a function of correlation and magnetic structure. All data were generated using the LOBSTER suite, which has been enhanced to process PAW-based data from Quantum ESPRESSO. With respect to manganese oxide, our results support previous studies confirming the system as an intermediate charge-transfer/Mott insulator. Regarding the slightly more correlated carbodiimide phase, the theoretical data also confirm the system as an insulator of the same type. For both MnO and MnNCN, the relative orderings of the various magnetic states do not depend on the U correlation parameter.

Despite being of the same charge-transfer/Mott insulator type, a direct comparison between MnO and MnNCN reveals both similarities and differences in their chemical bondings. For both chemical systems, the upper majority VB is comprised of antibonding Mn-O/Mn-N states that cancel, to some degree, the bonding states in the lower majority VB. In contrast, the entire minority VB is bonding, albeit smaller in magnitude. Nonetheless, as a consequence of the exchange hole, these coherently bonding interactions of the more diffuse minority orbitals contribute dominantly to the total bonding compared to the ones of the contracted majority orbitals, similar to what has been observed for the spin-polarized itinerant metals. In addition, our results concerning the charge distribution, the calculated band gaps, and also the dispersion of the VBs as observed in the local DOS and pCOHP plots furthermore clearly show that MnNCN is more covalent than MnO, in harmony with spectroscopic and electronegativity data.

The chemical-bonding analysis also provides a reason why MnO and MnNCN adopt, respectively, the AFM2 and AFM structures. Only for these do the correct magnetic ground states fully annihilate formerly antibonding states from the vicinity of the Fermi level, thereby strengthening the strong Mn-O and Mn-N bonds and optimizing them for these magnetic structures. Indeed, the size of the integrated COHP of the Mn-O and Mn-N bonds, although being on the order of just 1 eV and also being part of the magnetically indecisive band-structure energy on the order of 1000 eV, correctly ranks the magnetic states as they are trivially given by the total energy on the order of 10 000 eV. Hence, the Mn-O and Mn-N interactions are the decisive ones both for structure and magnetism.

PDMAEMA with an atactic stereochemistry was purchased from Polymer Source, Inc. Its number average molecular weight M n is 2.7 kg mol-1 (equivalent to a PDMAEMA chain with the degree of polymerization N = 20) and its polydispersity index is 1.16. The polymer was dissolved in Millipore water in concentrations spanning from 0 to 29 wt %. The pH of the solution was adjusted to 5.0.

Rheological measurements were performed on an Anton Paar MCR501 stress-controlled rheometer equipped with a Couette geometry (CC-17) with an outer diameter of 18.08 mm, a length of 25 mm, and a bob size of 16.66 mm. The solution was loaded in the rheometer at a temperature of 20 °C and then tetradecane was added above the solution to prevent water evaporation. The sample viscosity η was measured by performing rotation experiments at shear rates γ ranging from 100 to 0.01 s-1. The torque T decreased as a function of the shear rate, and the lowest measurable value was 0.01 μN m. For every concentration studied, the zero shear rate viscosity η0 was obtained by averaging the values obtained at the lowest shear rates, where the Newtonian plateau was obtained, before reaching the minimum torque.

The selectivity of a series of anions was determined at the aqueous interface for an anchored guanidinium amphiphile that is both positively charged and has the capacity to hydrogen bond. We have discovered that the guanidinium receptor binds preferentially to oxoanions in the order SO4 2- > H2PO4 - > NO3 - > NO2 - and has comparatively weak affinity to the halides in the order I- > Cl- ≈ Br-. The geometrical complementarity of hydrogen bonding between the oxoanions and the guanidinium is consistent with these oxoanions being preferred over the halides. The weakly hydrated guanidinium head group on our receptor interacts with highly hydrated anion sulfate and phosphate in contradiction to the qualitative rules set out by Collins. The novel low dielectric character of the interface allows intense Coulombic interactions between the dianionic sulfate and the monocationic guanidinium to likely offset the large dehydration penalty. While the phosphate is only monovalent leading to lower Coulombic stabilization, its hydration energy is also lower. VSFG and IRRAS provided an effective means to order the relative binding affinities of this series of anions by tracking changes in the interfacial water structure and relevant low frequency modes, respectively.

Our results show that the ordering of anions at the aqueous interface deeply depends on the specific recognition event. We observe that the ordering of oxoanions follow trends seen in anion recognition in which guanidinium has a geometrical preference for tetrahedral anions over others, such as, nitrate and nitrite. The observation of this trend at the interface supports the idea that the low dielectric medium present at the interface correlates with binding behaviors seen in low-polarity organic solvents. Yet, recognition principles alone do not appear to explain the selectivity of the entire series. Instead, we have invoked a combination of chemical (e.g.. ion recognition) and physical (e.g.. ion partitioning) effects and phenomena to rationalize our observations. The guanidinium functional group presented here drives strongly hydrated ions to the surface through a combination of electrostatic attraction and geometrical complementary.

We studied the PL characteristics of FAPbBr3 NCs by employing pressure-dependent multispectroscopy techniques. The steady-state absorption and PL spectra as a function of pressure show that FAPbBr3 NCs pass through Pm3m, Im3, and Pnma phases in turn, whose knee points are located at 0.77 and 2.03 GPa, respectively, which is also consistent with the pressure-dependent evolution of PL dynamics. Based on the two-carrier model, the analysis of PL dynamics suggests that free carriers and trapped carriers by deep defects together participate in the carrier dynamics. The appearance of deep defects in Pm3m and Im3 phases, acting as a nonradiative channel, can accelerate the PL dynamics and decrease the PL QY through capturing the carriers. In the Pnma phase, the carrier movement apparently enhances owing to the weakening of trapped carriers, while the PL QY also decreases. According to the dynamics and QY of PL at different pressures, it is found that the radiative lifetime prolongs with pressure. Apparently, applying pressure can effectively manipulate the PL characteristics and carrier dynamics. Furthermore, FAPbBr3 NCs in the Pm3m phase are suitable for photoluminescence devices and those in the Pnma phase can be applied in photovoltaic fields. These findings deepen the understanding of PL characteristics occurring in FAPbBr3 NCs and thus will be useful for broadening the application of optoelectronic devices based on perovskite materials.

Figure shows the experimental and theoretical XAS spectra of the benzene cation. The experimental spectrum was obtained as the logarithmic difference of absorption of the sample with and without UV pulse. The two experimental spectra taken over the range 0-50 fs and at 1000 fs delays between the pump and probe beams have similar structures but the peak positions shift slightly, as indicated by black arrows in the bottom panel. The theoretical spectrum agrees reasonably well with the experimental one after a shift of -0.7 eV is applied. The main difference from the XAS spectrum of the neutral (Figure ) is the presence of the low-energy peak (peak E at 281.3 eV) and a clear splitting of the dominant feature (peak A in the neutral, marked as peaks F and G in the cation), accompanied by red and blue shifts of the split peaks relative to peak A in the neutral. Inspection of the NTOs (given in the Supporting Information) reveals that peak E is derived from the 1sC → π transition, peaks F and G correspond to the transitions to the two π* orbitals (as in peak A of the neutral). Peak H′ has the same orbital character as peak B in the neutral. The splitting of the core → π* transition in the cation is expected (and observed theoretically) already at the symmetric FC structure, when the two π* orbitals are still exactly degenerate; thus, it arises due to the spin coupling via the presence of the unpaired electron in the π-subshell (the JT distortion will further modulate the splitting). Using theoretical values, peak G (G′) is blue-shifted by 0.4 eV relative to peak A (A') in the neutral, while peak H′ is blue-shifted by 2.9 eV relative to peak B (B′) in the neutral. A larger shift of the latter can be attributed to the Rydberg character of this transition: the compact valence orbitals are stabilized more than the Rydberg orbitals by the positive charge of the cation. The computed splitting between peaks F and G is 1.1 eV, which agrees well with the experimental value of 1 eV. This value is also close to the singlet-triplet gap in the neutral benzene (1.22 eV, computed with EOM-EE-CCSD/6-311 (2+,+) G** at the FC structure). Because both splittings are attributed to different spin coupling of the π and π* electrons, their magnitude should be roughly equal to the exchange integral between the respective orbitals. Thus, close agreement between the splitting of the core → π* transition in the cation and the singlet-triplet gap (between the two lowest ππ* states) in the neutral confirms their origin as due to spin coupling.

In addition to illustrating electronic signatures of the cation (manifested by the new low-energy peak and by the splitting of peak A), the experimental spectra (Figure , bottom panel) also reveal dynamics of the structural relaxation of the cation manifested by shifts in the positions of the 3 main peaks. At longer time delays in the experiment, peaks E and G move to higher energy ( ~ 0.2 eV) and peak F moves to lower energy ( ~ 0.3 eV), as indicated by the arrows in the bottom panel of Figure . The signs of the shifts follow the expectations from the MO diagram (Figure ): at the JT displaced structure, the half-occupied π-orbital moves to higher energy and the two π* orbitals split to lower and higher energy relative to their position in the FC region. The computed XAS spectra (shown in Figure S2 in the Supporting Information) of the cation at the FC and JT-relaxed structures show similar trends. As noted in the experimental paper, while the experimental time resolution is insufficient to capture the time scale due to a possible JT shift accurately, the effect of possible shifts in time is evident in the spectrum. An additional effect that could cause the shifts is vibrational structure, discussed further in the companion experimental paper.

Comparing the calculations at the symmetric FC structure and the relaxed JT minimum (Figure S2 of the Supporting Information), we observe relatively small differences: peak E is blue-shifted (0.31 eV), the relative intensity of peaks F and G changes slightly, and the splitting between the lowest transition under peak F and the transition under peak G increases by about 0.1 eV, consistent with the magnitude of the splitting computed for band A of the neutral (Figure ). Thus, the prominent doublet structure at 285 eV in the cation spectra arises due to the effect of the unpaired electron on the transition ( ~ 1-1.2 eV), while the structural relaxation leading to the splitting of π* orbitals has a much smaller effect ( ~ 0.1-0.2 eV). As in the case of the computed XAS spectrum of the neutral, the energy changes of the transitions due to the structural relaxation can be attributed to the energy change of the valence (occupied or virtual) MOs, because the energies of the core orbitals are much less sensitive to the structure.

We note that, due to the use of an open-shell reference in EOM-CC, the computed target excited states (which should be pure doublet states) are afflicted by spin contamination, which affects their computed positions and intensities. Spin contamination is significantly reduced upon inclusion of triple excitations in the ansatz. , Therefore, we carried out exploratory calculations at the CCSDT level in a minimal basis set and the results show a reduction of the energy separation and intensity redistribution of some lines, for instance the second stick line under the F band, which is the spin counterpart of the main transition of peak G. Importantly, these preliminary CCSDT calculations confirm the split nature of the 1s → π* band, and some dynamic shift of peak E and increase of splitting of bands F and G due to the JT distortion.

In summary, the effects of annealing on the microstructure of β-iPP with two different supermolecular structures and the resultant macroscopic physical property responses were compared. The results demonstrate that annealing promotes the occurrence of the second crystallization of β-iPP, which results in an increase in the crystallinity with increasing annealing temperature. Compared with the unannealed β-iPP samples, the annealed β-iPP samples exhibited enhanced chain-segment mobility in the amorphous region. It is interesting to observe that, at relatively low environmental temperatures and/or small tensile stresses, the annealed β-iPP samples exhibited accelerated creep deformation, even though the annealed samples had relatively higher crystallinities than the unannealed samples. It is suggested that the accelerated creep behavior is related to the reduction of the coupling force in the crystalline hard skeleton during annealing. However, at relatively high environmental temperatures and/or large tensile stresses, the creep deformation of β-iPP was found to be determined mainly by the crystallinity. The greater the crystallinity, the higher the creep resistance. Specifically, it was demonstrated that the creep resistance of β-iPP is also dependent on the crystalline morphology. Under all conditions considered in this work, the bundlelike spherulites exhibited higher creep resistance than the radial spherulites. This work thus provides valuable information for the potential industrial application of β-iPP objects.

Three quinoxaline derivatives with different chain length of carbonyl functional groups were studied for their inhibition characteristics on mild steel corrosion in 1 M HCl using both experimental and theoretical techniques. The following conclusions were drawn from the studies: 1. Both polarization and EIS studies revealed that the three compounds are good inhibitors of mild steel corrosion in 1 M HCl and the polarization study shows that the compounds are all mixed-type inhibitors. 2. Adsorption of the studied inhibitors is spontaneous, essentially chemisorption and obey the Frumkin adsorption isotherm. 3. SEM images show that the inhibitors adsorb on mild steel surface and protect the steel surface against acid attack. 4. Quantum chemical calculations revealed that the inhibitors have high proton affinity in acidic medium and the results agree with experimental data. 5. The results of the Monte Carlo simulations accord with the experimentally determined inhibition efficiencies of the inhibitors, i.e. PQDPP > PQDPB > PPQDPE. 6. PQDPP with the shortest carbonyl substituent having the least steric hindrance showed the best inhibition efficiency.

Near-UV photodissociation at 300 nm can be used to drive the formation of gas-phase metal-oxo ions of the (bpy) M-O+ type (M = Cu, Ni, Co) that spontaneously add water in ion-molecule reactions. The resulting [(bpy) Me-O + H2O]+ complexes are photolyzed by near-UV light to eliminate OH radicals, effectively cleaving the added water molecules. The gas-phase water splitting reaction is stoichiometric, as the [(bpy) M-OH]+ products do not photodissociate to reform the (bpy) M-O+ reactants. The [(bpy) M-O + H2O]+ ion structures, electronic states, and dissociations were characterized by photodissociation action spectroscopy and density functional theory calculations to elucidate the processes involved in water splitting. Further efforts are needed to reform the [(bpy) M-O]+ reactant ions and close the catalytic cycle.

The matrix approach for solution of the EGME was first used in 1983 by Scranz and Nordholm and has subsequently been extensively developed by a number of groups. - ,, In this approach the coupled differential equations described by the discretized form of eqs and are formulated as the following eigenvalue problem: 3 d d t n = Mn where n is a vector containing the grain populations of every species and M is a matrix whose elements comprise rate coefficients for the grain to grain energy transfer and reactive processes. In order to solve the master equation, the matrix M must be diagonalized; to exploit efficient diagonalization routines which operate on symmetric matrices, MESMER utilizes detailed balance to symmetrize M, forming a symmetric matrix S as follows: 4 S ij = M ij ( f i f j ) 1 / 2 = M ji ( f j f i ) 1 / 2 = S ji where f i is the equilibrium population of grain i. Within the matrix approach, solutions of eq take the form: 5 n ( t ) = U e Λ t U - 1 n ( 0 ) where n(0) contains the initial conditions for each grain at time zero (i.e.. n i (E i ,0)), U is matrix of eigenvectors obtained from diagonalization of M, and Λ is a diagonal matrix of the corresponding eigenvalues.

In order to illustrate the graining process and the makeup of n and M, a schematic is shown in Figure for a simple fictitious system involving two wells, (each with two energy grains) and a single bimolecular source term (A + B ↔ C ↔ D). This figure not only provides insight into the matrix formulation of the EGME; it will also help to understand the implementation of the KMC algorithm within MESMER described in section d. In Figure the k ij in M simply represent an effective rate coefficient for transition between grains i and j regardless of whether the transition is due to reaction or energy transfer. The Figure schematic neglects the details of how the effective rate coefficients are obtained. The matrix M can be divided into different blocks and these are color coded to identify the different regions. The lead diagonal marked in green represents the total loss from each grain g or source term S; the first row and column (blue) give transitions between the source term and the grains of the other isomers in the system (in this case between s 1 and grains g 2 and g 3 in species C), the blocks marked orange deal with energy transfer between the different grains of C and D respectively, and the purple blocks correspond to reactive transitions between C and D. It should be noted that in the absence of tunnelling k 24 and k 42 would be 0 since these grains span energy regimes entirely below the reaction threshold connecting C and D. In practice, typical EGME simulations will have many more grains than shown here, and the matrix M will be significantly more complex; however, this figure serves to illustrate the key features of the matrix representation of in its discretized form.

Solution of eq gives time-dependent grain populations; however, it is often desirable to have a more coarse grained representation of this microcanonical detail, e.g.. into phenomenological rate coefficients. In the matrix approach, defining these phenomenological rate coefficients is facilitated using methods related to the work of Bartis and Widom. Broadly, these Bartis Widom methods exploit time scale separations in the eigenvalue spectrum and lump the associated eigenvectors so as to uniquely define macroscopic rate coefficients between all pairs of species in the system. So long as there is a good time separation in the eigenvalue spectrum, then it is often possible to calculate a course-grained kinetic representation, which exactly reproduces the time-dependent microcanonical grain populations. -

We revealed the effects of supramolecular encapsulation on the photophysics and photostability of highly fluorescent 2,6-diacetoxy-9,10-bis (arylethynyl) anthracene dimeric guest, G2. In both liquid and polymer matrix, free-G2 fluoresces in the planar conformation. In contrast, within the rigid confines of the polymer environment, the excited-state planarization of G2@(Cap)2 is prevented by the bulky Cap host. Consequently, G2@(Cap)2 in polymer is forced to emit in the twist conformation. Such a phenomenon was absent in the monomeric guest G1, because the torsional degree of freedom between two 2,6-diacetoxy-9,10-bis (arylethynyl) anthracene monomeric units is absent in G1. Despite the different photostabilities of the free guests, the photostabilities of their encapsulation complexes were remarkably similar, suggesting that the thermal stability of the boronic ester bond dissociations in the host (rather than the photostability of the guest) dominates the photostability mechanism. The excellent photostability and brightness of the encapsulated 9,10-bis (arylethynyl) anthracene derivatives within the self-assembled boronic ester cavitand capsule could be exploited in single-molecule fluorescence-based spectroscopy and assay, advancing the applicability of these complexes to fluorescence-based single-molecule detection.

There were several potential sources of error that limited the quantitation of the results. The mass of explosive used to make the powders was 10-15 mg where the measurement accuracy was ~1 mg (scale precision was 0.1 mg, but stability and reproducibility limited confidence to 1 mg). In addition, the KBr pellets were not completely homogeneous upon pressing. Although we are averaging over 3 mm of a 7 mm pellet, concentration variations of 10% in the area observed are likely. Because of these limitations, the actual number of molecules in the irradiation area was known at the ±10% level. The FTIR beam and excitation laser beam oversampled the 3 mm sample aperture. Changes in concentration by FTIR could be computationally determined to the 2.5 part per thousand level. Intensity used in calculations was calculated by the average pulse energy divided by the pulse temporal fwhm divided by the area of the aperture, ignoring the temporal and spatially dependent intensity of each pulse. Upper bounds on quantum yield are given for molecules that did not measurably react over the entire exposure series of typically 5000 pulses. The quantum yield also depends on determination of the fraction of incoming photons absorbed. As Figure below illustrates, the scattering contribution to the apparent absorption is difficult to isolate from the pure absorption. Modeling the scattering with a frequency to the fourth power dependence did not match the data. If the absorption was large, the effect of scattering introduced small errors. If the absorption was small (such as P-Tz-Cl and DNP-Tz-Cl at 355 nm), the error in quantum yield due to uncertainty in quanta absorbed could be up to 50%. While this error was large, it allowed us to establish that the photochemical quantum yield was 0.002-0.008, which was sufficient to support our conclusions that establish the low probability of photochemistry in the material. Typical errors in quantum yield were closer to the 10% level, with similarly little impact on our conclusions.

The uncertainties in fluorescence quantum yield were determined by the standard deviation of fresh solutions at different concentrations measured on different days. The rhodamine 6G quantum yield standard was remeasured with each data set. Differences in solution absorption led to spatial differences in the excitation profile over the 1 cm long path length that affected fluorescence collection efficiency, causing some deviation in the resulting quantum yields. Redeterminations of the rhodamine 6G quantum yield using fresh solutions of different concentrations led to errors in apparent fluorescence quantum yields of 20%.

In conclusion, a novel TADF emitter having a very narrow emission spectrum with a fwhm of 48 nm was developed by a new molecular design approach interlocking donor moieties for restricted molecular motion. A high efficiency of 14.0%, a deep blue color coordinate of (0.14, 0.12), and a fwhm of 48 nm were achieved in the deep blue TADF device using a new molecular design approach.

Our Hg measurements in western Maryland indicate a strong regional upwind source. The 2006-2014 average concentrations of GEM, GOM, and PBM2.5 were 1.4 ± 0.2 ng m-3, 11.0 ± 15.5 pg m-3, and 5.2 ± 5.0 pg m-3, respectively (Table ). The large standard deviations for both GOM and PBM2.5 reflect their greater reactivity in the atmosphere and higher dry deposition rates compared to GEM. As a result, GOM and PBM2.5 can be removed from the atmosphere much faster and closer to their sources than GEM, which can be transported great distance from sources, leading to more dynamic and variable atmospheric concentrations of GOM and PBM2.5. The average GEM and PBM2.5 concentrations were similar to those reported for other sites in North America. However, the background concentration of GEM, GOM, and PBM2.5 were often impacted by short-term, high-concentration episodic events (Figure ). This suggests that the atmospheric Hg concentrations at PRAMS were influenced in part by the global background pool and a more dynamic pool of elevated Hg emissions from regional sources. This influence was very clear for GOM. The average GOM concentration at PRAMS was at the high end (upper 5%) of the range of GOM concentrations reported for other sites in North America. The average GOM concentration at PRAMS was most similar to GOM concentrations at an urban site in Salt Lake City, Utah (13 pg m-3) and a rural site in Athens, Ohio (13 pg m-3), downwind of a nearby power plant. , This comparison suggested that PRAMS has elevated concentrations of GOM most similar to sites directly impacted by local or regional sources of Hg. In addition, many of these high-concentration GOM events often coincided with elevated concentrations of SO2 and winds from the west of PRAMS. Both SO2 and GOM are produced from the combustion of coal. This suggests that the atmospheric Hg concentrations at PRAMS were strongly influenced by regional sources of Hg from upwind coal-fired power plants.

Pollution roses identified the regions that contributed significantly to the GOM and PBM2.5 concentrations at PRAMS (Figure ). These pollution roses showed that 50% (34 500) of the GOM and PBM2.5 concentrations were associated with winds from the west (225° to 315°) of PRAMS. Winds from these directions traveled over many power plant sources of Hg in Pennsylvania, Ohio, and West Virginia before arriving at PRAMS (Figure ). Winds from the southeast accounted for only 20% (6916) of our GOM and PBM2.5 concentrations at PRAMS. Winds from this region transport Hg to PRAMS from several small and highly dispersed power plant sources of Hg in Maryland and Virginia (Figure ).

From 2000 to 2008, annual power plant Hg emissions in the United States were relatively constant, ranging from 39 to 41 Mg yr-1 (Figure ). In 2009, however, annual power plant Hg emissions decreased to 31 Mg yr-1, which was 8.2 Mg lower than the emissions in 2008 and was the largest annual decrease over the past 15 years. From 2009 to 2012, total power-plant Hg emissions continued to decrease annually to the lowest levels (20 Mg yr-2) in 2012 and 2013, a 50% reduction from 2000. Similarly, power-plant Hg emission reductions from the upwind states of Pennsylvania, Ohio, and West Virginia were similar to the national emission reductions. However, the total power plant Hg emissions in 2012 from these three states were 70% or 7 Mg of Hg less than their Hg emissions in 2000.

There was a strong (r 2 = 0.942) linear relationship between the annual average SO2 concentrations at PRAMS and the annual power plant Hg emissions from Pennsylvania, Ohio, and West Virginia. This is not unexpected because coal is an important source of both SO2 and Hg, and, until recently, coal was the dominant fuel used by many power plants to generate electricity. This reduction in power-plant SO2 and Hg emissions were driven by many factors, including emission controls, economics, climate, and energy sources. By 2012, 64% of all coal-fired power plants had installed control equipment to comply with MATS, and 145 power plants retired. The recession and cooler summer temperatures in 2009 coincided with the onset of a decrease in the use of coal to generate electricity. For example, between 2009 and 2013, production of electricity from coal decreased 17%, while electricity production by natural gas increased 25%. The change in fuel source was driven by the increased availability and lower cost of natural gas and the need to meet the CAIR and MATS emission reductions. The combustion of natural gas releases much less SO2 compared to coal because of the lower sulfur content in natural gas.

The reductions in United States power-plant emissions could be seen in the frequency of the short-term episodic events of GEM, GOM, PBM2.5, and SO2 (Figure ). An episodic event is defined as the time period in which the atmospheric concentrations started at background concentrations and rapidly increased to concentrations that were 90% greater than the background concentrations, followed by a return to the background concentration. The frequency of the high-concentration episodic events decreased for GEM, GOM, PBM2.5, and SO2 between 2008 and 2009 (Table ). The most extreme example is for GEM with close to 15 000 events per year from 2006 to 2008 and between 1000 and 3500 events each year from 2009 to 2014 (Table ). This pattern also occurred for GOM and PBM2.5. However, the number of events for PBM2.5 increased to 329 in 2014, which was similar to the frequency in 2009 (Table ). For SO2, the number of events continuously decreased from nearly 1700 events in 2006 and 2007 to 44 events in 2013 (Table ).

After 2009, there was also a reduction in the maximum event concentration of GOM, PBM2.5, and SO2 (Table ). For example, the maximum event concentrations for GOM and SO2 were typically greater than 100 pg m-3 and 40 ppbv for events in 2007 and 2008, respectively (Figure ). Starting in 2009, the maximum event concentrations for GOM and SO2 were typically less than 50 pg m-3 and 20 ppbv, respectively (Figure ). These changes coincided with the first substantial reduction in power plant Hg emissions in the United States in 2009, which was a 26% reduction in Hg emissions compared to 2007 and 2008 (Figure ).

The annual (2006-2014) average GOM concentrations at PRAMS were strongly correlated (r 2= 0.964) with the sum of the power-plant Hg emissions in Pennsylvania, Ohio, and West Virginia. The average annual GOM concentrations were highest in 2007 (18.8 ± 23.9 pg m-3) and 2008 (17.4 ± 18.1 pg m-3), which coincided with the highest annual power-plant Hg emissions that occurred from 2006 to 2014 (Table ). The average annual GOM concentration decreased to 11.2 ± 14 pg m-3 in 2009, which coincided with the first and largest annual power plant Hg emission reduction in the United States (Figure ). The average annual GOM concentration continued to decrease until reaching the lowest concentration of 4.7 ± 7.0 pg m-3 in 2013, which was not significantly different than the annual average concentrations in 2014. Thus, from 2007 and 2008, the annual GOM concentrations at PRAMS decreased each year until it reached the lowest concentrations in 2013 and 2014. In 2014, the annual average GOM concentration was 14 pg m-3 lower than the average in 2007, which was a 75% reduction in the average annual GOM concentrations at PRAMS.

For SO2, there was also a statistically significant decrease in the annual average concentrations from 2006 to 2012 and a strong correlation with annual power-plant Hg emissions (r 2 = 0.952) from the upwind states of Pennsylvania, Ohio, and West Virginia (Table ). Over this time period, the annual average SO2 concentrations decreased from 4.9 to 1.2 ppbv (Table ). From 2012 to 2014, the average annual concentrations were not significantly different at approximately 1.2 ppbv. Our SO2 data showed that the lowest annual average concentration occurred in 2012. Thus, the annual average concentrations of SO2 at PRAMS were 75% or 3.7 ppbv lower in 2012 than in 2006. This was a relatively large reduction and strongly suggested the emission reduction strategies of CAIR were very effective at reducing the concentrations of SO2 at PRAMS.

Over the 2006-2014 period, the average annual GEM concentrations decreased from 1.5 ± 0.2 to 1.3 ± 0.2 ng m-3, a statistically significant difference (Table ). The highest annual average GEM concentrations (1.5 ng m-3) were in 2006, 2007, and 2008, and the lowest concentrations were in 2009, 2013, and 2014. From 2008 to 2014, the annual average GEM concentration decreased 200 pg m-3 or 13%. This decrease is similar to the reduction in GEM concentrations reported for several sites in Canada. Although the GEM reduction at PRAMS is smaller than the GOM reduction on a percentage basis, it is a larger reduction on a mass basis (note that GOM is reported in pg m-3, whereas GEM is ng m-3). Hence, it is larger than the combined reduction in the atmospheric concentration of GOM and PBM2.5 ( ~ 17 pg m-3). The annual average concentrations of GEM were strongly correlated with power plant emissions from OH (r 2 = 0.821). This suggests that even though the atmospheric GEM pool at PRAMS is strongly influenced by global Hg pool, reductions in the Hg emissions from upwind regional sources contributed to the reductions in the GEM concentrations at PRAMS, particularly the frequency of high-concentration episodic events. However, the maximum GEM concentrations during the episodic events remained unchanged over our sampling period. One potential explanation is that some of the maximum GEM concentrations at PRAMS may be from Hg sources not considered in this study.

The annual average PBM2.5 concentrations decreased from 7.3 pg m-3 to 4.0 pg m-3 for a 43% reduction (Table ). The highest average annual PBM2.5 concentrations were in 2007 (7.3 pg m-3) and 2008 (6.8 pg m-3) and coincided with total United States power-plant Hg emissions of 39 Mg yr-1. In 2009, the U.S. power-plant Hg emissions decreased to 31 Mg yr-1, and the annual average PBM2.5 concentration decreased to 4.9 pg m-3. This large reduction (8.2 Mg yr-2) in emissions coincided with this 3 pg m-3 reduction in annual average PBM2.5 concentrations at PRAMS. However, all subsequent reductions in power-plant Hg emissions had little to no additional effect on the PBM2.5 concentrations because the annual concentrations ranged between 4.0 and 4.3 pg m-3, while the emissions decreased from 28.6 to 20.3 Mg yr-1. In 2014, the annual average concentration of PBM2.5 increased to 6.1 pg m-3, while U.S. power-plant Hg emissions were at their lowest levels in years. In addition, the correlation (r 2 = 0.786) between annual power-plant Hg emissions (Pennsylvania, Ohio, and West Virginia) and annual average PBM2.5 concentrations was statistically significant. This suggests that the PBM2.5 concentrations at PRAMS are influenced by regional reductions in power-plant Hg emissions. However, other factors, such as emissions from other sources or atmospheric reactions that produced PBM2.5, likely contributed to the elevated PBM2.5 concentrations in 2014.

The strong correlations between reductions in power-plant Hg emissions from the upwind states of Pennsylvania, Ohio, and West Virginia and reductions in the atmospheric concentrations of GEM, GOM, and PBM2.5 at PRAMS suggest that power-plant compliance with EPA's air pollution control policies have been effective for achieving improvements in downwind air quality. Full compliance with MATS, which includes a 90% reduction in power-plant Hg emissions, is expected to lower the concentrations of GOM, GEM, and PBM2.5 even further. However, global reductions in GEM emissions may be needed to further reduce the atmospheric concentrations of GEM in the United States.

GaN is usually produced and assembled under ultraclean conditions. We perform DFT calculations to systematically investigate the stability of water molecules adsorbed on the GaN(0001) of coverage from 0.1 to 5 ML, providing insight into the interaction of wetting layers and the GaN surface. Our results indicate the strong interaction between water molecules and bare GaN, especially in the 1 ML case, the binding energy is high to -1.3 eV/H2O. Such strong interaction between H2O and the GaN (0001) severely distorted the hydrogen bond between water molecules, thereby no regular monolayer and bilayer ice phase can form on the GaN(0001) surface although we have tried several configurations. GaN is likely to wet by 1 ML water even under very low water partial pressure. The wetting coverage below 1 ML coverage is strongly dependent on the interaction and symmetry of GaN(0001), and the wetting is not continuous; only some special coverage can appear. Thus, the wetting coverage below 1 ML can be controlled by tuning the water partial pressure and temperature. One ML of coverage is a magic adsorption layer with the widest windows for P-T. However, the amount of water over 1 ML is not strongly related to the interaction with GaN(0001), thus they are hard to control because of the narrow P-T window. We also insightfully interpret the origination of the high stability of 1 ML water wetting. Water wetting should be considered in the production and fabrication of GaN devices. On the other hand, water wetting also can be effectively used to tune the work function of the GaN(0001) surface.

Au2 + and Au2H+ species were produced. By performing tandem MS on both species with a narrow mass selection window (Δm ≤ 1 Da), we were able to distinguish the reactivity of Au2 + and Au2H+, as shown in Figure . Both species are stable in the presence of pure buffer gas, and there is no evidence of the bonding of water molecules or oxidation in the mass spectrum. After the introduction of CO in the trap, the gold dimer becomes unstable and dissociates when reacting with CO. The products observed are Au (CO)+ and Au (CO)2 +. The reaction kinetics show that the Au (CO)+ is formed on a timescale faster than 0.1 ms. The onset of Au (CO)2 + comes after 10 ms of trapping time, and it increases while the abundance of Au (CO)+ decreases indicating that the bigger complex is formed from the smaller one by the addition of a CO molecule. The complexes with more CO remain low in intensity even at longer trapping times, and only slight indications of these species can be detected in the mass spectrum. It was shown that Au2 + in reaction with trace amounts of CO at 70 K in the ion trap leads to the observation of Au2(CO)+ as well as Au2(CO)3 +. Kinetics measurements for the Au2 + with CO reaction were also performed at room temperature. Terasaki and co-workers observed that Au2 + adsorbs CO followed by the cleavage of the Au-Au bond. The amounts of Au (CO)+ and Au (CO)2 + produced by the reaction of Au2 + with CO under multiple collision conditions as a function of storage time were reported. Our results are in agreement with this previous work.

Unlike Au2 +, the Au2H+ does not dissociate during reactions with CO. New species are formed by the addition of CO to the precursor complex. They correspond to the generic formula, Au2H (CO) n +, where n = 1, 2. The hydrogen atom seems to stabilize the complex and prevent dissociation. Furthermore, the Au2H+ species show lower reactivity than Au2 +/Au+. Figure shows the reaction rates for Au2H+. It takes trapping times of more than 50 ms to observe some increase in the abundance of the CO complexes, and the relative intensity of the products remains low even at trapping times longer than 1 s, at both high and low CO concentrations. From the reaction rates in Figure , the reaction constants (k's) were calculated (Table ) by normalizing the reaction rate obtained from the slope of plots by the number of CO molecules per cm3. The helium pressure in the LTQ trap given by the constructor is P LTQ = 1 mTorr (0.133 Pa). The CO pressure is P LTQ %CO and is equal to 9 × 10-3 Pa [for 5% of CO, e.g.. 6.8% concentration (v/v)]. The volumic concentration of CO is given by nV CO = P LTQ %CO/k B T, where k B is the Boltzmann constant and T = 300 K, i.e.. 2.2 × 1012 cm-3. The k values found depend only slightly on the pressure (0.1-5%), and perhaps saturation effects occur for 5% CO. The k values are 2-5 times higher than the published values by Terasaki, which is attributed to uncertainty on the total pressure in ion traps.

The high-resolution spectroscopic survey of the H3Σu --X3Σg - electronic transition of Si2 in the 380-520 nm range has yielded an accurate determination of spectroscopic constants for both X3Σg - and H3Σu - states. The spectral resolution (0.04 cm-1) has enabled to fully resolve the triplet spin-splitting structures in individual rotational transition lines and, consequently, to experimentally determine the spin-splitting effect in both states for the first time. Comparable values (λ ≈ 1.5 cm-1) of the spin-spin interaction constants for both X3Σg - and H3Σu - states are found, which may originate from the 3p atomic orbital interaction in the triplet Si2 molecule. A series of isotopologue band spectra of 29Si28Si and 30Si28Si have also been measured. The good agreement between the experimentally determined spectroscopic constants of the isotopologue bands and those calculated from the main isotopologue 28Si2 indicates that the H3Σu --X3Σg - transition system of 29Si28Si and 30Si28Si can be reasonably reproduced by the mass-scaling rule. Spectroscopic parameters for the H3Σu --X3Σg - (v′, v″) transition system, including the Franck-Condon factors (q v′v″), the Einstein coefficients (A v′v″), and the oscillator strengths (f v′v″) are also determined from the experimental results and the RKR calculations. The agreement between the experimentally measured and calculated dispersed fluorescence spectra indicates that the RKR calculations with the molecular constants determined in this work can accurately reproduce the potentials of both states. Like the well-known C2 molecule, accurate molecular data for the X3Σg - and H3Σu - states of Si2 are now available, providing a benchmark in future ab initio calculations on Si2 and likely other small silicon clusters.

A series of circular micropatterns of thermoresponsive islands of varied diameters and gaps on PEI-precoated glass coverslip was fabricated, and NIH 3T3 cells were cultured on the patterned surfaces to investigate cell detachment behavior by temperature reduction. Compared with continuous thermoresponsive coatings, this work has demonstrated that cells could detach from discontinuous thermoresponsive coatings which were patterned on cell-adhesive substrate. Semiquantitative calculation data demonstrated that cells could detach from the patterned surfaces when the thermoresponsive area is just about 20% of the cell spread area. The size-dependent behavior of cell detachment on micropatterned substrates has potential applications in pertinent fields such as cell chips and biomodeling.

We identified the chemical nature of the Fe2O3 surface state that is likely responsible for the reported 580 nm absorption peak. ,,, First, we ruled out a peroxo chemical species intermediate previously hypothesized to participate in the reaction mechanism because the large distance between two surface oxygen sites prohibits this bond formation. After considering several possible adsorbates, we conclude that the chemical group corresponding to the observed absorption could be an *Fe-O -type bond, an O p and Fe d hybridized state with a radical on O. This bond is created after two hydrogen cleavages of an adsorbed water molecule. We suggest that the Fe2O3 system could have an electron occupying this hybrid state resulting in a Fe (IV)-O bond. We therefore provide theoretical support to one hypothesis expressed previously in the literature, that the surface state's chemical identity is Fe (IV)-O, which is related to an intermediate in the water oxidation mechanism. - ,,,

In conclusion, new fundamental insights into the ligand-metal mixed MOs at molecule-electrode interfaces are disclosed by considering the LFE. The FMO of -C-C-Au has contributions from the π x orbital of the ethynyl moiety and the d xz orbital of gold, in contrast to the C-Au σ-bond with contributions from the s and d z 2 orbitals. The PDOS reveals that the FMO involves d orbitals not only from the contacted gold atom but also from neighboring and underlying gold atoms. Accordingly, a bias voltage applied to the electrodes induces a change in E FMO. Such a pinning effect is pronounced for the -C-C-electrode terminal but silent for the other side of the electrode-N-C- contact, where the ligand-metal orbital mixing LUMO shows no discernible PDOS from the gold substrate. To observe the LFE on the I-V bias characteristics of molecular junctions, model compounds with one and two -C-C- units are synthesized, where the latter bears better energy matching and exhibits a larger energy-level splitting. The superior ELA for butadiynyl anchored junctions, along with the pinning effect, renders the measured nominal currents at V bias > 0.9 V larger than the narrower ethynyl junctions. The I-V bias curves for the former show larger RRs and smaller onset voltages than the latter, as demonstrated by the transmission spectra simulated by NEGF-DFT calculations and STM-BJ-based measurements. The simulation results suggest that the magnitude of currents and the RRs are strongly influenced by the geometry of the atomic arrangement at the molecule-electrode contact, which remains a challenge for single-molecule devices.

In summary, nitrogen and oxygen codoped porous carbon material was obtained. The codoping method reduced the dosage of KOH. Moreover, the obtained NOCKs exhibited high CO2 capacity (6.77 mmol g-1 at 0 °C and 4.46 mmol g-1 at 25 °C), high dynamic adsorption performance, and excellent regenerability. The porous structure with the V micro/V meso ratio in the range of 2.64-3.36 contributed more to CO2 adsorption. Additionally, the experimental results and DFT calculations demonstrated that the codoped nitrogen and oxygen had a synergistic effect on enhancing CO2 adsorption performance of carbons, and the physical adsorption mechanism on the heterogeneous surface of adsorbents was confirmed. Therefore, NOCKs are a promising sorbent material for CO2 capture on a large scale.

The LiFePO4 cathode and graphite anode are compacted by hydraulic apparatus at 10-250 MPa to obtain high-density electrodes. Compared to the reported work which focuses on improving the tap density by chemical synthesis, our work here focuses on the manufacture of high-density electrode laminates with improved compaction density by physical or mechanical method (i.e.. hydraulic compaction). The highest density of LFP cathode and graphite anode free from damage are 3.2 and 2.0 g/cm3 with 250 MPa loading, respectively. Moreover, the electrochemical performance of compacted electrodes is improved significantly. The discharge capacity of compacted LFP and the charge capacity of compacted graphite at 2C rate increase to 140 and 349 mAh/g, respectively. By increasing the compaction density of electrode pieces, the volumetric energy density of LFP/graphite battery cell can reach as high as 733 Wh/L, which is even higher than LCO and NCM. In summary, this work provides an approach to improve the volumetric energy density of Li-ion batteries instead of calendering for industrial application.

To uncover the mechanisms of the UV-light promoted removal of As (V) by sulfide, batch experiments were performed in a photochemical reactor (Shanghai Jiguang Special Lighting Appliance Factory, China) equipped with a water jacket containing a 1000-W UV high-pressure mercury lamp (35 × 1 cm2) in the synthetic wastewater. The detailed description of the lamp was provided in the SI (Figure S1). Twelve quartz colorimetric tubes containing 100 mL of the prepared solutions were placed around the mercury lamp and were maintained at a constant temperature under magnetic stirring (25 ± 1 °C). Control experiments were performed in the dark in quartz colorimetric tubes wrapped with aluminum foil. Unless otherwise specified, the concentrations of H+ and arsenic in all simulated wastewater were 1.84 M (0.92 M H2SO4) and 1.33 mM, respectively. Na2S 9H2O was used as the S (-II) source.

At prescribed time intervals, 10 mL of the samples was removed with a plastic syringe and immediately filtered through a 0.22 μm cellulose acetate membrane. The samples were split into two. For the identification and analysis of monothioarsenate, 5 mL samples were characterized by wavelength scanning in the range of 190-400 nm using a UV-vis spectrophotometer (DR6000, HACH, U.S.A.) and measured by ion chromatography hydride-generation atomic fluorescence spectrometry (IC-HG-AFS). S (-II) not only interferes in the determination of monothioarsenate when using a UV-vis spectrophotometer, but also affect the formation and transformation process of monothioarsenate (eqs 5 and 6, Table ). Thus, before analyzing monothioarsenate, excess sulfide was removed from the samples by air stripping for 5 min. We found that the residual S (-II) was below 0.1 mM after air stripping. For the analysis of the residual total arsenic (TAs), 1 M NaOH was added to the other 5 mL samples to obtain a final pH of 11 and quench the reaction. Then, CuSO4 was added to the above alkaline solution to remove sulfide by forming a precipitation through the reaction between Cu (II) and S (-II). The dose of CuSO4 was 10% higher than the nominal molar concentration of sulfide used in the experiments. The suspension was filtered again through a 0.22 μm membrane after 10 min of reaction for analysis of the TAs. For analysis of the precipitates, the precipitates obtained in the As (III)-S (-II) or As (V)-S (-II) mixed solutions after 24 h of reaction in the dark or 10 min of reaction under UV irradiation were centrifuged and freeze-dried.

To further verify the availability of the UV-light promoted method in real wastewater, the experiments were also conducted in a submerged UV-light reactor equipped with a 32-W UV low-pressure mercury lamp (30 × 0.5 cm2, Foshan Comwin Light & Electricity Co.. Ltd.. China.) (Figure S2). The main emission wavelength of the lamp is 253.7 nm (Figure S3). Prior to As (V) removal, As (III) and other heavy metals in the real wastewater were precipitated by H2S gas and the precipitate was centrifuged (SI). The residual H2S was removed from the samples by air stripping. After the above treatment, 99.9% As (III) was removed, and the concentration of As (V) decreased from 60.8 mg/L to 55.9 mg/L. Then, As (V) removal experiments were conducted by adding additional S (-II) (Na2S) in the submerged UV-light reactor, in which As (V)/S (-II) ratio was 1:7.5.

We applied the "grafting-from" macromonomer approach to functionalize PS culture substrates with thermoresponsive OGEA bottlebrush coatings via surface-initiated photografting under bulk conditions. As the first report utilizing this technique, we obtained bottlebrush coatings with structure- and temperature-dependent wetting properties, which we adjusted via the grafting procedure, irradiation time, and the molecular weight of OGEA macromonomers, which governs the obtained bottlebrush structure. Culture experiments with HDFs showed that adhesion of cells to the substrates at 37 °C can be tuned via the coating procedure and structure and that confluent HDF sheets can be harvested from the bottlebrush substrates at 20 °C, likely via the temperature-induced rehydration of thermoresponsive OGEA side chains. Because of the broad spectrum of attainable properties, the coatings developed in this work constitute excellent prospects for cell sheet fabrication and as "smart" substrates for various tissue culture and biomedical applications. The versatility of the presented photografting process with respect to the copolymerization of OGEA macromonomers of different molecular weights and comonomer compositions potentially allows the manufacture of thermoresponsive coatings with finely tuned properties matching the specific substrate requirements of various cell types. In summary, the presented coating strategy does not only constitute an efficient and scalable process for the manufacture of PGE-based thermoresponsive coatings but further embodies a method to extend the attainable coating properties in terms of introducing novel layer architectures. In the future, this might not only offer an extended applicability of PGE-based coatings for the fabrication of new types of cell sheets but also enable an in-depth investigation of the underlying mechanism of cell sheet detachment, especially regarding the roles of temperature-induced macroscopic swelling versus changes in coating hydration on the nanoscale.

No Chl triplets were observed at room temperature in both of the two studied LHCs upon excitation in the Q y band of Chl a, proving that their quenching by carotenoids is highly efficient. , In both LHC II and acpPC, the major proportion of Chl triplet states is quenched very efficiently even at temperatures down to 77 K. These Chls are probably protected by luteins in the central binding sites in LHC II, or peridinins, which likely replace luteins at the same site in the case of acpPC. This efficient quenching prevents the accumulation of Chl triplet states, and therefore, the temperature dependence of the quenching of these Chl triplets would be difficult to study. A small portion of Chls in both complexes, which increases with a decrease of temperature, but never exceeds 7%, is not quenched at all. This is probably caused by a temperature-dependent conformational change, which interrupts singlet EET from these Chls further along the energy-transfer chain and thus increases the probability of triplet-state formation. This is further corroborated by the fact that the fluorescence of Chl b in LHC II and Chl c 2 in acpPC has been observed at low temperatures, but not at 295 K, when both pigments efficiently transfer their excitation energy to Chl a. It also suggests that the red-most Chls are among those efficiently protected by carotenoids at low temperatures, similarly as it was observed for other LHCs at room temperature. Thus, for LHC II, the Chl triplets were either quenched as efficiently as at 295 K, or not quenched at all, and therefore, it was not possible to study the temperature dependence of the DET. A third subpopulation of Chls, however, which was observed only for acpPC, is quenched with a temperature-dependent transfer time that decreases from ~130 ns at 77 K to ~17 ns at 225 K and could not be resolved at higher temperatures. This dependence could be sufficiently fitted only by eq . Therefore, we believe that it reflects the intrinsic temperature dependence of DET. The same ~130 ns DAS also exhibits a strong band at 680 nm, the origin of which was explained by the emission of Chl a. We propose that triplet-triplet annihilation is responsible for the generation of singlet states of Chl a at late nanosecond times, the presence of which was proven by the observation of DF. Thus, a part of the Chl triplets resolved in the temperature-dependent ~17-130 ns DAS component is quenched by carotenoids and another part by triplet-triplet annihilation. Because triplet-triplet annihilation was observed to occur only at low temperatures, it does not represent a quenching mechanism relevant under physiological conditions. This behavior seems to reflect a difference in the structure between LHC II and acpPC, including a larger distance between some of the Chls and carotenoids in acpPC leading to less intense interactions between these pigments.

A so-called interaction peak can be observed for many LHCs, including LHC II, at wavelengths corresponding to the Q y band of Chl a, but it decays with a lifetime of carotenoid triplets. It is probably caused by an altered electric field generated by the carotenoid in the triplet state, which decreases the extinction coefficient of the nearby Chls in its ground state. We did not observe the interaction peak in acpPC at room temperature. This supports the above-mentioned idea of a less intense interaction between the carotenoids and Chls in acpPC, which lead to the temperature-dependent quenching of the Chl triplet states. However, four different interaction peaks could be resolved for acpPC at 1.8 K, indicating that the strength of the interaction depends on temperature. Unfortunately, the necessity to use a larger number of DAS components for fitting of our low-temperature data led inevitably to a decrease of the signal-to-noise ratio and made interpretation of the weak features beyond 600 nm difficult.

In acpPC, the triplet states of Chl a were observed to be quenched by three subpopulations of carotenoids, most likely peridinins (one rising with an ~5 ns component and two with ~ 130 ns component, including peridinins in a polar environment), which may fit the three subpopulations of peridinin identified by deconvolution of the absorption spectrum at 77 K. The combination of low temperature and time resolution thus allowed to distinguish another peridinin triplet in addition to the two triplets resolved previously. , Although we cannot exclude that diadinoxanthin is involved in triplet quenching as well, we believe that its main role is that of a xanthophyll cycle pigment. From a comparison of Figures and b, it seems that the decay of carotenoid triplets exhibits a rather different temperature dependence in the case of LHC II and acpPC. However, most probably, the only difference is that the plateau with a constant lifetime, which extends over 70 K in the case of acpPC, is shorter for LHC II. This difference might be related to differences in the structures of both complexes.

In summary, three kinds of phenyl-containing sulfobetaine surfactants 3-((4-(alkoxy)-3,5-dimethylbenzyl) dimethylammonio)-2-hydroxy-propane-1-sulfonate were synthesized and characterized by ESI-HRMS, 1H NMR, and 13C NMR spectrometry. Their thermal properties showed that all these three surfactants exhibit high thermal stability and are difficult to decompose below 245 °C. The results of surface tension indicated that the cmc and γcmc of C n OBSb (n = 12, 14, and 16) decreased with the increase of the hydrocarbon chain length. The lowest value of cmc and γcmc were 0.0015 mmol/L and 28.32 mN/m in C16OBSb. In terms of surficial and thermodynamic parameters (pC 20, cmc/C 20, ΔG mic 0, and ΔG ads 0), it could be found that C n OBCb surfactants with longer hydrocarbon chains tended to adsorb at the air/water interface rather than aggregate into micelles. The DLS and cryo-TEM results showed that C n OBSb molecules could spontaneously aggregate into large vesicles in aqueous solution at very low concentrations over the cmc, and the diameter of vesicles was in the range of 100-400 nm. The IFT measurement showed that C n OBSb surfactants possess strong capability in lowering the oil/water IFT against Xinjiang crude oil. Ultralow IFT could be achieved by C12OBSb at different salinity and temperature.
