The solubility equilibria leading to the formation of the known ternary Na j Ca k Mg m (UO2) (CO3)3 xH2O (cr) solid species Liebigite, Swartzite, Bayleyite, and Andersonite were also critically reviewed. After careful analysis of the results in the previous papers followed by additional calculations, we obtained new, updated values for the solubility products (log K 0 s , 298 K) of these solids: log K 0 s = (33.9 ± 1.0), (33.4 ± 2.0), (31.7 ± 1.5) for Liebigite, Swartzite, and Bayleyite, respectively. The authors of this paper propose these values as better estimates with respect to the ones reported to date. Nonetheless, new solubility studies on these systems may be required in order to obtain even more reliable solubility data.

Solubility data calculated in this paper, together with U (VI) speciation data, provide a comprehensive picture of the most relevant reactions involving U (VI) in a seawater environment. With respect to the prospective recovery of uranium from seawater using poly (amidoxime) collection systems, these data provide useful insights by helping to assess the affinity of U (VI) toward the amidoxime binding sites in conditions closely simulating the real systems. Among different amidoxime moieties, the cyclic glutaroimide-dioxime is currently considered as the best candidate for this task. , The data in this paper, in combination with the speciation model for the formation of UO2 2+ complexes with glutaroimide-dioxime, - indicate that the concentration of this ligand in seawater should be ca. 0.100 M, in order to effectively compete with the formation of Ca2(UO2) (CO3)3(aq) and Mg (UO2) (CO3)3 2-.

A thermobalance Q500 from TA Instruments was used to obtain the CO2 uptake capacity of the sorbents under a flow of 50 mL/min containing 92.5% CO2 (N2 as balance) at a carbonation temperature of 600 °C. In addition, the CO2 uptake performance of sample 900-5-2 was evaluated under different CO2 concentrations, ranging from 4% to 92%, keeping constant the total flow, in a thermobalance Setsys Evolution from Setaram. For these experiments, the carbonation time was 120 min.

Carbonation-regeneration experiments were carried out using TGA under different absorption (525 or 600 °C carbonation temperature and either pure CO2 or 4% CO2/N2) and regeneration (either pure N2 or a mixture of 70% CO2/N2) conditions. For these experiments, carbonation time was 120 min and regeneration time was 30 min.

Figure shows the schematic diagram of the electric N2O5 production system from air dried by molecular sieves (4 Å, 1/16 inch pellets). The plasma module consists of a high-temperature (HT) plasma reactor, low-temperature (LT) plasma reactor, high voltage power supply, flow switches, and other electronic control units. Compressed air stored in the cylinder is supplied to the HT and LT plasma reactors, and both air flow rates are fixed at 1 L/min. The electric field in the air discharge plasma selectively heats the electrons to ~104 K, leading to molecular dissociation to form radicals and subsequent reaction products. - The HT plasma reactor, designed to elevate the gas temperature with the discharge coupling power and heat recovery, mainly exhausts nitric oxide (NO) and nitrogen dioxide (NO2). The LT plasma reactor, designed for lower power and a large heat loss to avoid nitrogen dissociation and to enhance O3 production yield, ,,, mainly exhausts O3. Details of the plasma devices are described in the following paragraph. The subsequent mixture and reaction processes in the perfluoroalkoxy alkanes (PFA) tube enhance N2O5 production from NO x and O3. The PFA tube is used to increase the reaction time (t mix) of the mixture gas up to 24 s, of which the length and inner diameter are varied for analytical purposes. The plasma effluent mixture is flown through a gas cell with a 5 m long optical path for Fourier-transform infrared (FT-IR) absorption spectroscopy for reactive species analysis as described in our previous works. ,

Figure shows the optical images, schematic drawings, and characteristics of the portable plasma module (W700 mm × H 250 mm × D 155 mm), powered by a general AC power input. The HT plasma reactor has double concentric glass/quartz tubes (OD: 12 mm, ID: 10 mm/OD: 6.1 mm, ID: 4.1 mm) for heat exchange and dielectric barrier discharge (DBD). The DBD plasma is generated by applying AC high voltage (13.6 kVp-p, 12.5 kHz) between a central SUS wire (φ 0.5 mm) and a grounded SUS pipe (OD: 9.5 mm, ID: 7.5 mm) [Figure S1 (a)]. The discharge coupling power, measured using a 22 nF capacitor inserted between the SUS pipe electrode and the power supply ground, was approximately 44 W [Figure S1 (c)], corresponding to the adiabatic temperature rise (zero heat loss assumption) of approximately 2000 K. The countercurrent heat exchange design is employed to preheat air before the DBD section and cool to mitigate the thermal stress to the polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) insulation structure. These allow a drastic decrease in the O3 formation yield and increase in NO x formation, enabling selective NO x supply from the HT plasma reactor as shown in Figure (e). The LT plasma reactor has a typical DBD geometry powered with a voltage- and frequency-variable AC supply (HVG-4P-EE-M-RN-200-0, Hikaridenshi Co..Ltd.. Japan) [Figure S1 (b)]. Relatively high voltage ( ~ 7.8 kVp-p) and low frequency ( ~ 5.7 kHz) DBD stabilizes the low DBD coupling power (3.4 W), enabling an O3 dominant supply from the LT plasma reaction [Figure (f)]. These DBD systems can contribute to long-term durability and the high stability, allowing stable species composition in continuous operation at least 6 h with repeatability at least over 6 months.

This contribution presents a simple thermodynamically inspired relation to model the viscosities of polymer solution, as a function of composition. The intrinsic viscosity of the polymer in the solvent of interest plays a central role for that purpose; it enables the introduction of a reduced polymer concentration (c~ = c[η]), accounting for the spatial extension of the polymer coils in solution and for the thermodynamic quality of the solvent. Incorporating ideas concerning changes in the free volume of the mixture, compared to that of the pure solvent, yields the following relation: ln η rel = c ~ 1 + p c ~ + q c ~ 2 where η rel is the viscosity of the solutions relative to that of the solvent. Only two adjustable parameters (p and q) are required to cover the entire concentration range in case the intrinsic viscosities are known from independent measurements or can be calculated by means of the Kuhn-Mark-Houwink equation from the molar mass of the polymer. In case such information is lacking, the intrinsic viscosity is accessible from the measured concentration dependence of η by treating [η] as a third adjustable parameter, in addition to p and q.

Detailed literature data concerning the viscosities of polymer solution, as a function of composition reported in the literature for seven different systems in wide ranges of molar masses and temperatures, were evaluated according to the above relationship. In all of these cases (uncharged polymers and one polyelectrolyte in a saline solvent), the parameter p is positive and the parameter q is negative. For six of the seven systems, the values of p and q yield points of inflection in the composition dependence of the viscosities: At low polymer concentrations, η increases less than exponentially with rising c, whereas it increases more than exponentially for high concentrations. Solutions of poly (dimethyl siloxane) (PDMS) in its pentamer assume a special place in several ways; this exceptional position is tentatively explained in terms of the high flexibility of PDMS.

A more detailed analysis of the data reveals that the values of the parameters p and q show a clear dependence on the distance of the measurement temperature to the glass-transition temperature (T g) of the polymer, such that the viscosity of the solution becomes infinitely high at T ≈ T g. For polystyrene solutions in dibenzyl ether, this feature was used to determine the concentrations at which the solutions solidify at temperatures below the T g value of the pure polymer. The results are in good agreement with corresponding literature data.

The analysis of the viscometric behavior according to the proposed relation also provides access to the generalized intrinsic viscosities {η}, i.e.. to the effective hydrodynamic specific volume of the polymer at arbitrary polymer concentrations. Within the range of high dilution, it is possible to determine the coil dimensions as a function of c. However, once the reduced polymer concentration surpasses a critical value, the {η} data can no longer be considered to be characteristic for individual molecules. In that case, they must be reinterpreted as kinetically determined dimensions of flow units.

In view of the general importance of quantitative information concerning the viscosities of polymer solutions, as a function of concentration, methods enabling forecasts would be of great help. The general features apprehended by the present analysis should be a first step in this direction. It goes without saying that many more systems must be studied, including solutions of co-polymers and of macromolecules with nonlinear architecture.

Our combined I/V-LEED and STM measurements clearly indicate that the V2O3(0001) surface is covered by vanadyl groups under typical UHV preparation conditions. This is in marked contrast to conclusions derived from ion scattering experiments by Window et al. , While the surface could be oxidized to show a (√3 × √3)R30° LEED pattern indicative of one of the √3 structures, we were not able to prepare an O3 terminated surface due to the formation and sublimation of V2O5 at the required preparation conditions. Through atomically resolved STM images we could distinguish two different types of surface defects. While the surfaces are never completely free of defects, the number of defects could be reduced by annealing in UHV or in an oxygen atmosphere depending on the type of the defects.

We have determined surface Debye temperatures for V2O3(0001) by using them as fit parameters in the structural optimizations of the I/V-LEED calculations. This method avoids the shortcomings of the kinematical determination through temperature-dependent measurements of the LEED intensity. Using five different Debye temperatures, we obtained values of ΘD,surf ≈ 300 K for the atoms in vanadyl groups, ΘD,surf ≈ 400 K for the top oxygen trilayer and ΘD,bulk ≈ 600 K for the bulk. The good agreement with the literature value of ΘD,bulk = 580 K indicates the reliability of this method.

We observed the reactivity differences between bilayer graphene with two identified stacking modes by reacting it with 4-NBD diazonium salts. The 4-NBD grafting reaction on tBLG was found to be almost 5 times more reactive than that on AB-stacking graphene. We attribute this reactivity difference to variations in the electron distribution and DOS between these two stacking modes. In addition, the reaction rate of the two stacking modes of graphene can be fitted as an exponential growth model along with a kinetics-dominated effect. These results provide a positive way to control the electronic properties and tune the bandgap of graphene bilayers. The methodology presented herein will provide a method to control the electronic structure of bilayer graphene.

We have investigated the reaction mechanism of CH (X2Π) + propene via ab initio CCSD (T)-F12/CBS//B3LYP/6-311G (d,p) calculations of the PES and computed unimolecular rate constants of various isomerization and dissociation reaction steps of the C4H7 radicals, as well as reaction product branching ratios both at a zero-pressure limit under single-collision conditions and at p = 5 Torr and T = 300 K. At both sets of conditions the calculated branching ratios appeared to be similar but they strongly depend on the initial reactive C4H7 complex formed in the entrance channel. If the reaction is initiated by CH addition to the double bond in propene or by CH insertion into the terminal sp2 C-H bond or into the C-C bond, 1,3-butadiene (CH2CHCHCH2) + H are the dominant products ( ~ 85%) and ethene (C2H4) + vinyl radical (C2H3) are minor ( ~ 11%) but non-negligible products. A small amount ( ~ 4%) of 1,2-butadiene + H is also produced. The reaction mechanism in this case is found to be the following: CH + C 3 H 6 → CH 3 - cCH CHCH 2 → CH 3 CHCH CH 2 → 1,3 -butadiene + H → 1,2 -butadiene + H CH 3 CHCH CH 2 → C H 2 CH 2 CHCH 2 → ethene + C 2 H 3 → 1,3 -butadiene + H Here, the double bond addition leads to a cyclic C4H7 intermediate which rapidly ring opens to CH3CHCH CH2 and the latter loses an H atom to form 1,3- or 1,2-butadiene. CH3CHCH CH2 may also be directly produced by CH insertion into the terminal sp2 C-H or single C-C bonds. Alternatively to the H loss from this intermediate, it can undergo an H migration to CH2CH2CHCH2 and then decompose to either ethene + C2H3 or 1,3-butadiene + H. CH insertion into a C-H bond in the terminal CH3 group would lead to the CH2CH2CHCH2 complex directly and then the major reaction products are predicted to be ethene + C2H3 radical (67-77%) and 1,3-butadiene + H (20-30%). If CH inserts into the middle sp2 C-H bond, a branched CH3C ( CH2) CH2 complex is produced and it will predominantly decompose by splitting the methyl group, which makes allene + CH3 radical nearly exclusive reaction products (99%). Although the double bond addition and all C-H insertion channels may occur without entrance barriers, a comparison of the calculated reaction mechanism with the experimental PIMS measurements, especially for the isotope-labeled CD + C3H6 reaction, clearly indicate that the CH addition channel dominates. Then, the computed branching ratios are in agreement with the experimental results by Loison and Bergeat who observed the relative yield of the H elimination products as 78 ± 10%. However, our results quantitatively disagree with the PIMS experiments by Trevitt et al.. who observed a nearly 100% yield of the C4H6 + H products and also found 1,2-butadiene + H (25 ± 5%) and 1-butyne + H (12 ± 3%) to be significant minor reaction products. Here, the deviation of the theoretical results from experiment can be rationalized in terms of the dynamical factors (i.e.. by deviation from the statistical behavior), which favor direct dissociation of the CH3CHCH CH2 precursor by H loss, especially to 1,2-butadiene, over its isomerization to CH2CH2CHCH2 followed by the production of ethene + C2H3 radical. If CH insertion into the middle sp2 C-H bond also has some contribution and produces a small quantity of allene + CH3, the amounts of ethene + C2H3 radical and allene + CH3 radical might be then below the 5% detection limit in the PIMS experiments. 1-butyne might be formed through secondary H assisted isomerization of 1,2-butadiene. Overall, the calculations confirm that the CH + C3H6 reaction could be a major source of 1,3-butadiene at low-temperature and low-pressure conditions in the interstellar medium and planetary atmospheres.

We have simulated ultrafast nonadiabatic population relaxation from S2 to S1 using A-FSSH simulations of the dual fluorescent molecule DMABN. Our results are largely consistent with previous theoretical calculations, , though we have gained several new pieces of insight. First, decoherence is found to not play an important role in propagating these dynamics due to the rapid excited-state relaxation and subsequent energetic separation of the first two excited states. Second, we ran simulations of DMABN in the presence of a MECN molecule and found that the ultrafast relaxation was largely unaffected by the solvent, in agreement with time-resolved fluorescence measurements of DMABN in MeCN. Third, we introduced a physically motivated diabatization procedure that is capable of converting the TDDFT excited (adiabatic) states into excited (diabatic) states of La and Lb character (which are diagonal with respect to the rotationally averaged transition dipole operator). Transforming the mixed quantum-classical density matrix into this diabatic representation, the population relaxation from La to Lb was found to be somewhat slower than the adiabatic states and consistent with the decay of the ensemble-averaged transition moment; specifically, our calculations predict a decay in the emission on the order of 15 fs (rather than 11 fs). Fourth and finally, we investigated the dynamics of the diabatization angle for all relaxation events through the CI. We found that 16% of the trajectories that we simulated fully circled the CI clockwise, 18% circled counterclockwise, and the remainder did not circle the CI at all. From these numbers and the fact that the majority of the electronic relaxation occurs within 30 fs according to our TDDFT functional, we hypothesize that if geometric phase effects are important in larger molecules, the 21 atom molecule DMABN will be an ideal test case for higher-level calculations, both for the electronic structure and the nuclear dynamics. It remains an open question as to whether or not we can predict an observable to prove such effects with nonlinear spectroscopy.

H2V3O8-rGO composites were synthesized successfully through a facile and time-saving hydrothermal process. The graphene oxide precursor acts as a conducting, reducing, and structuring agent. The formation mechanism of the composites is investigated in detail that may go through an "adsorption-nucleation-reduction-recrystallization" process. The H2V3O8-rGO composites exhibit a high specific capacity of 246.3 mAh/g at a current density of 0.05 A/g, and superior cycling stability even at rate as high as 1.0 A/g, which can be ascribed to the unique nanostructure of the composites and the presence of rGO sheets. Because of the excellent electrochemical performance, the H2V3O8-rGO composites should be further explored as potential low-cost, long-lived cathode materials for Li-ion batteries.

To show the effectiveness of our proposed MC-ML algorithm, it was applied to experimental data collected from various studies. For the case study, we selected UiO-66 and the M-MOF-74 (M = Ni, Mg) series as representative MOF materials. - The experimental methane uptakes at 298 K, SA, and V p were collected from the studies (Table S3), and then methane uptakes at other temperatures were predicted using the MC-ML algorithm. The obtained isotherms were compared with the experimental isotherms reported in the same study. To visualize the strength of the MC-ML approach, GCMC simulations were also conducted for the crystallographic structures of the UiO-66 and MOF-74 series. The crystallographic structures of the UiO-66 and MOF-74 series were collected from the CoRE-MOF database.

As displayed in Figure a, methane uptake calculated from the GCMC simulation have large discordances with the reported experimental methane uptakes for the case of UiO-66. This is because UiO-66 usually has diverse defects when it is synthesized, and determining the exact microscopic structure in the sample is almost impossible. , Owing to these reasons, the experimentally measured SA and V p values deviate from those predicted from the perfect crystal structure (Table S4). Similarly, the GCMC simulation failed to predict the experimental methane uptakes because it performs calculations based on perfect crystal structures.

In contrast, methane uptakes predicted from the MC-ML algorithm match well with the reported experimental methane uptakes of UiO-66 (Figure a). This is because in the MC-ML algorithm, methane isotherms are not predicted on the basis of the coordination geometry of perfect crystals but are based on experimentally measured SA, V p, and methane uptakes at 298 K, which reflect the defective nature of the samples. Hence, the MC-ML algorithm provided much more precise predictions of experimental methane uptakes at 308 and 318 K. These results clearly reveal the strength of our MC-ML strategy compared to the conventional GCMC simulation. Even for the experimental situations for which GCMC simulations fail to provide good predictions, MC-ML can provide reliable predictions using experimentally measured properties as their inputs.

Another typical case for which the GCMC simulation fails to predict precise adsorption capacities of MOFs is the case of structures with OMSs, such as the M-MOF-74 series. As shown in Figure b-d, the methane uptakes of Ni-MOF-74 and Mg-MOF-74 calculated from the GCMC simulation are much lower than those measured experimentally. This is because the transportable force fields do not reflect the electron effect of OMS, and thus they underestimate the interactions between OMSs and gas molecules. However, similar to the case of UiO-66, the MC-ML predictions for methane isotherms of Ni-MOF-74 and Mg-MOF-74 at 283, 313, and 343 K are very close to the experimental isotherms reported in Dietzel et al. (Figure b,c). This is because there are other structures whose methane uptakes calculated from the GCMC simulation are similar to the experimentally measured methane uptakes of the MOF-74s (Table S5 and Table S6). On the basis of the data, the algorithm could suggest Q st that corresponds with the experimentally measured methane uptakes. One interesting fact is that MC-ML can deal with an Mg-MOF-74 (Bao) sample, whose BET SA of 1174 m2/g is very different from that of Mg-MOF-74 (Dietzel), 1542 m2/g (Figure d). The difference in SA between the two experimental samples might be due to the presence of some defects, partial collapse, or residues in pores. The traditional GCMC simulation cannot reflect the role of the disorders in experimentally prepared samples. In contrast, MC-ML accurately predicted the methane isotherms at 278 and 318 K for two different Mg-MOF-74 samples with varied SAs.

Three structural polymorphs of the stoichiometry Li2Ni2TeO6 have been synthesized and their electrochemical performance evaluated. All three structures exhibited a higher voltage than expected for the Ni2+/3+ redox couple of around 3.9-4.1 V owing to strong Te-O covalent bonding. None the structures synthesized approached the theoretical capacity of the Li2Ni2TeO6 composition of 151 mA h g-1, but the disordered orthorhombic structure showed the best electrochemical performance.

The disordered structure was the easiest to synthesize owing to its low energy of formation relative to other possible atomic arrangements such as a T#2, O2, or O3 layered structures of Li2Ni2TeO6. Lithium and nickel cation mixing hinders the conduction of lithium along ⟨110⟩ pathways in the disordered structure that would appear if lithium and nickel did not mix, but the ability to extract lithium in an electrochemical cell demonstrates that the tunnels are not completely blocked when the material is prepared.

T#2-layered Li2Ni2TeO6 was synthesized by an ion exchange reaction with P2-layered Na2Ni2TeO6. However, computations and ex situ X-ray diffraction of the material showed a quick and severe phase transformation from T#2 to O2 stacking upon lithium extraction from the structure is favorable and indeed occurs. The transformation seems quasi-reversible at first but is incomplete until lithium can no longer be inserted/extracted from the material in a meaningful capacity. The O2 phase does not seem electrochemically active in the 2.8-4.4 V voltage range of this study. The capacity fade of the T#2 material upon transformation to the O2 phase is greater than even the capacity fade of the O3-layered material which undergoes severe nickel transfer from the transition metal layer into the lithium layer. Other than Ni2+ transfer, the O3-layered phase does not undergo any further structural transformation upon cycling.

The nickel transfer in the T#2 and O3 layered structures was relegated to transfer of Ni2+ to an adjacent lithium layer via a tetrahedral or octahedral site. For the disordered structure the transferred nickel rests in the ⟨110⟩ tunnels. The barriers for nickel diffusion in each structure were low and similar to each other even with varying mechanisms. This result suggests that Ni2+ transfer may plague any layered structure that it inhabits despite its octahedral-site preference energy. The unidentified phase formed as well as the O2 layered phase upon delithiation of the T#2 structure may be the result of a surface reconstruction that inhibits lithium insertion/extraction into the O2-layered phase.

In summary, we have studied the effect of TMAO on the growth of an amyloid fibril formed by peptide NNQQNY from the Sup35 prion protein using molecular dynamics simulations. We found that TMAO stabilizes the locked state of the peptide in the protofibril compared with the free monomer state, in which the peptide is in solution. In the presence of TMAO, the basin corresponding to the locked state on the free-energy surface, projected onto the CVs RMSD and d cm, is stabilized compared to that in the free state (Figure B,C). The locked state basin on the free-energy surface moved to higher RMSD values due to the direct strong interaction of TMAO with the plane of the aromatic hydrocarbon ring present in the side chain of the Tyr residue. In the locked state, the surface of the aromatic ring available to interact with TMAO decreases. As a result, the Tyr residue in the peptide flips out from its locked position to interact with TMAO, and this results in a higher RMSD for the locked peptide on addition of TMAO. Analysis of the interactions of TMAO with the residue Asn reveals that TMAO has indirect interactions with Asn and is preferentially excluded from the protein surface compared with water (Figures and ). The exclusion of TMAO from the Asn residue surface is minimized in the aggregated state. As a result, TMAO stabilizes the dimerization of Asn residues (Figure A), which promotes the stabilization of the peptide in the locked state.

The Gln residue, which is a higher homologue of Asn, with an additional -CH2 group, interacts favorably with TMAO. However, the dimer of Gln is not destabilized, unlike the dimer of the residue Tyr, as the number of TMAO molecules interacting with Gln does not decrease upon dimer formation (Figure S6). The increased stability of Gln dimers in the presence of TMAO might be due to the strong interaction of TMAO with water. The stabilization of compact conformations (folded or aggregated) by TMAO in peptide chains primarily composed of amino acids with amide functional groups in the side chain (Asn and Gln) can also be due to the reduced number of hydrogen bonds between the -C-O group in the amide and water. The premise is that TMAO interacts strongly with water, as a result of which the number of hydrogen bonds between water and the -C-O group decreases and the side chains prefer to form intramolecular hydrogen bonds or hydrogen bonds with other peptide groups, resulting in the stabilization of compact or aggregated protein conformations.

All calculations were performed using Vienna ab initio simulation package (VASP) , with the projector augmented wave (PAW) , pseudopotential method. The spin-polarized generalized gradient approximation (GGA) with the Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof (PBE) exchange-correlation function was chosen. All structures were fully relaxed using conjugate gradient method without symmetry constraints for both spin-polarized and spin-unpolarized cases, until the Hellmann-Feynman force acting on each atom was less than 0.01 eV/Å. The kinetic energy cutoff for plane-wave basis set was set to 500 eV. A large vacuum spacing (more than 15 Å) was taken to prevent mirror interactions. The Brillouin zones were sampled with 0.1 and 0.08 Å-1 spacing in reciprocal space by the Monkhorst-Pack scheme for geometry optimizations and further property calculations, respectively. They corresponded to 19 × 19 × 1 and 29 × 29 × 1 k-point meshes for (1 × 1) GaN ML unitcell.

Given that besides ferromagnetic (FM) and nonmagnetic (NM) states, antiferromagnetic (AFM) states may also appear, we considered four atoms (F, O or N) adsorbed symmetrically on each (2 × 2) GaN ML supercell as the model for high coverage (Θ = 1/2) and (4 × 4) supercell for low coverage (Θ = 1/8). The adatoms were initially placed at four possible adsorption sites (TN, TGa, H, bridge) at a height of about 2 Å from GaN plane (as displayed in Figure ). The average adsorption energy was defined as follows: 1 E a = ( E GaN + 4 E A - E GaN + 4 A ) / 4 where E GaN was the total energy of bare 2D GaN supercell, E A was the energy of an isolated adatom in the vacuum, and E GaN+4A was the total energy of 2D GaN supercell with four adatoms. The interaction energy between adatoms were estimated by 2 E I = E a - ( E GaN ′ + E A - E GaN + A ) where E GaN ′ and E GaN+A were the total energies of 10 × 10 2D GaN supercell without and with an adatom at the same site, respectively.

We have presented the first study of a lithium ion-doped IL incorporated into a MOF and investigated its phase behavior and ionic conductivity. Moreover, for the first time, we have studied the dynamics of lithium ions inside the micropores of the MOF in terms of the self-diffusion coefficient of the lithium ions. XRPD measurements suggest that the (EMI0.8Li0.2) TFSA is incorporated into the micropores of ZIF-8. 19F solid-state NMR measurements show that the motion of the TFSA- anions was gradually suppressed inside the micropores by lowering the temperature, which indicates the absence of the apparent freezing transition. In contrast, the motion of the Li+ cations showed a steeper decrease than that for the TFSA- anions below 193 K. This is explained by the phase transition of the Li+ cations with other ions or the inner surface of ZIF-8 into a solid phase inside the micropores. This explanation is consistent with the results of the DSC measurements, in which the endothermic heat flow was obtained at the onset temperature of 200 K. The ionic conductivity of the (EMI0.8Li0.2) TFSA inside the micropores was 2 orders of magnitude lower than that of the bulk (EMI0.8Li0.2) TFSA. This result suggests that the ionic conductivity is drastically enhanced by the conductive paths for the ions, which are strongly connected with increasing concentrations of the guest ions. The activation energy for the self-diffusion coefficient of lithium ions in ELT@Z 100 is comparable with that in ELT-bulk. This result suggests that Li+ cations can diffuse with low activation energy through the micropores because of the exchange of the solvating TFSA- anions, similarly to the Grotthuss mechanism. The lithium ion-doped IL@MOF system provides a novel ion conductor to study the conductive mechanism of lithium ions.

We have discussed recent developments of "smart" hybridization probes that couple target recognition with fluorescence signaling for imaging of RNA in live cells. We have focused on hybridization probes containing a DNA stain such as thiazole orange as a reporter label, preferably linked as a surrogate of a canonical nucleobase. However, it is important to note that there are many alternative probe concepts, and we have tried to mention a few. We have emphasized the need for synergistically improving both the fluorescence enhancement and brightness. For example, we made our FIT probes brighter by combining the highly responsive TO nucleotide with a slightly red-shifted, highly emissive fluorophore. The use of local constraints-introduced by LNA-in the vicinity of the dye nucleotide offered an alternative for improving the brightness, and importantly, the concept extends to dyes spanning the cyan to red spectral region. Recent proof-of-feasibility studies have demonstrated imaging of mRNA, miRNA, and lncRNA in living cells and tissues. The authors envision that the next step will be to turn hybridization probes into tools that allow quantitative measurements of RNA concentrations in single live cells.

In this work, the established limiting current technique was analyzed comprehensively and adopted for the liquid-solid mass transfer measurements in solid foam packed reactors operated with descending gas and liquid flow. Based on the literature review and preliminary experiments, an optimized setup was applied to a reactor packed with solid foams made from SiSiC and embedded nickel foam electrodes of similar morphology. In particular, the effects of various electrode configurations were addressed for two different foam pore densities. The LSMT was studied simultaneously at three axial positions for a wide range of gas and liquid velocities. Besides providing comprehensive data on the effective LSMT coefficient in trickle and pulse flow, a detailed analysis of the dynamics during the passage of liquid pulses was carried out. Thereby, the time series of electric currents revealed dynamic behavior differing significantly from the liquid holdup time-series.

By introducing a compartment model for the interaction of pulse-induced holdup and mass transfer fluctuations, the dynamic behavior was simulated successfully. The model revealed that the higher inertia of the electric current is attributed to the comparatively large static holdups in solid foam packings. The explorative study furthermore indicated that the liquid properties affect the mass transfer dynamics significantly.

In terms of measured specific LSMT rates, the solid foam clearly outperforms conventional packings of similar specific surface area. Even though, the elevated LSMT rates are also attributed to larger operation windows in terms of gas and liquid flow rates due to the low pressure drop of the solid foams.

In conclusion, an advanced protocol of intramolecular aziridination reaction has been developed to synthesize 2-oxa-7-azabicyclo [4.1.0] hept-3-en-1-yl carboxylates from their corresponding 4-H-pyrans and spiropyrans using iodosyl benznene as the exclusive oxidant in the presence of various aromatic as well as aliphatic carboxylic acids and triethylamine. Regardless of its broader substrate scope, this methodology offers a very simple, robust, and diastereoselective route to construct pyran fused NH-aziridine molecular scaffolds. Good functional group tolerance of the oxidant makes this protocol suitable to introduce high skeletal and stereochemical diversity in the product NH-azridines. Their potent synthetic efficacy has been discovered by efficiently transforming them into biologically relevant novel pyrano oxazolone and pyrrole derivatives under mild reaction conditions.
Carbon chain increase reactions for platform molecules based on our own experimental results are discussed in more detail in the following paragraphs.

As is common in bioprocess experimentation, the reactors initially went through a startup phase with variable performance before approaching stable performance. Solely for the purpose of facilitating discussion, the long-term experimental period of the three parallel PBRs inoculated with environmental samples from FL, NC, and IL can be described across three general phases of operation based on performance observations: phase I (rapid change), SRT0 to SRT2 from 0 to 16 days; phase II (moderate change), SRT2 to SRT8 from 16 to 62 days; and phase III (stable performance), SRT8 to SRT10 from 62 to 82 days (a full list of sample names and the day and time of sampling can be found in Table S2).

The detailed mechanisms for photoinduced intermolecular hydrogen transfer have been investigated using combined DFT/TDDFT computation. In this study, we have presented three possible hydrogen transfer pathways to explain the experimentally observed accelerated photodegradation of CD in the presence of CT. We have identified two local minimum dimers which could account for the intermolecular hydrogen transfer; both dimers would undergo excitation energy transfer process from the T2 state to the T1 state, with the complex evolved from CD + 3CT to 3CD + CT. After the excitation energy transfer, migration of the hydroxyl hydrogen on the cyclohexane ring of CD molecule to the nitrogen atom on CT had the lowest energy barrier in terms of hydrogen transfer. Hydrogen migration pathways at alternative reactive sites of the cyclohexane ring have also been described, yet with considerable higher energy barrier. The results implied that the intermolecular transfer of hydroxyl hydrogen on the cyclohexane ring could be the major mechanism for CT-catalyzed phototransformation of CD.

NPA charge and population of the CD/CT complex along the reaction pathways and counterpoise corrected energies of CD and CT molecules as well as the dimers showed that intermolecular electron transfer had facilitated the subsequent proton transfer for reaction pathway 3 as compared to pathways 1 and 2. The results obtained were in good agreement with previous experimental and computational study on intermolecular hydrogen transfer from pharmaceutical compounds to dissolvable organic matters. Comparisons on electrostatic potential and corresponding molecular distribution could explain the different energy profiles because of different transfer mechanisms for electron and proton.

Theoretical studies on the intermolecular interaction of agrochemicals is currently limited, and the mechanisms are not well understood. However, such issues must be taken into consideration when developing and applying new agrochemical molecules. The computational study of intermolecular hydrogen transfer between CD and triplet CT molecules contributes to understanding the photochemical processes and assessing the risks of efficiency loss by mixing agrochemicals; some of the methods and conclusions are transferrable to similar systems such as herbicides reacting with DOMs in surface water. Further studies on intermolecular electron transfer and electrostatic attraction between molecules might provide better insight into the behavior of similar interacting compounds.

In conclusion, the metal organic framework of ternary metal-terephthalate containing three metals, viz.. Co, Cu, and Ni, as the metal center and terephthalic acid (H2 bdc as organic linker) (CoCuNi-bdc/NF) and its single metal counterparts (Co-bdc/NF, Cu-bdc/NF, and Ni-bdc/NF) have been prepared on a Ni-foam substrate via a one-step facile hydrothermal reaction. The resulting metalorganic frameworks (MOFs) differed in their morphologies. The triple cation MOF had a worm-like nanofiber morphology having a diameter of ~80-100 nm. A similar morphology was shown by Cu-bdc/NF samples, but fibers appeared to have fused together. Co-bdc/NF formed as uniformly distributed nanofiber network bundled on the edges of plate-like structures of width ~500 nm, and Ni-bdc/NF displayed mixed structures consisting of smooth and dense sheet-like and petal-like morphologies with lengths of ~3.4 μm and widths of ~300 nm. The triple cation MoF when used as a charge storage electrode showed one of the highest specific capacities ( ~ 321.3 mAh/g; 2892 F g-1) in an aqueous alkaline electrolyte (6 M KOH). This high capacity of the triple cation MOF has been attributed to the morphology of the samples. Also, all MOF electrodes showed lower series resistance (CoCuNi-bdc/NF, ~ 0.28 Ω; Co-bdc/NF, ~0.31 Ω; Cu-bdc/NF, ~ 0.37 Ω; and Ni-bdc/NF, ~0.47 Ω), thereby demonstrating superior solvated ion transfer from the electrolyte to electrode.

Supplementation of water-soluble polymers has a positive effect on the hydrolysis of both lignin-free substrates and lignin-containing substrates. With the addition of 10 mg polymer/g-substrate addition, up to 25.4% increase in glucan hydrolysis and 13.2% increase in xylan hydrolysis were achieved depending on the type of the substrate and polymer. The optimum level of polymer loading is 10 mg polymer/g-substrate for all of the polymers. Higher hydrolysis yields were obtained with nonionic polymers (PVP, PVA, and PEG) than ionic polymers (PEI and C-PAM) for all substrates. Nonionic polymers are effective for both lignin-free and lignocellulosic substrates, whereas ionic polymers are effective only for lignin-free substrates to some extent. The major reasons for the digestibility improvement with the polymer are the improvement in cellulase activity and reduction in unproductive binding of cellulase to lignin. The results indicate that up to 67% of enzyme usage (from 15 to 5 FPU/g-glucan) can be reduced with the addition of polymers.

The chemical dynamics simulations reported here are for CH4* → H + CH3 dissociation using the DHS analytic potential energy surface (PES) developed previously. , There is another PES for the CH4 system; , however, use of the DHS PES is appropriate for the model simulations reported here. The classical unimolecular dynamics for CH4 on the DHS PES are ergodic and an initial classical microcanonical ensemble dissociates exponentially with a rate constant in agreement with RRKM theory. An initial quantum microcanonical ensemble in the classical phase undergoes rapid IVR, forming a classical microcanonical ensemble, which dissociates with classical ergodic dynamics. In the work presented here quasiclassical microcanonical ensembles are prepared for CH4* on the DHS PES and CH4* dissociation is simulated at two total vibrational energies E total of 131 and 133 kcal/mol. The total angular momentum J is zero. For one simulation protocol, the dynamics are purely classical and the calculated rate constants versus energy are the classical microcanonical, RRKM values. For the other, a product ZPE constraint is imposed, so that if CH3 does not contain ZPE at a H---CH3 separation of 6 Å, the momenta of the H and CH3 atoms are reversed and the reactive system is sent back to the vibrationally excited CH4* phase space. The total lifetime of a vibrationally excited CH4* molecule is then taken as the total time it takes to form products with ZPE in CH3, including any additional time after revisiting the CH4* phase space. Except at the high energy classical limit, the resulting average lifetime of the CH4* molecules will be longer than the classical value. There are two important issues to consider for this simulation: i.e.. does this average lifetime agree with the quantum RRKM value, and with this ZPE constraint does the dissociation of the CH4* molecules remain exponential as described by RRKM theory?

We define agrifood as outputs of the agriculture and animal production sectors (of the NAICS industry classification) that are subsequently consumed either directly or processed and embodied in various food items eaten. Current local capacity (CLC) for a certain agrifood item is calculated by dividing the total "local" production of that agrifood item (within the area designated local) by the local demand. We focus on current local capacity-as it is in the present time. 1 current local capacity ( CLC ) = current local production current local demand

CLC thus represents the balance between current local production and current local demand, both represented in agrifood equivalent units; however, local production may not feed current local demand with today's supply chain configurations, hence the terminology of current local capacity. The steps in computing CLC are described below.

First, the region to be analyzed is clearly defined (i.e.. cities, counties, states, etc.). This study focused on major metropolitan statistical areas (MSAs) of the conterminous United States (Census), which are aggregated counties containing a total population of 50 000 or more, centered around at least one large urban core. To reflect previous foodshed and local capacity efforts, only household demand was considered for CLC calculations in eq , consistent with the goal of nutritional self-sufficiency. We address four select agrifood commodities that are often the focus of local production efforts, i.e.. fruits, vegetables, dairy (in raw milk equivalents), and eggs.

Second, we estimate household agrifood demand (denominator of eq ) for which five methodologies are available, but none address all together: varied diets, granular food item detail, delineations between direct and embodied agrifood demand, as well as pre-consumer losses. The five methods are the following: (1) Individual consumer-level food intake surveyed by the Center for Disease Control's National Health and Nutrition Examination and Survey (NHANES). , The food items eaten recorded by NHANES reflect real-world dietary habits by different sociodemographic groups and can be converted to raw agrifood commodity weights (i.e.. bushels of corn harvested instead of ounces of canned corn eaten) using the Environmental Protection Agency's (EPA) Food Commodity Intake Database (FCID). (2) The Food Availability Database (FAD) estimates national household food demand through mass balance by totaling production, net withdrawals from long-term storage, and net imports. The FAD is only available at the national scale; it focuses on total available food for human intake, but may not represent actual dietary intake with detail on food items eaten as seen in NHANES. FAD contains useful statistics on processing losses and post-consumer waste, by food item. (3) Sub-national economic input-output (IO) tables track expenditures by industries and households at smaller geographic scales, and model imports to urban areas (e.g.. IMPLAN used by Chavez and Ramaswami in 2013), but such modeled datasets are expensive to acquire. (4) Complete-Diet Modeling , can effectively model ideal/conceptual household demand but does not represent actual U.S. diets, and hence was not included in the analysis. (5) Last, the Bureau of Labor Statistic's Consumer Expenditure data can provide basic food demand at the household level by tracking monetary expenses, but the data are frequently aggregated in public datasets-either geographically or by food groups.

After considering all the above approaches, this paper innovated upon the NHANES approach by first delineating food items eaten into two categories: (a) food eaten directly ("fresh" or minimally processed agrifoods) and (b) food items generated from complex processing or complex supply chains (with significant embodied agrifoods), the sum of which yields total direct-plus-embodied agrifood demand of an average U.S. diet. See Figure S1 and Table S2 for method details. The food items eaten (assessed from NHANES) were converted to raw agrifood equivalents using EPA FCID, upon which various Food loss factors (pre-harvest and post-harvest, including post-consumer ) are also incorporated , to assess overall agrifood demand (direct-plus-embodied-plus-loss). The annual mean consumption of each food item in NHANES was tabulated using the two-day survey results (food consumed within and outside the home), using statistical weighting to extrapolate individual-level consumption to a national per capita average.

The delineation of food eaten into the two categories (direct/potentially direct and processed food with complex supply chains; see Table S2) provided a novel approach to compare the NHANES-derived methodology with other surveys to assess survey errors , and to also align the derived agrifood demand with national apparent consumption data.

The direct intake of agrifood items estimated from the NHANES-derived methodology shown in Figure S1 incorporating post-consumer loss factors matched well with another independent bottom-up data survey on food purchased by household (i.e.. consumer expenditure surveys (CEX), when surveys had sufficient granularity for "apple-to-apple" comparisons); see left side of Table . The total direct-plus-embodied agrifood requirements computed in our methodology from individual-level food recall surveys, upon which pre- and post-consumer losses were applied, were also then compared with national apparent consumption (determined as the sum of total production and net imports on a per capita basis reported by the USDA and FAS to assess coherence (see Table , right side). The analysis (in Table ) allows for an internally consistent set of both agrifood consumption and production data across all U.S. counties, on the basis of which we are able to assess the production-consumption dynamics across all U.S. counties and MPOs. This is a key methodological contribution.

As with any survey, CEX and NHANES suffer from recall errors and under-reporting of "guilty" foods. We estimated a rough magnitude of these errors by reviewing errors in the CEX as reported in the GHG consumption-based footprinting literature. Researchers have found that CEX studies under-report compared to personal consumption estimates (PCEs; derived largely through retailer sales accounts) by ~30% when considering all food purchased for human consumption-including "guilty" food items like alcohol, which show the greatest discrepancy. The differences are less (20%) for the expenditures on "fruits and vegetables", and even lower (+3%) for reporting of "fruits" (when comparing CEX and PCE) (personal communication and spreadsheet provided by Taylor J. Wilson, BLS). These comparisons suggest that survey recall errors with NHANES may also be of similar magnitudes, ranging from 3% (for healthy foods) to 30% overall. Nevertheless, the ranges of direct food purchases estimated from our NHANES-derived method are consistent with the PCE-corrected consumer expenditure data, and the direct-plus-embodied agrifood demand computations are also consistent with national production-import data. These findings (in Table ) demonstrate that our methodology is internally consistent across estimates of consumption and estimates of production plus net imports, and aligned with national datasets, with likely errors ranging from 3% to ~20% in agrifood demand estimates for the four items studied in this paper.

The nominal CLC was computed for both total direct-plus-embodied agrifood equivalent demand (CLCdirect+embodied) and also estimated for only the direct part of the demand (CLCdirect): CLC direct+embodied = current local agrifood production at MSA level / current local direct+embodied agrifood demand of MSA households 2a 2b CLC direct = current local agrifood production at MSA level / current local direct agrifood demand of MSA households

The last step to compute CLC requires agrifood production data at the county level (for the numerator in eq ), provided by the USDA Census of Agriculture and other USDA surveys (accessed from the USDA QuickStats Database), aggregated to obtain local production for select crop and crop categories within the MSA boundary. The census of Agriculture catalogues all agricultural operations that produce more than $1000 worth of agricultural product. Smaller commercial urban farming operations, community gardens, and household gardens are often excluded in the Ag Census; the potential impact of these smaller local production operations is evaluated briefly in the Results section. The USDA sometimes does not disclose production for specific crops for counties which contain only a small number of producers, for privacy concerns. The undisclosed data was modeled using simple mass balance technique (similar to the way GDP is modeled by Sherwood et al. in 2017); first allocating for the unaccounted-for production at the state level (when available) across the counties with undisclosed data, and then allocating the remaining unaccounted-for production at the national level to the counties where state and county data was withheld or unavailable. Overall, greater than 95% of total production was accounted for at the state level for all agrifood categories studied. At the county level, 11% of the total fruit, 25% of the total vegetable, 40% of total egg, and 12% of total milk production, nationally, were undisclosed and modeled. The nominal current local capacity at the MSA level (CLCdirect+embodied,MSA) was computed from eq , by dividing local production by the local total agrifood demand (direct plus embodied) for the same administrative unit, i.e.. the MSA.

We also explored the sensitivity of CLCdirect+embodied to expanding boundaries of local production at varying radii of 25, 50, 75, and 100 miles around the population-weighted center of the metropolitan areas, based on various definitions of local from people's perception of local, , popular culture, , distance traveled by farmers to farmers' markets, and previous studies conducted by cities to analyze their local food capacity (see Table S1). Two scenarios were created to accomplish this. A non-competitive scenario allocated all food produced in the surrounding counties to the demanding MSA, after subtracting the household food demand needs of the surrounding counties. The non-competitive scenario informs the draw that single MSAs can have on their surroundings. However, as we are analyzing actual capacity,competition between multiple MSAs drawing on the same hinterland counties must be assessed and was done by proportionally allocating excess production in the hinterland counties to the multiple demanding MSAs based on their respective demand.

The sensitivity analyses were repeated to assess the current local capacity for only the direct portion of agrifood demand, yielding a CLCdirect, with MSA boundaries as local production areas (eq ). While CLCdirect+embodied assesses the current potential for local production to meet the total demand of raw agrifood equivalents in our diet (offering a full mass balance perspective), the latter estimate (CLCdirect) addresses local production capacity to meet the demand of food items which are typically less processed, presenting a more realistic assessment of local capacity from an operational and policy perspective.

The nominal current local capacity (CLCdirect+embodied), computed using MSA boundaries for local production and local household demand, was further evaluated in Rstudio (utilizing the regression package) to explore statistical correlations with various features of the urban system, such as demographic information (total population, percent population foreign born, population density, and median income), agrifood inputs (average solar radiation per day, precipitation, and water input for irrigation), total land area of MSA, and MSA-level economic data (percent of total GDP from agricultural sector), and the presence of local- and state-level policies promoting urban agriculture-collated from previous literature reviews ,- and combing state Web sites. To assess if MSA characteristics by total area, by population size or by population density, impact current local capacity, these relevant parameters (sourced from U.S. Census Bureau) were also included in the analysis. After filtering for redundantly correlated variables, the remaining variables, as seen in Table S2, were assessed to provide added insight on factors that might influence the current local capacity across all 377 U.S. MSAs analyzed.

In this study, we have investigated the macroscopic swelling of and accompanying free-volume changes in TO-CNF films. While these films swell according to expectation when subjected to 90% RH water vapor, swelling is reduced when the film drying temperature is increased. This observation is attributed to higher film density, as verified by SEM and suggesting enhanced hornification. In marked contrast, the total free volume of fully dried films is not affected by the drying temperature even though the pore size decreases and the pore number density increases with increasing drying temperature. Suspension sonication prior to casting serves to increase the free-volume pore size due to a combination of disruption and size reduction of the TO-CNF fibrils. Subjecting TO-CNF films to various RH levels reveals free-volume pore filling at low levels ( < 33% RH). As the RH is increased, free-volume pores expand. At RH levels beyond ~53%, water likely creates new free-volume pores and behaves as free water inside the film, thereby eliciting a free-water PALS signal. This conclusion is supported by comparing PALS spectra with free-volume intensity and lifetime calculations. Lastly, swollen films that are subjected to redrying exhibit slight free-volume pore size hysteresis. This study establishes a direct relationship between macroscale and nanoscale water sorption in TO-CNF films prepared under several different conditions.

In conclusion, we have demonstrated a simple, rapid, and generic surface-confined film formation strategy utilizing coordination-driven self-assembly of simple phenolic building blocks, such as gallic acid, pyrogallol, and pyrocatechol. The structural simplicity of the ligands allowed for a more in-depth evaluation of their contribution to the film formation process. These molecular hybrid films might provide a versatile multifunctional platform for a range of applications, including catalysis, energy, and optoelectronics. Moreover, the biological relevance of the phenolic ligands, combined with the dynamic metal-ligand interactions, may make them of interest in the biomedical sciences.

The development of new ionic liquid metal catalysts proved to be very promising, yielding polystyrene with high conversions within a few minutes of synthesis and low catalyst concentration, well below those reported in the literature and generally required in industrial processes. The largest number-average molar masses were obtained using the BMI Sn3Cl7 catalyst, while the iron-based catalysts presented the smallest molar masses, due to the abruptly occurring reactions. In addition, using the catalysts BMI Nb2Cl11 and BMI Zn3Cl7, it was possible to form polystyrene with two polymeric populations of different molar masses and mass fractions.

T g values below 65 °C are characteristic of low-molar-mass polystyrene and the plasticizing effect of residual catalyst cannot be taken into account, as the presence of catalyst was not observed by 1H NMR analysis. FTIR and 1H NMR analysis confirmed obtaining polystyrene, and the NMR technique also revealed that the end group of the polymeric chain is a chlorine-bonded methyne group and some chains have the terminal indanyl group. The deconvolutions indicated the presence of three to four active catalytic species in the iron-based catalysts and BMI In2Cl7. Investigations of the polymerization mechanism by ESI (+)-MS (/MS) permitted detection and characterization of key intermediates and the positive IL effect on its formation and stabilization.

The experimental protocol employed to synthesize the polymer materials through bulk polymerization presented a few differentials: (i) the use of ILs, the low catalyst/monomer molar ratio, and the absence of organic solvents and/or initiators favor more sustainable processes; (ii) cost reduction and yield of high-purity products; and (iii) high yields in a few minutes.

These results are quite promising, including beneficial ecological and economic characteristics and opening a wide range of applications of these catalysts in homogeneous and heterogeneous polymerization reactions and cationic polymerization of other vinyl monomers and ring-opening polymerization.

All experiments designed to identify treatment effects (i.e.. addition of NTA or cysteine, or no ligand) were run with the same algal batch, preacclimated to the same N source (i.e.. the same population of algal cells was used for the different treatments), and thus for a given test any difference in metal uptake rates is not associated with biological factors such as a batch-to-batch variation in the membrane-bound transport system for the metal. Moreover, the majority of the tests (typically each with three replicates) were repeated with different algal batches two to five times to ascertain the reproducibility of the results (SI Table S2).

Measured MeHg concentrations and literature-reported energy contents of prey from the EPO and WPO are significantly different between epipelagic and mesopelagic zones (Figure ). Surface-associated prey have significantly higher energy density (6.6 ± 2.0 SD kJ g-1 ww) and lower MeHg concentrations (0.05 ± 0.01 μg g-1 dw), than mesopelagic prey (4.2 ± 0.84 kJ g-1 ww; 0.13 ± 0.06 μg MeHg g-1 dw) (p < 0.01, Tukey's HSD test). Species classified as primarily diel vertical migrators have intermediate MeHg concentrations (0.08 ± 0.01 μg g-1 dw) and energy density (5.4 ± 1.1 kJ g-1 ww) values which are not significantly different from surface or deepwater prey (p > 0.05, Tukey's HSD test).

THg in PBFT ranged from 0.61 to 1.93 THg (μg g-1 dw; mean 1.31 μg g-1 dw ±0.37). MeHg measurements showed that THg in PBFT was predominantly in the form of MeHg (99% MeHg ± 6% SD). Prey THg ranged from 0.01 to 1.76 THg (μg g-1 dw), with an overall mean of 0.13 μg g-1 dw ±0.19. Correlations between size and age of PBFT and MeHg concentrations were analyzed, and these relationships were not statistically significant.

The fraction of THg in muscle tissue as MeHg (%MeHg) in prey species was also high (85% ± 18%), and reached 100% in several prey species (Pacific mackerel Scomber japonicus, market squid Doryteuthis opalescens, blacktip squid Gonatus onyx, and armhook squid Gonatopsis borealis). The range of %MeHg in prey fish and squid (mean 90% ± 9%; range 74%-100%) was significantly higher than in pelagic crustaceans (57% ± 9%) (Mann-Whitney U-Test, p = 0.0044). Pelagic red crab (Pleuroncodes planipes) had the lowest %MeHg (32% ± 6%).

In prey, both Δ199Hg and δ202Hg values generally decrease with increasing depth (Figure a, SI Figure S1). Slopes of Δ199Hg/δ202Hg in muscle tissue of prey species in the EPO (1.50 ± 0.02 SE) and WPO (1.77 ± 0.06 SE) are shallower than experimentally determined slopes of photodemethylation in lab studies (2.43 ± 0.10 SE) and for muscle tissue in pelagic fish from the CPO (2.64 ± 0.24 SE) , (Figure a). The highest Δ199Hg and δ202Hg values are found in surface foraging fish, including flying fish (Exocoetidae spp.) in the WPO and Pacific mackerel (Scomber japonicus) in the EPO (Figure a and SI Figure S1). The Δ199Hg values of flying fish ( ~ 5‰) observed in the central Pacific Ocean (CPO) are higher than those in surface fish in the EPO and WPO ( < 3‰) (Figure a).

Hg isotope values of PBFT in this study fall between prey in the WPO and EPO (Figure b). Some δ202Hg and Δ199Hg values measured in individual PBFT overlap with surface-associated prey, and others overlap with deeper mesopelagic prey (Figure b). Bayesian mixing model results for Hg isotopes indicate that 28% diet is from mesopelagic prey for this PBFT data set (including both the EPO and WPO). The mesopelagic prey proportion ranges from 19% to 53% across individual PBFT (median estimates; see SI Table S5 for credible intervals). There is a statistically significant (linear regression, P = 0.004) decline in the growth rate of PBFT, and increase in muscle tissue MeHg burdens (linear regression, P < 0.001), with increasing proportion of mesopelagic prey as determined from Bayesian mixing model results (Figure ). PBFT growth rates based on measured length and otolith-derived age varied from 0.18 to 0.25 cm d-1, with a mean of 0.017 cm d-1 ± 0.02 SD. Proportion of mesopelagic prey in diet explains approximately 22% of the variability in PBFT growth and 59% of the variability in PBFT muscle MeHg burdens (Figure ).

Given the high oxidant levels during SOA generation, it is first worth briefly considering the representativeness of our results compared to previous SOA chamber studies. We compared ACSM mass spectra from β-caryophyllene and terpinolene experiments against reference chamber ozonolysis SOA spectra for the same precursors. A detailed analysis is provided in section S5 of the Supporting Information. Briefly, Pearson correlation coefficients between experimental and reference spectra range between 0.54 and 0.97, and thus, we do not believe the higher oxidant levels make the results presented here less representative than previous OFR work at lower oxidant loadings. Upon passage through the thermodenuder, the correlation degrades. This is expected because only the least volatile SOA fraction is retained.

Figure shows O:C and H:C ratios from the bypass scans for each experiment, with constant OSC lines plotted at OSC = -1.0, - 0.5, and 0.0. Measured OSC values range between -1.0 and 0.13, with a mean (standard deviation) of -0.65 (0.41). Typically, the OSC of atmospheric OA falls between -2.0 and 1.0 and, for monoterpene ozonolysis SOA in particular, between -1.1 and 0.5, comparable to values presented here. In our study, a lower organic loading results in OA with the highest oxidation state, consistent with previous studies of monoterpene SOA, , while OA formed at higher loadings typically has an OSC of approximately -1.0. Viscosities generally decrease with an increase in mass loading, as indicated by the color scale and marker sizes in Figure .

There is no clear trend between O:C or H:C ratios and either x ELVOC+LVOC or viscosity (Figure ), and no statistically significant relationship between OSC and viscosity was observed at 95% confidence among our nonsystematic set of conditions (Figure S4a). OSC and x ELVOC+LVOC are weakly correlated (Figure S4b), with a higher OSC associated with a lower x ELVOC+LVOC. This is perhaps a surprising result, given that trends of increased OSC and lower volatility (so likely higher x ELVOC+LVOC) have been observed; however, our study was not systematic, and changes in SOA characteristics other than OSC (e.g.. molecular weight) may be primarily driving this trend. Qualitatively, OSC values of ≥0.0 tend to be associated with lower viscosities at 30 °C, while a broader range of viscosities are observed at more negative OSC values (Figure S4). A previous study of biogenic SOA produced in a flow tube reactor employing dark ozonolysis also revealed a perhaps counterintuitive relationship between OSC and viscocity.

Viscosity increases with an increase in molecular weight and with an increase in the degree of functionalization of the organic compounds. ,,,,, Therefore, it is possible that our approximated oxidation states do not reflect the functional group composition of the aerosol and that our results may be at least partially explainable by oligomerization or other particle-phase processes that increase the mean MW while reducing the mean O:C ratio and OSC. Our OSC values are derived from O:C ratios, which have been previously reported to be a poor proxy for T g. An increasing MW is also associated with SOA aging , and is correlated with both lower vapor pressures, including in components of common SOA systems, and higher T g values. , For example, Yli-Juuti et al. hypothesized that low volatility α-pinene SOA consisted of oligomerized monomers with similar O:C ratios. Therefore, oxidation state in SOA does not seem to be the key factor in determining its viscosity.

Figure plots the common logarithms (log10) of viscosities (at 30 °C) against x ELVOC+LVOC fractions. Values for x ELVOC+LVOC range between 0.36 and 0.79, while observed viscosities at 30 °C range between 6.2 × 105 and 8.0 × 108 Pa s (all in the "semisolid" range). Dry monoterpene-derived SOA typically has room-temperature viscosities of ≥106 Pa s, ,- comparable to values presented here. β-Caryophyllene SOA generally had a viscosity higher than those of other SOA for nonconditioned experiments at lower loadings ( < 200 μg m-3); for example, experiment 11 versus experiment 5 (limonene) and experiment 6 (terpinolene) had viscosities of 2.1 × 107 Pa s versus 3.1 × 106 and 3.2 × 106 Pa s, respectively. Temperature-conditioned OA has a volatility that is lower (i.e.. higher x ELVOC+LVOC) and a viscosity that is higher than that in unconditioned experiments with the same precursor. For example, β-caryophyllene SOA conditioned at temperatures of 60, 100, and 120 °C has x ELVOC+LVOC values of 0.65, 0.79, and 0.84, respectively (Figure S2), with 30 °C viscosities of 1.2 × 108, 2.3 × 108, and 3.7 × 108 Pa s, respectively. Although the expected relationship between volatility and viscosity is unknown, a simple log-linear relationship was explored. The correlation between log10(viscosity) and x ELVOC+LVOC [log10(viscosity) = mx ELVOC+LVOC + b, where m = 4.7 ± 2.3, b = 4.7 ± 1.4, and R = 0.69] suggests that higher volatility (represented here by lower x ELVOC+LVOC) is associated with lower viscosity in these laboratory-generated biogenic SOA. This relationship implies that increasing x ELVOC+LVOC by 0.1 increases the corresponding viscosity (at 30 °C) by ~200%. Similar relationships hold for other single-parameter representations of OA volatility [e.g.. C*eff, C*mean, and C*p (see section S3 of the Supporting Information and Figures S5-S7)]. Viscosity increases exponentially with a decrease in temperature, ,, and one would expect that the slope of log10(viscosity) and x ELVOC+LVOC (or other volatility metrics) would become more pronounced at lower temperatures. Sensitivity analysis in TD data fits (assuming different ΔH vap and α values) results in shifts in volatility and suggests that fits may be especially sensitive to the assumed α, but the observed slopes do not change significantly (section S4 of the Supporting Information).

Figure shows that increased aerosol mass loading (C OA) generally results in OA with higher volatility and lower viscosity. For example, nonconditioned limonene at mass loadings of 250 and 830 μg m-3 have x ELVOC+LVOC values of 0.46 and 0.43, respectively (with corresponding 30 °C viscosities of 3.1 × 106 and 6.2 × 105 Pa s, respectively). An increased C OA causes higher volatility OA to condense into the particle phase, which is the likely driver for the decrease in OA viscosity in higher C OA experiments. This reduction in viscosity with higher mass loading is consistent with the observations of Grayson et al. for chamber-generated α-pinene SOA. In addition, Jain et al. observed a 30% decrease in particle bounce (corresponding to lower viscosity) at higher C OA. These results suggest that future numerical parametrizations relating viscosity and volatility of SOA must also consider mass loadings, especially if based on laboratory experiments conducted well above atmospheric concentrations.

Regardless, if molecular weight is the key moderator of viscosity, our results suggest that a "molecular corridor"-style framework ,, may enable a robust characterization of SOA viscosity based on MW and volatility, for example, in modeling frameworks that include a VBS component [e.g.. Community Multiscale Air Quality (CMAQ)]. Additionally, our results suggest that a liquid-phase state is likely not applicable for this type of SOA under dry conditions, consistent with previous viscosity measurements for an environmental chamber-generated biogenic SOA system ,, and common highly oxygenated SOA proxy species. , Therefore, condensed-phase concentrations of semivolatile and low volatility OC may be overpredicted (and gas-phase SVOCs underpredicted) for similar SOA systems if instantaneous equilibrium partitioning theory is assumed, particularly in desert, polar, and upper atmospheric regimes where environmental conditions favor higher viscosities. , The results presented in this work may be less applicable in more humid environments where plasticization due to water uptake may dramatically reduce viscosity at near-surface temperatures ,- and tend to reduce the extent of diffusional inhibition. , Future work should refine these estimates by systematically varying oxidation conditions, loadings, and humidity and refining volatility determinations.

The VLEs of three pure pyridinium-based ionic liquids were investigated by classical MD simulations at 700-850 K. The compositions and relative abundances of the ionic clusters existing in the vapor phase were identified and correlated to the cation-anion interaction energy. It was found that most evaporated ions exist as ion pairs (more than 40% in any RTIL). The vapor phase of [BPY] [TFSI] at 700 K contains most ion pairs, 71%. This percentage decreases down to 44% when temperature increases up to 850 K. Due to the vapor density increase at higher temperatures, ion pairs tend to fuse, giving rise to larger ionic aggregates, up to eight ions. However, the fraction of such large aggregates is very small, usually below 1%. It is yet unclear whether they can be detected by modern experimental techniques. Studies of the lifetimes of the six to eight ion aggregates in all RTILs may constitute an interesting extension of our present work.

Interestingly, the amount of ion triplets and neutral ion quadruplets exceeds the amount of single ions in most systems. Thus, single ions in the vapor phase-both cation and anions-are relatively unstable. The size of the ionic aggregates is generally proportional to the density of the vapor, which is, in turn, proportional to temperature. The reported results are in general agreement with the earlier reports , on the vapor of the imidazolium-based RTILs, showing that ion pairs constitute the dominant species.

The reported data are important from the fundamental standpoint, providing information on the vapor composition of ionic liquids. Vapors of molecular substances contain individual molecules, and vapors of inorganic melts contain mostly ion pairs (with modest admixtures of neutral ionic quadruples and neutral ionic sextets). - ,- In comparison, vapors of RTILs exhibit a more complicated structure that needs to be accounted for while building analytic theories. For instance, the saturated pressure at given conditions depends on the density of evaporated particles, rather than on their size and mass. From the practical point of view, information regarding VLE is important for lubrication, coating, and separation applications.

In this work, we simulated and analyzed the photoinduced nuclear and vibrational dynamics of a pyranine molecule in aqueous solution. We combined ground and excited state ab initio molecular dynamics with a time-resolved vibrational analysis, based on the wavelet transform.

Our approach showed important advantages, including the possibility of investigating time-resolved vibrational dynamics of the chromophore in aqueous solution, naturally taking into account anharmonicity and coupling of modes. Transient vibrational features can be easily correlated to the structural relaxation and the molecular dynamics in real time.

Within the class of photoacid molecules, pyranine is classified as weak. Indeed, the origin of pyranine photoreactivity cannot be simply interpreted and explained in terms of the electronic density redistribution responding to the external perturbation. On the other hand, nuclear dynamics turns out to be preparatory and essential in promoting the ESPT reaction.

Our findings support the hypothesis that the nuclear photorelaxation of pyranine is finely controlled by the activation of transient vibrational modes at low frequency. The most important stage of the skeleton relaxation is completed in about 500 fs, in agreement with FSRS data. In particular, the exchange of the order among C-C bonds occurs according to a complex vibrational dynamics, showing oscillatory patterns that are out of phase and modulated by modes below 200 cm-1.

We also individuated modes playing a role in optimizing the structural rearrangement of the pyranine and water molecule hydrogen bonded to the O-H group. In particular, a ring out-of-plane wagging (108 cm-1) and a ring deformation mode (280 cm-1) support the rearrangement of the intermolecular orientation and distances. As a consequence of the ultrafast relaxation, the pyranine-water couple is tighter and better oriented for the ESPT, occurring at later times.

Iron-methane cluster complexes are produced in a laser ablation source and studied with a dual time-of-flight reflectron mass spectrometer, previously described in detail. , For these studies, the ion source was modified to promote creation of larger clusters. Ions are formed by laser ablation of an iron rod (Sigma-Aldrich, 99.8% pure) and subsequent clustering in an expansion gas mixture that comes from one or two pulsed valves (Parker, series 9). The primary valve, whose gas mix consists of 1-10% methane in helium at 60-140 psi backing pressure, introduces gas before ablation. This mixture travels through a 2.5 mm ID, 20 mm long tube and then interacts with gas from the secondary valve (1-100% methane in helium at 10-20 psi backing pressure). This fast flow reactor design has the advantage of giving independent control over the methane concentration as well as reducing the possibility of ablation laser and resulting plasma fragmenting methane. The gas then flows through a 50 mm long, 2.5 mm ID aluminum nozzle to help induce more collisions and larger cluster formation. Various nozzles are used, mainly consisting of a long straight section followed by a 10° cone in order to promote formation of the desired ions.

The ions undergo supersonic expansion into vacuum, cooling to a rotational temperature of ~10 K. The ions then pass through a skimmer into the extraction region of a Wiley-McLaren time-of-flight mass spectrometer. Ions are all accelerated to 1800 V kinetic energy, are rereferenced to ground potential, and enter a field-free flight tube section. An IR laser system photodissociates the mass-selected ions at the turning point of the reflectron. The parent and photofragment ions are reaccelerated out of the reflectron, traveling through the field-free region where they finally impact upon a 40 mm diameter dual microchannel plate detector. The ion masses are determined from their characteristic flight times. The IR laser system is an optical parametric oscillator/optical parametric amplifier (LaserVision) that is pumped by a Spectra Physics GCR-190 Nd:YAG operating at 10 Hz. The system is tunable from 2200 to 5000 cm-1 and produces ~6 mJ per pulse near 3100 cm-1. In the reflectron region, a multipass mirror setup allows for the IR beam to cross the ion beam ~15 times. In order to properly calibrate the laser wavelength, well-known CH4 absorptions are used.

The ion signal is amplified and acquired on a gated integrator or digital oscilloscope. A LabView program averages the data and scans the IR laser. The photodissociation spectrum is obtained by measuring the normalized fragment ion signal (fragment ion signal divided by the parent ion signal and IR laser fluence) as a function of wavelength. The photodissociation spectrum is the product of the photodissociation quantum yield and the absorption. The only fragments observed correspond to the loss of one or more intact CH4. Depending upon the ion, 0.2-20% photodissociate. For some ions, a variant of the ion collection program is used in which the ablation laser operates at 20 Hz while the photodissociation laser runs at 10 Hz. The gated integrator then collects laser on and laser off signals on alternate shots. This is used for more accurate background subtraction and is particularly useful for some of the heavier ions where the mass gate does not completely remove lighter parent ions with the same flight time as the fragment.

Calculations are carried out with the Gaussian 09 program package. Optimized geometries of the ions are computed using the B3LYP, BPW91 and M11L density functionals and the 6-311++G (3df,3pd) basis set. All reported energies include zero-point energy. The calculated vibrational frequencies are harmonic, whereas measured frequencies include anharmonicity. To account for this effect, computed frequencies are scaled by the ratio of the experimental and calculated C-H stretching frequencies of isolated CH4 (ν1 = 2917 cm-1, ν3 = 3019 cm-1): 0.963 for B3LYP, 0.979 for BPW91 and 0.971 for M11L.
