In conclusion, we have investigated the neutral and radical cation/anion states of a syn/anti mixture of 1a and related compounds substituted at the 5,11-position with an ethynyl group in solution state. To investigate the effect of the ethynyl group in solution state, the unsubstituted structure of 1a and a variety of ethynyl-substituted compounds 1b, 1e, and 1f were synthesized. All of the compounds were confirmed as mixtures of syn/anti structures by 13C NMR or single-crystal X-ray crystallographic analysis. The parent structure of the syn/anti mixture, ADF, exhibited an absorption spectrum and cyclic voltammogram similar to those reported for pure anti-1a, suggesting that the syn and anti structures exhibit similar physical properties. The absorption spectra of all the ground-state compounds in the solution state under ambient condition did not change, suggesting that the ADF structure and substituted moieties are highly stable. According to the fluorescence lifetimes and quantum efficiencies of 1a and its ethynyl-substituted analogues, the ethynyl group enhanced the fluorescence lifetime and radiative quenching; however, sterically larger substituents favored nonradiative quenching. The fluorescence spectra of the radical cation and anion states exhibited new peaks at 550-1400 nm for the radical cation state and at 550-1100 nm for the radical anion state, respectively. The stabilities of both radical states increased with increasing size of the substituent group in the alkylsilyl moieties. DFT computation results showed that the πSOMO-π * and π-πSOMO transitions were the primary contributors to the radical state of the first excitation.

In conclusion, we have prepared a stimuli-responsive hydrogel that exhibits a large thermal hysteresis in volume phase transition, which is due to the intermolecular interactions of the MC scaffold. To achieve the combination of thermally responsive PNIPAm with MC to form a high thermal hysteresis hydrogel, we grafted PNIPAm chains onto an MC backbone and concurrently cross-link the PNIPAm.

The prepared PNIPAm-g-MC exhibited a thermal hysteresis of 10 °C, which results from the stable hydrophobic junctions in the MC backbone. By combining PNIPAm-g-MC with photothermal MNPs, a material capable of programmable volume change initiated by light-triggered shrinking and recovery through excessive cooling was prepared. A bilayer actuator comprising PNIPAm-g-MC/MNP as the active layer and PAAm as the passive layer was successfully fabricated. We demonstrated that static bending of the fabricated actuator in response to light irradiation is possible, meaning that the material has the ability to memorize its irradiation history and have that memory erased by cooling.
The programmable hydrogel platform developed may be applied to the fabrication of new types of origami, microvalves, and drug delivery systems.

The thermal camera-thermocouple dual temperature measurement method developed in this work allows for real-time high temperature (300-1000 °C) measurements in MW-heated catalytic reactors. This method was applied for a temperature distribution study in a platinum-on-carbon catalytic bed used for methane dry reforming. For this purpose, a custom-designed microwave cavity was employed to focus the microwave field on the catalyst bed and monitor its temperature in a 2D fashion by means of a thermal camera. The effect of different factors affecting the temperature measurements and emissivity values under microwave heating was investigated. The effects of camera range, the presence of different media and reactant gases in the process domain, object-to-camera distance, heating system, and microwave field distribution were discussed in detail. The multiparameter emissivity dependence in such a complex reaction system does not ensure correct temperature recording by the thermal camera alone; therefore, at least one contact sensor is highly recommended. The developed method successfully detected hot spot generation and provided an explanation for the nonhomogeneous heating profiles during MW processing. Careful handling and continued temperature monitoring with a thermal camera is very helpful to avoid potential risk hazards in MW-heated catalytic reactors.

The relation betweeen the miscibility of polymers in a mixture of two solvents and the solvent quality is analyzed by comparing the computed constant volume spinodal curves T = T(ϕB o, r o = const) with the computed second osmotic virial coefficient B 2 ( T , r oo = r o = const . ) and B 2 ( r oo , T = const . ) for these systems. The free energy parameters used in our illustrative calculations are taken as Δh A = -35 kJ/mol, Δs A = -105 J/(mol K), Δh C = 20 kJ/mol, and Δs C = 105 J/(mol K). This choice corresponds to solutions in which the solvation of polymers B by the solvent A is promoted upon cooling, whereas the solvation of polymers B by the solvent C is enhanced upon heating. The values of Δh A, Δs A, Δh C, and Δs C are very similar to those used in our previous studies of self-assembly and polymer solvation. , The effective interaction parameters χAB and χ CB between systems exhibiting polymer B and the solvents A and C, respectively, are assumed, for simplicity, to be equal χAB = χBC = 260/T, while the effective interaction parameter χAC between the small-molecule solvents A and C is fixed as χAC = 500/T to induce cononsolvency. The polymerization index N of polymer chains B is selected as N = 1000, and the eight adjustable parameters of the theory are kept fixed in the illustrative calculations. Calculations with a larger polymerization index N ≫ 1000 would permit the use of much lower effective interaction parameters {χ αβ } to generate the same spinodal curves.

Figure presents spinodal curves for the binary A/B and C/B polymer mixtures and for the ternary A/B/C polymer solution specified by the relative initial solvent composition r o = 5 (i.e.. by the majority which is solvent A in the A/B/C mixture before solvation). While both binary systems are taken as miscible over wide ranges of temperature and the initial polymer concentration ϕB o, the ternary solution exhibts a rather large closed-loop window of immiscibility (see Figure ). The second osmotic virial coefficient B 2 for the latter system (see green curve in Figure ) vanishes at two different Θ temperatures T Θ (1) and T Θ (2), becoming negative when T lies between T Θ (1) and T Θ (2) and being positive otherwise, i.e.. when T > T Θ (2) and T < T Θ (1). The Θ temperatures T Θ (1) and T Θ (2) provide the limits approached by the upper and lower critical solution temperatures T c (1) and T c (2), respectively, for high mass polymer solutions. Figure also displays, for comparison, the temperature variation of B 2 for a binary A/B polymer solution which is characterized in Figure by a small imiscibility region (see the red curve in Figure ) and by a much narrower difference ΔT Θ ≡ T Θ (2)-T Θ (1) (see the red curve in Figure ) than ΔT Θ for the ternary polymer solution (see the green curve in Figure ). The magnitude of ΔT Θ just provides meassure of immiscibility for systems exhibiting reentrant phase diagrams and presenting a more universal touchstone of immiscibility for various systems than the difference ΔT c ≡ T c (2) - T c (1) between the upper and lower critical solution temperatures because both T c (1) and T c (2) strongly depend on the molecular weight of the polymer. The second osmotic virial coefficient B 2 for the UCST binary polymer solution C/B, whose phase diagram is denoted by the blue curve in Figure , vanishes only at a single Θ temperature T Θ. (The temperature variation of B 2 ( T ) for the C/B mixture is omitted from Figure to avoid overlapping of the Θ points of the C/B and A/B/C solutions.)

Complementary information about general trends in miscibility of ternary A/B/C polymer solutions that emerge from Figures and can be deduced by considering the second osmotic virial coefficient B 2 ( T = const . ) as a function of the composition of the pure solvent mixture maintained in osmotic equilibrium with the polymer solution. Figure provides examples of plots of B 2 ( T = const . ) versus r oo for two temperatures coinciding with the Θ temperatures T Θ (1) and T Θ (2) deduced from Figure . The green and red curves, B 2 ( ϕ A oo , T = T Θ ( 2 ) ) and B 2 ( ϕ A oo , T = T Θ ( 1 ) ) of Figure intersect each other at a common point with the abcissa B 2 = 0 and the ordinate r oo = 5. Surprisingly, the second virial coefficient B 2 ( ϕ A oo , T = T Θ ( 1 ) ) also vanishes for r oo = 0.942. Figure resolves the seeming inconsistency in the presence of multiple Θ points by depicting the temperature variation of B 2 for a ternary A/B/C polymer solution with r o = 0.942. More specifically, Figure manifests the presence of three separate Θ temperatures T Θ (1), T Θ (2), and T Θ (3) for this particular system. Interestingly, the Θ temperature T Θ (2) of Figure coincides with the lower Θ temperature T Θ (1) = 279 K for the ternary polymer solution with r o = 5 in Figure . Figure also suggests that the ternary polymer solution (r o = 0.942) should be miscible at temperatures T for which B 2 ( T ) becomes positive, i.e, ranging from T Θ (1) to T Θ (2) or exceeding T Θ (3). The existence of these three separate Θ temperatures becomes more understandable by reference to the system's phase boundary depicted in Figure . The phase diagram of this particular system combines a UCST branch at low temperatures and a closed-loop region of immiscibility at higher temperatures, thereby directly predicting the appearance of three characteristic temperatures for phase separation, and thus of three separate Θ temperatures. Notice that Figures and are perfectly consistent and reflect the well-known thermodynamic regularity that miscibility and imiscibility occur, respectively, at temperatures for which B 2 is positive and negative. Measurements of B 2 , thus, can provide crucial information about miscibility when direct experimental determination of the phase diagrams may be very tedious as is in the case of ternary mixtures. The merging of the intermediate T Θ (2) and the lower Θ temperatures T Θ (1) for ternary systems with r o = 0.942 and r o = 5, respectively, is also easy to comprehend because it emerges from the shrinking of the closed loop region of immiscibility upon decreasing r o. As indicated in Figure , changing r o from r o = 5 to r o ≈ 1 leads to impoved miscibility through a significant decline in the upper critical solution temperature, while the lower critical solution temperature practically remains constant. Correspondingly, T Θ (2) for polymer solutions with r o ≈ 1 (see Figures and ) coincides with T Θ (1) for solutions with r o = 5 (see Figures and ).

This Account summarizes our recent work on developing genetically encoded multifunctional photo-cross-linkers to facilitate the investigation of CDC-client interactions. The introduction of a Se-based cleavable linker into the photo-cross-linking probes expanded the current toolkit, which facilitated the development of new strategies such as CAPP-DIGE and IMAPP to profile the native clients of HdeA/B as well as to characterize their client specificities and interaction interfaces. The genetically encoded photo-cross-linking strategy was also employed by other researchers to investigate the transient or dynamic PPIs within bacterial cell envelope. This work uncovered versatile and dynamic PPIs that play important roles in biological processes. Since a growing number of proteins have been shown to interact with their binding partners under disordered conditions, - the advantages for simultaneous client identification and binding interface mapping with our newly developed multifunctional probes will be highly valuable in studying these proteins. However, the genetically encoded photo-cross-linking strategy is not without limitations. For example, it may not be suitable for trapping very fast PPI changes, and such a covalent-capture method offers limited information regarding the interaction affinity. Nevertheless, considering that our photo-cross-linkers are highly compatible with various proteomic strategies, we expect these probes to find broader applications in diverse areas. The addition of other novel functional groups to the photo-cross-linkers may further expand the versatility of this toolbox. Finally, the unique Se-bearing cleavable linker may be valuable for tool development in other fields that also require small-sized but highly biocompatible and chemically cleavable linkages.

In this work, we demonstrate how the phasor approach can be used for quantification of multiple components. This approach requires prior knowledge of the phasor positions of the components. The approach works as long as the third component does not lie in the line joining the other two phasor positions. If a polygon can be formed with each of the contributing species at the vertices in a phasor plot and the phasor cloud is inside the polygon, multicomponent analysis can be applied. The difficulty to resolve multiple components is related to their phasor positions. If a point is in between two other phasor points lie and on the line joining the two phasor positions, then that point cannot be resolved in three components because it is due to the linear combination of only two components. In this method, data acquired with only one excitation frequency can be resolved into multiple components and their quantitative contribution can be calculated. The only other method that, in our knowledge, can calculate more than two components from FLIM data also uses a phasor approach and is based on non-Euclidean geometry. Our approach is a simple technique based on the projection of phasor cloud to different axes and can be easily employed during phasor analysis.

In this paper, we have analyzed the isomeric distribution of a binary complex between pFP and CPA produced under a supersonic jet expansion by means of vibrationally resolved LIF spectroscopy. To corroborate our findings, the spectrum of the pFP-NH3 complex, which is known to be produced in single isomeric structure, has been measured under the same expansion condition by the LIF method. It is known from earlier vibrational spectroscopic studies that the bare CPA molecule can have two distinct isomeric structures owing to the internal rotation of the amine group with respect to the cyclopropyl ring, and the present study reveals that complexation of CPA with pFP, where the two molecules are bound via O-H N as well as additional weak H-bonding, does not alter the isomeric distribution of the molecule drastically, and the observation is consistent also with the prediction from the electronic structure theory. This study allows us to conjecture further that similar conformational distribution of CPA might be retained also in solutions where similar intermolecular interactions prevail.

In the measured LIFE spectrum, the spectral red shift of the S1 ← S0 origin transition of the pFP moiety for the endo conformer of the complex (816 cm-1) has been found to be 80 cm-1 larger compared to that for the pFP-NH3 complex. The difference has been attributed to the larger proton affinity of CPA compared to that of ammonia and also to the larger value of hyperconjugative charge transfer interaction energy as obtained from NBO analysis. Furthermore, unlike the pFP-NH3 complex, the low-frequency bands for the intermolecular vibrational modes of the pFP-CPA complex appear with much larger intensities in the FE spectrum, and this has been attributed to a significantly large change in the geometry of the complex upon electronic excitation for the latter. The same is also manifested as a long progression in the DF spectra when the intermolecular stretching fundamental is excited. With the aid of the PGOPHER spectral fitting program and optimized geometric parameters as obtained from electronic structure calculation by the CAM-B3LYP/6-311++G (2d,2p) method, the σ n 1 progressions of the measured spectra have been satisfactorily simulated.

We used substance flow analysis (SFA) as a method to track and quantify the direct carbon flows in the system under study. When modeling the life cycle carbon emissions of the wood utilization system as it is within the given temporal window, we followed the principle of attributional life cycle assessment (ALCA). , The functional unit chosen was harvested wood (t C). In order to model the carbon impacts of the studied wood utilization system, we separated the respective technosphere from the ecosphere. This was done using a no-human-intervention land-use reference system within the studied temporal window, - here reflecting no-harvest of forest over the studied 100-year time horizon. To quantify the forest C sink impacts, we applied the relative carbon (RC) indicator introduced by Pingoud et al. over a 100-year time horizon (RC100). The indicator describes cumulative reduction in the forest carbon sink per the amount of carbon harvested from forest, both over the given time horizon.

We compared the life cycle carbon emissions of a wood utilization system to those of alternative materials and energy, serving equivalent (comparable) function with harvested wood products. By deducting the life cycle carbon emissions of alternative products from those of wood utilization system, it is possible to consider an extended carbon balance. The balance describes how efficiently, in theory, the overall wood utilization system in Finland functions in climate change mitigation. In this system expansion, the avoided life cycle carbon emissions of alternative products are considered as "substitution credits" of the wood utilization system. We assumed that the substitution is perfect, implying that the total amount of consumption of goods does not change in response to the production of goods. We considered "substitution credits" from material and energy use of wood when available. For functions served by traditional paper products, we assumed that there are no functionally equivalent products to be substituted. However, we assumed that traditional paper products are recovered and used as energy at the end of their life cycle, thus achieving "substitution credits" from energy use.

Second, we studied the uncertainty and sensitivity of the results to the input parameter uncertainties using the Monte Carlo simulation. It is a method in which a probabilistic analogy is used to solve deterministic problems of uncertainty. It performs a deterministic computation of the input parameters for a selected number of the samples (here 10,000) from each probability distribution. Then, it aggregates the samples as probability distributions. To characterize the probabilities (P), we used the IPCC terminology: virtually certain refers to 99-100%, very likely to 90-100%, likely to 66-100%, about as likely as not to 33-66%, unlikely to 0-33%, very unlikely to 0-10%, and exceptionally unlikely to 0-1% probability, respectively. To measure the contribution of a single variable to the uncertainty of the carbon emissions, we used Spearman's rank correlations (ρ) between each of the variables and the result values (see Supporting Information (SI) SI2 for more information). We used MS Excel software and its add-in @Risk application to carry out all the calculations.

The single crystal XRD analysis of three TBPO hydrate crystals grown from the TBPO-H2O mixtures with different TBPO content reveals their belonging to the orthorhombic system with Pbam space group. All three studied structures are extremely similar and refined on the basis of the water framework with idealized unit cell composition 4H 4P 4T 14D 148H2O. The structural stoichiometry is TBPO 34.5H2O. The location of the TBPO guest molecules has been refined for the first time. The stoichiometry of TBPO (33.6 ± 0.9) H2O is obtained in analytical determination of the crystal composition. The discrepancy between the analytically determined and structural stoichiometry is likely to be attributed to the structure defects, which cannot be revealed by the routine single-crystal XRD analysis. The dissociation temperature of 280.0 K and dissociation enthalpy of 253.1 ± 4.7 J g-1 for TBPO 33.6H2O semiclathrate hydrate were measured by DSC. The obtained dissociation enthalpy is higher than ΔH diss = 217.5 J g-1 for TBAB 38H2O ionic clathrate hydrate, which have already been successfully used for air conditioning technology.

TBPO + CH4 double hydrates were synthesized from TBPO-H2O mixtures in the range 14.9-55.8 wt % TBPO at a methane pressure of 8.5 ± 0.5 MPa and temperatures of 274 ± 1 and 286 ± 1 K. The maximum included methane volumes 61.6-74.6 mL/g were observed for the TBPO + CH4 double hydrates synthesized from ~26-30 wt % TBPO aqueous solutions. The obtained value exceeds at least by a factor of 1.5 the methane capacity of THF + CH4 and TBAB + CH4 double hydrates. It was shown by the PXRD method that TBPO + CH4 double hydrate belongs to the same structural type as the simple TBPO hydrate. No meaningful differences in the unit cell parameters of the double and simple TBPO hydrates were observed in the PXRD experiments. The molar H2O:TBPO ratio is about the same in the simple TBPO and double hydrate. The study of the Raman spectra of the TBPO + CH4 double hydrate and simple TBPO hydrate showed that CH4 molecules selectively occupy the small D cages in the TBPO + CH4 double hydrate. At a methane pressure of 8.5 ± 0.5 MPa, the degree of the small D cages occupancy did not exceed ~85% for the TBPO + CH4 double hydrate. We have not found structural evidence of the existence of several structural types of hydrates in the studied systems that was suggested earlier. The obtained results indicate that the TBPO-H2O binary system has a potential for application in gas separation technology and as cold storage and transportation media.

We prepared hybrid nanoparticles by selectively anchoring PNIPAAM polymer at the outer surface of halloysite. The synthetic route endowed a large surface density of polymer onto the nanotubes. Temperature-responsive features were observed as the PNIPAAM corona undergoes a coil-to-globule transition at the LCST. The hybrid nanocarrier shows Brownian diffusion as well as electrophoretic mobility strongly dependent on temperature. The wettability of the solid composite surface was also temperature responsive, the water spreading being the dominant phenomenon compared to the adsorption in pristine halloysite. We performed in vitro tests simulating the gastro-intestinal transit of the proposed delivery system loaded with curcumin, a natural anticancer molecule. The results showed a targeted release of the active species into the intestine. This study is encouraging for designing biocompatible thermosensitive materials based on halloysite nanotubes and PNIPAAM with hollow nanocavity available for controlled release.

The DM mass balance for the Norwegian agriculture-based food processing, human consumption, and waste subsystems (Figure ) shows that cumulative AFW (in red) accounts for roughly 17% of sold food. The largest losses of AFW were found at human consumption with 92 kt DM/year. In fact, these losses were more than AFW from food processing, wholesale and retail combined (63 kt DM/yr) and roughly 10% of total consumer purchased food. Food processing, retail and human consumption were significant contributors to AFW, with 33 kt DM/yr, 29 kt DM/yr and 92 kt DM/yr respectively, whereas losses from wholesale were comparatively negligible (1 kt DM/yr). With approximately 1100 kt DM/yr of food sold by wholesale and imports of 780 kt DM/yr, the degree of self-sufficiency lies at about 30% in Norway. However, domestically produced food has a high share of animal products and is exported in large amounts (300 kt DM/yr).

For the baseline energy scenario (Figure ), we found the largest energy flows were grazing (41 PJ/yr), net inputs to plant production (32 PJ/yr) and manure (26 PJ/yr). Additionally, the results highlighted that about 80% of domestically produced plants is used for animal feed (17 PJ/yr), whereas 20% of produced plants go to human consumption (4 PJ/yr). The highest energy recovery potential was found to be manure at 26 PJ/yr, as this secondary resource can be used as biogas feedstock. In terms of PE, the cumulative baseline PE was 14.5 PJ/yr, which was relatively low as compared to the biomass flows. However, in terms of waste, cumulative PE was more than double exported waste and waste to incineration combined (7 PJ/yr). Additionally, compared to cumulative AFW, cumulative PE was about three and a half times as large with 14.5 PJ/yr versus 4 PJ/yr. The largest PE consumer was food processing at 10 PJ/yr.

The AFW recycling scenario only significantly affected a few flows relative to the base scenario. Organic waste for biogas production increased from 1 PJ/yr to 5 PJ/yr due to the diversion of AFW to biogas production. Similarly, produced biogas increased from 1 PJ/yr to 4 PJ/yr and the return of residuals to agriculture increased from 0.4 PJ/yr to 0.9 PJ/yr. While the relative return of biogas residuals increased substantially from the base scenario to the AFW recycling scenario, this had a minimal effect on the net inputs to plant production (32.3 PJ/yr versus 32.0 PJ/yr). The increase in biogas production was coupled with an increase in biogas PE of 0.4 PJ/yr to 1 PJ/yr and cumulative PE from 14.5 PJ/yr to 15.2 PJ/yr.

The AFW prevention scenario resulted in considerable savings relative to the base scenario. The net inputs to plant production reduced by 19% from 32 PJ/yr to 26 PJ/yr. Similarly, plants for human consumption reduced from 4 PJ/yr to 1 PJ/yr. This was due to the high fraction of plant products in AFW, with the largest fraction of AFW being fresh fruit and vegetables, and the assumption that trade was held constant. Plants for feed reduced by 12% (17 PJ/yr to 15 PJ/yr) and animal products decreased by 9% (11 PJ/yr to 10 PJ/yr). Processing wastes decreased from 2 PJ/yr to 1 PJ/yr and organic household waste decreased from 11 PJ/yr to 2 PJ/yr. This was due to the drastic decrease in food waste as a result of prevention measures. While produced biogas decreased substantially from 1 PJ/yr to 0.2 PJ/yr, this was met with a decrease in cumulative PE from 14.5 PJ/yr to 13.6 PJ/yr.

For the baseline P scenario (Figure ), we found that the largest P flows were manure (12 kt P/yr), grazing (7.8 kt P/yr) and imported mineral P (7.8 kt P/yr). Similar to energy, the results showed the high fraction of produced plants for animal husbandry feed (4.2 kt P/yr) versus plants for human consumption (0.9 kt P/yr). The flow with the highest theoretical potential for P recovery was manure, however, this is unfeasible due to the spatial distribution between P deficits and P surpluses and P surpluses requiring long and costly transport distances, as discussed in Hamilton and colleagues. The net addition of P to agriculture soil stocks (NAS) for the baseline was determined to be 10 kt P/yr.

The AFW recycling scenario resulted in a 6% decrease of imported mineral P (7.8 kt P/yr to 7.3 kt P/yr) due to the return of P in biogas residuals that displaced primary P consumption (increase from 0.4 kt P/yr to 0.9 kt P/yr). This resulted in a 17% decrease of NAS from 10 kt P/yr to 8.3 kt P/yr. Organic waste to biofuels increased from 0.4 kt P/yr to 1 kt P/yr. Exported waste decreased relative to the base scenario from 1.7 kt P/yr to 1.6 kt P/yr and waste to incineration/landfill decreased from 2.7 kt P/yr to 2.4 kt P/yr.

The AFW prevention scenario resulted in a substantial reduction in the throughput of P. Imported mineral P decreased by 14% (7.8 kt P/yr to 6.7 kt P/yr) due to the reduced demand for plant products for human consumption (from 1 kt P/yr to 0.5 kt P/yr) and animal husbandry feed (4.3 kt P/yr to 4.0 kt P/yr). Similarly, grazing decreased by about 4% (7.8 kt P/yr to 7.5 kt P/yr) and manure decreased by 8% (12 kt P/yr to 11 kt P/yr) due to the reduced demand for animal products. While the return of food processing waste and sewage sludge decreased from 1.8 kt P/yr and 1.3 kt P/yr and residuals from 0.4 kt P/yr to 0.3 kt P/yr, this was met with as much as a 33% reduction in the NAS (10 kt P/yr to 6.7 kt P/yr). Additionally, exported waste and waste to incineration/landfill decreased by 27% (4.4 kt P/yr to 3.2 kt P/yr, combined).

The domestic energy requirement was higher for the AFW recycling scenario, closely followed by the baseline scenario, whereas the AFW prevention scenario most effectively reduced cumulative energy demand. However, the domestic energy requirement indicator needs to be interpreted (Figure ) with caution, because it does not include PE for waste incineration, landfill and waste export. Overall, for both energy and P, AFW prevention resulted in the lowest impacts. The primary reason for this was the reduced demand for animal and plant products, resulting in both reduced upstream production impacts and downstream waste treatment impacts. Combined, this resulted in savings beyond the gains from producing secondary products (biogas and secondary fertilizer from sewage sludge and food processing wastes) from AFW recycling. Therefore, while AFW recycling does provide savings relative to the baseline, the effect is minimal. Based on our results, AFW prevention is preferable for the highest reductions in overall energy and P impacts compared to the present.

In general, most of the G4-binding ligands are known to be end-stackers that bind to the ends of the G-tetrads or form interactions in the loops. At variance with end-stackers, another class of ligands can bind to the grooves of the G4 DNA but ligands that selectively recognize G4 grooves are much more limited. , Large, flat aromatic planar molecules stack on G-tetrads through extensive π-π stacking with them, whereas small nonplanar molecules have the probability to bind to the external region between the successive G-tetrads of G4 DNA. Various studies suggest that there is no general rule that explains the drug-G4 DNA binding and a sequence-dependent interaction could also be important. ,

Among various such small molecules, fisetin and naringenin, the two dietary plant flavonoids have immense biological potential. ,,, In this Article, we have investigated the interaction of these two flavonoid molecules with G4 and duplex DNA structure using multispectroscopic approaches. UV-visible absorption results show that the binding of fisetin with G4 DNA does not involve end-stacking interaction, but it is possible that fisetin forms complexes with G4 structure in the external surface of the G4 DNA through stacking interactions with some portions of the bases. Upon the addition of increasing amounts of duplex DNA to fisetin, smaller spectral shifts were observed compared to G4 DNA, suggesting a higher interaction of fisetin with G4 DNA than that of duplex DNA. We also performed both steady-state and time-resolved fluorometric studies to elucidate the binding of fisetin with different DNA structures. We observed that the generation of tautomer species of fisetin is much more in a G4 environment than that in duplex DNA, which is a clear indication that fisetin experiences a more hydrophobic environment in the G4 DNA matrix. Steady-state anisotropy studies also indicate that the motional restriction of fisetin is much higher in G4 DNA than that of duplex. From the time-resolved fluorescence decay studies, we observed an increase in the average lifetime (⟨τ⟩) of fisetin in DNA environments, but the value is higher in G4 DNA than that of duplex DNA which also indicates the higher interaction of fisetin with G4 DNA. Time-resolved anisotropy measurements also support our previous results, showing higher rotational correlation time (τr) of fisetin molecules in G4 DNA environment.

As naringenin is nonfluorescent, we were not able to perform fluorometric measurements. Thus, we used FID assay using TO as an external probe to evaluate the binding affinity of naringenin toward different DNA structures. We found that naringenin displaces a higher percentage of TO from the duplex DNA environment than that of G4 DNA, which indicates a higher interaction of naringenin with duplex DNA. This result was also supported by the absorption studies where we observe a higher hyperchromic effect at the absorption maxima of duplex DNA in the presence of naringenin.

From molecular docking studies, we found that fisetin and naringenin both primarily exhibit stacking interaction with some of the external bases of the parallel G4 structure and it was also observed that both of the molecules show minor groove binding ability in duplex DNA. Despite possessing quite similar structural backbones, fisetin exhibits preferential interaction with G4 DNA in comparison to the duplex, while the reverse occurs for naringenin. Molecular modeling studies clearly demonstrate that the spatial structures of the flavonoids may cause these differences in the G4 binding. The more coplanar conformation of fisetin may be responsible for the strong binding of this flavonol with the G4. However, due to the absence of a C2-C3 double bond in the C-ring, naringenin adopts a significant noncoplanar conformation relative to the ring A/C plane, resulting in a poor binding with the G4 structure. Interestingly, fisetin forms a greater number of H-bonds with G4 than that of naringenin which may also lead to the higher affinity of fisetin toward G4 than naringenin. The present study elucidates, for the first time, the role of C-ring planarity on the preferential binding of G4 DNA by flavonoids. This study also exemplifies the application of dual emission behavior of flavonoids to probe selective G4 DNA recognition and lays the basis for further applications in this direction. To the best of our knowledge, this may be the first report of two closely similar structured flavonoid molecules showing sharply contrasting selectivity for binding with different DNA structures. These studies may enlighten the understanding of specific interaction of small molecules with DNA structure, helping the drug discovery process.

Finally, we note that it might be of interest to explore the prospects of the sensitive "two-color" fluorescence of fisetin (and other fluorescent flavonoids) as a novel tool for the detection and quantification of G4 DNA, for instance, in human cancer cells. This can conceivably emerge as a viable alternative to the existing antibody based approach which has already been established. Interestingly, there have been a few recent studies illustrating the use of fluorescent probes of synthetic origin for visualizing G4 DNA, , but to our knowledge, to date, there are no reports on the applications of flavonoids or other natural product based compounds for such a purpose.

We performed analyses to elucidate the toxicity of sediments in Flanders to H. incongruens. According to initial TU results (Figures S5, S7), NH3 (TU = 0.1) contributed most to H. incongruens growth inhibition. Other contributors were Ni and Cu (TUs ≤ 0.1), whereas the individual TUs of Zn, Cd, CrO4, Hg, and Pb were ≤0.01. Predicting the % growth inhibition via initial TU using initial (standard) EC50 values (Table , Section ) yielded maximal explained variance lower than 30%. Initially, speciation calculations (eqs , ) did not appear to improve these results. In contrast to Figure S7 (wherein there is a low contribution), organotins are among the species most highly correlating with H. incongruens % growth inhibition (Figure S9).

We then performed "semiempirical" analyses to further elucidate the toxicity of sediments by letting γ i EC50 values fit the growth inhibition data (Section ). This "calibrating" procedure allowed a robust TU analysis for H. incongruens. According to the semiempirical analysis, too, NH3 dominates the TU (TU = 0.3). Additional toxic pressure arises from organotins (as represented by tributyltin, TU = 0.3). Then, the contributions from Ni and Cu appear minor ( ≤ 0.1) (Figure ). Inclusion of chemicals other than NH3, HPO4 2-, and By3SnOH2 only marginally improved the fit. Instead, we found a positive influence by HPO4 2-, i.e.. growth-promoting (TU = -0.3).

After calibration, we found that speciation calculations (eq ) significantly improved the results (Figure B,C). Then, NH3, organotins, and HPO4 2- explain up to 90% of the observed variance in the % growth inhibition for water bodies throughout Flanders. We established γ i EC50 values for NH3, HPO4 2-, and TBT cation (By3SnOH2 +) at 150,000-39,000 and 0.003 ng/L. The relative importance of the toxicants differs between water bodies. In general, there is a higher toxic pressure in West Flanders than in inland regions (Table S4). In general, predictions for H. incongruens growth inhibition are more precise for "uniform" (e.g.. large rivers and canals) water bodies than for small "nonuniform" water bodies.

This work was aimed at the plant-wide control of an amine gas sweetening plant. The plant comprises two gas absorption columns in which the sour gases are absorbed from natural gas, two solvent regeneration columns, and two heat exchangers. DMPC was implemented on this network for the start up of the plant with and without disturbances and measurement noise. The optimal architecture for DMPC was obtained from a modularity maximization algorithm which separates the two stages of absorption and regeneration as different subnetworks. The performance of DMPC on the optimal decomposition was compared with that of a fully centralized MPC architecture, a decentralized MPC architecture, and distributed MPC on the suboptimal decomposition obtained from the modularity maximization algorithm. The closed-loop performance of DMPC implemented on the optimal decomposition was found to be comparable to that of CMPC and superior to the other architectures for all the control problems considered. The computation time for solving the optimization problem was also reasonably low (larger than only the decentralized MPC architecture) for DMPC based on the optimal decomposition. This work, thus, demonstrates a promising path for designing practically implementable model based controllers for large-scale tightly integrated plants. Future research will address the state estimation problem, further improvement and validation of the model based on plant data, and the real-time implementation of the proposed control structure.

Abundant models are available that address different aspects of estimating the eutrophication impact category for LCA and LCIA. Therefore, to limit the scope of the paper and provide a succinct review, criteria were developed to select models for this analysis. A list of candidate F&T and LCIA models was created based on the results of Google Scholar and Google Web searches for peer-reviewed publications and model documentation published between 2007 and 2017. The searches combined the keywords "eutrophication" and "(nitrogen OR phosphorus OR nutrient) AND (pollution OR fate OR impact OR hypoxia)". Sources were added if they were referenced by multiple authors in the original search. Priority was given to models actively maintained and updated, regularly used, especially in the United States, applied by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), and considered to have potential to contribute to LCIA of eutrophication.

Each model was documented using a spreadsheet to assess its suitability for estimating eutrophication-related impacts in LCA. Refer to the Supporting Information for rubric details. General metadata documented included model type, institutional origin and ongoing support, public availability, and aspects of scope, including geographic coverage, time step, and spatial resolution. Nutrient-related metadata included model representations of nutrient loading sources, nutrient species or groupings tracked, transport and removal mechanisms (i.e.. processes that facilitate or minimize transport, respectively, through the biosphere), and nutrient transformation processes (which change the form or speciation of a nutrient). Figure illustrates the relationship between nutrient input, transport, removal, and transformation as N and P cycle through the biosphere. Ideally, F&T models and LCIA methods would reflect accurately and precisely all relationships shown in Figure . Due to practical factors, however, such as lack of model sophistication, lack of site specificity, and technical challenges associated with determining spatial and temporal distribution of releases and emissions, simplifying assumptions must be made. The approach taken in this Review is to include as much scientific detail as necessary and available and continually work toward methods and models that more-realistically reflect observed environmental processes.

A theoretical study of doping of CPs was performed with DFT calculations using the GGA (PBE) functional. Trends obtained from PBE are similar to those from other types of functionals. Two atomic dopants, namely Li and Cl, were used to facilitate n-type and p-type doping. The CPs PTh and PPy and their analogs (S replaced by O, Se, and Te in PTh, and N replaced by P, As, and Sb in PPy) were investigated. Structural and electronic changes upon doping were analyzed with molecular and periodic calculations. Slight variations in geometry parameters and band gaps were observed between periodic and molecular calculations. However, the observed trends are more or less the same, and the two types of calculations complement and augment each other. Successful doping was confirmed by observed structural changes in the CPs. Muliken population analysis was used to evaluate the amount of charge gained or donated by the dopants. The band structure diagrams obtained from periodic calculations show upward or downward shifts in the Fermi level with Li and Cl, respectively. A decrease in HOMO-LUMO gaps was observed upon doping. This is particularly prominent in PTh and analogs. These new materials will be useful for various device applications.

The ESPT mechanism of the 2,6-DAI (H2O) n (n = 2-4) clusters was investigated based on the geometric structures, electronic spectra, photophysical properties, and potential energy curves using the DFT and TD-DFT methods. By calculating the bond length and IR vibrational spectra of the geometric structure, the intermolecular hydrogen bond in the S1 state was enhanced significantly. The absorption and fluorescence spectra are consistent with the experimental results, which indicate that the calculation methods are valid. The corresponding frontier MOs of 2,6-DAI (H2O)3 and 2,6-DAI (H2O)4 clusters was analyzed to qualitatively discuss the charge distribution and transfer. This analysis further revealed the possibility of the ESPT process. A detailed analysis of the potential energy curve shows that the ESPT reaction of the 2,6-DAI (H2O)3 clusters occurs in the type A process, whereas that of the 2,6-DAI (H2O)4 clusters occurs in the type C process because of the optimized stability of 2,6-DAI (H2O)3-PT and 2,6-DAI (H2O)4-PT clusters. The ESPT reaction of 2,6-DAI (H2O)3 and 2,6-DAI (H2O)4 clusters is a consistent mechanism by optimizing the transition state in the S1 state. In addition, similar values were obtained for the energy barriers. The type A process of 2,6-DAI (H2O)3 clusters in the S1 state is 13.16 kcal/mol, whereas the type C process of 2,6-DAI (H2O)4 clusters in the S1 state is 13.14 kcal/mol. Thus, 2,6-DAI molecules in an aqueous solution participate in the ESPT process in these two forms (2,6-DAI (H2O)3-PT and 2,6-DAI (H2O)4-PT clusters).

In this paper, several trajectory-based time-domain methods of CW EPR spectral simulation based on MD simulations of spin-labeled proteins were presented. Three models of MD-derived spin-label dynamics of differing complexity (direct MD, HBD, and HMM) were examined and compared across three different proteins and two spin labels with very different mobilities: R1 and TOAC.

When compared with experimental data, the direct method worked very well for both slow motion in TOAC-phospholamban and faster motion in R1-T4 lysozyme, indicating sufficient conformational sampling in each MD trajectory. In general, more advanced sampling methods such as umbrella-sampling and replica-exchange dynamics will be needed to ascertain complete sampling.

Regarding the approximate methods (HBD and HMM), the HMM method is, in general, superior as it can account for multiple time scales for transitions between spin-label orientations, whereas the HBD method only uses a single rotational diffusion tensor and an orientational potential energy. Given its stark simplicity, the HBD method performed surprisingly well. However, for the very restricted, multisite jump-like motion of TOAC-polyalanine as well as for both R1-labeled systems, the HMM method was clearly superior compared to the HBD method, indicating the flexibility of the HMM method for spin labels with different types of dynamics. For these reasons and due to its consistent performance, we conclude that the HMM method is the preferred approximation for simulating EPR spectra from MD simulations, both for R1 and TOAC labels.

The computation times for the faster-motion spectra of R1-labeled proteins using HBD were about 50 times longer than with HMM. The bottleneck in the HBD method is the interpolative evaluation of the torque term at each time step. This is a second reason for which the HMM is preferred.

To the authors' knowledge, TOAC-labeled proteins had not been studied via MD simulation prior to this work. The results given here show that the dynamics of TOAC in α-helical sites can be accurately modeled as two- or four-site exchange between twist-boat and chair conformations.

Finally, a key practical aspect of the present work is that all three models of spin-label dynamics as well as the ability to directly interface with MD simulation data have been implemented in a time-domain CW EPR spectral simulation software suite in the freely available software EasySpin. This allows anyone to perform similar spectral simulations using dynamical orientational trajectories from any MD program and test different models of spin-label dynamics of nitroxides or any other spin system on a single platform.

We showed how ultrasound reduces dispersion in micropacked-bed reactors by two orders of magnitude. Sonication produces partial fluidization of the bed even at high flow rates, continuously modifying gas channels and reducing liquid dispersion. Direct visualization and RTD experiments confirm that ultrasound can remove common gas channeling phenomena by promoting a dynamically dispersed gas phase flow. A more thorough study under a variety of hydrodynamics conditions is still necessary to assess contributions to mass transfer, the nature of gas-channeling, and the potential for enhancing heterogeneous catalyst reactions. The effects of short ultrasound pulses applied during transient initial bed operation might also present an interesting area of exploration to reduce variation in bed packing and ensure a more uniform packing for longer runtimes. To mitigate any surface damage of the catalyst due to cavitation or friction, more data are essential to quantify the acoustic attenuation in unsaturated porous media and optimize the design of micropacked-bed sonoreactors. The efficient use of ultrasound unlocks new pathways for multiphase reactor design, enabling near-plug-flow operation with enhanced phase homogenization in microscale-packed beds.

This Account tells a story about the discovery of mesoionic pyrido [1,2-a] pyrimidinone insecticides from a high throughput screen, their optimization, side chain evolution, and ultimate identification of two compounds for commercialization development, i.e.. triflumezopyrim (4) as a potent hoppercide to control rice hopper species and dicloromezotiaz (5) for lepidopteran pest control. During the optimization, a number of significant breakthroughs were achieved. Such advancements include side chain changes from n-propyl to 2,2,2-trifluoroethyl to 2-chlorothiazol-5-ylmethyl and 5-pyrimidinylmethyl groups which demonstrate potent hoppercidal activity for commercialization. Significant improvements to lepidopteran activity was seen with 2-chlorothiazol-5-ylmethyl side chains, combined with a "magic methyl effect" for 9-methyl substitution with this side chain chemotype. Successful identification of triflumezopyrim (4) and dicloromezotiaz (5) for commercialization development demonstrates that compounds binding to the orthosteric site of nAChR can provide not only a powerful tool to control hopper species, but also a useful tool for lepidoptera pest control, using an underexploited mode of action. More profoundly, commercialization of these compounds dismisses the notion that such colored organic compounds cannot be developed as pesticides, particularly for foliar usage. Discovery of mesoionic insecticides provides yet another successful example of identifying biologically active agents from HTS screen, while the optimization and potency improvement through side chain evolution will provide inspiration for future optimization programs and SAR studies. The success of our discovery program on mesoionic compounds, combined with the unique structure of such compounds and their intriguing physical properties, may stimulate interests in mesoionic compounds not only for other agrochemical discovery programs, but also for human drug discovery and other science disciplines looking for substances and materials with unique properties.

In summary, we have shown that charged helicoids are more stable than flat ribbons in electrolyte solutions under the assumption of a constant-area transformation. This transformation is the most reasonable one as it keeps a constant charge density, σ. The stabilizing electrostatic free energy for twisting the ribbon and the elastic energetic penalty have similar orders of magnitude. In the case of nanoribbons formed by amphiphile self-assembly, the electrostatic contributions will be relevant for flexible ribbons (thin ribbons with low Young's modulus), large surface charge densities (highly charged amphiphiles), and low ionic strengths (which promote large twisting periods that involve low elastic penalties). Even in the case where the spontaneous twisting of the ribbon results from molecular chirality, electrostatic interactions may be relevant and shift the optimal twisting period. This situation can be recognized in experiments as a dependence of the twisting period on the ionic strength of the solution.

The fact that the helicoid is a minimum free-energy surface in aqueous solution is unexpected if we consider that a one-dimensional string of charges minimizes its energy in the fully stretched conformation. However, twisting the nanoribbon into a helicoid (keeping a constant and homogeneous charge density) results in an increase in its perimeter. We, therefore, ascribe the stability of the helicoid to an increase in the number of charges near the edge, which are more stable than those near the axis. This simple argument successfully explains many of our numerical results, but one should note that there still remain open questions, for example, why the helicoid is the only twisted shape that can be more stable than the flat ribbon and why pairwise-additive electrostatic models fail to capture the effect. In conclusion, the results of this work provide new insights into the role of electrostatics in the shape development of soft materials.

A one-electron + CPP (core pseudopotential) calculations for the Mg+He van der Waals system was performed using the effective potential approach. The Mg2+ core and the electron-He interactions were treated using semilocal pseudopotentials, which reduced the ion to only one valence electron, for which an SCF calculation is sufficient. In addition and due to the only one valence electron, large Gaussian basis sets for Mg and He atoms were used. The Mg2+He core-core interactions were determined at the CCSD (T) level of theory using the Molpro program. The spectroscopic constants of the Mg2+He ground state were derived and compared with the available studies to validate its accuracy and its use in the modeling of the Mg+He system. For a better description of the Mg2+He interactions at intermediate distances where the minimum of several states of Mg+He are located, this potential was fitted to the Tang and Toennies analytical expression. In addition, the spin-orbit effect was incorporated using the semiempirical approach of Cohen and Schneider. As a result, a splitting in energy, transition energy, and transition dipole moment and an insignificant shift in the equilibrium distances of some states were observed. A comparison between our results and the previous studies, - especially for the X2Σ+ and the A2Π states, has shown good agreement. The accurate data produced for the ground state of the Mg2+He and Mg+He ionic dimers will be used to generalize structural and dynamical studies of large Mg2+He n and Mg+He clusters and immersion of the Mg2+ and Mg+ ions into helium nanodroplets. However, the results of the excited states of the Mg+He dimer will be used to investigate the broadening effect of the Mg+ spectrum by collision with the He gas. This will stimulate experimental investigations for these dimers and clusters.

Solid extractants consisting of poorly crystalline Zr (IV)-coordination polymers based on BTP and carboxylate-substituted derivatives have been prepared. The use of HF as a mineralizer resulted in crystalline mixed-phase compounds whose structure could not be resolved. Of the materials studied, the poorly crystalline ZrBTP-x phases prepared in the absence of fluoride showed superior performance in the extraction of trivalent lanthanides and tetravalent Th even in greater than 3 M HNO3. Under such highly acidic conditions, the compounds remained stable and displayed enhanced selectivity for heavy lanthanides, suggesting that they might be useful for actual applications. In addition to excellent selectivity for the mentioned trivalent elements the ZrBTP-x compounds showed extremely fast kinetics and good capacities. It remains to be seen if appropriate choice of conditions could result in materials suitable for the extraction of trivalent actinides from radio lanthanides. Work addressing column dynamics of granulated materials and the extraction of radiolanthanides and actinides from Purex-type raffinates is underway. Thermal treatment of the lanthanide and Th-loaded extractants results in formation of highly crystalline pyrophosphates with the general formula AIVP2O7 and where Zr, Th, and the lanthanides occupy the A site. Such materials are expected to be highly insoluble and therefore suitable for radioactive waste repository disposition after suitable conditioning.

In this study we have presented new homology models of E2 and E3BP monomers of human pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (hPDC) core. We showed that the previous E2-EM model is not stable and not accurate enough. To validate our new models, extensive MD simulations were conducted on E2 and E3BP. For a more quantitative and mechanistic assessment several dynamic and structural properties such as rmsd, rmsf, R g , and secondary structure analysis were carried out. Overall, both models, especially the E2 model, showed very good structural stability and consistency within the extended simulation time in comparison to the low-resolution cryo-EM model (E2-EM). The active site of the new E2 model showed a much higher stability (rmsf = 0.16 nm) than that of E2-EM (rmsf = 0.30 nm). Further the protein interactions and the anchoring effect were studied in dimers of E2 and E3BP where the monomers were oriented as in a 60-meric core to mimic the same interactions. The anchoring effect was observed by simulation of wild-type (WT) and truncated E2 (E2-t8) and E3BP (E3BP-t7) versions. In both WT subunit dimers, the original orientation was well preserved and the C-terminals were tightly bound to the hydrophobic pockets. On the contrary, upon elimination of the C-terminals, within a short simulation time the two monomers lost their mutual orientation in both cases and detached from their binding pockets. The detachment was shown by the distance increase between the C-terminals and the hydrophobic pockets in E2-t8 and E3BP-t7 in comparison to those in WT. Further, a dramatic decrease in the number of hydrophobic interactions in the truncated versions proved a dominant hydrophobic force in the dimers interaction and in the core assembly. This phenomenon is shown for the first time from our simulations at the molecular level for hPDC subunits. The results correlate well with earlier experimental investigations on other PDC species with 20 identical E2 containing trimers; for human PDC however, no experimental proof was reported so far. In our group experimental work is ongoing in this direction, and our preliminary results indicate the disassembly of hPDC for several double truncations, e.g.. E2-t8 and E3BP-t7, for the first time (data not shown).

Our atomistic models will serve as a starting point for building higher-scale models of the hPDC core and complex system, i.e.. at coarse-grained and meso scale, which will allow exploring them on a scale of different order of magnitude in size and time for the design of multienzyme systems. This will further enable targeted manipulation of such complex enzyme system and thus create the foundation for the synthesis of artificial complexes and enzyme cascade in the future.

Through these studies, a new set of bioconjugation reactions has been developed based on oxidative coupling pathways. Many of these reactions are the first of their kind, providing both useful methods for synthetic group attachment and design leads for future strategies. Taken as a whole, these methods offer a particularly attractive set of features. First, they exhibit very high coupling rates, with typical reactions occurring in 2-20 min even at micromolar concentrations. This capability avoids prolonged exposure to the reaction conditions, minimizes opportunities for biomolecule denaturation, and is highly advantageous for time-critical applications, such as radiolabeling. In addition, the rapid rates of these reactions are only minimally influenced by steric factors, allowing the efficient coupling of full-sized biomolecules in similar amounts of time. Our studies have indicated that the products are highly stable with respect to hydrolysis, reducing agents, oxidants, and strong nucleophiles. The oxidative strategies described herein also rely on easily prepared, inherently water-soluble functional groups and use oxidants that can be easily removed from the product mixtures. Most significantly, by subtly changing the reaction conditions, the reactant structures, or both, these methods can be used to target a variety of natural and unnatural functional groups with high selectivity, offering a greater range of substrates for which they can be used, as summarized in Figure . Considering the broad range of electron-rich aromatic and heterocyclic molecules that has yet to be explored in this chemistry, it is likely that many additional transformations can be discovered through the application of the reaction development workflow that has been established. The development of new oxidative coupling strategies and the synthesis of complex biomolecular materials through their use are proceeding apace in our laboratory.

This study has used pilot plant data and process modeling to investigate the industrial scale use of scCO2 extraction and fractionation of biocrude for the recovery of renewable chemicals from a lignin-rich HTL biocrude.

It was confirmed through pilot plant extraction and fractionation trials that it is possible to effectively model the extraction characteristics of a multicomponent biocrude by a series of individual solute-solvent binary interaction parameters regressed from experimental VLE data.

Aspen Plus process and economic models of four design scenarios were developed to compare supercritical extraction with conventional distillation of biocrude. These models indicated that two-stage scCO2 extraction of biocrude combined with multiple-stage evaporation to remove water and recover catechol (process scenario P-1) generates 16.7% and 11.8% more total profit annually than SFE single stage (P-2) and distillation combined with evaporation (P-4), respectively. Distillation alone (P-3) did not produce any profit, rather gave a negative value for annual total profits of about 6.3 million USD. At base plant capacity of 22.8 tonne/hr, however the IRR values of 15.0%, 14.7%, -2.1% and 15.3% were obtained for P-1, P-2, P-3 and P-4, respectively. Solvent/biocrude ratio will have considerable impact on total profits of SFE process in relation to distillation combined with multistage evaporation.

These results suggest two main areas of future investigation to further improve the profitability of industrial scale scCO2 recovery of chemicals from biocrude: 1. HTL production of biocrude should be tailored to produce fewer compounds but in large amounts rather than more compounds in small amounts. This will simplify the postextraction treatment for further purification of products. 2. Modeling of the scCO2 extraction (i.e.. prefractionation) process itself is needed to identify extraction conditions with improved yields and product composition profiles.

An Omicron STM chamber was used to obtain STM images, and a preparation chamber connected to the STM chamber was used for sample cleaning, annealing, and catalyst surface preparation by vapor deposition. A Cu(111) single crystal (Princeton Scientific Corp) was cleaned by repeated cycles of Ar+ ion sputtering followed by annealing at 850 K. Zr was vapor-deposited using a commercial metal evaporator (Scienta Omicron). Two different vapor deposition pathways were applied to investigate the growth modes of ZrO2 on Cu(111): (1) Zr was vapor-deposited on Cu(111) at 300 K and then oxidized at 600 K in a 5 × 10-7 Torr oxygen ambient and (2) Zr was vapor-deposited on preoxidized CuO x /Cu (111) at 600 K in a 5 × 10-7 Torr oxygen ambient. Deposition of Zr on preoxidized CuO x /Cu (111) without O2 in the background led to oxygen-deficient systems, which have to be oxidized to get ZrO2/CuO x /Cu (111). All STM images were obtained at room temperature, using a Pt-Ir tip.

XPS analysis was performed to follow the oxidation state of zirconium using a commercial SPECS chamber for ambient-pressure X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (AP-XPS) equipped with a PHOIBOS 150 EP MCD-9 analyzer (Mg Kα X-ray source) and a homebuilt XPS with a Scienta SES 100 spectrometer (Al Kα X-ray source), which are located at the Chemistry Division in Brookhaven National Laboratory. Zr was vapor-deposited on Cu(111) or preoxidized CuO x /Cu (111) surface at the same conditions as those used for the STM samples. For the XPS spectra, Zr 3d, Cu 2p, O 1s, and C 1s regions were collected for each surface. The binding energies were calibrated by the position of Cu 2p. The Zr or ZrO x coverage was determined by attenuation of the primary peak of the Cu substrate. The XPS spectra of the samples were collected under UHV (10-9-10-10 Torr) or under an O2 pressure of ~1 × 10-6 Torr.

The structural confinement effects of hydrophobic [C6mim] [PF6] entrapped in the hydrophilic nanopores of silica ionogels had been systematically probed. [C6mim] [PF6]-based silica ionogels were manufactured through a nonhydrolytic IL-based sol-gel route with TEOS as precursor and formic acid solvolysis. In the investigated systems, SAXS and BET had identified that three distinct pore morphologies (i.e.. H2-type nanopores with various radiuses, H3-type slit-shaped capillary nanopores with board sizes, and H4-type narrow slit-like nanopores) embedded within the fractal silica framework could be constructed through mediating n IL/n TEOS ratios. Neat [C6mim] [PF6] molecules would self-organize into a nanoscale segregation in the bulk, leading to a observable low-Q peak at scattering vector q = 3.67 nm-1 in the WAXS profile measured here and a characteristic length of 1.71 nm. H2 and H4 nanopores would destroy this nanoscale segregation of confined ILs, originating from narrow pore sizes; however, the broad H3 pores could allow the existence of nanoscale segregation of confined [C6mim] [PF6] even subject to the rough topography on wall surface. Furthermore, the confined [C6mim] [PF6] molecules within H3 nanopores also exhibited a more close packing than bulk ones, as evidenced by the smaller characteristic lengths of 1.55-1.65 nm than that of bulk one (see inset in Figure ). It is believed that the repulsive interfacial interactions between anionic [PF6]- and silanol cause this press of confined IL. Besides, the change of pore morphologies embedded within the ionogels with various n IL/n TEOS ratios is postulated driven by the minimization of the [PF6]-/silanol repulsive interfacial energy and IL release entropy gain.

This paper proposes to use probabilistic graphical model for process monitoring. A graphical model can be constructed using process knowledge or identified from data using different techniques. Different from a previous work, this paper decomposes the graphical structure into a hierarchical structure using the conditional dependency among variables. The joint density of process variables can then be transferred into multiplication of several conditional densities and a low dimensional density. The conditional density can be estimated from data using a nonparametric kernel method and the low dimensional density can be estimated using KDE. As compared to other work, this method is distribution free; it is more capable in localizing the faulty variables. Application to a blast furnace iron-making process shows that the proposed method can better isolate the faulty variables than PCA-based contribution plots.

The evolution of electronic states on the surface and in the near surface area for NaF on air-deposited and annealed PCBM and P3HT films has been investigated, and a concentration depth profile for a thick layer of NaF on both organic materials was obtained. The salt did not appear to dissociate or induce doping in the organic materials. Changes in the interfacial dipole between the salt and organic layer was observed for both PCBM and P3HT. Within the probing depth of XPS, the dipole changes are similar to those observed for LiF2. No contaminants were observed in XPS; however, it is suspected that trace amounts of water were present in the salt upon deposition as indicated by the MIES results. This appeared at the outermost layer for both deposition methods. There was a significant difference occurring in the near surface area when sequential depositions were performed as compared to a single thick NaF deposition as indicated by UPS. The single thick deposition of NaF revealed DOS similar to that seen in the literature, whereas the sequential depositions appeared to be more complex and attributed to a convolution of changes in the interfacial dipole along with possible water trapped by this deposition method. The interfacial dipole appeared to be affected by the deposition method at the outermost layer as well, with the sequential depositions inducing the outward facing component of the dipole parallel to the surface normal to become more positive for NaF/P3HT and less positive for NaF/PCBM. Although the possible water content is clearly undesirable for OPV devices, the changes in interfacial dipole induced by the deposition method could have an effect on charge injection in OPV devices as the dipole is one of the proposed and accepted mechanisms enhancing electron injection into the electrode. We believe further experiments with testing devices would only be appropriate for thin NaF layers, as the thick layers were seen to induce fluorination of the organic materials and damage the conjugated π states of PCBM. This fluorination of the organic materials and lacking conjugated structure in the fullerene with thick layers of NaF could possibly be part of the reason for the drastic differences in device efficiency noted in Ahlswede's work for thick layers of LiF versus NaF, with LiF being clearly superior for device function when a thicker interlayer was used. The enhanced ability of NaF (compared to LiF) to induce an electron redistribution within the organic materials could possibly be related to the enhanced performance of devices for thin layers of salt; however, further experiments involving electrode deposition are required to observe how the electronic redistributions change once the electrode material is present.

The growth mechanism of the NaF appeared to be similar to that observed for LiF2 as shown in the NICISS results, and it is concluded that films of the salt grow in an island-like manner, but diffusion also possibly occurs.

A concentration-swing frequency response apparatus was used to study diffusion rates of several C10 hydrocarbons in BPL activated carbon. Micropore diffusion was the rate limiting mass transfer mechanism for each adsorbate at various concentrations. Predicted local isotherm slopes from the CSFR experiments agreed well with those calculated from adsorption isotherms for hydrocarbon molecules. The diffusion coefficients were found to be highly concentration dependent, and a Darken analysis was used to predict a lower limit for diffusivity in the Henry's law regime. The lower limit of the diffusivity of C10 hydrocarbons in BPL activated carbon at room temperature is about 1 × 10-12 m2/s, although values can be orders of magnitude faster at higher concentrations. For the molecules studied, the order from fastest to slowest diffusion was n-decane > limonene > perfluorodecalin > decalin > α-pinene. QSAR correlations were performed to relate diffusivity to specific molecular descriptors. Size exclusion based sieving effects were not observed as the wide pore size distribution of BPL activated carbon was larger than any molecular dimensions. However, molecular shape factors based on rigidity of ring structures showed good correlation with diffusivity, with the more rigid molecules diffusing more slowly.

In this study, new potential chitosan-based surfactants for bitumen emulsions were introduced. At first, the controlled depolymerization of chitosan was investigated to reach the cationic head of the future surfactant suitable for further functionalization. Thus, the functionalization of COS-oxime by different fatty epoxides including epoxidized cardanol, a reaction that as far as we know was never described in the literature before, was investigated. Oligomers with DP5, DP10, and DP15 grafted with cardanol were obtained with a maximum DS of 12, 8, and 2%, respectively. It was shown that direct oil-in-water (60/40) emulsions stable for 24-48 h, with 15 μm medium size droplets can be obtained with DP10-cardanol acting as a surfactant. To improve the stability of emulsions, the amount of surfactant could be increased to reach a higher quantity of active species. Studies on pH influence might also be led.

This work showed a way to obtain potentially biobased and biodegradable COS amphiphilic structures that have been of great interest in these last decades. These products have proved their potential for cationic surfactant substitution in bitumen emulsion applications.

In this paper, VMQ foams reinforced by chemically reduced graphene (rGO) and 3-aminopropyl triethoxysilane functionalized graphene (FG) were prepared and their cell morphology, mechanical properties, and deformation recovery capability were compared. The FTIR, XRD, and XPS results characterized the structures of rGO and FG. Rheological results showed that the matrix strength was improved about 2 times by rGO and 6 times by FG owing to the stronger compatibility and interaction between FG and the silicone rubber matrix. The higher matrix strength was helpful in preventing the shrinkage of cell walls so that the cell size of VMQ/FG foams was larger than that of VMQ/rGO foams under the same foaming conditions. At 1 wt % graphene loading, the density of VMQ/FG foam is one-third of the VMQ/rGO foam. Meanwhile, the great improvement in matrix strength of VMQ/FG foam contributed to resisting the external pressure better than VMQ/rGO foam so that the specific compression strength of VMQ/rGO foam and VMQ/FG foam increased to 0.85 MPa cm3/g and 1.21 MPa cm3/g from 0.62 MPa cm3/g of the pure sample. Moreover, VMQ/FG foams showed better deformation recovery capability with 2% permanent compression set and could recover in less than 0.5 h after constant shape variable (50%) and certain temperature (70 °C) treatment. In addition, VMQ/FG foam exhibited improvements in tensile strength (130%) and the corresponding elongation at break (140%) compared to VMQ/rGO foams. The silicone rubber foam with good resilience prepared via this method has good application prospects in high and low temperature scenarios.

There is a clear need for efficient computational algorithms for the uncertainty analysis of gene expression models. In this work, we proposed and investigated new approaches for Bayesian parameter inference of stochastic gene expression parameters from single-cell data. We employed adaptive tuning of proposal distributions in addition to delayed acceptance MCMC and reduced-order modeling. Numerical tests confirmed that the reduced models can be used to significantly speed up the sampling process without incurring much loss in accuracy. While we have only focused on smFISH data in this work, we plan to extend our algorithm to other types of data such as time-course trajectories using time-lapse fluorescence microscopy, for higher-throughput but lower precision single-cell measurements available using flow cytometry, and eventually for lower throughput but higher content data using single-cell sequencing.

In this study, we have primarily focused on the effect of the imidazolium cation tail length on the nanostructural reorganization and dynamics of [R n mim] [Ac]/water binary mixtures, and their consequent influence on the anomalous densities of this IL family. We observed that the density change exhibited by different ILs of this family could be clearly demarcated into two regimes (Figure ). While the increased structuring among the polar components (cation headgroup, anion, and water) led to the initial rise in density in the first regime (X w ≤ 0.5), the role of the alkyl tail became evident in the second regime of higher water concentrations. As a result, the density of [emim] [Ac]/water binary mixtures showed a turnover at X w = 0.5, whereas, for longer-tailed [bmim] and [hmim] cations, the turnover was shifted to X w > 0.7 (see Figures , , and ). As evident from Figures and , the spatial correlation in the polar domain maximizes at X w = 0.5, beyond which the nanostructuring continues to grow only in cations with longer alkyl chains due to water-induced tail aggregation (Figures - and Figures S4-S6, Supporting Information). This differential nanostructuring caused by varying cation tail lengths could explain the different turnover points in the measured densities of [emim] [Ac]/water and [bmim] [Ac]/water binary mixtures. ,

Acetate anion-water interactions were found to play a key role in structuring the polar domain of the binary mixtures in agreement with earlier studies. , An in-depth analysis showed that the pattern of these interactions changed with water concentration, which intricately controlled not only the initial rise but also the subsequent turnover in density of [R n mim] [Ac]/water binary mixtures. When present in low concentrations, isolated water molecules occupy locations between adjacent anions and form water-mediated hydrogen bonded anion bridges (Figure a). As more and more hydrogen bonded bridges are formed (Table ), the spatial correlation among the IL anions (and consequently among the cation head groups) increases, leading to a steady rise in density up to X w ~ 0.5. Upon further dilution, the incoming water disrupts the water-mediated anion bridges and increasingly forms bifurcated anion-water hydrogen bonds, leading to decreased anion structuring and a decline in the density. However, this density turnover is shifted to higher concentration in longer-tailed cations, due to water-induced tail aggregation, as described above. The dynamics of these mixtures also exhibited a similar turnover at moderate water concentration.
We found that the effects of Fe3+ on arsenopyrite oxidative dissolution are threefold.

In summary, a porosity modulation approach was successfully developed for the synthesis of a series of 2D COFs for efficient volatile iodine adsorption. Based on separation results, we found that the iodine uptake capacities on COFs were not only determined by their pore volumes but also significantly related to intrinsic pore sizes. Both should be regulated simultaneously to work in concert when designing new COFs adsorbents. The resultant optimized COF with a pore volume of 0.84 cm3 g-1 and pore size of 4 nm exhibits a high-performance iodine uptake of 4.0 g g-1 at 75 °C and under ambient pressure, where full pore access of iodine can be successfully achieved. We anticipated that this study could help to get a better understanding of volatile iodine adsorption on porous crystalline COFs and evidently advance their separation applications.

The high-pressure phase transition behavior of [C4mim] [I] was investigated using high-pressure Raman spectroscopy. We observed a peculiar phase transition in [C4mim] [I] under high pressure: liquid phase → high-pressure glassy phase → partial crystalline phase. Therefore, the present results provide new type of high-pressure behavior of ILs in the scientific community on high-pressure systems. The reddish-brown precipitate was probably due to concentrated I3 - and/or I2 species that were observed above 12 GPa. The conformation of [C4mim]+ is essential to control the formation of iodide precipitations by iterative modulation. Up to 16.7 GPa, [C4mim] [I] showed pressure-induced partial crystallization from the glassy state. Of note, a polyiodide-like reaction without additional I2 is possible under external pressure. As mentioned in the Introduction, polyiodide formation may be important for the application of ILs in DSSCs. Regarding additional pressure-induced reactions in ILs, Ribeiro and co-workers , have reported a polymerization reaction of the allyl group in allylimidazolium-based ILs with iodide and dicyanamide. Combined with these results, we believe that the investigation of chemical reaction of ILs under high pressure is expected to contribute to the development of high-pressure synthesis techniques using ILs.

The development of in vivo monitoring strategies for biologically important species in brain chemistry is challenging but required for progress in understanding the roles that biomolecules play in pathological and physiological processes. Rationally tailoring functional surfaces, as well as designing specific molecules, has greatly improved the sensitivity and selectivity of biosensors for distinguishing between biomolecules and fulfilling the demanding requirements for in vivo measurements. The electrochemical ratiometric strategy has established fascinating approaches for the in vivo quantification of Cu2+, pH, O2, and glucose with high accuracy.
