Our TPD studies reveal how the H coverage and desorption temperature track with the alloy surface structure. This work provides a fundamental understanding of ensemble effects in Pt-Cu alloys on the uptake and release of H2. This in turn yields guiding principles for the design of Pt-Cu alloy catalysts that maximize the efficient low-temperature uptake, spillover, and release of hydrogen while minimizing the amount of precious metal required to activate hydrogen.

Two independent trials of periphyton exposed to a single pulse of 1, 5, 10, and 20 μg L-1 arsenate resulted in consistent decreases in dissolved As concentrations. Dissolved As concentrations dropped rapidly over the first few days of exposure and stabilized at roughly 50% of their initial concentrations (Figure A,C) by days 2-4. Uptake of As into periphyton was not monotonic and did not always mirror dissolved As concentrations. In both trials, the periphyton exhibited transient periods of decreasing As concentrations (Figure B,D). In trial 1, this occurred briefly at days 4-5 before increasing again and reaching its maximum fold increase relative to water (6,000-9,000-fold) (Figure A). Ratios of periphyton As to mean dissolved As decreased with increasing dissolved As concentrations. In trial 2, the maximum As bioconcentration was observed on day 4 (4,200-5,400) but decreased to 3,200-4,200 by day 10 (Figure B). Ratios of periphyton As to mean dissolved As were more consistent in this trial and did not trend with dissolved concentrations.

To test whether periphyton-bioconcentrated As was trophically available to an invertebrate grazer, we reared the mayfly N. triangulifer on the periphyton diets described above along with residual aqueous As (see SI for dietary and aqueous exposure characterization). Very low radioactivity was measured in the larvae corresponding to 0.0006-0.005 μg of As per individual (Figure ). Although these individuals were not weighed to avoid handling stress, if we assume approximately 1 mg dry weight (average for developmental stage), we estimate that tissue As concentrations were 18-35% lower than As concentrations in periphyton, suggesting significant biodilution. When assayed again as subimagos, radioactivity could not be detected and, therefore, As concentration could not be quantified.

Assimilation efficiencies (AE) of As from periphyton in N. triangulifer and other invertebrate grazers varied among species tested (Figure ). N. triangulifer had the lowest assimilation efficiency (22 ± 8.5%) followed by Pleurocera sp. (28 ± 10%), Corbicula fluminea (57 ± 12.7%), Maccaffertium sp. (60 ± 13.2%), and Isonychia sp. (75 ± 8.5%). Hydropsyche betteni did not acquire enough radioactivity from labeled periphyton until 15 h of exposure and therefore only had 8 h on clean food for excretion. Thus, our estimate of 71 ± 6% as an AE for this species may be an overestimate and is not included in Figure .

Periphyton treated with arsenate by static renewal for 5 days and analyzed using X-ray fluorescence mapping (XRF) revealed that As was not strongly correlated with Si, P, S, K, Ca, Ti, Mn, Cu, or Zn (data not shown). Conversely, As and Fe were largely colocalized across the sample area analyzed (Figure A) and showed a strong correlation (R = 0.92; Figure B).

Biological fluids, such as serum or plasma, contain a multitude of peptides, proteins, lipid, DNA, and other molecular components that may complicate characterization of PEGylated products by mass spectrometry. To address this issue, a sample clean up step is generally required to completely or partially remove interfering substances before mass spectrometry analysis. These procedures can be labor intensive, particularly when attempting to obtain intact mass information of large molecules present at low ng/mL levels. Our method circumvents complicated sample cleanup steps, allowing direct collection of intact molecular weight information of PEGylated products in biological fluids. Following removal of contaminating debris by either centrifugation or treatment with acetonitrile and centrifugation, biological fluids containing PEGylated products are directly analyzed using RP-LC/MS with a postcolumn addition of DEMA. Samples are injected under mobile phase conditions employing a high level of acetonitrile (approximately 50%) to resolve the PEGylated products from biological components.

Figure shows the total ion chromatograms obtained for monkey serum or 2 mg/mL BSA solution spiked with 10 μg/mL of 15, 20, 30, and 40K free PEG, 15 and 20K PEGylated 6K Peptide, and 20K PEGylated Lys. The control sample, containing only monkey serum (Figure d), showed one peak in the retention time window of the PEGylated products, while seven peaks were detected for the spiked monkey sera without (Figure a) or with (Figure b) acetonitrile precipitation prior to the injection. A similar elution profile was obtained for the PEGylated products spiked into PBS buffer containing BSA (Figure c). The peak detected in the control sample was also found in the spiked monkey sera and eluted close to the 15K PEGylated peptide peak. No specific ions at significant levels above baseline were detected (see Figure ), and it was concluded that this peak does not interfere with the characterization and quantitation of the 15K PEGylated product.

Plasma or serum contains hundreds of proteins with a broad dynamic range from <10 pg/mL (interleukin) to >10 mg/mL albumin that can possibly interfere with the intact mass detection of PEGylated products. , Despite these complexities, our methodology does not suffer from limitations with analyte detection. Two chemical principles make it possible for a simple reversed phase HPLC step to remove almost all serum proteins and capture the PEGylated products of interest for mass spectrometry analysis. First, PEGylated products are very soluble in water or in water-acetonitrile mixtures, but they are also very hydrophobic allowing favorable interactions with the reversed phase column resin. Most of the serum or plasma proteins do not bind to the column resin if the samples are injected at more than 45% acetonitrile in the mobile phase. Second, lipids, fats, or hydrophobic low mass molecules in the plasma or serum will bind to the resin but they either need a much higher percentage of acetonitrile to elute from the column or their ions are in a lower m/z range than PEGylated products when analyzed following postcolumn addition of DEMA. While the plasma or serum samples containing PEGylated products could be directly injected for LC/MS analysis, it is preferable to mix the sample with acetonitrile in a ratio of 1:1 (v/v) to precipitate plasma or serum proteins before the injection to avoid potential clogging of the HPLC system.

These spiking studies also provide insight into the range of pegylated products that can be evaluated with our methodology. As shown in Figure , the 20K PEGylated 6K Peptide eluted earlier than 20K PEGylated Lys, while 20K free PEG eluted last. This interesting elution profile whereby PEGylated products containing larger peptide or protein molecules conjugated to a constant PEG size have shorter retention times on reversed phase columns has been previously observed. On the basis of this published data and the results of the spiking studies reported here, our method is suitable for analyzing peptides and proteins conjugated with PEG in the size range of 15 to 40K. Since molecular design strategies typically employ PEGs of this size, our method is broadly applicable to most peptide or protein products.

Further studies were conducted to assess method capability. The linearity over a range of concentrations was determined by evaluating the recovery of the PEG conjugates. Samples were prepared containing varying amounts of 20K PEG-6K Peptide and 20K PEG mixed with 2 mg/mL BSA solution or monkey serum. Standard curves were prepared by plotting the known concentrations of the PEGylated conjugates and their corresponding MS signal intensities as shown in Figure . The mass intensities were extracted from the top 15 most intense mass ions corresponding to each concentration. By comparing the results obtained for samples spiked into 2 mg/mL BSA solution, the recoveries of PEGylated product were determined to be nearly complete at the range of 1 μg/mL or lower in serum. The observed sample loss may be due to surface absorption and/or slight precipitation caused by the acetonitrile sample treatment procedure beyond this range of spike concentration. These experiments also demonstrated that the limit of quantitation (signal/noise ≥10) is approximately 10-20 ng/mL PEGylated product (data not shown). It should be noted that the exact limit of detection or quantitation is dependent upon the sensitivity of the mass spectrometer or HPLC conditions (e.g.. increasing injection volume or using small diameter column) employed.

To demonstrate application of our methodology, studies were conducted using two model peptides, PPA and glucagon, each pegylated with a 20 kDa PEG moiety. These conjugates were synthesized using two different types of PEGylation chemistries. PEGylated PPA was prepared through alkylation of the sulfhydryl group of a cysteine residue with 20K mPEG-IAM. The PEGylated glucagon sample was synthesized by reacting 20K mPEG-PNP with the amino side chain of a lysine residue. Each pegylated product was characterized following incubation in serum to evaluate the effectiveness of the method for detecting specific structural changes. The results of these experiments are presented in the following sections.

We performed an in situ X-ray scattering experiment to reveal the behavior of the FL-MoS2 flakes during the Langmuir film formation. Relying on the evaluation of the width of the pole figure profile and surface pressure during the compression, five principal stages of the Langmuir film formation were identified. During stage I, the MoS2 flakes are randomly distributed and the film compression does not lead to an increase in the surface pressure. No tilting of MoS2 flakes affecting the pole figure width was observed. Stage II is associated with a slight increase in the surface pressure, elastic modulus, and width of the tilt angle distribution of the FL-MoS2 flakes. During this stage, the FL-MoS2 flakes agglomerate into islands and start to collide, forming a continuous (closed) layer at the end of this stage. At stage III, the surface pressure and elastic modulus increase rapidly with further compression. A significant broadening of the distribution of the flake tilts is observed as the increasing surface pressure forces the flakes to flip up and slide onto each other. During stage IV, the surface pressure reaches the critical pressure Πc for the monolayer collapse. A maximum in the elastic modulus and the saturation of the broadening in the flake tilt distribution are observed, and the formation of a second layer relaxing the accumulated stress starts. Subsequently, at stage V, the increase in the surface pressure is slowed-down, the elastic modulus drops rapidly, and the flake tilt distribution evolution is reversed, becoming narrower.

After the transfer of the Langmuir film in the fourth stage close to the critical surface pressure Πc onto a solid substrate, a narrowing of the flake tilt distribution and uniaxial texture improvement was observed. This improvement is caused by the stress relaxation during the free drying of the transferred film on the solid substrate, i.e.. without the force action of the barriers.

Summarizing, the results obtained explain in detail the formation and collapse of the Langmuir film of the rigid FL-MoS2 flakes, which is different from the behavior of conventional organic molecular Langmuir films. The results and conclusions can be extended to a large family of inorganic Langmuir films of other rigid 2D materials with direct implications for the optimization of the deposition process depending on the envisaged application.

Four new polyaramides have been efficiently prepared by postpolymerization modification via a simple esterification reaction of poly (hexafluoroisopropylidene hydroxyisophthalamide) (PA) with acid chlorides under mild conditions. In this approach, a wide variety of acid chlorides with bulky pendant groups can be employed to tailor a variety of polymeric structures otherwise not obtainable. Furthermore, the synthesized polyamides exhibit good solubility and processability for film preparation in most common aprotic solvents, and they also show high mechanical and thermal stability. Depending on the bulky pendant group, the synthesized polyamides were highly permeable (13.2-31.4 times higher for CO2) and more permselective (3.4-4.5 times higher for CO2/CH4 and 2.0-2.3 times higher CO2/N2) in comparison with the precursor polyamide, PA. Gas-induced plasticization over the pressure range up to 10.17 bar tested was not observed. Thus, the postpolymerization method will be useful in the evaluation of structure-property relationship, incorporating more bulky and rigid pendant groups, to enhance gas transport through the membranes.

As shown in Figure , the experimental SOPLIM setup is in fact a modified laser-scanning confocal FLIM. It consists of six subsystems: the inverted microscope (Olympus IX81, Japan), the scanner (B&H DCS120 system, Germany), the 405-nm picosecond pulsed laser, the detectors D1, D2, and D3, the ultrafast time-correlated single photon counting (TCSPC) system (B&H Simple-Tau-153-DX-7, Germany), and the PC and software (B&H SPC-Image, Germany). The inverted microscope provides the stage and the objective. The objective focuses the excitation laser (bold solid line) coming out of the scanner onto the sample lying on the stage, and the resulted fluorescence (bold and thin dash line) and SOP (thin solid line) are then collected by the same objective and sent into the scanner along the light path of the excitation laser. Controlled by the scan controller card that is installed in the PC, the scanner guides the excitation laser emitted from the 405-nm picosecond pulsed laser to the objective, and the resulted fluorescence (bold and thin dash line) and SOP (thin solid line) to the detectors D1, D2, and D3 respectively. Detector D1 is a liquid-nitrogen-cooled infrared photomultiplier tube (IR-PMT R5509-43, Hamamatsu, Japan) and is used together with an 800-nm cutoff filter glass to specifically detect the SOP in the wavelength range of 1240-1340 nm. Detectors D3 (HPM-100-50, B&H, Germany) and D2 (HPM-100-40, B&H, Germany), with their response wavelength ranges being 380-890 nm and 300-720 nm, respectively, are high-speed hybrid PMT detectors and used to detect the UV-visible fluorescence from the sample. Point-scanning function is realized when the galvanometer mirror of the scanner moves the focus of laser on the focal plane of the objective by altering the direction of the laser beam. After entering into the scanner, the fluorescence (bold and thin dash line) and the SOP (thin solid line) pass through the pinholes and arrive at the detectors. The resulted electric signals of the detectors are then acquired by the TCSPC system. The scan controller card and the TCSPC system are driven by the PC and software, and the data acquired by the TCSPC system are handled by the software SPC-Image to simultaneously generate the intensity and lifetime images of the sample, as well as the time-dependent luminescence trace for every point of these images.

Two schemes, nonconfocal SOPLIM and confocal SOPLIM, were designed to perform SOP imaging. In nonconfocal SOPLIM scheme, detector D1 is placed at location 1, and meanwhile, a dichroic mirror DM1 that reflects infrared and transmits visible light is placed between the objective and the tube lens of the scanner to separate fluorescence and SOP; then, the SOP is focused by lens 1 onto the detector D1, and the fluorescence is conducted to detectors D2 and D3 along the optical path of the scanner. The function of lens 1 is to ensure that all the SOP reflected by the dichroic mirror DM1 can be collected by detector D1. In confocal SOPLIM scheme, the dichroic mirror DM1 and the reflecting mirror RM1 that appear in nonconfocal SOPLIM scheme are removed, and detector D1 is placed at location 2 and behind the pinhole PH1 of the scanner, and SOP needs to be transmitted in the scanner before it is detected by the detector D1. This is the simplest scheme for upgrading a FLIM to a SOPLIM, for the confocal SOPLIM is no more than a general FLIM in which one of its detection channels that should have been used to detect fluorescence is changed to detect SOP. Compared to the confocal SOPLIM, the advantage of the nonconfocal SOPLIM lies in that the SOP can be detected as much as possible because the SOP loss in the scanner has been avoided.

The sample on the stage is a layer of loose C60 powder (purity 99.9%, Sigma-Aldrich), formed by randomly splashing C60 powder over a slide (see Figure ). The reason C60 is selected lies in that (1) solid C60 itself is a high efficient sensitizer and very easy to produce O2(a 1Δg) under ambient atmosphere. (2) According to ref , the O2 molecules in C60 solid are trapped in the octahedral interstices of the face-centered-cubic lattice, and the time needed for O2 molecules diffusing out of a C60 film with 200 Å thickness is as long as about 40 s (half-life) at room temperature. Thus, it can be considered that the number of O2(a 1Δg) molecules produced in a point is "fixed" during the period (28.8 ms, see below) when the SOP lifetime is measured for this point. Therefore, the spatial heterogeneity of C60 sample can be labeled with the distribution of O2(a 1Δg), or in other words, the singlet oxygen imaging for C60 sample becomes possible. The photoluminescence of C60 (C60-PL) is a kind of fluorescence. The C60-PL in 600-900 nm range is detected by the detector D3, and other luminescence shorter than 600 nm is detected by the D2. The numerical aperture and magnification of the objective (UPLSAPO, Olympus, Japan) are 0.16 and 4×, respectively. The pulse width and repetition rate of the picosecond pulsed laser are about 100 ps and 80 MHz, respectively. Measured with a power meter, the laser power at the focus of the objective is 0.187 mW, corresponding to 2.34 pJ/pulse.

The spectra of SOP and C60-PL were acquired in nonconfocal SOPLIM scheme by using an IR-CCD spectrograph that substituted for the detector D1 at location 1. The IR-CCD spectrograph consists of a monochromator (SpectraPro-2500i, Acton Research Co.. USA) and a liquid-nitrogen-cooled infrared charge coupled device (IR-CCD) camera (7498-0001, Acton Research Co.. USA). When the spectrum of SOP was acquired, an 800-nm cutoff filter glass was placed in front of the IR-CCD spectrograph to eliminate the interference of the second-order diffraction of visible light on grating; and when the spectrum of C60-PL was acquired, the filter was removed and meanwhile the dichroic mirror DM1 was replaced by a 50/50 beam splitter.

The C60-PL lifetime was measured by TCSPC technique. Note that the laser pulse period is 12.5 ns. It is out of question to measure the C60-PL lifetime (several hundred picoseconds, see below) and a general fluorescence lifetime (several nanoseconds order) under the repetition rate of 80 MHz. However, TCSPC technique is not suitable for the SOP lifetime measurement because the SOP lifetime in C60 powder is as long as several milliseconds (see below), much longer than the pulse period. Fortunately, the technique that simultaneously records the lifetime images of short-lifetime fluorescence and long-lifetime phosphorescence in a laser scanning system has been maturely commercialized at present. Here it is briefly described as follows. Suppose that the resident time of laser beam at a point is T pxl. T pxl can be divided into two parts, T on and T off, that is T pxl = T on + T off, and T off is much greater than T on. Within the time of T on, the laser is turned on and the short fluorescence lifetime is measured with TCSPC technique, and meanwhile the luminophor of the phosphorescence is accumulated on the irradiation of the laser; then, within the time of T off, the laser is turned off and the luminophor of the phosphorescence accumulated within the time of T on begins to decay, and the corresponding phosphorescence decay trace is recorded by the multichannel scaler integrated in the TCSPC system.

In summary, the hybrid structure TiO2-G/TiO2 NRAs:Eu3+, Tb3+ /Cs2CO3 /CdS was successfully synthesized. The results revealed that TiO2-G/TiO2 NRAs:Eu3+, Tb3+ /Cs2CO3 /CdS shows significantly enhanced photocatalytic activity compared to other samples. The success is attributed to the much improved electron-hole separation and light utilization of the TiO2-G/TiO2 NRAs:Eu3+, Tb3+ /Cs2CO3 /CdS. The improvement of performance for photocatalysis gives us a new insight on studying photocatalytic materials. Furthermore, the photocatalysts grown on carbon textiles make the collection and recycle of photocatalysts much easier.

By combining three complementary surface characterization techniques (SEM, OEMS, and XPS), we elucidated the interfacial reaction mechanisms for Pred-based electrodes during the first lithiation. We observed three main phenomena: (i) the release of phosphine gas (PH3) caused by multiple surface reactions; (ii) electrolyte reduction; and (iii) surface layer passivation (i.e.. the formation of an SEI). We demonstrated that the native surface layer composed of P2O5 reacts with water traces (present in the organic electrolyte) to form a highly reactive layer of H3PO4. Once this process is initiated, it will generate an electrochemical reduction leading to Pred and water, which will then react further to regenerate H3PO4. This process will continue until reaching potential below 1 V, where the SEI starts to be formed. The thickness and insulating character of the SEI inhibit PH3 gas release. Combining different surface sensitive techniques leads to understand the changes in the electrode/electrolyte interface during cycling in order to properly engineer and stabilize this interface and prevent gas releases that would raise concerns over battery safety.

The feasibility of using a novel nano gemini imidazolium IL surfactant, namely 1,1′-(butane-1,4-diyl) bis (3-octyl-1H-imidazol-3-ium) bromide, for reducing the IFT of crude oil/water was studied. The synthesized gemini IL was characterized and a nanosize structure was revealed.

The used IL gives low IFT values for the system owing to its unique molecular structure. Temperature assists this phenomenon at low IL concentrations, whereas no sensible change was attained at concentrations close to the cmc. The emulsification index showed that the gemini IL could form stable emulsions, useful for CEOR applicability.

The used IL was much more effective in salty waters with very close to seawater content, which is important in utilizing seawater for enhanced oil recovery. This abnormal salt effect was attributed to the fact that salts can neutralize the positive charge of the IL head groups and ease the adsorption at the interface. In this regard, alkaline pHs provide more IFT reduction.

To reproduce the experimental data of salt-free cases, the Frumkin adsorption isotherm was applied consistently. Accordingly, the maximum interface excess and the adsorbed molecular repulsion were increased with temperature. However, an inverse variation was relevant to the adsorption tendency. The adsorption thermodynamic parameters were determined, confirming that the IL adsorption and micelle formation were spontaneous due to the freedom of the hydrophobic part of the gemini IL molecules. Associated entropy and adsorption energy show different variation trends with the IL concentration and temperature.

In summary, it can be declared that the used nano gemini imidazolium IL represents a high potential for lowering the crude oil/water IFT and that salt addition provides a synergistic effect in IFT reduction.

The synthesis of boehmite-RGO composites was accomplished, and the composites have a high surface area that is almost 20% better than that of RGO. Herein, condensation occurs between the Al-OH of boehmite and the surface -OH of GO, and the cross-linked boehmite nanorods are successfully anchored and adequately cover the surface of RGO sheets, as proven by XRD, FTIR, BET, SEM, and TEM analyses. Then, different amounts of CuO were deposited on the boehmite-RGO composites to produce CuO/γ-Al2O3-RGO adsorbents. XRD characterization confirmed that the boehmite was converted to the γ-Al2O3 phase and that CuO molecules were uniformly dispersed on the surface of the boehmite-RGO composites. Then, DBT adsorption tests were carried out with a model diesel oil and confirmed that the addition of CuO significantly enhances organosulfur uptake and results in the highest adsorption capacity reported for regenerable graphene-related materials. The regeneration stability of the CuO/γ-Al2O3-RGO adsorbent is effectively improved in comparison with that of pure RGO. All the results show that a higher absolute organosulfur capacity can be accessible by exploring methods to synthesize boehmite-RGO composites with a higher intrinsic surface area, which could be utilized as supports for transition metals and their oxides for organosulfur adsorption.

Based on the spironolactone-water-acetone ternary phase diagrams at nine temperatures from 5.0 °C to 45.0 °C, conclusions can be drawn that the stable form gradually changes from form II to hydrate with increasing water content, and the phase region of hydrate decreases as the temperature increases. The water activity and equilibrium constant were calculated and verified these conclusions. RDF plots from MD simulation explain the formation of different solid forms; water molecules have a tendency to form clusters at low water fractions while forming hydrogen bonding with spironolactone at high water fractions, which results in an anhydrate form and a hydrate form, respectively. Consequently, the desired solid forms of spironolactone can be controlled by the ternary phase diagrams when thermodynamic factors are predominant: away from the eutectic point, the stable form at corresponding solvent ratios can be obtained, whereas, at the eutectic point, form II and hydrate nucleate concomitantly at all the investigated supersaturations. However, the final form is not only controlled by thermodynamics, but also by kinetics. Around the eutectic point, concomitant nucleation occurs at high supersaturations, because of the balance between thermodynamics and kinetics, whereas the thermodynamically favored form-the hydrate-nucleates alone at low supersaturations. The results presented in this report can provide instructions to control the formation of target forms and avoid concomitant crystals, which contribute to increasing the product's quality.

In conclusion, NC-Ph3-CN molecules deposited on Cu(111) at RT form upon cooling chain and honeycomb structures that coexist. Unlike the NC-Ph5-CN molecules, which align along the second nearest neighbor directions of the substrate, the molecules with three phenyl rings are oriented along two main directions deviating from the high symmetry ones and having a relative probability that depends on the resulting bond length between CN end group and Cu coordination atom. We explain the different behavior of the two molecules through the interplay between the gain in energy obtained by forming a straight CN-Cu bond with the right length and the one given by having the phenyl rings and hydrogen and nitrogen atoms placed on favorable adsorption sites on the surface. In the case of NC-Ph3-CN the directionality of the metal coordination bond and the registry of the metal atoms with the substrate dominate over the registry of the molecule, while for NC-Ph5-CN this balance is inverted. We also investigate the properties of the LUMO and LUMO+1 for the two networks, demonstrating that the different molecular orientations influence the energy of these orbitals. Moreover, the central phenyl ring of the molecules has a tilt that depends on the molecular orientation, giving rise to distinctive appearances of molecules and to an asymmetry in the spatial distribution of the LUMO across them. As a last point, we showed the networks that are obtained upon changing the molecular coverage.

In this study, we have calculated the homolytic C-H bond cleavage of CH4 over periodic structures of [FeO]2+-ZSM-5, [Cu2(μ-O)]2+-ZSM-5, and [Cu3(μ-O)3]2+-MOR zeolites by using six known meta-GGA functionals combined with the D2 method of the dispersion correction. The reaction involves an adsorption state referred to as reactant complex (RC), a transition state (TS), and a radical intermediate state (RI). For all studied active species, the CH4 adsorption energies calculated by the SCAN-D2 and MS-D2 functionals are found to be slightly stronger than those calculated by the TPSS-D2 and RTPSS-D2 functionals due to their natural abilities to well describe weak interactions. Also, through PDOS analysis, we are able to resolve the dispute on the most favorable electronic structure of the active species where [FeIV-O]2+, [CuII 2(μ-O)]2+, and [CuII 2CuIII(μ-O)2(μ-O )]2+ are found to be the preferred electronic structures.

In the reaction over the [FeO]2+-MFI, the SCAN-D2 and MS-D2 functionals predict an RI that is more stable than RC and thus result in a lower TS, consistent with the previous computational results using the hybrid B3LYP and HSE06 functionals. , However, on the contrary, the TPSS-D2 and RTPSS-D2 functionals predict the otherwise, i.e.. RC is more stable than RI, which is consistent with our previous work using the PBE-D2 functional. To get an idea of how the energy trend should be like, we discuss the mechanism of RI formation. By performing PDOS analysis, we found that the C-H bond cleavage over the [FeO]2+ active species proceeds through the electrophilic attack (EA) mechanism where the α electron from the C-H σ orbital is transferred to the α-LUMO (Fe-O σ* antibonding orbital) of the active species, thus resulting in an elongated Fe-O single bond and reduction of the FeIV-O to a FeIII-OH species. Since it is widely known that FeIII, with its symmetry half-filled 3d5 electronic configuration, is more stable than FeIV, the formed RI (FeIII-OH + CH3) should be more stable than RC (FeIV-O + CH4). Thus, the SCAN-D2 and MS-D2 functionals, in this regard, predict a correct energy trend, owing to their ability to treat well a stretched Fe-O σ-bond, which has a mixture character of strong and intermediate-strength bonds. As a consequence of RI's high stability, TS in the EA mechanism involves an insignificant distortion of the CH4 geometry.

In contrast to the EA mechanism, the C-H bond cleavage over the [Cu2(μ-O)]2+-MFI and [Cu3(μ-O)3]2+-MOR proceeds through the hydrogen-atom transfer (HAT) mechanism where the β electron from the C-H σ orbital is transferred to the β-LUMO (CuII-O-CuII π* antibonding orbital) of the active species. However, since the [Cu3(μ-O)3]2+ species involves an oxyl (O ), the electron transfer results in a reduction of the O to an oxide (O2-), forming an RI of CuII 2CuIII(μ-O)2(μ-OH) + CH3 that preserves the stability of the Cu2+ centers. On the contrary, [Cu2(μ-O)]2+ species involves only O2-. Thus, when the electron transfer occurs, it would form an RI of CuI-OH-CuII + CH3 that is much less stable than RC due to a reduction of one of the Cu2+ centers to a less stable Cu+. This explains why O is more reactive than O2- and clarifies the critical role of radical character at the active O atom on the reactivity of the active site toward CH4 activation through the HAT mechanism. , In contrast to TS in the EA mechanism, that in the HAT mechanism involves a significant distortion of the CH4 geometry and a partial formation of the O-H bond due to an endothermic nature of the reaction from RC to RI. Observing the energy profiles for [Cu2(μ-O)]2+-MFI and [Cu3(μ-O)3]2+-MOR, we found that only the SCAN-D2 functional predicts an energy trend inconsistent with those calculated by the rest of studied meta-GGA functionals and the B3LYP and PBE-D2 functionals. ,, This discrepancy is attributed to an overestimation imposed by the SCAN-D2 functional on the Cu-O-Cu bond strengths, which causes the β-LUMO acceptor orbital to locate at a lower energy.

Overall, the SCAN-D2 and MS-D2 functionals are as good as the hybrid B3LYP functional for reasonably predicting an energy trend of the CH4 activation over the [FeO]2+-MFI. In contrast, the TPSS-D2, RTPSS-D2, and MS-D2 functionals are best for treating the CH4 activation over the [Cu2(μ-O)]2+-MFI and [Cu3(μ-O)3]2+-MOR, as they predict an activation barrier consistent with the experimental value and an energy trend consistent with the logic of reaction mechanisms described above.

The effect of high-dose gamma irradiation on the chemical composition, morphology, and vibrational and optical properties of MoS2 crystals under ambient conditions has been systematically evaluated. The deconvolution of XPS spectra as a function of radiation exposure shows that the surface of the MoS2 crystal undergoes significant oxidation via a series of intermediates to ultimately yield MoVIS y O x and sulfate species. Oxidation of MoS2 is driven by reactions involving the products of adsorbate radiolysis such as water and adventitious carbon. Moreover, edge-selective radiolytic etching of the uppermost layer of MoS2 crystals is observed after irradiation with an absorbed dose of 500 kGy, evidenced by correlative optical microscopy and Raman and PL spectroscopy. The observed etching is facilitated by the higher reactivity of active edge sites and the lower rate of reaction between the products of adsorbate radiolysis and MoS2 layers further from the interface. A blue shift and a line width decrease of the out-of-plane A 1 ′ vibrational mode are observed upon irradiation of 1 L MoS2 with an absorbed dose of 500 kGy and are attributed to p-doping. The mechanism of p-doping is expected to involve the adsorption of O2 molecules onto radiation-induced vacancies and subsequent charge-transfer interactions. Consequently, the p-doping of gamma-irradiated 1 L MoS2 significantly alters the optical properties of the crystal as A- trions are observed to dissociate into neutral A excitons. In addition to the oxidation, etching, and doping of MoS2 crystals observed at lower doses, upon irradiation with an absorbed dose of 1000 kGy, monolayer MoS2 crystals are completely etched from the substrate. Hence, our results provide fundamental insights into key radiation damage mechanisms occurring at the MoS2 crystal surface as well as the threshold of the material's radiation hardness in the ≤1000 kGy range. Additionally, we demonstrate that the radiolytic degradation of MoS2 is accelerated in the presence of adsorbed water due to the production of reactive radical species.

We conclude that gamma irradiation of MoS2 results in the adverse changes in the physical and chemical properties, which would lead to a gradual degradation of MoS2-based device performances. For example, vacancies produced by the radiation-induced displacement damage will introduce defect states within the band gap of MoS2. In FETs, such vacancies would act as scattering centers for charge carriers, thus reducing carrier mobility, while radiolytic oxidation would change the chemical composition of MoS2, resulting in deviation from the expected current-voltage characteristics of a pristine MoS2 device. In optoelectronic devices, radiation-driven doping would change the intensity of PL, i.e.. alter the quantum efficiency of the PL process, and PL emission energy of the device, i.e.. alter the wavelength of emission.

We summarize that, owing to their appreciable radiation stability, 2D MoS2-based devices are promising candidates for a variety of demanding nuclear and space applications. However, appropriate consideration must be given to protective shielding and required device operation times as well as to the presence of common adsorbates, such as water, on the surface of MoS2 during radiation exposure.

The pH-dependent and 80 pH-independent equilibrium constants of the thiol-disulfide redox reactions between glutathione and the three important biogenic thiols were determined. The pH-independent species-specific redox equilibrium constant was implemented for the first time for thiol-disulfide systems; these values characterize the redox processes at the microspecies level. The 80 different species-specific equilibrium constant values provide sound means to predict thiolate oxidizabilities, a key parameter to understand and influence oxidative stress. The delicate task of medicinal antioxidants lies in their confinement: ROS (reactive oxygen species) surplus has to be eliminated, while physiological disulfides in proteins and peptides have to be kept intact. The major difficulty in designing effective antioxidants without decomposing the physiological disulfides in biomolecules is that the redox potential of the latter could not be determined at this point in time. The correlation between the redox and acid-base properties now serves as a basis to quantify reducibility of disulfide moieties in physiological proteins and peptides, thus allowing the development of potent, selective antioxidant compounds.

In conclusion, the desire to design a molecular entity which possesses exclusively halogen and chalcogen bonding with a complete absence of hydrogen bonding and π π interactions has been accomplished. In addition, the dominance of the chalcogen bond over the halogen bond is established employing the charge density methodology, which also brings out the feature that halogen bonds are more direction prone than chalcogen bonds. This study serves as a unique example of the display of polymorphism in a system devoid of both strong and weak hydrogen bonding as well as stacking interactions.

Spectroscopic and thermodynamic studies of myoglobin in the presence of GdmCl, HGA, and dodine have been performed to understand the role of different parts of the denaturants in the unfolding of myoglobin. Gdm+, unfolds myoglobin at ~2.0 M concentration whereas the HGA and dodine denature myoglobin at millimolar (mM) and micromolar (μM) concentrations, respectively, which suggests that the increase of carbon chain on Gdm group drastically decreases the amount of denaturants for the unfolding of myoglobin. The CD data indicate that all of the denaturants decrease the secondary and tertiary contents of myoglobin and behave as chaotropic agent. However, decrease in the tertiary structure of myoglobin is significantly higher in the case of dodine and HGA than for GdmCl. Thermodynamic and spectroscopic data suggest that Gdm+ accommodates between the helices of myoglobin and breaks the hydrogen bond between the proteins during the denaturation of myoglobin. In contrast, the long alkyl chain of dodine and HGA approaches the surface of the helices of myoglobin, which creates the strong hydrophobic interaction causing the unfolding of myoglobin.

Our work bears significance in two separate aspects. First of all, we present a simple formula in terms of macroscopic parameters that empowers one to predict and quantify the presence of amplification effects in an association reaction. We show the source of this effect and its upper limit. This result could change the perception of many biological mechanisms studied in subcellular structures.

We also provide a formula to directly estimate the macroscopic association constant from nanoscale experiments. Our approach expands and potentially simplifies the analysis of complex formation in nanocompartments. It also provides mathematical tools that could help in design of experiments allowing researchers to overcome existing limitations.

The experimental setup has been described in detail in earlier work. , Here, we will present a brief summary of the main components of the apparatus and give a short explanation of the technique used to prepare the ions and record the photofragmentation electronic spectra. The protonated parent ion (ABH+ or dmaABH+) is produced in an electrospray source from a solution of water/methanol (1:1 in volume) at a concentration of 0.1 mM, containing a trace of acetic acid. We tried to observe the formation of dimers by increasing the concentration of the solution but no cluster signals were found in the mass spectrum. The ions formed in the source are injected into a cryogenically cooled Paul trap through a mass gate. It takes several tens of milliseconds to cool the ions to a temperature of about 40 K by collisions with cold He atoms pulsed into the trap. After this time, a first laser pulse is triggered and photodissociation of the cold parent ions takes place. Ionic fragments as well as the remaining parent ions can be extracted from the trap and mass-analyzed in a time-of-flight (TOF) mass spectrometer and their intensities quantified as a function of the laser wavelength. In addition, the ion fragments can be cooled by introducing a second He pulse in the trap 1 ms after the fragmentation laser pulse and probed by a second laser pulse triggered after a delay of some tens of milliseconds. Well-resolved electronic spectra of cold daughter ions can be obtained in this way. To ensure proper cooling conditions in the trap (product ion temperatures as low as those of parent ions, namely T < 40 K), a solution of benzylamine was occasionally electrosprayed in the source and the absence of vibrational hot bands in the benzylium ion (m/q = 91) spectrum (produced by photofragmentation of protonated benzylamine) was verified. One or more specific photofragments can be removed from the ion trap by exciting their axial micromotion applying specific auxiliary dipolar radiofrequencies, according to a procedure recently implemented in the setup.

Two optical parametric oscillator (OPO) lasers (EKSPLA model-NT342B) were used in the experiments, operating at a 10 Hz repetition rate and having 8 cm-1 of spectral resolution and a scanning step of 0.02 nm. The lasers were focused to a 2 mm2 spot in the trap and the OPO pulse energy was roughly 0.5 mJ.

Ab initio calculations were carried out with the TURBOMOLE program package, making use of the resolution-of-the-identity (RI) approximation to evaluate the electron-repulsion integrals. Ground state (S0) equilibrium geometries of protonated species were optimized at the MP2 (second order Møller-Plesset perturbation) level of theory using the cc-pVDZ (correlation-consistent polarized valence double-zeta) basis set. Vertical excitation energies, oscillator strengths, and equilibrium geometries of the lowest excited singlet states were computed at the CC2 (second-order approximate coupled cluster) level, because standard time-dependent DFT (density functional theory) is well-known to produce substantial errors in representing charge transfer (CT) excited states. Moreover, we have chosen the RI-CC2 method because it proved useful in describing the electronic transitions of similar aromatic ions with nitrogen functional groups. , In all the calculations the starting geometries had Cs symmetry and were constrained to distinguish between π or σ orbitals and A′ or A″ excited states. In the case of the benzenediazonium ion fragment, adiabatic excitation energies were calculated in addition to the vertical excitation values. For doing this, the energies of the ground and the first two excited states were computed for the optimized S1(A′) and S2(A′) excited state geometries, in Cs symmetry. Additional excited state optimizations were performed for this system and protonated azobenzene, relaxing the condition of maintaining Cs symmetry and allowing nonplanar geometries.

The reliability of vibrational contributions obtained from QC computations has been demonstrated in the pioneering work by Pawlowski et al. : as a matter of fact, an accuracy of 0.001 Å on bond lengths can be obtained as soon as a correlated ab initio method in conjunction with triple-ζ quality basis sets is used. Several subsequent studies have shown that methods rooted in the DFT in combination with double-ζ quality basis sets are able to reach the same accuracy at a greatly reduced computational cost, thus extending the applicability of this approach to large systems. , In particular, in ref , a systematic benchmark study on small molecules has been carried out to evaluate the performance of the B3LYP/SNSD level of theory in the derivation of vibrational corrections. This evaluation was based on the comparison with vibrational corrections computed at the CCSD (T) level in conjunction with basis sets of at least triple-ζ quality. The overall conclusion was that B3LYP/SNSD corrections lead to results that reproduce very well the best r e SE geometries. As an example, Figure collects the results for cyclobutene, the cis form of acrolein, and pyridine, thus comparing a selection of r e SE bond lengths determined using CCSD (T) and B3LYP vibrational corrections. It is observed that the bond lengths agree within 0.001 Å, with the exception of a very few specific cases. For all examples of Figure , the electronic corrections to rotational constants were also considered, which are, for example, mandatory to fulfill the planarity condition for the moments of inertia in cis-acrolein.

A key point in the determination of SE equilibrium structures is the robustness of the fitting program. Furthermore, an important step toward a widespread use of the semiexperimental approach is the availability of a user-friendly tool. Both requirements are well fulfilled by the recent "Molecular Structure Refinement" (MSR) software, which is specifically designed for computing equilibrium structures based on a nonlinear least-squares fit of the moments of inertia for a given set of isotopologues. Among the wide range of features of the MSR software, an important one is the implementation of a black-box generation of a set of totally symmetric vibrational modes (A 1 internal coordinates) to be used in the structural determination. Indeed, as pointed out by Demaison et al.. the most effective choice to describe the molecular configuration is by means of the set of A 1 coordinates selected from a set of nonredundant internal symmetry coordinates. In addition, the method of predicate observations has also been implemented in the MSR program. While the reader is referred to ref for all details, Figure shows the program structure of MSR, which is part of the virtual multifrequency spectrometer (VMS).

As a sort of conclusion, ref demonstrated that the computational bottleneck of the semiexperimental protocol, which is the calculation of the cubic force field required for vibrational corrections, could be overcome by using the B3LYP/SNSD level. Indeed, the differences in the r e SE geometrical parameters obtained using B3LYP/SNSD and CCSD (T) vibrational corrections show a nearly Gaussian distribution with standard deviation and mean absolute error of 0.0009 and 0.0007 Å for bond distances and of 0.08 and 0.05° for angles, respectively. The small standard deviations shown by B3LYP/SNSD vibrational corrections are therefore fully satisfactory for accurate geometrical parameter determinations, the values given above being clearly comparable with the intrinsic errors of the fitting procedure itself. The evaluation of r e SE for a set of 47 molecules containing the most common organic moieties led to the definition of a database of accurate molecular geometries, , the so-called B3se database, to be used as references for benchmark calculations as well as for the validation of low-level models affordable for large systems. In particular, refs and made use of the B3se database for benchmarking recently developed density functionals. In subsequent studies, it has been shown that even better results can be obtained employing the B2PLYP functional in conjunction with a triple-ζ basis set (B2se set), and the database was extended to compounds containing sulfur. The reader is referred to the database Web site (http://smart.sns.it/molecules/), where all information can be downloaded.

Even if the topic will not be further addressed, it is worthwhile mentioning that semiexperimental equilibrium constants can also be used for benchmarking low level, in particular DFT, models. A significant example in this respect is provided by ref . The last comment concerns other experimental techniques for structural determinations, which also suffer from the proper analysis of vibrational effects. Among them, gas-phase electron diffraction and X-ray crystallography deserve a particular mention, the latter also showing the additional issue of crystal packing to be taken into account. In these cases, vibrational corrections can be evaluated to correct computed equilibrium geometries in order to derive structures that are directly comparable to experimental values.

The interface between Li cathode materials and LLZO is of significant interest to the solid-state battery development. Several studies have focused on identifying the secondary phases and compositional profiles across the interface. The present work focuses on systematically studying the effect of annealing temperature on the LCOLLZO interface using thickness-controlled thin films and interface-sensitive detection methods. XPS, SIMS, HAXPES, and STEM EDX results show that Co and La diffuse extensively across the LCOLLZO interface. As a result of annealing in air up to 500 °C, the most likely reaction products at this interface are Li2CO3, La2Zr2O7, and LaCoO3, as identified by XRD, XAS, and EXAFS. The interface reaction width was found in HAXPES and in situ XPS measurements to be less than 20 nm at 250 °C and close to 100 nm at 500 °C. These reaction products at the LCOLLZO interface are detrimental. Depth profiling of Li across the interfaces shows that the reacted interfaces block Li transfer, leading to an eightfold increase in the interface impedance. The exposure of LCO and LLZO to the atmosphere induces Li2CO3 formation; however, the Li2CO3 on the surface could be completely removed by heating the sample to 350 °C under an O2 atmosphere. The thin-film cathode geometry and the interface-sensitive measurement techniques allow us to observe the formation of interface reaction products at temperatures much lower than in traditional ceramic sintering and bonding processes. Our results indicate that processing conditions at lower temperatures, short time scales, and in CO2-free environments are highly desirable for obtaining ceramic cathode-electrolyte interfaces that enable fast Li transfer and high capacity.

With the assumption that the solid sample after a short reaction time should exhibit higher catalytic activity, the activeness of Zn/ZnO interface was demonstrated by a two-step experiment, in which Zn reacted with NaHCO3 in the first-step for different reaction times, and hydrogen was introduced to the reactor in the second-step to reduce NaHCO3. As expected, the yield of formate after 5 min in the first-step reaction was 38.4%, which was higher than that after 2 h in the first-step reaction (23.0%). These results evidenced the catalytic activity of Zn/ZnO structure.

The size dependence of the internal conversion rate in J-aggregates has been deduced with the help of the exciton model and the energy gap law. The scaling relations of the aggregate electronic properties with length were derived and verified by semiempirical calculations in the frame of the TD-LC-DFTB method.

We predict that for weakly coupled J-aggregates the nonradiative rate should decrease quickly with the delocalization length N. For strong coupling the rate increases since the energy gap law prevails. Some experimental evidence for this phenomenon could be found in the temperature-dependent measurements on BIC J-aggregates. In summary, trends of the internal conversion rate in oligomers can be rationalized in terms of the electronic coupling between the monomers and the length of the region over which the exciton is delocalized.

Step-by-step, we have come to a deeper understanding of the specific roles of higher-energy electronic excited states in a broad range of photophysical and photochemical phenomena. The relaxations from these states may follow different routes, and one of these routes can be the direct start of a photochemical reaction competing with internal conversion to the excited state of lowest energy. This range of phenomena, known as anti-Kasha photochemistry, is well-documented in gas-phase reactions, whereas in the condensed phase, it can be observed only under specific conditions. We show that these conditions are determined by kinetic factors: the photochemical transformation should be among the fastest reactions in the studied systems, triggered by electronic excitation to a higher energy state, with a rate comparable to or higher than that of other ultrafast events such as vibrational relaxations and radiative and nonradiative processes between upper excited states.

The discovery and characterization of deviations from classical Kasha-type routes of relaxation from the high-lying electronic states must stimulate the in-depth investigation of basic ultrafast events that are responsible for such behavior. Moreover, targeted material design based on proper knowledge of the conditions in which these effects operate could lead to a variety of practical applications. One of them could be based on the efficient use of absorbed high energy, avoiding its release in the form of heat in Sn → S1 transitions and making the photochemical reactions controllable and productive. Another is exemplified by the on/off switch applying excitation wavelength-dependent intensity ratio for phosphorescence (P) versus fluorescence (F) (see section ). By setting a threshold for the P/F ratio, the fast off-on switch can be achieved by one- and two-photon processes being accessed to S1 and S n states, respectively, with different P/F ratio. A similar concept can be applied as the bifunctional bioimaging, in which one-photon excitation is for the fluorescence imaging while two-photon excitation to the S n state gives more triplet state population for the photodynamic therapy. We thus demonstrate that the exploration of anti-Kasha effects opens up an unexpectedly broad range of possibilities for selective control of photoreactions by changing the excitation energy in both single-photon and multiple-photon modes. The ramifications in view of applications are awaiting their realization, offering real challenges and new chemistry to researchers.

Progressions of peaks in the OH stretch region are seen in the IR spectra of several water-anion complexes. Qualitatively, this can be understood in terms of anharmonic coupling between the OH stretch and the intermolecular rocking modes. In this work, we explore the utility of one-dimensional adiabatic models for describing these progressions. Specifically, we generated relaxed adiabatic rock potentials for HCO2 - (H2O), NO3 - (H2O), and CS2 - (H2O) with zero or one quanta of OH stretch. The resulting potentials were used to calculate the OH stretch spectra. For CS2 - (H2O), our calculations gave one strong and one very weak peak, consistent with experiment from which only a single peak is seen in the OH stretch region. For HCO2 - (H2O) and NO3 - (H2O), which do exhibit progressions experimentally, we found that agreement with the experimental peak spacing dramatically improved when variable reduced masses obtained from the Wilson G-matrix procedure were employed. With a variable reduced mass, the calculated peak spacings for HCO2 - (H2O) are about 15 cm-1 larger than those observed experimentally, while the overestimation of the spacings is larger for NO3 - (H2O).

Treating vibrational anharmonicity in molecules and clusters with strong anharmonic couplings remains a challenging theoretical problem. The adiabatic model presented and applied in this study can provide a semiquantitatively accurate descrption of the progressions that arise in the case of strong coupling between low- and high-frequency modes, while having only modest demands in terms of the required electronic structure calculations. Our results suggest the need to systematically explore the applicability of higher dimensional adiabatic models to the vibrational spectra of clusters such as NO3 - (H2O).

The use of double-well rather than single-well N = 1 potentials results in progression lengths in much better agreement with experiment. This is a consequence of the energy levels above the barrier having very low intensity. However, the use of the double-well potentials while not having a major impact on the peak spacings of HCO2 - (H2O), worsens the agreement with the experimental peak spacings in the case of NO3 - (H2O). This is further evidence of the need to go beyond a one-dimensional treatment for NO3 - (H2O) within the context of a reduced dimension adiabatic model.

In situ high-pressure angle-dispersive X-ray diffraction experiments at room temperature and the first-principle calculations were performed on semiconductor photocatalyst BiOCl. In the compression process, a tetragonal to tetragonal isostructural phase transition was observed at 15.1 GPa. BiOCl completely transforms into the high-pressure phase at pressures above 22.1 GPa, with discontinuous structure parameters in the transitional region of 15.1-21.1 GPa. The redistribution of Bader charge between Bi, O, Cl ions under high pressure induces this isostructural phase transition, according to the ab initio calculation results. The crystal and electronic structure evolution processes of the HPT phase of BiOCl are different from those of the LPT phase. These high-pressure structural transition behaviors in BiOCl are helpful for us to understand the structural evolution and physical property patterns for the other similar compounds upon compression.

The material SrCo0.9Nb0.1O3-δ (SCN) holds significant promise as an air electrode for solid oxide electrochemical cells. SCN appears to have slightly more favorable thermodynamic stability limits than BSCF, although both materials exhibit a slow oxidative decomposition under likely operating conditions. For SCN, this decomposition is thermodynamically favored when the oxygen stoichiometry 3-δ is greater than ~2.58, or in other words, when the average formal oxidation state of Co is greater than ~3.0+. The partial molar enthalpy and entropy of oxygen fall in the ranges -56 to -134 kJ/mol-O and 54 to -86 J/K mol-O, respectively, for 3-δ values ranging from 2.650 to 2.516. The electronic conductivity of SCN is 60 to 320 S cm-1 under the conditions studied, comparable to that of La0.8Sr0.2MnO3-δ and higher than that of BSCF. At fixed gas composition, the p-type electronic conductivity of SCN decreases with increasing temperature as a result of decreasing hole concentration from reduction of the oxide. The activation energy (i.e.. enthalpy of hole migration) decreases linearly with increasing average cobalt valence, and it exhibits no change in behavior upon crossing a formal cobalt valence state of 3+, consistent with a high degree of cobalt 3d and oxygen 2p orbital hybridization. The thermal expansivity of SCN is comparable to that of BSCF, but SCN has a larger chemical expansivity and thus a slightly larger total expansivity.

The effects of a hydrotropic salt, sodium salicylate (NaSal), on the dynamics of DTAB-based cationic micelles are studied and reported here. The diffusion coefficient of whole DTAB micelles obtained from the dynamic light scattering experiments at room temperature is found to be slower with the addition of NaSal. This is consistent with the earlier small angle neutron scattering (SANS) results - which suggested that the addition of NaSal induces growth of DTAB micelles. Observed QENS data were explained by a model consisting of two distinct motions. The slower motion is identified as the lateral motion, and the other one corresponds to the segmental motion of the surfactant. Lateral motion is found to be Fickian in nature, and segmental motion is described using a model in which a fraction of surfactant hydrogen atoms undergoes localized translational diffusion within spherical domains. It is observed that the addition of NaSal significantly affects the lateral motion of DTAB, whereas segmental motion remains almost unaffected. These observations are found to be consistent with our atomistic molecular dynamics simulation results. They suggest that lateral motion of the surfactant is hindered because of the stronger association of the salicylate ion with the charged headgroup of the surfactant and its location at the micellar surface. However, segmental motion of the surfactant is localized in nature and mainly dominated by the segmental motion of the alkyl chains which does not have much of an effect because of the addition of NaSal. This study clearly demonstrates the effects of the addition of hydrotropic salt on the nanoscopic dynamics of micelles and establishes the correlation with its microstructure.

As seen in Figure , the square pyramidal {Cu (terpy)}2+ is a simple building unit that could coordinate to the organophosphonate ligands via its empty basal and apical coordination sites producing near 90° corners. - In addition to limiting the number of potential phosphonate coordination, fixing the coordination angle to the metal center helps the predictability of the ultimate structure as well. To date, no systematic studies have been reported to test this hypothesis. We have recently reported the synthesis and crystal structures of tetrahedral methane tetra-p-phenylphosphonic acid (MTPPA), which is a remarkable ligand possessing a negative charge range between 0 and -8, thus providing a pH controlled platform for the oligomerization of Cu-P-O polyhedra in one, two, and three dimensions. , Tetrahedral cavities of MTPPA are expected to form large void spaces when they are connected via the metal center to form two- and three-dimensional frameworks. - Therefore, we have used the MTPPA ligand to coordinate over the two empty coordination sites of square pyramidal {Cu (terpy)}2+ and {Cu2(pbterpy)}2+ building units to form our hybrid frameworks of one-dimensional [{Cu (terpy)}2(MTPPA-H5) (MTPPA-H6)] (4.25 H2O) (H3O) and two-dimensional [{Cu2(pbterpy)} (MTPPA-H4)], where 2,2′:6′,2″-Terpyridine = terpy, and 4′,4⁗-(1,4-Phenylene) bis (2,2′:6 ′,2″-terpyridine) = pbterpy. This study is the first report utilizing the novel MTPPA ligand to form the corresponding metal complexes with Cu (II).

The first crystal structure of [{Cu (terpy)}2(MTPPA-H5) (MTPPA-H6)] (4.25 H2O) (H3O) (Figure ) consists of two similar one-dimensional zigzagged chains of [{Cu (terpy)} (MTPPA-H5)] and [{Cu (terpy)} (MTPPA-H6)] (Figure and Figure S1). The extra negative charge is counterbalanced by a hydronium ion and it has no significant contribution to the overall structure. The tau-descriptor (τ5) values for Cu1 and Cu1A atoms are 0.12 and 0.13, which indicate slightly significant distortion of the geometry (τ5 = 0 for an ideal square pyramid and τ5 = 1 for an ideal trigonal bipyramid). Both chains are formed by the coordination of single phosphonate oxygen arm originating from the two ends of the tetrahedral MTPPA-H6 and MTPPA-H5 ligands. MTPPA-H6 ligand has two full protonated phosphonate ends, while each of the two remaining single-protonated phosphonate end has overall -1 charge.

The analogous one-dimensional zigzagged [{Cu (terpy)}/organophosphonate] pattern observed in 1 was previously seen in aliphatic organophosphonates as well. , 1 was synthesized under hydrothermal reaction conditions. The adjustment of initial pH = 1 has increased the protonation level of the MTPPA ligand providing overall -2 negative charge limiting the growth in one dimension. The second two-dimensional compound [{Cu2(pbterpy)} MTPPA-H4] was synthesized using the solvothermal methods in DMF ( Figure and Figure S2). The TOPOS analysis of 2 indicates that the one-dimensional chain figure observed in 1 has retained its character. The one-dimensional chain structures observed in [{Cu (terpy)} MTPPA-H6] (1) were connected by the second copper originating from the {Cu2(pbterpy)}4+ unit to form the two-dimensional network of 2 (Figure ). The tau-descriptor (τ5) values for Cu1 and Cu2 atoms are 0.06 and 0.02, which indicate no significant distortion of the geometry when compared to complex 1. The tetrahedral MTPPA-H4 in 2 was observed as a result of the incorporation of the second Cu (II) in {Cu2(pbterpy)}4+, which has produced the three distinct phosphonate ends. The first phosphonate end in 2 has a fully protonated R-PO3H2 unit, the second group is fully deprotonated R-PO3 -2 providing overall -2 negative charge, while the remaining two phosphonate adhesive units are half protonated R-PO3H-1 providing overall -2 negative charge. Half protonated phosphonate units of MTPPA-H4 linker follow a similar zigzagged one-dimensional chain pattern to that observed in 1. In conjunction with {Cu2(pbterpy)}4+ the fully deprotonated R-PO3 -2 unit of MTPPA-H4 is connecting the previously observed one-dimensional pattern in 1 to form the two-dimensional 2. The additional connectivity originated from the fully deprotonated phosphonate end in 2 has also produced the one-dimensional void chanel of {Cu2(MTPPA-H4)} via the {Cu2(pbterpy)}4+ end. The overall driving force behind the formation of the two-dimensional structure of 2 is the deprotonation of MTPPA-H6 ligand in 1 to accept the second Cu (II) originating from the {Cu2(pbterpy)}4+, which is analogous to {Cu (terpy)}2+.

As shown in Figure , the expansion of the framework into two dimensions has produced the second distinctive void space at the center of [{Cu2(pbterpy)} (MTPPA-H4)] macrocycle with solvent-accessible voids occupying 21.0% (666.7 Å3) of the unit cell volume (3171.3 Å3) obtained using the PLATON. Analysis of solvent accessible voids in the structure was performed using the CALC SOLV within the PLATON software package with a probe radius of 1.20 Å and grin spacing of 0.2 A. Van der Waals (or ion) radii used in the analysis are C (1.70 Å), H (1.20 Å), N (1.55 Å), and P (1.80 Å), respectively. Topological analysis has shown that complex 2 had 3,3,4L34 topology with the point symbol of {4.6.8} {4.62.83} {62.8}. The TOPOS analysis clearly shows how the one-dimensional zigzagged chain is connected to form the two-dimensional network (Figure a and b). Furthermore, 2D sheet adopts -AAA- stacking to generate a 3D supramolecular framework.

TGA studies of [{Cu (terpy)}2(MTPPA-H5) (MTPPA-H6)]. (4.25 H2O) (H3O) shows three successive weight losses as seen in Figure S3. The initial decrease of 7.1% is associated with loss of water molecules (4.9% calculated). The partial loss of terpyridine starts at 300 °C. Concurrent decomposition of MTPPA and terpyridine units start at 400 °C. The sharp decomposition of organic units continues until ca. 500 °C with total 56.1% weight loss of terpy + MTPPA components (58.5% calculated) and the decomposition of inorganic components continues to 800 °C. TGA of [{Cu2(pbterpy)} MTPPA-H4] shows similar pattern as seen in Figure S4, where the decomposition of organic units start at ca. 300 °C and the slow decomposition of organic components continues until 900 °C with overall ca. 60% weight loss (65% calculated).

This is the first report incorporating the tetratopic methane tetra-p-phenylphosphonic acid as a tetrahedral organophosphonate linker to produce the one-dimensional [{Cu (terpy)}2(MTPPA-H5) (MTPPA-H6)] (4.25H2O) (H3O) (1) and two-dimensional [{Cu2(pbterpy)} MTPPA-H4] (2), respectively. In addition, we provide an alternative approach for conventional SBU based MOF chemistry, by using a square pyramidal {Cu (terpy)}2+ building unit as prefixed corner junction points providing a limited number of coordination sites on Cu (II) from the basal plane and the apical position for the phosphonate binding to perform controlled oligomerization. This methodology has produced two compounds in one and two dimensions. The one-dimensional chain structure observed in 1 was connected into two dimensions upon the incorporation of the second copper originating from the ditopic pbterpy ligand. Blocking the copper coordination sites with tripodal organoimine ligands has increased the predictability of the ultimate structure in metal-organophosphonate chemistry while tetrahedral MTPPA ligand and long linker molecule pbterpy produced void spaces in the two-dimensional framework of 2. We are currently working on the pH optimizations to fully deprotonate the MTPPA ligand to enhance the formation of three-dimensional porous frameworks in this system.

Untargeted metabolomics can be used to provide insight into the toxic activity of environmental pollutants in organisms, as they can enable exposome compounds to be detected and potential biomarkers of altered tissue metabolism to be characterized. , In the current study, the structural annotation of molecular features detected in in vivo SPME extracts revealed changes in the composition of endogenous compounds among three groups of fish (i.e.. control group, low-dose group, and high-dose group). After 1 day of the experiment, 277 features (peaks appeared in all samples within group) were detected in the control group, with masses ranging between 102 and 878 m/z (Figure a); after 14 days of the experiment, the number of detected features increased to 325, with a range of molecular masses between 104 and 928 m/z (Figure a). This increase in detected features could be related to the development and growing processes in juvenile rainbow trout. Conversely, analysis of the high-dose group revealed a lower number of detected molecular features and lower range of molecular masses than the control group. The high-dose group had 99 detected features after 1 day of the experiment, with masses ranging from 102 to 628 m/z, and 112 detected features after 14 days of the experiment, with masses ranging from 102 to 540 m/z (Figures c and c). This difference may be attributable to the altered fish's metabolism caused by higher doses of BaP. Interestingly, the low-dose group initially had 82 detected molecular features (masses ranged from 109 to 695 m/z) (Figure b), which was similar to the results obtained for the high-dose group. However, in the low-dose group, after 14 days the number of molecular features increased to 380 with masses ranged from 104 to 901 m/z (Figure b). This change may suggest the presence of an adaptive mechanisms in the metabolism that is responding to low pollutant levels in the surrounding environment.

The presence of BaP and its active metabolites in fish muscles affected several metabolic pathways mainly related to energy metabolism and osmotic regulation. As previously reported, the metabolism of amino acids is tightly regulated within the cells and is susceptible to alterations caused by environmental pollutants. ,, Indeed, the application of in vivo SPME revealed distinct differences in amino acid composition between the three groups, which indicates that the metabolism of these endogenous compounds is highly sensitive to BaP (Table ). In the control group, several amino acids were extracted using SPME probes, including proline and its derivative -5-oxoprolinate, as well as proline dipeptides. Moreover, an intermediate of proline metabolism, l-4-hydroxyglutamate semialdehyde, was also detected in the control group of fish. In contrast, the muscle tissue of the fish that had been at 10 ng/L of BaP for 14 days only showed the presence of free tryptophan and proline (SI, Table S1), with the level of the latter found to be 10 times higher than the level of free proline in the control group. In vivo SPME sampling also revealed differences in lipid metabolism in analyzed groups of fish. Among the detected lipids, two crucial intermediates in the β-oxidation of fatty acids, carnitine and its estrified form, acylcarnitine, were present only in the control group. In the low- and high-dose groups, only the presence of carnitine was detected, which suggests that BaP causes disturbances in lipid metabolism within the muscle cells. Moreover, several specific metabolites that are active in fatty acid transformation, such as l-2-aminoethyl seryl phosphate (l-serine phosphoethanolamine), which participates in glycerophosholipid metabolism, were detected only in the low- and high-dosage groups. The observed changes in the metabolism of lipids and amino acids are indicative of BaP's strong impact on energy metabolism, which is consistent with previous observations. ,

In addition, BaP also altered the osmotic regulation of the fish in the low- and high-dose groups. Hypotaurine, taurine, and betaine are typical osmolytes that participate in various metabolic pathways of osmotic regulation in aquatic organisms. It has been demonstrated that exposure to BaP causes reductions in several compounds that participate in osmoregulation, including branched chain amino acids, dimethylamine, betaine, and taurine, due to its ability to disturb the fish's osmotic mechanisms. ,, Indeed, in vivo SPME facilitated the detection of hypotaurine, taurine, and betaine exclusively in the control group after the first day of the experiment. Moreover, a short-lived and labile precursor of taurine, cysteic acid, was also detected in the control group. Interestingly, taurine was detected not only in the control group (SI, Table S2) but also in the low-dose group after 14 days (SI, Table S1), which may suggest the existence of adaptive metabolic pathways in fish in response to exposure to lower BaP's level in the surrounding environment. The lack of the osmolytes in the high-dose group may be indicative of an imbalance in osmoregulation, which confirms previous findings. ,

Apart from the observed disturbances in the tissue components involved in muscle metabolism and osmotic regulation, additional unique and untypical compounds were captured by SPME probes. For example, the formation of arachidonoyl serinol, a metabolite of endocannabinoid (2-arachidonoyl glycerol), was observed in the high-dose group after day 1 and day 14 of the experiment (SI, Table S1 and Table S2). The exclusive presence of this unique compound in the high-dose group may indicate that higher doses of BaP (10 ng/L) can significantly impact the endocannabinoid system, which can also be used to distinguish this group from the other two. In contrast, 2′,3′- cyclic CMP and glucose-6-phosphate, which are crucial intermediates of multiple biochemical pathways, were present exclusively in the control group. Additionally, the end products of nicotinamide metabolism, N1-methyl-4-pyridone-5-carboxamide (4PY) and N1-methyl-2-pyridone-5-carboxamide (2PY), were initially only detected in the control group; however, after 14 days, they were also detected in the low-dose group. The low-dose group's metabolomic pattern underwent significant changes over the duration of the experiment and ultimately came to resemble that of the control group after 14 days. This change may imply the presence of adaptive mechanisms developed by the fish over time exposed to low concentrations of BaP. Conversely, the control group's metabolic profile remained relatively constant, although some differences in metabolite composition were observed, possibly related to the growth and development processes.

The presence of several of the above-mentioned endogenous components extracted using SPME probes was not reported in prior toxicological studies. In vivo SPME provided real-time extraction and the capturing of short-lived compounds, and it was able to reveal unique and altered metabolites that were related to time-dependent and dose-dependent exposure to the pollutant. The observed differences in signaling pathways may lead to the identification of tissue-specific compounds (biomarkers) that are formed as a consequence of altered metabolism. These findings demonstrate that in vivo SPME can be applied in real-time to monitoring the exposome in aquatic organisms.

For an alarm time node sequence, the time interval has to be represented by two consecutive nodes. It is seen that traditional XOR operations can rarely be adapted to treat alarm time node sequences. To deal with this problem, a novel approach of alarm similarity analysis based on block matching degree is presented here.

First, the length of an alarm time window should be determined according to the actual industrial process and the specific alarm data. Generally, there may exist a time delay between two correlated alarms due to the propagation or response time. This time delay reduces the correlation coefficient and thus may mask the correlation between these variables. To eliminate this influence, time delay should be assumed and the maximal correlation coefficient can be computed; this would be regarded as the real correlation. Second, the block matching degree is used to calculate the similarity of the two alarm time node sequences. A value of the similarity measure is obtained by assuming a certain time delay for the alarm time series. Thus, the absolute maximum value can be regarded as the correlation coefficient and the corresponding lag as the estimated time delay between these two alarms.

Therefore, the maximum absolute value of ϕ a b ( k ) can be regarded as the correlation coefficient between alarm a and alarm b, and the corresponding time delay k is the estimation between two alarms. Mathematically, we can compute the maximum and minimum values ϕmax = max k {ϕ ab (k),0} ≥ 0, ϕmin = min k {ϕ ab (k),0} ≤ 0, as well as the corresponding arguments k max and k min.Then the estimated certain time delay λ from a to b is 4 λ = { k max , ⁣ if ϕ max ≥ - ϕ min k min , ⁣ if ϕ max < - ϕ min

The actual time delayed cross-correlation is ρ = ϕ ab (k), in which ρ ∈ [-1,1], and the sign of ρ indicates that the correlations are positive or negative. All of the common similarity measure methods in Table have been tested, and the comparative experiment was carried out in case 1. The Sorgenfrei coefficient similarity measure is taken as an example to illustrate.
The detailed algorithmic steps are presented as follows.
Step 1. Consider two alarm time series X and Y, by partitioning sequences; the time node sequence can be calculated, as shown in Figures and Figure .

Step 2. Assume a certain time delay k for the alarm time series. Comparing the first blocks of the two sequences, the longer one is used as the first time domain. As shown in Figure , X⃡ 1 is longer than Y⃡ 1 , so the length of X⃡ 1 is used as the first time domain, and is called L 1.

Step 3. If the block crosses the time domain, it is partitioned into two parts. Because Y⃡ 3 crosses two time domains L 1 and L 2, Y⃡ 3 is split into Y⃡ 3.1 and Y⃡ 3.2 . The start node of Y⃡ 3.1 is the third node Y⃡ p 3 of sequence Y⃡ , and the end node of Y⃡ 3.1 is X⃡ p 2 , which is the end node of the time domain L 1. At the same time, the start node of Y⃡ 3.2 is X⃡ p 2 too, as shown in Figure .

Step 4. Calculate the corresponding parameters N 1 L 1 , N 2 L 1 , and C L 1 in time domain L 1. N 1 L 1 = X⃡ p 2 - X⃡ p 1 N 2 L 1 = ( Y⃡ p 2 - Y⃡ p 1 ) + ( X⃡ p 2 - Y⃡ p 3 ) C L 1 = ( Y⃡ p 2 - Y⃡ p 1 ) + ( X⃡ p 2 - Y⃡ p 3 ) 5
Step 5. Calculate the length of the time domain from the second one to the end, and then repeat from step 2 to step 4.
