Step 6. Calculate the sum of N 1, N 2, A, and C in each time domain separately, and then get N 1, N 2, A, and C of the whole sequence as follows: N 1 = N 1 L 1 + N 1 L 2 + .. + N 1 L n N 2 = N 2 L 1 + N 2 L 2 + .. + N 2 L n C = C L 1 + C L 2 + .. + C L n 6
Step 7. Calculate the estimated certain time delay λ and the actual time delayed cross-correlation ρ1,2, as shown in Figure .

Guest-host LC systems containing naphthopyrans are known to undergo an increase in order when exposed to UV light, resulting from the conformational change from the closed form to the open form of the guest molecules. After removal of the UV excitation, the photoinduced population of the open form reverts to the closed form. Here we have investigated the kinetics of the thermal relaxation of the naphthopyran derivative G1. The decay rate is host dependent and increases with temperature. At room temperature, the decay rate was 0.18 s-1 in toluene, 0.039 s-1 in 5CB, and 0.014 s-1 in 8CB. The temperature dependence followed an Arrhenius behavior within each phase of the guest-host LC systems. Larger activation energies are observed in the ordered phases of the 5CB and 8CB hosts than in their isotropic phase. In addition, relaxation rates were larger in a nonmesogenic solvent than in mesogenic ones. The results indicate that the ring-closure process of the class of naphthopyran molecules studied here is very sensitive to the nature of the environment, including the amount of local order and the viscosity. The observed trend in activation entropy suggests that the change in geometry from the open form to the transition state requires a larger reorganization of the solvent molecules in ordered solvents than in an isotropic environment. This could be due to a change in the free volume or of the solvation sphere around the naphthopyran molecules in a liquid crystalline environment as a result of the anisotropic nature of the guest-host intermolecular interactions.

The sensitivity of the G1 dynamics on the type and order of the solvent could prove useful in tailoring the properties of photoresponsive systems or as means to probe perturbations to the local order of guest-host LC systems.

Plants were exposed to either CBZ, LTG, EP-CBZ, or DiOH-CBZ (single-solute experiments), or to CBZ and LTG (bisolute experiments) for up to 96 h, maintaining a pH of 6-7 in all experiments by adding 4-(2-hydroxyethyl)-1-piperazineethanesulfonic acid (HEPES) to the nutrient solution at a concentration of 5 mM. During this time, the nutrient solution was not replenished and continuously aerated. The plants exhibited a healthy root system throughout the entire cultivation and experimental period. The nutrient solution was sampled at 1, 3, 6, 8, 24, 48, 72, and 96 h for the CBZ and LTG single-solute experiments and CBZ and LTG bisolute experiments, and once after 72 h for the EP-CBZ and DiOH-CBZ single-solute experiments. The plants exposed to CBZ in the presence or absence of LTG were sampled at 8, 24, 48, 72, and 96 h; the plants exposed to the metabolites were sampled after 72 h. The experiments were conducted in 5 replicates for each sampling time. At each sampling time, a whole plant was sacrificed for sap sampling and plant analyses. After plants were detopped, xylem sap was collected over a period of approximately 15 min after detopping, collecting 2-3 mL of sap from each plant, while roots were still in the nutrient solution, first drops being discarded. Then roots and shoots were washed, weighed and frozen at -20 °C until extraction.

CBZ and LTG uptake and translocation in a bisolute experiment was also tested comparatively at pH of 4.5 and 7.5. In this experiment, the exposure time was 48 h. To maintain pH 7.5, HEPES was added to the nutrient solution at a concentration of 5 mM. To maintain pH 4.5, 2 (N-morpholino) ethanesulfonic acid (MES) was added at a concentration of 5 mM. Since the MES buffer alone was not capable of maintaining a steady, low pH, the Ca (NO3)2 4H2O (2 mM) in the nutrient solution was substituted with 0.8 mM NH4NO3, 1.2 mM Ca (NO3)2 4H2O, and 0.8 mM CaCl2 in the low pH treatment, so that the N was composed of 20% NH4 + and 80% NO3 -.

The presented study considers water-assisted proton transfer in the nucleoside inosine. MP2/6-31+G (d,p), SCS-MP2/6-31+G (d,p), CPCM/MP2/6-31+G (d,p), and CPCM/SCS-MP2/6-31+G (d,p) calculations show that in the gas phase and in water solution, the most stable is the amino-oxo tautomer A (6-keto form) followed by the imino-hydroxy tautomer B1 (6-hydroxy form). The syn-conformer of tautomer A is more stable than the anti-conformer. The changing of the tautomeric form of the hypoxanthine moiety does not change the conformation of the nucleoside. The rate constant of the water-assisted proton transfer A → B1 in inosine, k = 5.64 × 101 s-1, is sufficiently large to generate imino-hydroxy tautomer. The time necessary to reach the equilibrium concentration of the 6-keto and 6-hydroxy tautomeric forms was calculated to be 2.10 × 10-6 s.
Following the reaction path show in Figure it can be concluded that the solvent-assisted proton transfer in inosine is realized through the asynchronous concerted mechanism.

In this work, we find that different positions of the C 60 relative to the donor DRCNnT molecule can induce large variations in the complex's dipole moment, the energy of the charge transfer states, and the driving force for electron transfer.

A favorable driving force for charge generation is obtained when ΔG < 0. For some configurations of the D/A dimer, ΔG is near or greater than zero, which hinders the electron transfer from the donor to the acceptor. For the face-on orientation, ΔG < 0 occurs when C 60 is near the central group of the A-D-A molecules. This configuration favors the hybridization between the HOMO of the donor and the LUMO of the acceptor which decreases the energy of the CT1 state. Considering the edge-on orientation, negative values of ΔG are obtained when the C 60 is aligned close to the positive partial charges of the donor's molecule. In this case, the magnitude of the complex's dipole moment increases. The electrostatic potential energy associated with this dipole moment induces a downward shift of the acceptor's LUMO, which decreases the energy of the CT1 state so that ΔG < 0.

Our analysis using the DFT and TD-DFT methods employed for some configurations of D/A dimers was complemented by molecular dynamics (MD) calculations. We applied MD to simulate the deposition of DRCN5T/C 60 films formed by solvent evaporation. Those simulations indicated that the face-on and edge-on dimer's configurations that tend to have very negative driving forces (as identified by our DFT and TD-DFT calculations) can be present in a real film. Moreover, we found that the lateral alkyl groups attached to the central thiophene ring of the DRCN5T molecule can behave like tweezers that guide the diffusive movement of C 60 toward the center of the molecule. This effect would favor the formation of dimers with C1-like configurations (that tend to have a negative ΔG). MD simulations also indicated that thermal annealing treatments increase the density and the size of the fullerene cluster in the blend (which is in agreement with the experimental observations).

It is common in the literature to associate a higher Δμge of the donor with a better photovoltaic performance of the OPV. Yet our results indicate that even when the donor is a centrosymmetric molecule so that Δμge ≈ 0, the best performance is obtained when ΔG tends to be more negative. Indeed we found a correlation between the magnitude of the driving force averaged over all tested dimer's configurations (ΔG ) and the measured power conversion efficiency (higher PCEs are observed when the ΔG is more negative). Here is important to mention that low CT1 energies can make ΔG more negative, but in some systems, it can also produce trapping states that are detrimental to the charge separation. - Hence a detailed description of the importance of the magnitude of the CT1 energy for charge separation needs a more sophisticated analysis involving, for example, Marcus theory to calculate the charge transfer rates. ,- Yet our results suggest that the calculation of ΔG for the dimer can be a sound and preliminary criterion to test possible combinations of donor and acceptor materials for photovoltaic applications even before they are actuality tested in the laboratory. Our results demonstrate the importance of the microscopy structure of the D/A dimer to define ΔG. It is clear then that a fine-tuning of the donor and acceptor relative spatial orientation can be a valuable strategy to improve the OPV efficiency.

The details for the 2D IR setup have been described previously. Briefly, the 4.0 W output of a 100 fs (fs) regenerative amplifier (Spectra Physics, Solstice) is used to pump a commercial optical parametric amplifier (OPA, Light Conversion, TOPAS). Signal and idler pulses are then used to pump a home-built, collinear difference frequency generation (DFG) module. The 25 μJ mid-IR pulses are centered at 1620 cm-1 and ~100 fs in duration. A wedged calcium fluoride beam splitter is used to split off about 5% of the light to be used as the probe pulse. The remaining 95% is used to generate the two pump pulses. Pump pulse pairs are created using a fully reflective germanium acousto-optic modulator (AOM) pulse shaper in the 4f geometry, described in detail previously. The Ge-AOM uses acoustic waves to shape the light in the frequency domain to generate a pulse-pair with computer-controlled time delays and absolute phase control. The pulse shaper is also used to compress the pulses in time by optimizing the second-harmonic signal from the mid-IR output with an AgGaS2 crystal. A four frame phase-cycling scheme is used to subtract the background and suppress pump scatter and the data are processed as in eq : 1 S 2 DIR = log S ( ϕ 1 = 0 , ϕ 2 = 0 ) + S ( ϕ 1 = π , ϕ 2 = π ) S ( ϕ 1 = π , ϕ 2 = 0 ) + S ( ϕ 1 = 0 , ϕ 2 = π ) where S 2DIR is the 2D IR signal, and ϕ i indicates the phase of the i th laser pulse. Pump and probe beams are overlapped spatially and focused on to the sample using parabolic mirrors. Timing between the pump and probe pulses, called the waiting time (t 2), is controlled by a motorized stage (Newport). The probe pulse is dispersed in a spectrograph and measured with a 64 element mercury-cadmium-telluride (MCT) array (Infrared Associates).

To calculate the couplings between discrete nitrate ester groups, a transition dipole coupling (TDC) model is employed that treats each chromophore as a point dipole. A similar method is employed in interpreting the spectra of peptides and proteins. ,, In this model, the coupling constant, βij between local modes i and j is calculated according to 2 β ij = 1 4 π ε 0 [ μ⃗ i μ⃗ j r ij 3 - 3 ( μ⃗ i r⃗ ij ) × ( μ⃗ j r⃗ ij ) r ij 5 ] Where μi is the transition dipole moment for chromophore i and r ij is the distance vector between chromophores i and j. DFT calculations were performed on an isolated PETN molecule using the B3LYP functional and a 6-31G (d,p) basis set in Gaussian '09. The local mode transition dipoles from the DFT results were used for TDC calculations. The transition dipole vectors are assumed to be the same for all nitrate ester groups and have the same direction relative to the N-O bond axis as determined from the DFT calculations. The crystal structure of PETN was used to calculate the vibrational coupling constants between each nitrate ester group in the crystal. From this, the one-exciton Hamiltonian is diagonalized to generate the normal-mode frequencies and eigenvectors, which were then used to simulate the linear FTIR spectrum.

Thin films of PETN used for both linear FTIR and 2D IR measurements were deposited by vacuum thermal evaporation in a custom deposition system. PETN powder was loaded into an effusion cell deposition source and the chamber was evacuated to a base pressure of ~10 -6 Torr. The effusion cell deposition source was heated to a temperature of ~130 °C. PETN evaporated from the effusion cell and deposited as a thin film on CaF2 substrates held in a cooled assembly. This substrate holder was rotated for uniformity. PETN thickness was measured using a surface profiler (Dektak XT) and determined to be ~ 1 μm thick.

This article shows that MMI is oxidized by chlorite and chlorine dioxide all the way through to desulfurization. Chlorite oxidation of MMI produces negligible amounts of the S-oxide (see Figure ) and no evidence of the sulfinic acid. The sulfonic acid is a major pathway of oxidation before formation of sulfate and N-methylimidazole. The lack of observation of substantial amounts of the sulfenic and sulfinic acids in the ESI-MS spectrum does not preclude their presence in the pathway and mechanism: it just means that these oxoacids are very unstable and are easily oxidized further. This was proven by the use of excess MMI over aqueous bromine in which both oxoacids are prominent (see Figure ).

In summary, we find a silicon-based highly efficient thermoelectric material Si2Te3, having figure of merit ZT = 1.86 under n-type doping. We resolve for the first time the ground state structure of this very important silicon-based chalcogenide. We predicted the most probable 8 lattice sites for silicon out of 28 possible octahedral voids in a unit cell of Si2Te3 containing 12 Te and 8 Si atoms. With the help of of Wyckoff positions corresponding to the space group P31c, out of total C (28,8) combinations of structures, the search was narrowed down to only 15 configurations. The ground state structure of Si2Te3, thus, obtained is a layered structure with excellent electronic and transport properties. Favorable electronic properties include combination of light and heavy bands, steep nature of DOS near the Fermi level, and large number of charge carrier pockets. These give rise to high electrical conductivity, low conductivity effective mass, and large thermopower, leading to high power factor in n-doped Si2Te3. Furthermore, low-lying optical branches in phonon spectra, low phonon group velocities and large negative Gruneisen parameters result in low lattice thermal conductivity. By integrating the effect of all these features, n-doped Si2Te3 exhibits high figure of merit ZT of 1.86 at 1000 K, which is comparable to some of the best known state-of-the-art thermoelectric materials. Hence, Si2Te3, with high ZT over wide range of temperature, can be a long sought silicon-based highly efficient thermoelectrics with strong possibility of integration into the existing electronic devices.

It has been commonly accepted that the electromagnetic theory of SERS gives a reasonable estimate for the expected range of EFs despite the rather widespread reported experimental EFs. Although the actual measured EFs are strongly affected by many factors (e.g.. the number of adsorbed Raman molecules or their distribution over the substrate's hot spots), there is a general consensus about the usability of the power law I SERS ~ E loc4 for making a reasonable estimate of the SERS EFs. As a result, when simulating the SERS response for plasmonic nanostructures with a variable PR around the laser excitation wavelength, one arrives at extremely strong EF variations (within one or 2 orders of magnitude), even for moderate detuning (within ±100 nm).

We have experimentally reexamined the above theoretical predictions by using a simple, reproducible, and controllable model of AuNRs with a variable aspect ratio. By contrast with the previously reported ensemble measurements, we have used the etching method to fabricate a set of samples with a constant width and concentration, while the nanorod length was finely shortened. Because all samples were prepared from the same original batch of nanorods, there were no problems with variations in particle morphology, impurities, and concentrations that would be typical of the previously used independent synthesis. With two independent methods we have confirmed the constancy of nanorod concentration ( ~ 7 × 1010 mL-1) in etched samples. The number of adsorbed NBT molecules per one nanorod ( ~ 104) has been determined by desorption of NBT molecules with DTT. For three etched samples (Set 3), we have found almost constant effective footprint ~0.55 nm2 of NBT molecules adsorbed on AuNRs. This remarkable result means that the topology of NBT adsorption is close to the monolayer packing density with the topological polar surface area of NBT 0.468 nm2.

With three independent sets of etched AuNRs and two measurement schemes (solution in a cuvette with waveguide spectrometers and sample drop on slides with a Raman microscope), we have come to similar conclusions. Namely, the experimental variations in the main SERS intensity of the adsorbed NBT molecules are quite moderate for nanorods with PRs varied around the laser wavelength of 785 nm within a wide range (650-925 nm). This finding is the first main result of our study. In order to account for this observation, we showed that SERS EF predictions must include orientation averaging and the effect of the Raman shift (beyond the common E 4-approximation). For PR wavelengths between 800 and 900 nm, both simulated and experimental EFs then show very small variations and are in remarkable agreement. However, for PR wavelengths between 650 and 800 nm, EM simulations still predict strong variations in the SERS intensity within 1 order of magnitude, which is in stark contrast to the experimental EFs. The exact reasons for such disagreement between measurements and EM simulations are unclear, and further work is needed to clarify the point.

In agreement with earlier results, we have also demonstrated that the reshaping of nanoparticles is a more important factor toward the highest SERS response than is the tuning of the plasmonic peak for on-resonance excitation. Specifically, the overgrowth of cigarlike nanorods to a dumbbell morphology increased the SERS response 5-fold. Thus, the rational design of shape morphology is more important for SERS optimization than the exact tuning of the PR to the excitation wavelength. In practice, detuning within ±100 nm may be quite acceptable. This is the second main finding of our study.

Finally, we have examined the Bg contribution to the measured SERS spectra from AuNR solutions, in analogy with the earlier data for single-particle measurements. In our case, the experimental range of the aspect ratio and PR variations were wider than those reported previously, , but the main features in the spectral behavior of the Bg were similar. This means that the previously suggested procedure for the Bg correction of SERS spectra could be applicable not only to single-particle spectra but also to ensemble measuring. The dependence of the Bg spectra on the particle aspect ratio is consistent with both the PL from an AuNR ensemble and the elastic light scattering of a very weak laser Bg by the same AuNR ensemble. This is the third main result of our study. However, further work is needed to explore this issue in detail.

We hope that the described reexamination study and the observed discrepancy between measured and predicted dependencies of the SERS intensity on the AuNR aspect ratio will stimulate further research on the plasmonically enhanced SERS of colloidal and single particles of various morphologies.

In this work, we explore the impact of the recombination model suggested recently by Burke et al.. in which interface recombination is a two-step process involving a charge-transfer state, on the J-V characteristics of organic solar cells. Toward that aim, we extended the model such that it can be employed also when operating the solar cell at external biases other than V oc. We demonstrate that the involvement of the intermediate CT states is a plausible origin of the apparently reduced Langevin recombination. The characteristic temperature dependence of the corresponding Langevin reduction factor γ is predominantly determined by the binding energy of the electron and the hole bound in the CT state and the spread of the CT-state energies due to disorder. Even when temperature-independent mobilities are assumed, the reduction of γ with increasing temperature can be qualitatively reproduced. For a quantitative prediction, however, additional knowledge about (at least) the actual temperature dependence and the degree of disorder in the CT-state energies is required. Moreover, for T > 150 K, the predicted evolution of γ-T coincides with the continuum model of Hilczer and Tachiya.

Once incorporated in device simulations, the model allows realistic J-V curves of bilayer OSCs to be quantitatively reproduced. It further demonstrates that the CT recombination model leads to qualitatively similar J-V curves as the reduced Langevin recombination model relying on encounter-limited bimolecular recombination. In both models, the interface recombination is shown not only to determine V OC, but also to affect the fill factor.

Future work will include the experimental determination of interface recombination in bilayer OSCs to further develop the theory presented in this article. Furthermore, the 2D drift-diffusion model presented here will be adapted to enaing of ble the model BHJ devices by taking bulk morphology effects into account.

To quantify the intensity of PFR, ~10 mg of prepared-BCs was injected into a micro pipet in an EPR instrument (Bruker EMX/plus spectrometer, Germany). The EPR signal in BC was also recorded after the reaction. Parameters related to EPR experiments are shown in the SI Text S4. To probe the role of PFRs in BCs and identify the impacts on Cr (VI) reduction or Cr (III) generation, H2O2 (100 mM) and different quantities of MeOH (100-200 mM) were used as electron competitors during the quenching tests. Benzoquinone (BQ, 100 mM) was added to probe the role of the superoxide radical (O2 -) due to the high reactivity of BQ toward O2 - (k 2 = 2.9 × 109 M-1 s-1). Pre-extraction was conducted prior to the kinetic tests by adding 10 mL organic solvent to 1 g BC three times to completely quench the PFRs.

In conclusion, supramolecular coordination polymeric hydrogels were obtained from self-assembly of small bis-terpyridine monomer with specific metal salts such as ZnC6H10O6 and Cu (OAc)2. However, other ion salts could not trigger the gelation. DTA can selectively discriminate Zn2+ ions by fluorescence enhancement in blue emission both in solution and gel among test ions. Otherwise, in the presence of Cu (OAc)2, DTA formed injectable, chiral, and electrochemical gels just at room temperature, which showed multistimuli responsive properties including both chemical and physical stimuli such as temperature, thixotropy, light, EDTA, KI, and sodium ascorbate. Therefore, the hydrogelation and corresponding properties such as fluorescence, chirality, and rheology can be modulated just by changing metal salts, which opened a new way for designing hydrogels with multiple needs. Notably, the ditopic ligand was comprised of a π-conjugated system without hydrogen-bonding sites or hydrophilic units, which was a typical paradigm for constructing novel π gelators in water. We believe that these dynamic polymeric gels can be used for biologically relevant materials and soft actuators toward external stimuli in the future.

At any instant of time the droplet is situated over two consecutive electrodes covered by a layer of dielectric material. In order to initiate motion, voltage is applied to the front electrode, whereas the rear electrode is kept grounded. The droplet is considered to be perfectly conducting. Fringing effects of the electric field from the sides of electrodes are neglected. The dynamic response of the droplet to the actuation is studied by mass averaged velocity. The internal circulation and variation of the local flow properties inside the droplet are neglected. Thus, the droplet is considered to be a nondeformable single liquid mass moving under electric field in this simplified analytical model. In the present model the junction of the two neighboring electrodes is considered as the origin of the one-dimensional reference frame for drop movement. A 1 and A 2 are the areas covered by the droplet on the front and rear electrodes, respectively (Figure b) and are functions of the displacement of the droplet front end from the end of the rear electrode. Considering the droplet as a spherical cap (or a portion of a sphere) and its footprint as a circle, the areas A 1 and A 2 can be calculated from the geometry as follows: A 1 ( x ) = r 2 cos - 1 ( 1 - x r ) - ( r - x ) r 2 - ( x - r ) 2 1 A 2 ( x ) = π r 2 - A 1 2 Considering ϕ as the equilibrium contact angle, the radius (r) of the droplet can be written as r = [ 3 ∀ sin 3 ϕ π ( 2 - 3 cos ϕ + cos 3 ϕ ) ] 1 / 3 3 where ∀ is volume of the droplet.

The capacitor formed due to the presence of the dielectric layer between the droplet and electrode is considered to be of parallel plate type in nature. The network of capacitor formed in the present configuration (Figure ) is shown in Figure . The capacitance C 1 and C 2 can be calculated as C 1 = k A 1 ε 0 d 4 C 2 = k A 2 ε 0 d 5 where k, d, and ε0 are the relative permittivity, the thickness of the dielectric layer, and the permittivity of vacuum, respectively.

The traversing droplet also encounters forces opposing its motion along an inclined surface. This opposing force is incorporated in the present model as the contact line friction by following the work of Ren et al. and Bahadur et al. Here, the contact line resistance is taken to be linearly proportional to the velocity (molecular kinetic theory; v = γ ( cos θ s - cos θ d ) ξ ). The values of μl and ρf are considered to be 8.9 × 10-4 Pa s and 1.2 kg/m3. The Re is calculated as Re = ρ f v D m μ f 11 where D m is the diameter of the cross section of the spherical segment (droplet) having maximum area. Thus, for a hydrophilic surface it is the footprint diameter of the droplet. On a hydrophobic surface, D m is considered as the diameter of the droplet which takes the shape of a portion of a sphere due to high contact angle. Details of the derivation of the projected area and droplet radius for a constant volume of liquid are presented in Appendix S1 (Supporting Information). As air is considered as the filler fluid, the contribution of drag force is low in the present case. However, the inclusion of the drag force term facilitates the model to be applicable for different filler fluids with various densities.

Due to the presence of microdefects on the solid surface, the contact line gets pinned during the initiation of motion. Experimental studies show that contact angle raises at the advancing front and reduces at the retracting wetting front. The difference in the contact angle is known as contact angle hysteresis. This produces a loss in capillary forces. A threshold actuation voltage is required to initiate the movement of the droplet. Following the work of Berthier et al. and Ahmadi et al.. the resistance force due to contact angle hysteresis is included as the last term in eq . ϕth is the threshold contact angle due to electrostatic actuation at the onset of motion which can be expressed as ϕ th = cos - 1 [ r cos ( ϕ - α ) - l 2 cos ( ϕ + α ) l 1 ] - α 13

l 1 and l 2 are shown in Figure . α is the angle of hysteresis, which can be defined as the difference between the contact angle made by the advancing and retracting wetting fronts at the same electric potential. Based on the experimental data presented by Berthier et al.. the value of contact angle is taken as 7°.

Considering the upward direction is positive, the equation of motion of the droplet in along the incline can be expressed as m d 2 x d t 2 = F act - F opp 14 where m is the mass of the droplet. Solving the above equation, the displacement and the velocity at a particular time instant can be determined.

In Figure we have shown the diminishing nature of the actuation force for a representative case as the droplet moves toward the junction of the electrodes. Hence the droplet starts to traverse toward the actuated electrode but slows down as its mass center moves toward the junction. Eventually it faces no actuation when the mass center is sitting over the junction. This seizes the droplet motion further. To continue the movement of the droplet, an arrangement needs to be made for the continuation of the actuation force. An intelligent electrode design and the subsequent switching scheme is one option to sustain the actuation. In the present study, we have designed an array of stripped electrodes (as shown in Figure ) and proposed a switching mechanism so that the droplet mass center, despite moving forward, will never reach the junction between the actuated and ground electrodes. It is assumed that, for a continuous movement, by switching the actuated electrodes, overlap of the drop over the actuated electrode is kept constant.

As a half-life extender, HSA has several beneficial features, such as very low immune response and good degradability. In this study, we investigated whether HSA is an effective serum half-life extender as an alternative to popular PEG molecules. Site-specific incorporation of AzF into sfGFP and bioorthogonal click chemistry achieved the site-specific conjugation of HSA or PEG molecules to sfGFP, generating three novel sfGFP conjugates (sfGFP-HSA, sfGFP-PEG20, and sfGFP-PEG30). Standard protein purification chromatography was applied to purify sfGFP conjugates in a high purity. The three sfGFP conjugates (sfGFP-HSA, sfGFP-PEG20, and sfGFP-PEG30) exhibited the fluorescence comparable to or even greater than that of sfGFP-WT. Therefore, we concluded that HSA or PEG molecules can be conjugated to a target protein without compromising the critical property of the target protein. In mice, the serum half-lives of sfGFP-HSA, sfGFP-PEG20, and sfGFP-PEG30 were 13.5, 11.0, and 14.3 h, which were 9.0, 7.3, and 9.5 times greater than that of sfGFP-WT, respectively. These results indicated that the extension of the serum half-life of sfGFP upon HSA conjugation is comparable to those of relatively large PEG molecules (20 kDa and 30 kDa). Combined with the previous case of uricase, these results also indicated that HSA conjugation seems a general approach to enhance the serum half-life of a protein in vivo. Finally, we concluded that HSA can be an alternative to PEG for extension of the serum half-life with additional benefits of low immune response and good degradability. Handling or chemical modification of HSA during the albumination process may lead to slight denaturation, which may be sufficient to generate an immune response. Therefore, more studies on immune responses of denatured HSA would be required to further develop albumination as a tool to enhance the serum half-life.

We designed two spatially segregated catalytic nanocompartments to support a cascade reaction between them, mimicking sequential reactions between biosystems. By an elegant selection of the enzyme combination, we applied these catalytic nanocompartments in tandem to decrease uric acid and H2O2, both involved in various pathologic conditions ranging from gout to oxidative stress. A thorough analysis of the factors affecting the overall efficiency of the cascade reaction between CNCs indicated the protective role of the compartments, which provide a shield for the encapsulated enzymes, especially important in biological fluids and cellular environment. For the first time, a kinetic evaluation of a cascade reaction between segregated reaction spaces at the nanoscale has been achieved. We elucidated the limiting factors for the overall reaction: (i) the diffusion through the membrane pores inserted into the walls of the compartments and (ii) the probability of the products from the first reaction to encounter CNCs containing the second enzyme and reach the encapsulated enzyme molecules. A balance is necessary between the protective role of the nanocompartments and the factors that decrease the efficiency of the cascade reaction for translational applications. This cascade reaction in separate compartments has been successfully performed in serum and then used to decrease both uric acid and the derived H2O2 from the cellular milieu as a first step toward medical applications. Our study is the first one that proves that a two-compartment cascade reaction acts in cellular conditions, thus contributing to the understanding of the design of complex catalytic compartments to cope with biological requirements.

In summary, we have shown that diselenide containing hydrogels are readily obtained from the reaction of a partially hydrolyzed poly (2-ethyl-2-oxazoline) with selenolactone. This was possible thanks to the reactivity of selenolactone toward secondary amines. The diselenide content can be easily varied by adjusting the quantity of γ-butyroselenolactone added and allows tuning the cross-link density and thus the swelling degree of the gels. The obtained hydrogels were also found to possess good adhesion properties to porcine skin and to undergo on-demand dissolution in the presence of either oxidative or reductive substances. For instance, by adding an excess of H2O2, an oxidant already commonly used as disinfectant and for cosmetic applications, the hydrogel can be completely dissolved, without any trauma or pain for the patient. This is a very important feature considering that burn wound dressings need to be changed regularly. The dressing can always be formed in situ to adapt perfectly to the wound shape and keep it moist. Moreover, the hydrogels were shown to be light responsive, enabling further reshaping if needed. All these properties, combined with the lack of toxicity, make this material very interesting for further studies toward burn wound dressing applications.

We investigated the separation performance of two 3D-printed ZIF-8 monoliths, with a different fiber thickness and channel size, for the adsorptive biobutanol recovery from fermentation gas mixtures. Equilibrium adsorption isotherms of different ABE mixture components showed that the monolith fibers retained the high equilibrium capacity of ZIF-8 for biobutanol and a high hydrophobicity. The high selectivity of the printed monoliths for biobutanol could be confirmed via breakthrough experiments, using a model ABE mixture. Broader n-butanol breakthrough profiles were observed on the smaller fiber monolith at different flow rates. Via CFD simulations, it was shown that the smaller side channel size of the 250 μm monolith leads to an inhomogeneous gas velocity inside the monolith channels near the inlet of the monolith, possibly leading to the observed broadening of the n-butanol breakthrough profiles. However, simulations with fully unblocked side channels show that these side channels can also help in obtaining a uniform gas distribution throughout the structure. Furthermore, thermal regeneration allowed to fully restore the capacity of the ZIF-8 monoliths.

We report the synthesis of carboxylic acid-side-chain-containing N-acylated amino ester-based polyacrylates of different acylations (i.e.. N-acetyl, N-propionyl) and different side-chain lengths (i.e.. DP 1 and 2). This small library of polymers allowed for a detailed evaluation of the effect of molecular composition of carboxylated polymers on physicochemical and biological properties. Discrete monomers were prepared in a multistep process to resemble the molecular structure of previously reported rather disperse NPAE macromonomers obtained by SZWIP. All reported polymers were found to be water-soluble and pH-responsive and showed a cylindrical conformation in aqueous solution. Flow cytometry studies revealed that cellular association of the polymers was strongly dependent on their side-chain DP and acylation type. N-propionyl substitution (P (E n ), P (E2), P (E1)) generally led to a higher association than N-acetylation (P (M1)). Moreover, within the propionyl group, increasing the side-chain DP resulted in higher association. More importantly, the cellular fate of the carboxylic acid polymers was mainly dictated by the type of cyanine dye used for labeling. The direct comparison of Cy5- and sulfoCy5-labeled P (E2) and P (E1) revealed trafficking of the Cy5-modified polymers to mitochondria, while sulfoCy5 modification mainly resulted in colocalization with lysosomes (P (E1) > P (E2)).

In summary, we demonstrated the broad applicability of our previously introduced mitochondria-targeting strategy by translating it into discrete small organic COOH-containing monomers. This study highlights diverse opportunities to tailor the cellular interaction and fate of carboxylated polymers through adjustments of the molecular structure of the side chains and modification with various cyanine dyes, respectively. Typically, the modification of, e.g.. polymers and nanoparticles with dyes is considered problematic as it can trigger unwanted interactions with biological materials. In contrast, this study emphasizes the potential to exploit these interactions for the rational design of organelle-specific targeted nanomedicines.

In summary, hybrid rod-like nanoparticles consisting of the CNC as the core and polydopamine as the shell were prepared via oxidation-induced self-polymerization of dopamine in the presence of CNCs as the nanoscale templates. Performing the PDA coating at low dopamine concentrations is the key to realize conformal PDA coating of CNCs on the single particle level, leading to CNC@PDAs with a well-defined rod-like morphology and excellent colloidal stability while devoid of any pure PDA contaminations. Similar to the CNC templates, the CNC@PDA has well-defined liquid crystal behavior with clear phase separation that follows the classic nucleation and merging of nematic tactiods. Dependence of the LC behavior on the rod concentrations and ionic strengths is also qualitatively consistent with what is expected for charged rodlike particles. Differences between CNC and the PDA-coated ones in terms of the critical concentrations for the phase transitions can be explained by the difference in the effective diameters. Similar to CNC, the several kinds of CNC@PDA hybrid rods can still form a well-defined CLC phase with a pitch that is systematically larger than that of pristine CNC at the same concentrations and ionic strengths. The pitch of the CLC phase formed by the CNC or CNC@PDA rods has the general tendency to increase with increasing PDA thickness, suggesting weakening chiral interactions between the CNC@PDA rods. The surface charge differences and blurring effects exerted by the EDL cannot explain these phenomena, and it is the PDA layer and its thickness that have profound influences on the strength of the chiral interactions between the CNC@PDA hybrid rods. The PDA coating with increasing thickness can cover up some topological features such as chirality at the molecular level or geometrical chirality that drives the formation of the CLC phase.

In the case of Quebec, strategies that rely on the electrification of energy services using renewable energy are unlikely to "backfire" and create additional human health or biodiversity impacts (Figure ). This result is consistent with previous literature. The relative importance of the different cause-effect pathways (Figure ) is similar to a global assessment of anthropogenic emissions. The similarities suggest that energy services play a large role in global anthropogenic burden.

Novel PAEs containing high bioactive content via multiple pendant group attachments per repeat unit were successfully synthesized. With ibuprofen and mannitol as model bioactive and backbone, respectively, controlled bioactive release via polymer hydrolytic degradation was achieved. Furthermore, polymers were nontoxic to fibroblast cells and the released ibuprofen retained anti-inflammatory activity. As the first linear biodegradable polymers using polyols with high bioactive loading, these PAEs can be modified with respect to number of pendant groups, stereochemistry, and chain extender hydrophobicity, thereby altering release rate and thermal properties. With multiple pendant sites, additional molecules, such as other bioactives to achieve a synergistic effect and targeting moieties to afford efficient delivery can be incorporated into the polymer. Through this easily amenable methodology, a series of new, completely biodegradable polymers containing a myriad of different bioactives classes as pendant groups can be used to solve issues of low bioactive loading and burst release.

We extended the generalized stoichiometric model, which was first developed by Angenent et al. for n-caproate production, to predict the thermodynamic favorability of n-caprylate formation at different ethanol-to-acetate substrate ratios. Briefly, the model uses stoichiometric relationships to evaluate the moles of n-caprylate, n-caproate, n-butyrate, hydrogen gas, and ATP that would be produced based on the moles of ethanol and acetate provided to the microbiome. The maximum boundary for the metabolic flux is set to 10 mol of ethanol and acetate combined (by setting moles of ethanol to "a" and moles of acetate to "10 - a", see eq S1-2) and with a total of 20 mol of carbon for the substrate and the products. Thus, within this boundary, "a" identifies the moles of ethanol, but is always linked to acetate (representing a relative ratio between ethanol and acetate). We have made changes to the published model to include n-caprylate. We introduced a new term "c" for n-caproate, losing a predictable ratio between n-butyrate and n-caproate (Figure S1). This resulted in the overall stoichiometric eq (eq ): 1 a C 2 H 6 O + ( 10 - a ) C 2 H 3 O 2 - → b C 4 H 7 O 2 - + c C 6 H 11 O 2 - + ( 10 - 2 b - 3 c ) / 4 C 8 H 15 O 2 - + ( 30 - 2 a - 2 b - c ) / 2 H 2 O + ( 4 a + 2 b + c - 30 ) / 2 H 2 + ( - 30 + 4 a + 2 b + c ) / 4 H + + ( 30 - 2 b - c ) / 8 ATP

For our model, the stoichiometry of all metabolites (i.e.. ethanol, acetate, n-butyrate, n-caproate, and n-caprylate, molecular hydrogen, water, intermediary metabolites, redox mediators, and ATP) depended on the variables "a", "b", and "c". Similarly, the stoichiometry for reoxidation of reduced ferredoxin via H2-ase or Rnf and ATP synthase varied depending on the variables "a", "b", and "c", which determined the molecular hydrogen production and ATP production, respectively (Figure S1). The net consumption of one mole of water during acetate production from acetyl- CoA via substrate level phosphorylation (due to ATP hydrolysis) was considered when balancing the overall equation. Based on the overall stoichiometry and the ethanol and carboxylate concentrations that were measured in the effluent, the Gibbs free energy of the reaction was calculated, as well as the Gibbs free energy required for ATP formation. It was assumed that -72 kJ was required per mole of ATP produced, based on the estimate of Buckel and Thauer for ethanol-acetate fermentation to n-butyrate and n-caproate by C. kluyveri. We note that this value would vary based on the concentration of inorganic phosphate present in the bioreactor. If the Gibbs free energy of the reaction was more negative than the Gibbs free energy required for ATP formation, the reaction was deemed feasible (Figure S2).

For our model, we tested three scenarios by varying the values of "b" and "c" (i.e.. moles of n-butyrate and n-caproate in the stoichiometric equation). For scenario 1, we alleged that only n-caprylate was formed by the microbiome. For scenario 2, we alleged that 1 mol of n-butyrate, 1 mol of n-caproate, and 1.25 mol of n-caprylate were formed by the microbiome. Finally, for scenario 3, we alleged that 1.5 mol of n-butyrate, 1.5 mol of n-caproate, and 0.625 mol of n-caprylate were formed (Figure S2). We used the effluent ethanol and acetate concentrations that we had measured during the operating period for the thermodynamic calculations (i.e.. to calculate ΔG of the reaction with the stoichiometric model). Due to the relatively high ratio of ~220 for the effluent recycle flow rate compared to the influent flow rate of our bioreactor, we assumed that the effluent concentrations represented the mixed liquor concentrations in our bioreactor. Further details on the model assumptions and setup can be found in the Supporting Information.

For the most part, our model described what we observed experimentally. Similar to the trend observed by Angenent et al. for n-caproate production, our model predicted that higher ethanol-to-acetate ratios experienced by the microbiome led to more favorable thermodynamic conditions for chain elongation to n-caprylate (Figure S2). In other words, the Gibbs free energy of the n-caprylate formation reaction was more negative than the Gibbs free energy required for ATP production at higher ethanol-to-acetate ratios (Figure S2). In addition, the model predicted that higher ethanol-to-acetate ratios lead to higher ATP yields. At the higher ethanol-to-acetate substrate ratios of 275 and 16.9 g COD g COD-1 (183 and 11.3 mol mol-1) that we administered during periods 2 and 3 (Table ), the actual measured molar ethanol-to-acetate liquor ratios in the bioreactor effluent was 16.5 and 7.01, respectively (Table S3). At these ratios, our model predicted that formation of only n-caprylate was thermodynamically feasible (ΔG rxn > ΔG req for scenario 1 in Figure S2), as well as the formation of mixtures of n-butyrate, n-caproate, and n-caprylate (ΔG rxn > ΔG req for scenarios 2 and 3 in Figure S2). Indeed, we observed high n-caprylate-to-n-caproate product ratios of 5.9 and 2.0 g COD g COD-1 (4.3 and 1.5 mol mol-1) and n-caprylate specificities of 82% and 64% for our bioreactor during periods 2 and 3, respectively (Table S1).

During period 4 at an ethanol-to-acetate substrate ratio of 6.7 g COD g COD-1 (4.5 mol mol-1) (Table ), the ethanol-to-acetate liquor ratio declined to 3.11 (Table S3). At this ratio that was observed by the microbiome, the model predicted that formation of only n-caprylate was not thermodynamically feasible, but formation of a mixture of n-butyrate, n-caproate, and n-caprylate was (ΔG rxn > ΔG req for scenarios 2 and 3, but not scenario 1 in Figure S2). This mixed product spectrum was experimentally verified (Figure and Table S1). At the lowest ethanol-to-acetate substrate ratios that we maintained during the main period (i.e.. 3.6, 2.9, and 1.8 during periods 5, 6, and 7, respectively, Table ), the ethanol-to-acetate liquor ratios were also correspondingly low (i.e.. 1.4, 1.0, and 0.6, respectively, Table S3). At these liquor ratios none of the scenarios that we tested were thermodynamically feasible (Figure S2), ruling out considerable amounts of n-caprylate production from our thermodynamic model. However, we did observe lower n-caprylate production during periods 5 and 6 with specificities of 25.7% and 23.7%, respectively, but did not observe any n-caprylate production during period 7 (Figure and Table S1). These experimental specificities for periods 5 to 6 were, indeed, lower than the alleged specificity for our third scenario (i.e.. 1.5 mol of n-butyrate, 1.5 mol of n-caproate, and 0.625 mol of n-caprylate), which would have translated into a 35.3% n-caprylate specificity based on COD, and which was not possible according to our model (Figure S2).

Even though the predictions of our model are in agreement with the bioreactor performance, real care should be taken in using the model because of our oversimplifications and assumptions. First, we assumed that the effluent ethanol and acetate concentrations represented a uniform concentration in the bioreactor experienced by the microbiome. In fact, we saw different microbiome compositions at two different sampling locations in our bioreactor across the study period (discussed later in the text), which suggests that the substrate composition (i.e.. ethanol-to-acetate liquor ratio may have varied throughout the bioreactor height. Second, we developed a formula for the moles of ATP produced by our model assuming that the Rnf complex (ferredoxin-NAD oxidoreductase complex) found in C. kluyveri was being used to establish a proton gradient across the cell membrane and drive ATP production. Wang et al. have reported that under low ethanol and acetate concentrations ( ~ 1 mM), and therefore correspondingly lower reaction Gibbs free energies, C. kluyveri can adjust the activity of two enzymes (an electron bifurcating Nfn complex and a NADP+dependent β-hydroxybutyryl-CoA dehydrogenase) to decrease its ATP production requirements. Our current model does not account for this potential shift in ATP production (and lower associated Gibbs free energy requirements) in considering the thermodynamic feasibility of n-caprylate production. Third, our model was based on the reported metabolism of C. kluyveri, which may not represent the actual situation for our reactor microbiome. Fourth, this model was designed for a system with product extraction (e.g.. our bioreactor) where n-caprylate is continuously being removed from the bioreactor broth. Our model does not account for the effect of product toxicity on n-caprylate production, and therefore cannot be directly applied to batch systems without product extraction.

In summary, we have studied the nanoscale wetting behaviors of water molecules on some FCC metals. We have found that both the lattice constants and crystal surfaces greatly affect the wettability of FCC metals. Particularly, stable water droplets on water monolayers are found on crystal surface (100) of the metals Pd, Pt, and Al. The key to the water droplet on the water monolayer is the appropriate matching between the surface atoms arrangement and water molecules, which results in the rhombic ordered water monolayers. The ordered water structures reduce the number of hydrogen bond formed between the monolayers and other water molecules. In contrast, no water droplet can be found on other metal surfaces (Ni, Cu, Au, Ag, Pb) with (100) crystal surface and all of those metal surfaces with (110) and (111) crystal faces due to the lack of ordered water. Our work provides a better understanding of the wettability of some FCC metals and helps to expand our understanding of hydrophobicity and hydrophilicity and the "molecular-scale hydrophilicity" we proposed. Particularly, more attentions should be paid when the macroscopic surface contact angles on some specific solid surfaces with ordered water are measured in the experiments, where the apparent contact angles may reflect the wetting degree of adsorbed water, rather than the wetting degree of solid surfaces. We note that the metal surfaces are easily to be oxidized, which may affect the surface constituent and atomic arrangements. This may account of the fact that there is still lack of the direct experimental evidence of the room temperature "ordered water monolayer that does not completely wet water" on the mental surfaces. In applications, we have found that the ordered water monolayer that does not completely wet water can reduce the surface frictions at the hydrophilic surfaces. It should be noted that the work by Ho et al. presented direct slip length on the hydrophilic surfaces, which also shows the friction reduction at hydrophilic surfaces.

Deoxyfluorination with the PhenoFluor reagent arrived at a functional-group-tolerant reaction with a large substrate scope using a metal-free approach but features a crucial change in mechanism from Halex chemistry. Concurrent attack of the nucleophile and loss of the leaving group during aromatic deoxyfluorination limits charge buildup in the transition state and allows part of the exothermicity of leaving group loss to be released in the transition state. PhenoFluor and its associated reagents PhenoFluorMix and AlkylFluor have been thoroughly established to provide convenient and reliable access to a wide range of aryl and alkyl fluorides as well as alkyl aryl ethers. The major limitation of PhenoFluor deoxyfluorination is the need for stoichiometric amounts of an expensive reagent, which prohibits its application to synthesis on a large scale. More economical reagents, such as PyFluor and SO2F2, are preferable whenever less complex substrates are used. However, PhenoFluor deoxyfluorination can succeed when other methods fail and provides direct access to densely functionalized substrates in a reliable and predictable fashion. PhenoFluor deoxyfluorination with 18F holds promise to become one of the radiolabeling methods of choice for the synthesis of tracers for human PET imaging that are not amenable to classic SNAr or SN2 reactions. Several new methods for 18F incorporation are now available. In our opinion, at least the fluorination of boronic esters and PhenoFluor deoxyfluorination have shown the scope, functional group tolerance, robustness, and operational convenience to prove enabling to medical imaging. , However, further development of deoxyfluorination, especially in terms of facilitating ruthenium (de) complexation, are needed to allow 18F deoxyfluorination to fulfill its full potential.

Beyond synthetic utility, PhenoFluor chemistry gives fundamental insight into mechanistic features that permit an expansion of the substrate scope of aromatic nucleophilic displacement. Future endeavors should focus on how the lessons learned with fluoride can be applied to other nucleophiles to permit nucleophilic displacement in general to be feasible even with electron-rich aromatic substrates.

In summary, we have shown here that the surface binding energy of *HPO (OH) can be used as a good descriptor for the rational catalyst design to improve the oxidation efficiency of the hypophosphite fuel cell. The free energy changes ΔGs of hypophosphite dehydrogenation, phosphite oxidation, and hydride oxidation reactions are all found to be scaled very well to the surface binding energy of *HPO (OH). The key to optimize a better catalyst than Pd is to weaken both the Pd-P bonds and the Pd-H bonds simultaneously. Thus, a Pd-B catalyst, with B doping in the subsurface of Pd, has been proposed and the mechanism has been demonstrated. The experiment results confirm the theoretical prediction showing that the hypophosphite oxidation became easier and less hydrides were generated on the Pd-B/C catalyst as compared to the Pd/C catalysts. There is a notable increase in both the faradaic and energy efficiencies in direct hypophosphite fuel cell operation with a Pd5.3B/C anode. The present study provides a good example in designing efficient catalysts for liquid fuel cells based on hydrogen compounds "H n -X", where both HOR and XOR need to be taken into consideration.

The 355 nm photodissociation of N2O3 was detected in a VMII experiment when a gas sample containing nitrous acid was dehydrated. When a sample of NO and NO2 seeded in He was expanded into the VMII system, the photodissociation results were similar to those of dehydrated HONO. The vector correlations between μ, v, and J are all approaching the limiting values, indicating a very fast dissociation. A fast dissociation is understandable considering the energy of the 355 nm photon relative to the weak ON-NO2 bond. TDDFT calculations suggest that the observed dissociation comes from a nonplanar conformation of N2O3.

These experiments point to the value of DC-sliced VMII in photodissociation experiments for discriminating between or among multiple dissociation pathways or from multiple parent molecules present in an expansion. Linewidths can be used to differentiate between product Doppler profiles in a laser-induced fluorescence (LIF) experiment, but DC-sliced VMII has added resolution. The probe is quantum-state selective, like LIF, but the VMII detection is selective for both speed and direction of the photoproducts. Depending on the NO rovibronic state probed, NO+ ions from NO, NO2, HONO, and N2O3 are resolvable in the ion images. Since the DC-sliced VMII technique displays both speed and direction by the radial and angular components of the images, sorting out the NO+ from different precursors can be straightforward. This DC-sliced advantage was necessary to perform the first gas-phase photodissociation study of N2O3 reported here.

Our investigation of the feasibility of fluorinated analogues being substrates for sPLA2 shows that good degradability can be expected; water influx and accessibility to the hydrolytic site of the enzyme is predicted to be unperturbed in the bulk and therefore remains at a productive, high level. For the interface-adsorbed ES complexes, water accessibility can be decreased depending on the chemical topology of the bound substrate. Furthermore, because of the lowered barriers of the hydrolysis reactions of HF-ProAEL and F2-ProAEL when compared to those of ProAEL, the hydrolytic reaction is predicted to occur at a progressively faster rate. Hence, the addition of partially fluorinated phospholipid analogues allows for the rational design of liposomal vesicles of phospholipid mixtures with desirable physiochemical properties that are still subjects for sPLA2-triggered drug release.

Through NMR, GPC, ICP, viscosity analysis, and chemical scavenger tests, the aging mechanism was investigated for soybean oil under accelerated aging conditions. It was found that the formation of the superoxide radical played a significant role in soybean oil aging, since capturing the superoxide radical by benzoquinone would completely quench the aging process as well as adding 2,6-dibutyl-4-methylphenol to trap other radicals. The dissolved copper (II) cation was also found to play a significant role in soybean oil aging. Significantly, through NMR and GPC analysis, it disclosed that the polymerization process contributed a lot to the aging event, which led to the formation of significant amount of aged soybean oil having high MW with aging proceeding. The comprehensive mechanistic information disclosed in the present studies may have provided new clues for seeking new antioxidants to improve the oxidation stability of natural ester based insulating oils.

The present calculations employ the MCTDH , approach and its multilayer extension (ml-MCTDH). , Eigenstates of the Hamiltonian are obtained by block relaxation of state-averaged MCTDH or ml-MCTDH wave functions. The correlation discrete variable representation (CDVR) and its multilayer extensions ,, are used for the evaluation of the potential energy matrix elements. The MCTDH equations of motion are integrated using a constant mean field approach, the CMF2 scheme described in ref .

Note that in the present work the quasi-bound states of the F CH4 complex are computed using techniques developed for the calculations of bound states. No absorbing potentials or similar techniques are employed to limit the extension of the wave packet motion in the numerical simulations. The barrier toward decay into the HF + CH3 product channel efficiently prevents any motion into this channel on the time scale of the imaginary time propagation. Consequently, the eigenenergies obtained by the present calculations correspond to energies of very long-living resonance states. Since the lifetimes of these resonances exceed the time scale considered in the numerical calculations, explicit resonance lifetimes cannot be computed.

The block relaxation employs the imaginary time propagator e -Hβ with β = 5000 au in each iteration step. State-averaged (ml)-MCTDH wave functions with different numbers of wavepackets were used in the computations. Calculations with 13 wavepackets focus on an accurate description of the lowest states and are employed in the detailed analysis while calculations with 63 wavepackets provide a complete description of all quasi-bound states with energies below the reactant asymptote.

The time-independent ("primitive") basis sets used for the representation of single-particle functions are given in Table . Fast Fourier transform (FFT) schemes are used in the coordinates r, s, t, R, and Φ. Discrete variable representations (DVRs) are employed in all other coordinates. In the six coordinates describing the internal motion of the methyl fragment, ρ, ϑρ, φρ, θ, χ, and ϕ, harmonic oscillator DVRs are used. In the coordinate Θ, one has to account for singularities appearing in the kinetic energy operator at Θ = 0 and Θ = π. Here the cot-DVR introduced in ref is employed.

To obtain an accurate and efficient representation of the wave function, many MCTDH and ml-MCTDH calculations with different layering schemes and single-particle function basis set sizes have been tested. Diagramatic representations of the MCTDH and ml-MCTDH wave functions (for a detailed description of the diagrammatic notation please see ref ) used in the final calulations studying the quasi-bound state of the F CH4 complex are depicted in Figure . The representations corresponding to the basis sets A-F are shown in panels a-f, respectively.

Beside the 12D calculations studying the quasi-bound states of the F CH4 complex, also 11D calculations studying the F CH4 system in the limit of large R have been performed. These calculations are required to obtain the vibrational zero point energies in the asymptotic limit. They have been performed for all 11D analogues of the basis sets A-F to define the zero of energy for the corresponding 12D calculations. The 11D analogues of the 12D basis sets A-F are called A′-F′ in the following. The diagramatic representation of the wave functions used in additional asymptotic calulations discussed below is displayed in Figure . The corresponding basis sets are denoted Gn′ and use different values of the size parameter n. The basis sets G1′, G2′, and G3′ employ n = 1, 2, and 3, respectively.

Both Tc (VII) and U (VI) were fully soluble (5000 g, 5 min) in the no mineral control buffer solutions, while Np (V) showed modest removal from the 30 mM buffer with 80.4 ± 6.4% of Np (V) soluble in the buffer at 14 days (Figure ). This was despite the fact that PHREEQC modeling with both the SIT and LLNL databases predicted under saturation of Np (V) in the buffer solution at ~10-6 M Np (V). Similarly, in the cells only controls with no electron donor, Tc (VII) and U (VI) in the high carbonate system were, within error, fully retained in solution over the experimental time course, and Np (V) again showed only ~20% removal suggesting the cells alone did not provide any significant sorption or reduction capacity in these systems (Figure ). Interestingly, for U (VI) the low carbonate, cells only controls with no electron donor did show significant U removal ( ~ 70%). The XANES analysis for this sample confirmed the U was speciated as U (VI) (Figure ), and thus the removal was due to sorption of U (VI) to biomass again confirming no significant reduction capacity was retained in the electron donor free cell controls.

On reaction with minerals, the Tc (VII) system showed no removal by the unaltered minerals, while in the microbially reduced experiments, extensive Tc removal occurred (86.0 ± 3.6% by biotite and 89.1 ± 8.9% by chlorite) by the experimental end point (Figure A). For U (VI) in the high carbonate buffer with unaltered minerals, there was no removal with biotite and only modest removal with chlorite (20 ± 3%). This was similar to previously published data on 30 mM carbonate systems showing scant removal of U (VI) by unaltered chlorite over time scales of days. The U experiments with microbially reduced minerals in high carbonate buffer showed essentially no removal of U (VI) with biotite, while chlorite was slightly more reactive after microbial reduction with 37 ± 2% U sorbed to the solid phase after 14 days (Figure B). For U (VI) the experiment was run at relatively high (0.126 mM U (VI)) concentrations compared to Tc and Np systems (which were at ~ 1 μM concentrations). Even so, in terms of electron balance, there was a greater than 6-fold stoichiometric excess of mineral-associated, biogenic and thus reactive Fe (II) ( ~ 0.15 m mol per 100 mL experiment) compared to U (VI) (0.012 m mol per 100 mL experiment); the system reactivity was therefore not limited by reactive Fe (II) in the microbially reduced mineral experiments. For the low carbonate system, both the unaltered and microbially reduced minerals showed significant reactivity toward U (VI) with >80% removal in all systems, although it is clear that the microbially reduced phases showed the highest reactivity with essentially complete removal at 14 days (Figure C). The different behavior of U (VI) in the low and high carbonate systems is related to the influence of carbonate on the system as uranyl-carbonates are known to decrease U (VI) adsorption to mineral surfaces, lower the U (VI)/U (IV) redox couple, and retard the kinetics of U (VI)-reduction. , Indeed, recent work has highlighted the importance of aqueous, noncarbonate UO2 2+ as the most readily reducible aqueous uranyl species. These factors support the observations in our experiments that U (VI) reactivity is enhanced in the low carbonate systems compared to the high carbonate systems. Finally, the Np (V) reaction with unaltered biotite and chlorite showed slightly increased removal compared to the groundwater and cell only controls with 30.1 ± 0.7% and 48.4 ± 0.6% removal at the experiment end points. For both of the microbially reduced minerals, and in contrast to the parallel U (VI) experiment in high carbonate buffer, Np (V) was quickly scavenged to below the detection limit ( < 4 × 10-11 M) within 24 h (Figure D). Overall, the microbially reduced mineral phases showed enhanced reactivity to Tc (VII), U (VI) in low carbonate, and Np (V) with relatively poor reactivity in the U (VI) high carbonate system, the latter presumably as a result of the influence of carbonate on U (VI)-reactivity.

In this work, we report a comprehensive study on the gas-phase reactivity of aluminum clusters with benzene. It is found that Al n + clusters are more reactive than neutral and anionic counterparts and produce Al+Bz, Al+Bz2, and Al2 +Bz3 in large mass abundances pertaining to stable sandwiched complexes. Also observed are the larger cationic aluminum clusters reacting with benzene to form Al n +Bz products, among which Al13 +Bz shows slightly higher mass abundances than its neighboring Al n + clusters. To understand the underline cluster-benzene interactions, the reactivity of Al13 ±,0 and Al15 + clusters with benzene was systematically studied in both experimental and computational views. Geometry optimization, molecular orbital analysis, natural bond orbital (NBO) analysis, topological analysis, and noncovalent interaction plots based on independent gradient model (IGM) fully clarify the stable cluster-π interaction in Al13 +Bz. Also we illustrate the influences of charge and cluster size dependence for the stability of aluminum-benzene clusters. Distinctly from traditional ion-π interactions, cluster-π interactions are strongly influenced by the orbital interaction and the geometrical structure of the clusters, which mainly accounts for the enhanced stability of Al13 +Bz. Crucial insights into the nature of this interaction will expand the essentiality of noncovalent interaction and contribute to the discovery of new binding sites in some biological systems and functional materials, developing new ideas in drug designing, catalyst optimizing, etc.

Quantum chemical computations were performed to explore the kinetic behavior for the reaction of DME with NO to produce CH3OCH2 and HNO. A single transition state was located with NO capturing the out-of-plane H atoms, and it was confirmed that there appeared a weak hydrogen-bonding postreaction adducts lying lower than the separate products in energy. From direct kinetics study in the high-pressure limit, it could be argued that tunneling quickly became insignificant with temperature and variational effects had a greater contribution to the calculated rate coefficients at high temperatures than at low. Multiple structures and torsional anharmonicities due to the two highly coupled torsional motions in the transition structure played a critical role in the rate coefficient calculations. The Arrhenius activation energy for the reaction of DME with NO appeared to be highly temperature dependent. Additionally, the relationship of E a with T was not strictly linear. Accordingly, the four-parameter Arrhenius formula was employed to reasonably describe the MS-CVT/SCT rate coefficients including tunneling effect as well as multistructural and torsional contributions on the basis of the compound method CCSD (T)/6-311+G (2df,2pd)//B2PLYP/TZVP results over the whole temperature range of 200-3000 K.

To conclude, in this work we perform first principle ab initio calculation for the electronic and optical properties of phosphorene oxides P4O n . We found that the oxygen coverage affects the electronic and optoelectronic properties. In summary, the electronic and optical properties of phosphorene oxides P4O n are studied via ab initio calculation. The results indicate that electronic and optoelectronic properties of this system are controlled by the oxygen coverage.

In summary, to obtain different color changes for photochromic compounds, group modification and coordination with metals are common methods to achieve this goal. In this work, it is demonstrated for the first time that different coordination modes can lead to controllable color changes. Two compounds exhibit different photochromic behaviors: compounds with dicoordinated bipy groups show significant red-shift absorption compared to the compound with monocoordinated bipy groups after illumination. Thus, this method provides a new way to obtain the expected color changes by regulating the coordination modes of bipy groups for photochromic compounds.

Several new chemical and isotopic approaches have recently been developed and/or applied and are particularly promising for identifying sources of fluids and their migration mechanisms and pathways from deep reservoirs to shallow aquifers and the atmosphere in situations where the traditional tracers produce ambiguous results. Clumped isotopes of CH4 and noble gases show promise for more definitively distinguishing sources of natural gas (i.e.. microbial from thermogenic and abiotic), removal via various oxidation pathways, and fingerprinting gases from specific oil/gas reservoirs based on their formation temperatures. - High-resolution molecular and isotopic profiles of hydrocarbons obtained during oil/gas drilling provide information about potential gas sources and fingerprints, particularly from intermediate gas-bearing zones between target reservoirs and shallow aquifers. Advanced microbiological techniques allow characterization of microbial communities responsible for CH4 generation and hydrocarbon oxidation, and their response to introduction of HVHF fluids. Development of laser-based approaches for measuring noble gas radionuclides in groundwater provides more robust residence time constraints for potentially HVHF-impacted aquifers. More broadly, these emerging approaches may be applied to other subsurface extraction and storage issues, including new frontiers of energy and renewable alternatives (e.g.. subsurface storage of H2, anthropogenic CO2, and/or nuclear waste).

A new series of PIs were synthesized to examine the aggregate emission and OFET behavior. All molecules were thermally stable and showed electrochemical reproducibility. Solubility of the functionalized PIs in various solvents makes them promising for easy and inexpensive device fabrication. Bottom gate-top contact OFETs were fabricated by solution processing of the active layer. In the series of molecules, 1 and 4 containing electron-accepting bromine and nitro groups, respectively, showed very high mobility and on/off ratio. With the binary solvent system (THF/H2O), all molecules under study formed J-aggregates. The SEM images of the aggregates indicated the formation of well-defined nanostructures.
