The ternary system is composed of a polymer, which itself contains two specific fractions differing in, for example, weight, architecture, or semicrystallinity, and consequently which are forming a respective component, P1 and P2, in the ternary system. This is a simplified form to consider and investigate the polydisperse effect of polymers on the SLE.

It could be shown that the model is able to predict a critical molecular weight level, where SLE-based fractionation is becoming independent of molecular chain length, though the sensitivity in fractionation with respect to molecular architecture is kept even above the critical molecular weight level. This is the reason why SLE-based fractionation methods are efficient tools to separate high polymers according to their molecular architecture. A strong influence of branching on the ternary system could be shown, small deviations in branching number and order are causing strong solubility asymmetries between the polymeric pseudocomponents. Further, it could be revealed, that solvents with higher molecular weight and more complex architecture have a strong impact on the decrease of solubility and support solubility asymmetries between the polymeric pseudocomponents. This is highly relevant for tailored separation of molecules according to their different architecture. Hence, this work contributes to the theoretical understanding and provides additionally a theoretical base for SLE-based polymer fractionation techniques.

The mixing rules have a great impact on the description of vapor-liquid equilibrium for mixtures containing ammonia. An unexpected liquid-liquid phase separation easily occurs in VLE incorrectly when applying the EoS mixing rules and some EoS/G E mixing rules to ammonia + alkane or alkene systems. Among all the mixing rules studied in this paper, MHV1 gives the best VLE reproduction in all of the systems.

The group parameters of ammonia and the group interaction parameters among -NH3, -CH3, -CH-CH2, -CF3, and -CHF2 were determined by regressing the VLE data. It seems like the model based on UNIFAC is more suitable for systems containing ammonia.

The theoretical PCSAFT EoS showed both advantages and disadvantages for the mixtures concerned. It can predict the VLLE and VLE with only one interaction parameter once the successful regression of VLE data was done; however large deviations were displayed in R717 + R152a, 1-butene, or R125 systems.

As to the excess Gibbs functions, the MHV2 mixing rule obtains similar excess Gibbs function compared to the EoS type mixing rules. The Wong-Sandler mixing rules require a rather large contribution to the excess Gibbs energy from the second virial interaction coefficient. It seems that most models are only good for correlation purposes.

We report observation, using time-resolved FTIR emission spectroscopy, of vibrationally excited products following UV photolysis of pyrazine. Specifically, UV excitation of pyrazine at 308 and 248 nm resulted in spectra showing only vibrationally highly excited pyrazine but no photolysis products. When the excitation energy was increased to 193 nm, the spectra revealed emission bands assignable to HNC, HCN, and HCCH. The fact that vibrationally excited pyrazine does not appear in the spectra at higher excitation energy strongly suggests that the resulting photofragments are generated from vibrationally highly excited pyrazine in the ground electronic state, rather than from reactions on excited electronic states. Spectral fit analysis of the nascent products allowed a lower bound estimate of the HNC/HCN product branching ratio of ca. 0.07.

Ab initio calculations were used to characterize the energetically accessible reaction channels. A series of sequential and concerted reaction channels resulting primarily in the production of HCCH + 2HCN (or HCN + HNC) were predicted to occur on the S0 surface. Consistent with experiment, it was predicted that only excitation at 193 nm provides sufficient energy to initiate photolysis reactions leading to vibrationally excited products. However, excitation at 248 nm does provide sufficient energy for partial fragmentation to HCN + cyclopropene-imine following isomerization to pyrimidine, and it may provide just enough energy to surmount the minimal barrier to reaction (via a concerted mechanism) but not enough to produce vibrationally excited products. Finally, the experimental and theoretical data reported here indicate that 308 nm excitation predominantly produces vibrationally excited pyrazine with a negligible amount of photolysis products.

In the present work, we have made an historical account of the achievements in the theory and computations of phosphorescence and related spin-forbidden phenomena. Our notion is that although a lot of experimental data have been collected over the years, theoretical investigations shedding light on the principles and mechanisms of phosphorescence remained quite limited until the last couple of decades. The triplet origin of phosphorescence remained unproven until 1943, and the debates around the triplet-singlet nature of phosphorescence did not cease until 1958 when Hutchinson and Magnum discovered EPR absorption of the triplet state in crystals and finally could prove the paramagnetic nature of this triplet state. However, the main contribution to the establishment of triplet state spectroscopy belongs, independently, to Terenin, Lewis, and Kasha in the fifties.

Accounting for perturbation theory, phosphorescence gains intensity from spin-allowed S-S and T-T electronic transitions via the spin-orbit coupling mixing of the singlet excited states manifold (Sn) with the first triplet (T1) excited state and of the triplet excited states manifold (Tn) with the ground singlet (S0) electronic state. A proper account of spin-orbit coupling makes it possible to estimate the main parameters of phosphorescence, like the transition dipole moment, radiative lifetime, and rate constant for each of the spin sublevels of the triplet state. The best equipment for the theoretical study of phosphorescence of today is, in our opinion, the quadratic-response theory formalism implemented in the DALTON program package, where this method is accessible at the HF, MCSCF, or DFT levels and where the spin-orbit operator can be accounted for exactly or by various effective approximations. The quadratic-response theory rests on an implicit sum-overstate principle, which allows one to describe correctly and largely clarify the phosphorescence mechanism for a number of difficult cases such as dioxygen (magnetic phosphorescence), benzene (vibronically induced phosphorescence), porphyrins (external and internal heavy atom effects), and cyclometalated iridium complexes (spin-sublevel selectivity and tuning of transition dipole moment orientation).

The greatest challenge of computational phosphorescence of today is the purposeful design of novel materials for modern devices of organic electronics, especially for organic light emitting devices (OLEDs). The triplet states in OLED materials play a crucial role because upon electron-hole recombination 3/4 of the formed excitons reside in the triplet state. The involvement of triplet excitons for enhancing of photoluminescence is impossible without overcoming the spin prohibition for singlet-triplet transitions. Therefore, the search of novel effective schemes for triplet-to-singlet spin crossover is a very important topic for modern phosphorescence spectroscopy as well as for theoretical modeling. For today, the most hopeful pathway to enable the emission from triplets in OLEDs is the thermally activated delayed fluorescence (TADF) process acting through the reverse intersystem crossing (RISC) process. In this review, we have presented the recent achievements in this field and the theoretical background for some new schemes of TADF in binary systems like intermolecular triplet-singlet energy transfer and RISC between singlet- and triplet-state exciplexes. Finally, we also reviewed some photobiology applications of the triplet state. The field remains wide open, and there is much room for new theory and modeling with strong ramifications for the rational design of novel electronic and photonic devices. We hope that this review can contribute to the further progress in computational phosphorescence and raise the awareness of researchers on the principles of modern phosphorescence spectroscopy.

In this work, we have explored the behavior of two Na+ tagged hexosamines, glucosamine and galactosamine, under CID conditions. Our experimental results deliver the characteristic dissociation patterns, which extends the reference database for the LODES approach mentioned in the introduction. Although the identification of the anomeric configuration remains challenging for both hexosamines, the two hexosamines can be distinguished easily by observing the relative intensity between the MS signals associated with the 0,2A (m/z 143) and 0,3A (0,3X) cross-ring cleavage (m/z 112 and 113). The calculations in this study shows that this difference in the mass spectra is associated with the difference in the values for the "0,2 0,3 gap", i.e.. the difference in the barriers for the C-C scission steps of the 0,2A and 0,3A cross-ring cleavage, which in return is mainly a result of the different stability of the TS structures associated with the 0,2A cross-ring cleavage. Although there are other MS-based methods that aim at identifying monosaccharides including their chirality, e.g.. via the investigation of (transition) metal complexes formed with the sugar under study, - the fixed ligand kinetic method, , or the comparison of the reaction rates of lithiated sugars and water in a quadrupole ion trap, the present work provides, together with some earlier studies, an easier applicable method that can, not only be used on isolated sugar samples, but is also suitable for the identification of monosaccharides, which are produced from the CID of oligosaccharides in mass spectrometer and captured in an ion-trap.

A further aspect that can be seen from the computational calculations at MP2 level is that hexosamines are, in their reactivity, more like HexNAcs than hexoses. Both HexNs and HexNAcs share the feature that essentially all information on the anomeric configuration is lost under CID conditions, as the ring-opening is the dominating reaction for those sugars in ring-form. Also, the behavior of the linear forms of GlcN and GlcNAc are comparable, as both feature an energetically low-lying 0,2A cross-ring dissociation channel. The main difference between GlcN and GlcNAc is also easy to understand: The dehydration channel that dominates the dissociation of GlcNAc requires the H transfer to the NAc group that is not present in GlcN.

At the end, there is a technical aspect regarding the computational results that is worth pointing out: The circumstance that calculations at B3LYP level of theory could not reproduce the experimental observation as in earlier works ,, raises some questions about the quantum chemical methods. In light of the results of this study, it seems reasonable to put some efforts into investigating how the different computational methods affect the transition state calculations for sugars.

Results revealed that, during alkali treatment, the amount of aluminum deposited and/or exchanged for B increases, which can effectively avoid the excess etching of silicon and introduce mesopores into the zeolite to enhance the diffusion rate of reactants and target products and inhibit the formation of carbon deposits. An appropriate amount of aluminum can render the high selectivity of low-carbon olefins. With respect to olefin aromatization, the HBZ5-27-AT catalyst exhibits the best performance. During the 200 h stable period, the total selectivity of C2 =-C4 = is more than 70%, contributing to further olefin aromatization.

Compared to the traditional methanol-to-aromatic catalysts, the two-step coupled catalyst layers result in synergistic catalysis to produce aromatics, exhibiting clear advantages with respect to stability. When the filling ratio for the HBZ5-27-AT and18-3Zn-Z5 was 3:7, the reaction was stable for 194 h and the single-pass aromatic production increased from 0.15 to 4.98 g/g catalyst.

Therefore, the multi-stage aromatization of olefins is considered to be a potential method for transforming excess hydrocarbons to high-value aromatics. Aromatic hydrocarbons from methanol via lower olefins can hopefully obtain highly selective aromatic hydrocarbons with high stability of the catalyst.

In this Review, we have attempted to chronicle how chemistry education research has evolved over the years from an individual's ideas about how to improve student learning to a sophisticated research enterprise driven by data and evidence. In contrast to the era of personal empiricism, modern CER studies are grounded in an understanding of how people learn that has emerged from contemporary learning theories. It is now generally accepted in the CER community that knowledge is not transferred intact from instructor to student but rather is constructed in the mind of the learner. ,, This construction does not take place on a blank slate, as students arrive in our courses with background ideas and preconceptions that may or may not be appropriate. As a consequence, these pieces of knowledge may contain errors and unscientific ideas. We also know that many of these ideas cannot be "overwritten" merely by telling students the correct version. Although we do not have strong evidence for the mechanisms involved in construction and reconstruction of ideas, there is evidence that many learners do not have stable mental models about chemical concepts. Unlike experts, students' knowledge tends to be fragmentary and not well-contextualized; , most researchers therefore believe that students must be helped to connect and, if necessary, reweave their ideas to construct more coherent, robust understanding of atoms and molecules.

One way to facilitate the construction of more expert-like knowledge frameworks is to develop learning experiences that allow students to make connections to core ideas in chemistry. ,, Relationships between concepts that may be obvious to experts often go unnoticed by novices. Thus, explicit linkage of course content back to foundational disciplinary ideas can aid students in appropriately organizing their knowledge. Course content can be extended, adapted, and connected to core ideas in the context of scientific practices such as constructing and using models, analyzing and evaluating data, using evidence to construct and support claims, and constructing explanations. , Curricula that support students with explicit connections to core ideas in the context of scientific practices are more likely to build understanding. Gains in understanding are even more pronounced if these connections are built over time, scaffolded, and revisited as students' understanding deepens. ,,

Tasks (both formative and summative) that require students to make connections should support student construction of more expert-like frameworks. In this context, it is useful to remember that assessments send a strong message to students about what matters. - When everything is assessed, everything appears to be equally important, and students can be quickly overwhelmed by what appears to be a vast swathe of material. In such a scenario, there is no recourse for students but to memorize everything and regurgitate fragments of knowledge. Focusing on assessing fewer important ideas helps students develop deeper knowledge by encouraging intentional, Type 2 thinking about those concepts most fundamental to a discipline.

Weaving together resources into coherent and useful disciplinary knowledge is a difficult process that requires considerable effort on the part of the student. ,, Stated differently, development of expertise is inherently an active process. Indeed, there is strong evidence that learning environments designed to promote student engagement and interactions both among peers and with the instructor improve outcomes, particularly for lower-performing students. , The mechanisms of improvement may be explained by social constructivist learning theory: as students interact with each other and with more knowledgeable others, they have to consider their ideas, refine, reflect, and explain. There are many ways to bring about this kind of active engagement, and most of them have been shown to improve overall average course grades or performance on concept inventories.

While much of the aforementioned research is relevant to learning in general, there are particular difficulties with learning chemistry because all of the causal mechanistic drivers for phenomena of interest occur at the atomic and molecular level. Students can learn to make the connection between macroscopic properties of materials and the molecular level, but it requires a long chain of causal inferences-almost none of which can be intuited by experience. Students must make sense of representations and diagrams that attempt to convey ideas about things that cannot be seen, and so visualizations, structures, and other tools can impart not only meaning but also incorrect ideas that may hinder learning.

In this paper, we have studied NMA-water mixturess with linear and nonlinear IR spectroscopy. The lifetime of the amide I mode has been found to be similar to the previous reports of diluted and the bulk NMA solutions. We revealed that adding water to NMA leads to disruption of the HB chains of NMA molecules, which were recently reported to be present in bulk NMA. Instead, solvation results in the formation of water and NMA clusters where the amide I dynamics are "frozen", at least at the picosecond time scale. Curiously, only the frequency and rotational dynamics are frozen while the anisotropy is not and does decay at the ~1 ps time scale. This is because the excitation is mobile and therefore samples a few amide I modes with similar frequencies but different orientations. The former leads to constant CLS values (after the initial drop), as the excitations tend to be shared between vibrations with similar frequency, while the latter results in the anisotropy decay. It would be interesting to investigate if the water dynamics are frozen, too (similar to the recently reported "mayonnaise effect"); these experiments are underway.

In our opinion, the results obtained here could form a basis for understanding the hydration structure and (vibrational) dynamics of more complex biological systems than the NMA-water system studied in the current work. Real proteins may, for example, have charged groups at the surface, a complication that could be avoided using simpler systems such as NMA as a testing ground. We clearly find that even without an actual backbone or side chains the amide unit is experiencing a kind of hydrophobic collapse when exposed to water. This leads to disruption of the long-range ordered HB network between NMA molecules observed in bulk NMA and to clustering of both NMA and water molecules. The resulting spectral dynamics reflecting the HB dynamics, at least in the NMA phase, are "frozen" as compared to the dynamics in the bulk. This suggests that the hydrophobic collapse is an intrinsic property of the amino acid backbone units, which may of course be enhanced by hydrophobic side chains or suppressed by hydrophilic ones.

It has been reported that ACN coupled with n-hexane, which can precipitate the proteins but extract less lipid, has been used to extract BPA and its chlorinated derivatives from human adipose samples. In the present study, a similar liquid-liquid extraction (LLE) method was adopted. Because there are strong matrix effects when the extracts of decidua and chorionic villi samples are analyzed by only a LLE cleanup method, additional steps are necessary to eliminate potential interferences. In this study, freezing was used for the removal of lipid, which was precipitated after having been kept at -20 °C overnight and immediately centrifuged at -10 °C. Although the matrix effects were greatly improved, they were still as high as 68% (Table S2) when DCBPA and DCNP were analyzed. Thus, NH2 SPE cartridges were further tested for sample cleanup. Although 20:80 (v/v) MeOH/acetone, 50:50 (v/v) MeOH/acetone, and 80:20 (v/v) MeOH/acetone were used to elute the target chemicals from NH2 cartridges, 20:80 (v/v) MeOH/acetone was found to be the most effective for elution of all eight analytes with the lowest matrix interferences. Finally, a method using LLE coupled with freezing-lipid centrifugation and NH2 SPE was applied to prepare decidua and chorionic villi samples, with signal suppression rates less than 19% in all cases.

A recovery test was conducted by spiking each target compound at different concentrations, followed by the entire pretreatment procedure (n = 3). The method recoveries of 8 target analytes were 83-108% with a relative standard deviation (RSD) of 1-12% for 0.05 ng/mL, 84-118% with a RSD of 1-20% for 0.5 ng/mL, and 72-115% with a RSD of 2-19% for 2 ng/mL (Table ). A previously developed dansylation LC-MS/MS method, which demonstrated high sensitivity and low matrix effects in the analysis of BPA, NP and their chlorinated derivatives in food-contact papers (FCPs), was applied to the analysis of the same target analytes in decidua, chorionic villi, and plasma samples. As displayed in Table , the LOQs in plasma samples were 0.004-0.03 ng/mL for chlorinated NPs and 0.001-0.005 ng/mL for chlorinated BPAs, which are significantly lower than the LOQs of chlorinated BPAs in serum (0.05 ng/mL) reported in a previous paper. The method applied to the analysis of decidua and chorionic villi samples also showed high sensitivity, with LOQs of 0.02-0.3 ng/g, which are significantly lower than those reported in placental tissue samples (1.0-2.0 ng/g) or in adipose samples (0.5-3.0 ng/mL). , BPA and NP were detected in the procedural blanks (0.02 ± 0.01 ng/mL for BPA and 0.82 ± 0.40 ng/mL for NP in plasma samples; 0.59 ± 0.01 ng/g for BPA and 5.88 ± 0.64 ng/g for NP in decidua and chorionic villi samples), and their LOQs were 0.04 ng/mL for BPA and 1.20 ng/mL for NP in plasma samples, 0.03 ng/g for BPA, and 1.92 ng/g for NP in decidua and chorionic villi samples. The instrumental and method linearity was demonstrated using a nine-point (0.005, 0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.5, 2, 10, 50, and 100 ng/mL) calibration curve for each analyte with good precision (RSD ≤ 5%) and r 2 > 0.99. The signal-to-noise ratios for the lowest concentration on calibration curves of analytes were 10-26. Interday precision of all substances in decidua, chorionic villi samples, and plasma samples are within 20% for lower LOQ (LLOQ) level and within 15% for other levels.

In this work, we used DLS, cryo-TEM and ITC to investigate the interaction between DOPC vesicles and CNCs. All techniques consistently revealed the formation of pH-dependent CNC-liposome complexes. The complexes were formed only when the charge sign of the particles was opposite and the complexation was more pronounced at lower pH where the charge of the vesicles was higher. The stoichiometry, enthalpy, and binding constant of the interaction were obtained using ITC. The results led to the conclusion that the charge of the vesicles plays a major role in the interaction and determines whether the complexation will take place or not. For oppositely charged components, the more positive the charge of the vesicles, the more pronounced the association with the CNCs, as demonstrated by a higher K a value at pH 2. The origin of the measured heat in this case was attributed to the release of counterions from the hydration shell of the particles as the interaction takes place. For similarly charged components, the interaction was not favorable as indicated by the absence of measured heat. This combination of techniques was a useful approach to investigate the interaction between CNCs and lipid vesicles and may be applied to other types of complexes made from lipids and CNCs that present different characteristics in terms of charge and size. Further work is in progress using flat supported lipid bilayers in order to investigate the CNC-lipid interaction in a curvature-independent scenario and other types of lipids to get a broader perspective of the interaction.

Temperature, conductivity, pH, and dissolved oxygen or oxidation-reduction potential (ORP) were measured in the field using a YSI multiprobe (YSI, U.S.A). The probes were calibrated at the start of each day using YSI calibration standards. All 48 samples were analyzed for dissolved anions by ion chromatography on a Dionex IC DX-2100. The IC calibration was verified using a secondary Dionex 7-anion standard at varying concentrations. Only runs reporting values within 5% of the secondary standard were accepted. Major cations were analyzed by directly coupled plasma optical emission spectrometry (DCP-OES), and trace elements, including Mo, B, and Sr, were analyzed by inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS) on a VG PlasmaQuad-3. DCP-OES was calibrated to the NIST 1643e standard, which was used at varying concentrations throughout sample runs, and the ICP-MS was calibrated to OSIL Atlantic Seawater. All concentrations are reported to the instrumental precision of ±0.1 mg/L for major elements and ±0.1 μg/L for trace elements. We calculated detection limits by multiplying the standard deviation of repeated blank measurements by three and dividing by the slope of the external standard. Relative standard errors (RSE) were less than 10% for randomized duplicates on the DCP-OES and ICP-MS. Charge balances were <10% difference for all samples, except those samples missing alkalinity data.

Boron and Sr isotope ratios were measured using thermal ionization mass spectrometry (TIMS) at Duke University. Samples for B analysis were pretreated with 10% Optima hydrogen peroxide. The 11B/10B ratio was measured on single Re filaments as BO2 - ions in negative mode and normalized to the NIST SRM 951 standard. Boron isotope ratios are reported as 1 δ 11 B = [ 1 - ( B 11 / B 10 ) / ( B 11 SRM 951 / B 10 SRM 951 ) ] × 1000 with a precision of ±0.3‰ on repeated measurements of the NIST SRM 951 standard (mean = 4.0051, n = 65). Sr was preconcentrated by evaporation in a HEPA filtered clean hood and redigested in 3.5 N HNO3, then separated using Eichrom Sr-specific ion-exchange resin. 87Sr/86Sr ratios were measured on the TIMS in positive mode using single Re filaments with a precision of ±0.000006 on repeated measurements of NIST SRM 987 standard (mean = 0.71062, n = 98).

[4He], [22Ne], [40Ar]) were all less than ±1.46%. Helium isotopic errors were approximately ±0.0093 times the ratio of air (or 1.0293 × 10-8) for the 3He/4He ratio.

Groundwater residence time estimates were calculated using 3H-3He and radiogenic 4He in-growth techniques to determine the apparent ages using a simplistic piston-flow conceptual model following previously published methods. - ,- Tritium active waters indicate the presence of post-1950s (modern) water (recharged since the early 1950s). Excess 3He produced by the radioactive decay of 3H were calculated by in-growth methods using the measured 3He/4He and 4He concentrations and noble-gas derived amounts of excess air and recharge temperatures. , Further details of the modeling approached are described in the Supporting Information.

The FH compounds have the Heusler structure with a general formula X2YZ, where X and Y are transition metals and Z is a main group element. The structure has the Fm3m (225) space group, with the Y and Z atoms forming a NaCl structure, and the X atoms are in the tetrahedral sites of the YZ NaCl-like structure, see Figure A. The X atoms can also be regarded as forming two different face-centered cubic (fcc) sublattices, X1 and X2. The Y atom is located at (0, 0, 0), the Z atom at (1/2, 1/2, 1/2), and the X1 and X2 atoms at (1/4, 1/4, 1/4) and (3/4, 3/4, 3/4), respectively. The HH structure is closely related to the Heusler structure, where the X2 sublattice is empty, as shown in Figure B. The space group of the HH structure is F43m (216) and can be viewed as made of four distinct fcc sublattices, shown in different colors in Figure B.

For each of the matrix/NS phase pairs, we calculate the mixing energies, as detailed below. The calculations were performed using the Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof (PBE) generalized-gradient approximation, employing the projector augmented plane wave (PAW) method, , as implemented in VASP (Vienna Ab-initio Simulation Package). For our calculations, we used the OQMD scheme for performing VASP GGA-PBE calculation: 520 eV energy cutoff, 10-4 eV energy convergence criterion, and using spin polarization. Equivalent basis set size and other integration grids were used for each of the different sizes of supercells, and a k-mesh (Monkhorst-Pack) with KPPRA (k-point density per reciprocal atom) of 8000 was used. Every crystal structure, pure and alloyed, was fully relaxed, that is, cell volume, cell shape, and ionic positions. Note that the calculated energies are at zero temperature and pressure. In addition, for better estimate of the solubility between the two compounds, we also calculated the vibrational entropy of mixing (see section ), for which the phonon dispersion was required. The phonon dispersion was calculated using finite displacement method in 2 × 2 × 2 supercells with the Phonopy code.

The mixing of the host matrix with the NS phase is done such that the stoichiometry of the mixed system always lies on the tie-line between the two constituent compounds. A tie-line connecting two phases implies a stable two-phase equilibrium exists between those phases. In this paper, we generally look for the existence of a tie-line on the T = 0 K convex hull to determine stable two-phase equilibria. Mixing on the Y or Z site is performed by respectively substituting one of the Y or Z atoms with the mixing atom. However, keeping in mind the difference in number of atoms on X site in HH and FH compounds and the possibility of mixing between HH and FH, mixing on the X site requires explanation. The case of HH/HH mixing (or FH/FH) mixing is simpler, where one (or two) X atoms are substituted by the mixing atom. On the other hand, in the case of HH matrix and FH NS phase (HH/FH mixing), one atom on X1 site is substituted by the mixing atom and another mixing atom is placed in the neighboring X2 (vacant) site, thus keeping the stoichiometry of the system still on the tie-line between the two compounds. Similarly, in the case of FH matrix and HH NS phase (FH/HH mixing), the X1 atoms is substituted by the mixing atom and a neighboring X2 atom is removed leaving a vacancy, as this sublattice is vacant in the HH structure. For clearer picture of the mixing on the X site, in Figure we have shown an atomistic representation of the supercells depicting the mixing between different types of Heusler compounds.

Having in mind the large number of calculations that need to be performed, identifying the smallest possible supercell that can produce reliable results is important. Therefore, we considered five different sizes of supercells; for the case of HH structure, there are 12-atoms (conventional cell), 24-atoms (2 × 2 × 2 of the primitive cell), 48-atoms (rhombohedral bcc-style cell), 81-atoms (3 × 3 × 3 of the primitive cell), and 96-atoms (2 × 2 × 2 of the conventional cell). For the purpose of the supercell size study, we examined the mixing energies of the NiTiSn host matrix, as the most studied system experimentally, with four other compounds: NiZrSn, NiTiSb, Ni2TiSn, and Co2TiSn, as well as the mixing energy of NiZrSn matrix with NiTiSn. The mixing energies, ΔE mix XY(A)Z, between two Heusler phases, in this example two HH compounds, XYZ and XAZ, are calculated within the dilute limit using 2 Δ E mix XY ( A ) Z = E tot XY ( A ) Z - N Y - 1 N Y E tot XYZ - 1 N Y E tot XAZ where E tot XY(A)Z is the DFT total energy of a supercell of XYZ with one mixing atom, and N Y is the number of atoms in a particular sublattice (in this case the Y sublattice). E tot XYZ and E tot XAZ are the DFT total energies of the supercells of pure XYZ and XAZ, respectively. The calculated mixing energies of the matrix/NS phase pairs using different supercell sizes are summarized in Table .

Evidently, for each of the studied systems, the changes of the mixing energy when using 81-atom or 48-atom supercell are very small ( < 5%) compared to the mixing energy for 96-atom supercell. In the case of the 24-atom supercell, except for the NiTiSn/NiTiSb system that exhibits significant change in the mixing energy ( ~ 20%), the mixing energies for all other systems show small difference with respect to the largest supercell. Further decreasing of the supercell size influences only the mixing energy in the NiTiSn/NiTiSb and NiTiSn/Co2TiSb systems. The other three studied systems show that even at the smallest supercell, 12-atom, the mixing energy are converged, and the mixing energies change insignificantly compared to the largest supercell. This demonstrates that although using the 24-atom supercell can yield good results in some cases, the 48-atom supercell would give reliable results in most of the cases. Therefore, for the rest of the study, we used the 48-atom supercell.

The master equation calculations for the thermal decomposition of CH3CF3 in Ar and Kr were carried out using the single exponential-down model with the calculated values of α. For the temperature range of interest, the approximate solution to the two-dimensional master equation reduces the low-pressure limiting rate constants by ~10% compared to the one-dimensional calculations, but the rate constants become nearly identical with each other at pressures above 1 kPa (some comparisons are shown in Figure S4 in the Supporting Information). Therefore, the results presented below are from the one-dimensional master equation calculations.

The calculated and experimental rate constants for the Kr bath at 2000 K are shown in Figure . The data points of k orig shown are the rate constants derived by inter- and extrapolations from the three nearest points of the ST/LS data taken at pressures of 2.0, 4.7, 13, 47, and 73 kPa (15, 35, 100, 350, and 550 Torr). As seen, the master equation calculation cannot properly describe the pressure dependence of the rate constants. Such observation once posed a question as to the applicability of the RRKM/master equation model to this reaction. However, the present classical trajectory calculations suggest that the dissociation process indeed obeys the RRKM dynamics and there seems to be no significant faults in the collisional energy transfer model.

One possible explanation for this discrepancy is that the effect of vibrational excitation in the product HF was not taken into account in deriving the ST/LS rate constants. The ST/LS method measures the axial density gradient in a shock-heated gas. This gradient, dρ/dx, is proportional to the reaction rate and the heat of reaction with a correction for any changes in the mole number. The ST/LS rate constants were estimated by comparing the simulated density gradient profiles with the experimental profiles. Some extrapolation of the gradient profiles was made in their analyses to estimate the rate constant at time zero; therefore, the derived rate constants are sensitive only to the early gradients (after the end of the incubation delay).

The early part (where secondary decomposition of CH2CF2 is negligible) of the gradient profile of the shock-heated CH3CF3/Kr mixture has a relationship of 11 d ρ d x ∝ R 1 ( Δ H 1 - C p T ) where R 1 is the rate of , ΔH 1 is the heat of reaction of , and C p is the heat capacity at constant pressure. At 2000 K, ΔH 1 is 152 kJ mol-1 and C p T is 56 kJ mol-1 for 5% CH3CF3/Kr calculated using thermodynamic data taken from the thermochemical database. These values are comparable to the vibrational energies of the nascent HF molecules formed in the dissociation of CH3CF3. The classical trajectory simulations suggest that more than half of the HF is formed in vibrationally excited states with the distribution shown in Table . Therefore, correction is needed to account for the nascent vibrational energies of HF when the vibrational relaxation is not too rapid compared to the reaction.

If one assumes that the vibrational relaxation of HF is negligible in the early gradient profile, the rate constants can be corrected by multiplying a factor given as 12 f corr = ( Δ H 1 - C p T ) ( Δ H 1 + ⟨ E * ⟩ - C p T ) where ⟨E*⟩ is the average vibrational energies of the nascent HF formed. The nascent energies can be evaluated from the solutions of the master equations and the results of the trajectory calculations as 13 ⟨ E * ⟩ = ∫ 0 ∞ g ( E ) ⟨ E v * ( E - E 0 ) ⟩ d E - ⟨ E v ⟩ 14 g ( E ) = n ss ( E ) k ( E ) ∫ 0 ∞ n ss ( E ) k ( E ) d E where n ss(E) is the steady-state energy distribution of CH3CF3 obtained as a solution to the master equation, k(E) is the microscopic rate constants for the dissociation, g(E) corresponds to the energy distribution of the reactive flux, ⟨E v* (E x )⟩ is the average vibrational energy of the HF product as a function of the excess energy above the transition state, and ⟨E v⟩ is the average vibrational energy of HF at thermal equilibrium. Four values of ⟨E v* (E x )⟩ were calculated based on the vibrational quantum number distributions estimated from the classical trajectory calculations (Table ) at E x = 120, 150, 180, and 240 kJ mol-1, and were fit to a linear expression 15 ⟨ E v * ( E x ) ⟩ = a v E x + ⟨ E v * ( 0 ) ⟩ with the coefficient a v = 0.095 and the intercept ⟨E v* (0)⟩ = 31 kJ mol-1. These values indicate that roughly 20% of the energy is released from the (reverse) exit barrier and 10% of the excess energy above the transition state contributes to the vibrational excitation of HF.

The correction is valid as long as the vibrational relaxation of HF is negligible during the early part of the density profile. Unfortunately, the relaxation rate for collisions with Kr is not available in literature, but it is expected to have a similar (or slightly smaller due to the larger reduced mass) value to HF + Ar collisions for which the vibrational relaxation time upon shock-heating is reported. The sample gas mixtures of ST/LS contain a few percent of CH3CF3 that also affect the early relaxation rate. Assuming that the relaxation by CH3CF3 collisions has a rate constant of one or 2 orders of magnitude larger than Kr, a few percent of CH3CF3 has a relaxation rate comparable to that of the Kr bath gas. Furthermore, the vibrational relaxation rate should be larger for high ν. Therefore, the correction of the rate constant was made only for the ST/LS data that satisfy tentative criteria: k corr > 5k HF-Ar, where k corr is the corrected rate constant and k HF-Ar is the vibrational relaxation rate constant of HF in collisions with Ar.

An indication of the formation of vibrationally excited HF from was also observed in the ST/LA experiment as a short incubation period in the absorption profile of HF at the vibrationally ground state. In the ST/LA study, rate constants for were derived by interpreting the absorption profile using a kinetic model that included formation and relaxation of the vibrationally excited HF (denoted as HF* in ref ). The model was rather primitive because the distribution of the vibrational quantum numbers were not taken into account; the model attributed all of the HF formed to be HF* that relaxes with the same rate constant, k HF-Ar. To investigate the effect of explicitly considering the HF (ν) distribution, preliminary reanalysis was performed for the ST/LA data. The reanalysis assumed that the product HF (ν) distribution obeys that derived from the classical trajectory calculations at E ex = 405 kJ mol-1, and that vibrational relaxation occurs only for single quantum changes with rate constants of k(ν → ν-1) = ν k HF-Ar for ν = 1-5, as indicated from the Landau-Teller model and Schwartz-Slawsky-Herzfeld theory. This kinetic model is still somewhat primitive but provides a rough estimation of the effect of the HF (ν) distribution. The rate constants obtained from the present kinetic model typically differed by less than 5% from the original ones. Since the differences were well within the uncertainty and scatter of the rate constants, no correction was made for the ST/LA data.

The calculated ⟨E v* (E x )⟩ and the energy distribution of the reactive flux, g(E), at 2000 K are plotted in Figure . The integrations give ⟨E*⟩ of 37 kJ mol-1 at the pressure of 2.0 kPa and 41 kJ mol-1 at 73 kPa, which lead to a correction factor f corr of ~0.7. All of the 2.0 and 4.7 kPa data and the 13 kPa data at T > 1890 K meet the criteria of k corr > 5k HF-Ar, and their corrected rate constants are presented. The data at 47 and 73 kPa as well as the 13 kPa data with T < 1890 K were obtained at conditions where the rate of dissociation of CH3CF3 was in competition with the vibrational relaxation of the HF formed. No attempt was made to correct these data; it is difficult to retrieve the true rate constants that warrant quantitative comparison with theory.

The corrected rate constants at 2000 K are plotted in Figure . They showed excellent agreement with the master equation prediction. Figure shows the Arrhenius plot of the master equation rate constants together with the corrected ST/LS data and those of the ST/LA experiment. The calculated data at 2.0, 4.7, and 13 kPa were obtained with a Kr bath, and the others were obtained with Ar. The ST/TOF-MS data are not shown here for the sake of simplicity because they quantitatively coincide with the ST/LA data. The calculation satisfactory reproduces the experimental rate constants; most of the data lie within ±50% from the master equation prediction with no significant systematic deviations.

There are several sources of uncertainty in the predicted rate constants, such as explicit treatment of probability distribution for collisional energy transfer (including nonexponential distribution, effect of weak-collision in J, and dependence of the distribution on precollision J , ), anharmonic effect on the density of states, and accuracies of the reaction barrier height and the RRKM rate constant. The explicit treatment of the probability distribution results in weaker collisions and reduces the low pressure limiting rate constants, but its effect is expected to be minor for the present reaction, having a tight transition state, at the studied temperatures and pressures. Also, in the context of comparison with experimental data, it should be noted that a few percent of CH3CF3 in the gas mixtures of ST/LS experiments could affect the collisional energy transfer rate. The present calculation assumed pure Kr baths, but self-collision of molecules in general causes stronger energy transfer than collisions with monatomic bath gases, which may possibly compensate the effect of the explicit probability distribution.

The anharmonic effect on the density of states was partially incorporated in the present calculation by scaling the harmonic frequency. The scaling increases the vibrational (excluding the torsional mode) density of states of CH3CF3 calculated using the Beyer-Swinehart algorithm at the reaction threshold by a factor of 1.90 compared to the unscaled harmonic density. This value is close to the anharmonic correction to the density of state of C2H6 at its bond dissociation energy, 2.20, calculated by Nguyen and Barker. This indicates that the scaling factor of 0.95, which was derived to estimate fundamental frequencies, , can reasonably reproduce densities of states at high energies.

The accuracy of the RRKM rate constant was verified by the present classical trajectory calculation as shown in Figure . Quantum effects were not considered in the comparison between the (classical) RRKM and trajectory results, but the tunneling correction employed is expected to be sufficient because the tunneling plays only minor (though not negligible) role in the studied reaction at temperatures and pressures of interest; the correction factors, defined as the ratios of the corrected to uncorrected rate constants, were ~ 1.14 and ~1.07 at temperatures of 1500 and 2000 K, respectively, for pressures above 1 kPa. Uncertainty in the barrier height is estimated to be ±4 kJ mol-1, which was deduced from the uncertainties in the experimental rate constants at low temperature region. It is worthwhile to note that the agreement between the experimental and computed rate constants as seen in Figure could not be attained without using the barrier height revised in the recent study (previous master equation studies on this reaction , used the high-pressure limits that were factors of 2-3 larger than the present values).

Overall, the pressure-dependent rate constants for the thermal decomposition of CH3CF3 can be well reproduced by the master equation calculation on the basis of the RRKM theory. This study further demonstrated the ability of classical trajectory calculations to predict parameters for collisional energy transfer. The calculated rate constants over the temperature range of 1000-2400 K can be represented with Troe's formula as k ∞ = 3.33 × 10 14 exp ( - 37363 K / T ) s - 1 k 0 , Ar = 2.52 × 10 25 T - 8.985 exp ( - 32578 K / T ) cm 3 molecule - 1 s - 1 k 0 , Kr = 0.9 k 0 , Ar F cent = 0.08 where k ∞ is the high-pressure limit, k 0,Ar and k 0,Kr are the low-pressure limits for the Ar and Kr bath, and F cent is the broadening factor. Note that the expressions for k 0,Ar and k 0,Kr were determined from the rate constants calculated at pressures of 10-6-106 kPa, and do not necessarily represent the true low-pressure limits, which can only be reached at unrealistically low pressures (e.g.. 10-40 Pa) due to deep tunneling. The parametrized rate constants reproduce the master equation predictions with a RMS relative deviation of 13%. These rate expressions, as well as the recent recommendation for limited temperature and pressure ranges, can be used for possible application of CH3CF3 as a chemical thermometer, , or to reanalyze previous studies that employed this reaction to determine experimental temperatures.

In summary, the interfacial reaction process, dynamic morphology changes, and chemomechanical effects of the interphase between LATP and lithium metal are systematically investigated through ss-NMR, XRD, and in situ TEM. These results suggest the (electro) chemical transformation at the interface and the interphase is mainly composed of the Li3Al0.3Ti1.7(PO4)3 phase. This (electro) chemical transformation process leads to a significant enhancement of electronic conductivity and ignites continuous side reactions at the interface. High electron conductivity of the side reaction products can also induce the direct growth of lithium metal in/-passing through the interphase and accelerate the chemical and mechanical degradation of the electrolyte. What is worse is that the formation of the new phase and coupled mechanical stress will finally break up the electrolyte and its connection with the electrode, leading to a large internal resistance of solid-state batteries. An artificial layer with robust chemical and flexible properties is imperative to avoid the formation of an ion/electron mixed interfacial conductor and alleviate the corresponding mechanical stress. This is especially important to achieve a long cycle life of solid-state batteries. In conclusion, this work is beneficial for understanding the degradation mechanism for a number of solid electrolytes who are unstable with the lithium metal.

In conclusion, a three-dimensional GO (3D GO) supported Dawson polyoxotungstate catalyst P2W17/3D GO is prepared successfully through covalent bonding method. The three-dimensional network structure and large π-conjugated structure of 3D GO is beneficial to the dispersion of the active component and adsorption of DBT and THT by it, so as to make a contribution to the desulfurization. The ODS performance of P2W17/3D GO is much higher than that of P2W17/2D GO due to the favorable 3D reticular holes. DBT could be removed completely in 120 min under the most appropriate conditions, that is, 0.08 g of P2W17/3D GO, 333 K, 100 μL of H2O2, and complete oxidation of THT could be achieved in 30 min by 0.02 g of P2W17/3D GO and 100 μL of H2O2 at the room temperature and atmospheric pressure. Kinetics studies were carried out to investigate the rate constants of the ODS reactions. The ODS activities of P2W17/3D GO on different sulfur-containing compounds decreased in the order: DBT > 4,6-DMDBT > BT. Moreover, it is more important that the heterogeneous catalyst P2W17/3D GO shows good stability and reusability, and its catalytic activity remains almost unchanged after 5 cycles. Thus, covalent immobilization provides a promising way for the preparation of high efficient and stable POM catalysts for potential industrial application.

For the sake of brevity, in the main body of the present article, we will present only a skeletal outline of the computational methodology. The detailed description of the simulation setup, and a discussion of its accuracy, is relegated to the Supporting Information.

Calculations at the DFT level indicate that N8-H tautomer illustrated in Figure is by far the lowest-energy tautomeric form of BPP. This finding is in agreement with the structures of the BPP-A and BPP-G base pairs as determined by Okamoto et al. using 15N NMR spectroscopic measurements (see Figure ). Hence, in what follows, we take into account only the N8-H tautomer.

The present work demonstrates that WT insulin monomer and dimer and mutant monomers and mutant dimers lead to different spectroscopic and dynamical signatures for residues along the dimerization interface. This is found (to different extents) for all three approaches used for computing the frequency trajectory ("scan", INM, "map") and suggests that the overall findings do not depend strongly on the way these frequencies are determined. The center frequency and fwhm for insulin monomer are in qualitative (scan along CO INM) or even quantitative (scan along [CONH] INM) agreement with experiment which, together with earlier investigations of the spectroscopy and dynamics of and around NMA, ,, provides a validation of the computational model. It is noteworthy that, using one single parametrization for the -CO stretch and the multipoles on the [CONH] moiety of the peptide bond, the experimentally observed fwhm for the protein is correctly described.

Depending on the variant considered, X-ray experiments find exact or near-exact 2-fold symmetry for the insulin dimer. For the hagfish insulin dimer, an exact 2-fold axis was reported. This differs from the dimer structure of pig insulin for which it was reported that "the residues along the line of the local two-fold axes, apart from the B25 side chain, conform extremely closely to the two-fold symmetry[..]". It is notable that the violation of the exact 2-fold symmetry is due to residues B25 and D25 which also behave differently for the FFCFs due to different local hydration in the present work, see Figure .

Subsequent X-ray experiments then found that monomers M1 and M2 are not exactly symmetric. , In line with this, the present simulations confirm that on the picosecond to nanosecond time scale the dynamics at the dimerization interface (residues B24-B26 and D24-D26) is not symmetric in that the frequency maxima of the amide-I modes differ by several cm-1, contrary to residues away from the interface. This is relevant in the context of insulin function as it has been suggested quite early on that "..[the] ability of the insulin molecule to adopt different conformations may be an important factor in the expression of its biological activity..". Hence, the dynamical asymmetry found in the present work for WT and mutant insulin dimers may have functional implications.

The infrared spectroscopy for the WT and mutant monomers and dimers (at position 24) also shows considerable differences, see Figures C and . Consistent with earlier findings that the frequency shifts for WT and mutant protein/ligand complexes can be related to protein-ligand binding affinities, the present results lay the foundations to relate insulin dimer stability with infrared spectroscopy. Experimentally, such relationships will be more easily established for isotopically labeled 13C18O insulin as the spectral signatures are displaced from those of the most common 12C16O isotope. Also, further simulation studies of the infrared spectroscopy along the dimerization process for WT and mutant insulin dimers are required for a better understanding.

Finally, the role of water in general and at the dimerization interface in particular emerges as an important factor in the stability and spectroscopy of the dimer. It has already been found that mutations at position 24 allow water molecules to penetrate and destabilize the dimerization interface. The present work now establishes that this has also consequences for the infrared spectroscopy. Both frequency maxima and fwhm for residues at the dimerization interface for WT and the F24A mutant differ, see Figure . Also, for residues B25/D25 of the WT dimer, the local hydration differs appreciably (see Figure S20) which has direct consequences on the local dynamics as seen in the decay times of their FFCFs and the frequency maximum of B25 in the dimer which shifts to the red whereas that of D25 shifts to the blue relative to the insulin monomer (see Figure S3).

The fact that the stability differences between WT and the mutant (here at position B24) insulin dimer are also reflected in the spectroscopy and dynamics of WT and mutant insulin monomers and dimers suggests that spectroscopic investigations can be used to provide information about the association thermodynamics. This follows earlier suggestions for characterizing protein-ligand binding which are supported by atomistic simulations. For insulin, this is particularly relevant because except for the WT dimer direct thermodynamic information about its stability appears to be missing. Replacing a thermodynamic approach by a spectroscopic characterization is an attractive alternative. The present work suggests that combining quantitative simulations with modern experiments is a potentially useful way to obtain pharmacologically relevant information such as the strength of the modified insulin dimers.

This paper presented the integrated design and optimization of nitrogen recovery in natural gas processing where the LNG and NGL are produced, and the nitrogen is completely separated from natural gas to be vented to the atmosphere. On the basis of the structural analysis of component separation, largely two nitrogen recovery solutions, the integrated NRU and standalone one, were studied. The latter solution includes two process configurations of using an end-flash drum in producing LNG or using a stripping column at the same position. For the integrated solution, first the heat and mass transfer structure of the base case from previous research by B. Ghorbani et al. was improved in the direction of minimizing exergy destructions. Then, the new configuration for this option was optimized in terms of a specific power equivalent to the overall process efficiency through controlling major decision variables related to the heat and mass transfer satisfying product specifications. The improved design has a higher process efficiency with the specific power of 0.482 kW h/kgLNG which is lower by 26.2% than that of the base case of 0.653 kW h/kgLNG. Standalone solutions consisting of the end-flash option and stripping one which were newly designed in this study as design alternatives were optimized resulting in even lower specific powers as compared to the integrated one for both options of 0.454 and 0.401 kW h/kgLNG, respectively. Each option then reduced the specific power by 30.5% and 38.6%, respectively, as compared to that of the base case of the integrated NRU. All of these results are for the feed gas containing 5 mol % of nitrogen. For the evaluation of the process efficiency with varying feed gas compositions from various natural gas sources, each solution was optimized and compared with respect to the nitrogen content in the feed gas from 5 to 20 mol %. As a result, from 5 to around 17 mol % the standalone NRU using a stripping column has the priority over other options, and after that point the integrated NRU leads the standalone solutions in terms of process efficiency. These results may be reasonable guidelines to the process design of nitrogen recovery with various feed gases. In addition, the method this study used in design improvement and optimization may be applied to other chemical process designs.

The quantum theory of CENFs during coherent periodic tunnelling from R to P and back to R in molecules with asymmetric double-well potentials has been developed. The results are deduced from the solution of the time-dependent Schrodinger equation () as a coherent superposition of two eigenstates (); here, these are the two states of the lowest tunnelling doublet, but applications can be extended to analogous rather general superpositions of two eigenstates. This allows the periodic time evolutions of the resulting electronic and nuclear probability densities (EPDs and NPDs) as well as the flux densities (EFDs and NFDs) to be expressed in terms of simple sinusodial functions. These analytical results reveal various phenomena during coherent tunnelling, e.g.. all EPDs and NPDs as well as all CENFs are synchronous, not only in symmetric but also in asymmetric double-well potentials. Spatial symmetry of the EPDs and NPDs is broken, however, when the symmetric reference is distorted to a system with asymmetric double-well potentials. In spite of this symmetry breaking for EPDs and NPDs, spatial symmetry is conserved for CENFs. This is one of the most surprising results of this article.

The analytical results for tunnelling in asymmetric double-well potentials, which have been derived in this article, are valid during very long periods of time: the present applications are in the domains of kiloseconds. This is much beyond the capabilities of numerical techniques, which are taylored to rather short time domains of molecular reaction dynamics, typically pico-, femto-, or even attoseconds. -

Exemplary application to the Cope rearrangement of SBV shows that tunnelling of the ideal symmetric system can be suppressed by asymmetries induced by rather small external electric fields. In the present case, the amplitude of the critical field that yields the half tunnelling, half nontunnelling border is as low as 0.218 × 10-8 V/cm. Even slightly larger fields (say larger than 10-8 V/cm) suppress tunnelling completely. At the same time, the delocalized eigenstates of the symmetric reference, which can be regarded as Schrodinger's cat-type states representing R and P with 50:50% probabilities, get localized at one or the other minima of the asymmetric double-well potential, representing either R or P with 100% versus 0% probabilities.

We conclude this article with a related speculation that goes much beyond the present application to SBV: under prebiotic conditions, similar weak (as well as stronger) electric fields may suppress tunnelling between two forms (R and S or d and l) of enantiomers, e.g.. between d- and l-alanine. Instead, they should induce localizations of enantiomers in either one or the other form (e.g. L-alanine), thus destroying the ideal Schrodinger's cat state, which represents 50:50% of one and the other forms. This type of de facto symmetry breaking may have been an important early step during evolution (see the extended, in-depth discussions in refs - ). By extrapolation, the results of ref suggest an analogous breaking of parity by weak fields, combined with the generation of huge dipoles in highly excited Rydberg atoms or molecules.

Potassium bis (fluorosulfonyl) amide (K [FSA]; Tokyo Chemical Industry, purity >95%), potassium (fluorosulfonyl) (trifluorosulfonyl) amide (K [FTA]; Tokyo Chemical Industry, purity >95%), and N-methyl-N-propylpyrrolidinium bis (fluorosulfonyl) amide ([C3C1pyrr] [FSA]; Kanto Chemical, purity >99.9%) were dried at 80 °C under a pressure of 1 Pa prior to use. Mixtures of K [FSA] and K [FTA] were then prepared in a dry chamber (DAIKIN, HRG-50AR, dew point <-50 °C) by mixing the two powders and grinding them. K0.2[C3C1pyrr]0.8[FSA] RTIL was prepared by mixing K [FSA] and [C3C1pyrr] [FSA] in a molar ratio of 20 and 80, respectively.

Thermal transition temperatures were measured using a differential scanning calorimeter (DSC; Hitachi High-Technologies, DSC220) under flowing nitrogen gas at scan rates of either 10 °C min-1 or 2 °C min-1. The DSC samples were sealed in an aluminum pan in the dry chamber to avoid exposure to the air.

The densities of the samples were obtained using a 5 mL volumetric cylinder by weighing a sample and visually confirming its volume during heating. The viscosities of the samples were measured using an electro-magnetically spinning viscometer (Kyoto Electronics Manufacturing Co.. Ltd.. EMS-100). The samples were sealed in glass tubes in the dry chamber with a spherical Al probe, and all bubbles were removed, followed by heating and melting. The specific conductivities of the samples were measured by AC impedance spectroscopy with an AC perturbation of 10 mV using an electrochemical analyzer (HOKUTO DENKO, HZ-Pro). The sample was sealed in a cell with two Pt black electrodes (RADIOMETER ANALYTICAL). The cell constant was obtained by measuring the conductivity of the KCl-saturated standard solution using the cell, and the entire cell was placed in the dry chamber.

Electrochemical measurements were conducted using a stainless-steel cell (Hohsen Corp.. HS-2) in a two-electrode configuration with the potassium metal counter electrode, with the aid of the electrochemical analyzer. A glass separator (Nippon Sheet Glass, TGP010, thickness of 100 μm) soaked in the K-SCIL electrolyte was used, and the cells were assembled in an argon-filled glovebox (UNICO, UL-1800AA-KIZ, [H2O] and [O2]: < 1 ppm) to prevent any exposure to moisture and oxygen. The electrochemical window of the K [FSA]0.55[FTA]0.45 SCIL was determined by cyclic voltammetry at 90 °C using aluminum and platinum plate working electrodes. The limiting current density of K [FSA]0.55[FTA]0.45 SCIL and K0.2[C3C1pyrr]0.8[FSA] RTIL was determined on an aluminum plate working electrode by galvanostatic polarization at 80 mA cm-2 and 90 °C. Charge-discharge tests were conducted at 80 °C on a graphite electrode composed of natural graphite powder (SNO-10, SEC Carbon Ltd.. mean diameter of 10 μm) and polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) (KUREHA) binder (graphite:PVDF = 80:20 in the weight ratio) on a copper current collector. Powder X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns were obtained using an X-ray diffractometer (Rigaku Corp.. SmartLab, Cu Kα radiation, 40 kV, 30 mA) to investigate the intercalation/deintercalation of K+ into/from the graphite, respectively. The graphite electrode for XRD analysis was charged by a constant current/constant voltage mode (0.5 C (cutoff: 2.5-0.1 V)/0.1 V (cutoff: 0.1 C). The samples were then loaded in an airtight cell with beryllium windows under an argon atmosphere.
To determine of the activation energies, the alkylation of benzene with ethylene was conducted in the liquid phase using the laboratory rig that is shown in Figure .

The alkylation process usually involves several stages: dissolution of aluminum chloride in benzene in the reactor intensive mixing and furnace heating of the liquid raw materials to the process temperature feeding ethylene from the cylinder to the reactor

The alkylation is typically carried out at a temperature of 333-353 K and under atmospheric pressure. In the measurements, the alkylation of benzene with ethylene was studied at two temperatures: 346 and 353 K. The amount of supplied benzene was 80-90 g; the amount of catalyst is 0.1 g per 1 g of benzene; the ethylene feed rate is 22.4 mol/L, and the alkylation time is 1-1.5 h. The product was sampled every 15 min during 1 h. The selected samples were dried with calcium chloride and examined using gas-liquid chromatography.

The aim of this part of the work was to understand the kinetics of the AlCl3-catalyzed benzene alkylation. The chemical interaction of benzene and ethylene occurs on the surface of the powdered catalyst that is dispersed in the liquid. Thus, only a small portion of ethylene that is dissolved in the liquid phase takes part in the reaction. The concentration of ethylene in the solution is determined by the temperature and gas pressure. Owing to gas bubbling and intensive mixing of the reactants throughout the reaction volume, it was assumed that the concentration of the dissolved gas remains nearly constant during the experiment. Consequently, the changes in the reaction rates during the experiment are assumed to be solely determined by the variation of the inlet concentrations of liquid components.

To simplify the kinetic analysis of the reactions in the process, it was assumed that the process occurs in two irreversible stages: conversion of benzene to ethylbenzene and conversion of ethylbenzene to di-, triethylbenzenes. The reaction constants for the first and second reactions are denoted by k 1 and k 2, respectively.

Consequently, the measurements of the time of benzene half conversion and of the time of the maximum yield of ethylbenzene allow us to determine the rate constants of the first and second reaction stages.

The dependence of the reaction rate on temperature is described by the Arrhenius equation. , Thus, if the reaction rate constants are known at least at two process temperatures, the activation energy of the reaction of alkylation of benzene with ethylene can be calculated from the following equation: 3 E a = 2.303 R T 1 T 2 T 1 - T 2 ln ( k 1 k 2 ) In experiments carried out using gas chromatography-mass spectrometry analysis, the composition of each of the samples was determined. The Arrhenius plot for the reaction of benzene alkylation with ethylene is presented in Figure S1.
The samples analysis was performed according to the methods used by analytical laboratories of petrochemical enterprises, and meeting the ASTM standard.
According to the obtained data, the dependences "molar composition-reaction time" are obtained.

Further, the constants of first and second reactions were determined. The constant k 1 is associated with the half-transformation time of benzene and at a process temperature of 73 °C is equal to k 1 1 = 0.0154 min-1, at temperature of 80 °C k 1 2 = 0.0231 min-1.

The rate constants of the product B-ethylbenzene were determined as follows: several k 2 values close to k 1 values were chosen and then t max values were determined by eq . According to obtained data for t max = 60 min k 2 1 = 0.02675 min-1, and for t max = 40 min k 2 2 = 0.01880 min-1.
As a result of found rate constants k 1 and k 2 reaction stages, the following values of the activation energies were determined, E a1 = 135.5 kJ/mol and Ea2 = 131.9 kJ/mol.

A series of thin films containing different amounts of Si in the nanohybrid layer have been grown by pulsed laser deposition (PLD) at room temperature. Details about the PLD setup can be found elsewhere. Only the most important aspects of the fabrication process are described below. Nanosecond UV pulses, generated by an ArF excimer laser, were used to ablate alternately independent Si, Er, and Al2O3 targets, using the following sequence, depicted in Figure a. An amorphous Al2O3 (a-Al2O3) buffer layer, ~ 100 nm thick, was deposited onto both silicon and fused silica substrates simultaneously. In order to form the nanohybrid layer, first a small amount of Si was deposited onto the buffer layer. The deposited amounts of Si were suitable for the formation of a two-dimensional assembly of a-Si nanostructures in a Volmer-Weber-like fashion. Subsequently a single pulse on the Er target was used to deposit onto the a-Si nanostructures an areal density of about 2 × 1013 Er atoms/cm2, as measured by Rutherford Backscattering Spectroscopy (RBS). Such areal density corresponds to an amount of less than 2.5% of an atomic monolayer of Er (i.e.. the deposited Er atoms located in a single plane would cover less than 2.5% of the plane surface), ensuring that neither drastic Er clustering nor concentration quenching will occur. The Er areal density was kept constant for all the films. Finally, an ~10-nm-thick a-Al2O3 capping layer was deposited in order to fully embed the nanohybrid layer. Films with only Er, without prior Si deposit, were also grown in the same conditions for reference. All the films with the nanohybrid layer were characterized in the as-grown conditions; i.e.. no annealing was performed. Note that the Si amount incorporated in the films is very small and cannot be determined by RBS measurements due to the proximity in atomic number of Al (Z = 13) and Si (Z = 14). Therefore, an indirect method (that will be explained below) based on spectroscopic ellipsometry (SE) measurements has been used to identify and classify the films as a function of the amount of nano-Si (Q Si) in the nanohybrid layer. With this aim, the asymmetric design of the films, which can be considered as simple vertical photonic structures, has been chosen in order to enhance the sensitivity of SE to the presence of the nanohybrid layer.

The nanostructure of a selected thin film grown on a Si substrate has been investigated by cross-section transmission electron microscopy (TEM) characterization. Specimens for TEM observation were prepared by the lift-out technique in the Focused Ion Beam (FIB), using an FEI Strata Dual Beam 235. Bright Field transmission electron microscopy (BFTEM) images were first obtained at an operation voltage of 200 kV using a JEOL 2100 microscope. Then, energy filtered TEM (EFTEM) images were recorded at the Si plasmon peak energy (17 eV) and the Al2O3 plasmon peak energy (24 eV), using a JEOL 2010F microscope equipped with a Gatan GIF energy filter.

Information about the chemical composition of selected thin films grown on Si substrates has been obtained by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS). XPS experiments were performed in a PHI 5500 Multitechnique System (from Physical Electronics) with a monochromatic X-ray source (Aluminum Kα line of 1486.6 eV energy and 350 W power), placed perpendicular to the analyzer axis and calibrated using the 3d5/2 line of Ag with a full width at half-maximum of 0.8 eV. The analyzed area was a circle of 0.8 mm diameter, and the selected resolution for the spectra was 23.5 eV of pass energy and 0.1 eV/step for the spectra of the different elements. Since XPS probes only a region that is a few nanometers thick below the surface of the materials, in-depth information was obtained from the XPS spectra recorded after successive etching steps by a 3.5 keV Ar ion beam. All measurements were made in an ultrahigh vacuum (UHV) chamber with pressure at between 5 × 10-9 and 2 × 10-8 Torr.

Information about the near-UV-visible optical absorption of the nanohybrid layer in films grown on the fused silica substrates has been obtained by optical transmittance at normal incidence (angle of 0°) in the 1.55-4.1 eV range. In addition, SE measurements have been performed systematically on all the films grown on Si substrates. The SE spectra were recorded using a Woollam VASE ellipsometer, at angles of incidence of 65°, 70°, and 75° in the near-IR region (0.73-1.24 eV range) where both a-Al2O3 layers and nano-Si can be considered transparent with a photon energy-independent refractive index.

PL measurements have been performed in the near-IR (0.74 to 0.88 eV range) on the films grown on Si substrates using successively a continuous wave (CW) Ar+-ion laser and a solid-state CW Coherent Genesis CX355 laser as excitation sources in the visible (2.6, 2.54, 2.5, and 2.41 eV) and in the near-UV (3.5 eV), respectively. The excitation beam was S-polarized in both cases and impinged onto the film surface with a 34° and 54° incidence angle, respectively. The emitted light was collected at normal incidence using a confocal configuration, analyzed spectrally by a single grating monochromator and detected by an InP/InGaAsP near IR photomultiplier. The signal-to-noise ratio was enhanced using standard lock-in amplification techniques. Suitable interference filters were located at the entrance of the monochromator in order to avoid scattered laser light and PL of the lenses and Si substrate at energies higher than 0.7 eV to enter into the monochromator. By such means, the recorded PL spectra were free of stray light effects.

Accurate electronic structure methods were utilized to obtain the complete free energy profile of a model palladium catalyzed nucleophilic fluorination with cesium fluoride in toluene solution. The calculations with the trimethylphosphine ligand indicate a very high overall barrier (ΔG above of 40 kcal mol-1) in the case of both mono- and bicoordination of palladium by PMe3, indicating that this reaction is not feasible in usual conditions (temperature around 100 °C). The reductive elimination from the monophosphine complex is more favorable, and a potential ligand able to promote the catalysis requires that dimerization of the PdL (Ph) (F) intermediate does not take place. Nevertheless, this is not enough to make the catalytic cycle viable, which justifies the use of special monophosphine bulky ligands able to provide repulsive interactions with fluorine and phenyl groups in order to promote the reductive elimination process. In addition, the thermodynamics data from the present study also suggest that an alkene PdL complex is a better precatalyst than palladium (π-cinnamyl) chloride for generating the PdL (Ph) (Br) complex.

A phenomenological algae growth model is developed using first-principles, and uncertainties are added to the model to create a simulator to mimic the production vagaries of nature. This work also demonstrated a procedure to optimize the harvest time and the pond depth to make the process economically viable. Bootstrapping analysis is done to estimate the uncertainty associated with model parameters, and also to evaluate the range of optimized harvest time and pond depth. This work also demonstrated Leapfrogging as a viable technique for regression modeling, and for optimizing stochastic processes. The developed algae growth model also predicts the growth pattern of different strains of the same species, which provides evidence of model robustness. The method is demonstrated as functional and robust. The application reveals the need for experimental data related to biomass growth and economic values.

Furan, 2,3-dihydrofuran, and 2,5-dihydrofuran were obtained from Sigma-Aldrich. Oxygen was removed by the freeze-pump-thaw method, and neat liquid samples were sealed in stainless-steel cells with steel foil windows for muon irradiation. Clathrate hydrate crystals were grown under nitrogen from a mixture of organic liquid (5.88 mol %) and crushed ice made from oxygen-free water. The mixture was held for a few days several degrees below the hydrate decomposition temperature and subsequently stored in a freezer at -20 °C. Prior to muon spectroscopy the crystals were crushed to a fine powder in a cold nitrogen atmosphere and packed into brass cells with brass foil windows. Assuming that all the organic material was incorporated in the clathrate sample, there should be one organic guest molecule in each 51264 cavity. It is possible that some of the smaller (512) cavities contained nitrogen.

The muon spin spectroscopy experiments were performed at the TRIUMF cyclotron, in Vancouver, BC, using spin-polarized positive muons from the M15 and M20 beamlines. The muons are sufficiently energetic (4 MeV) to penetrate the thin metal windows of the cells and stop in the sample inside. The sealed sample cells were mounted in a precooled cryostat inserted in the HELIOS spectrometer, which consists of a superconducting magnet and a set of plastic scintillator detectors that register the passage of incoming muons and the correlated outgoing decay positrons. The spectrometer was oriented so that the beam enters along the axis of the solenoid magnet.

Two types of spectroscopy were performed: transverse field muon spin rotation (TF-μSR) and muon avoided level-crossing resonance (μLCR). For TF-μSR measurements, the muon beam is tuned for transverse spin polarization. Since the magnetic field is aligned along the beam direction, this means that the spins of stopped muons precess in a plane perpendicular to the field, in a manner similar to that for nuclear spins in NMR after a π/2 pulse. Unlike conventional magnetic resonance, however, TF-μSR employs a single-particle counting technique: muons are individually detected and the elapsed time between arrival of a muon in the sample and detection of its decay positron is recorded in a histogram. Because the angular distribution of positrons is a maximum in the direction of the muon spin, the lifetime histogram corresponding to each positron detector contains oscillations which reflect the passage of the precessing muon spins. Individual precession frequencies can be conveniently displayed in Fourier transforms, but quantitative data analysis involves fitting the original time spectrum. Because the HELIOS spectrometer has four positron detectors arranged in phase quadrature, complex Fourier transformation can be employed to produce a spectrum which distinguishes negative from positive precession frequencies.

Muon precession frequencies vary according to the local magnetic environment of the muon. When positive muons stop in water, ice, and most organic liquids, roughly half pick up electrons to become muonium atoms, and the other half become incorporated in diamagnetic molecules, typically through muon attachment and subsequent proton transfer. , Muons in diamagnetic environments precess at the muon Larmor frequency νμ (13.554 MHz per kG applied field), similar to proton NMR except for the higher frequency due to the larger muon magnetic moment. However, chemical shifts cannot be distinguished because of the substantial broadening due to the short lifetime of the muon. In contrast, electron-nuclear Fermi hyperfine interactions in free radicals are much larger, so muon precession frequencies can be used to distinguish between different muoniated radicals. At sufficiently high fields (typically a few kG), muoniated radicals exhibit two precession frequencies, νR1 and νR2, separated by the isotropic muon hyperfine constant A μ. 1 A μ = ν R 1 - ν R 2

Loss of signal can occur due to spin dephasing when muonium is transformed to a radical which has different precession frequencies. This puts a significant constraint on the ability to detect muoniated radicals by TF-μSR: the pseudo-first-order muonium reaction rate must be well in excess of 109 s-1.

The second type of muon spectroscopy does not suffer this limitation because in μLCR the muon spin polarization is aligned along the magnetic field, so there is no precession.
