In conclusion we hope that our new experimental data and modeling results will be useful for designing ILs as new entrainers for modern extraction technologies.

In summary, the wavepacket motion in the excited electronic state of CV was detected using the amplitude ripples in the SE and ESA transient signals by exploiting the phase change of the wavepacket when passing through the minimum of the potential. These vibrational coherences lasted for several picoseconds and appear unperturbed by internal conversion as indicated by the absence of any shift in the node position in the ESA and SE signals along the waiting time, until these coherences completely dephase within a time scale of >10 ps. The slow dephasing of the vibrational wavepacket in the excited state and the invariable node position is a reflection of slow intramolecular vibrational relaxation, which in turn suggests weak coupling of this normal mode to other modes of CV (i.e.. very weak anharmonicity). The system is an ideal example of a weak coupling regime, wherein the excited and ground electronic states interact weakly with each other, and hence coherent nuclear motion generated in the excited state stays there until it dephases completely without facing a reactive internal conversion. The system instead internally converts to the ground state through Fermi's golden rule transition following exponential rates.

A series of highly dispersed Pd/Hβ catalysts with different metal and acid site properties was prepared by the weakly capping growth approach. The acid/metal balance was confirmed to be the key factor for benzene hydroalkylation. The relationship between the acid/metal molar ratio and the CHB yield was established, and the best cyclohexylbenzene yield of 32.8% was obtained at an acid/metal molar ratio of 22.4 μmol of H+/μmol of exposed Pd. In addition, the correlation analysis of acid types and properties indicates that the weak acid and Lewis acid greatly affected the benzene conversion, and the strong acid and Brønsted acid more impacted the alkylation process. The Pd/Hβ catalyst prepared by WCGA showed excellent stability compared with that prepared by dry impregnation, which demonstrated good application for industry.

Glass samples with compositions of (30 - x) Na2O xAl2O3 70SiO2 (x = 0, 10, 15, and 20 mol %) doped with 1 wt % CuO were prepared by a melt-quenching technique. More specifically, mixtures of commercially available SiO2, Na2CO3, Al (OH)3, and CuO of analytical reagent grade were melted in a covered corundum (α-Al2O3) crucible at 1550 or 1650 °C for 6 h. After removal from the melting furnace, the samples were annealed at 600 °C for 15 min, followed by cooling naturally to room temperature in the furnace. The glass samples with the thickness of ~1 mm were cut and polished using the slurry of diamond particles ( ~ 1 μm). Heating the glass samples in H2 gas was performed in a fused silica tube furnace, through which 100% H2 gas flowed at a rate of ~5 mL/min. The glass composition is hereafter shown as the nominal one without quantitative analysis.

27Al and 1H MAS NMR experiments were carried out using a JEOL ECX 800 MHz spectrometer equipped with an 18.79 T magnet. The pulverized glass samples were sealed in a ZrO2 rotor of 3.2 mm diameter and spun at a rate of 20 kHz to 208.5 MHz. 27Al MAS spectra were collected with an excitation pulse of 0.6 μs, 30° pulse width for AlCl3 aqueous solution, and 2.0 s pulse delay time. The chemical shifts (CSs) were referenced to 0 ppm of the external 1 M AlCl3 aqueous solution. 27Al 3Q MAS NMR spectra were obtained using a three-pulse sequence employing z-filter. The spectra were collected with a 2.7 μs triple quantum excitation pulse, 0.9 μs conversion pulse, 15 μs selective pulse, and 0.5 s pulse delay time. 1H MAS NMR spectra were measured using depth pulse sequence to suppress probe background signals. The MAS frequency was at 20 kHz, and the spectra were collected with a 3 μs excitation pulse, 90° pulse width, and 4 s pulse delay time. 1H chemical shifts were recorded from tetramethylsilane, Si (OCH3)4, of the external reference.

A JEOL ECX 500 MHz spectrometer equipped with an 11.75 T magnet was used for the 29Si MAS NMR measurement. The spinning frequency, excitation pulse, pulse width, and pulse delay time were 10 kHz, 3.4 μs, 90°, and 20 s, respectively. The 1H-27Al CPMAS NMR spectra were obtained with a contact time of 2.0 ms, pulse delay time of 7.0 s, and scanning numbers of 73 000. For the case of 1H-29Si CPMAS NMR spectra, these values were 3.0 ms, 7.0 s, and 46 000, respectively.

Fourier transform infrared (FT-IR) spectra were collected using a Jasco FT-IR4600 spectrometer. The formation of the OH bond was verified on the basis of the absorption spectra in the range of 4000-2000 cm-1 for platelike samples with ~1 mm thickness.

In conclusion, we demonstrated that the polyanion sublattice of the LiFePO4 triphylite is prone to the PO4 3- → mO2- + nOH- substitution under hydrothermal conditions. Ultimately, the hydrotriphylite solid solutions Li1-x Fe1+x (PO4)1- y (OH)4y are obtained. Being prepared at reductive conditions, the hydrotriphylites contain a relatively small fraction of ferric iron, and the charge compensation for the PO4 3- → [(OH)4]4- substitution occurs through decreasing the Li/Fe ratio that, in turn, introduces the strong and unequivocal correlation between the Fe fraction at the M1 position and P deficiency. This puts forward the hydrotriphylite-type substitution as the main factor causing Li deficiency and increasing Fe population of the Li diffusion channels, which can reach up to 12%.

The defect chemistry of the LiFePO4-based materials appears to be much richer than previously thought, and the polyanion sublattice should no longer be considered an inert component of this important battery material. Our results call for a reconsideration of many previous observations, such as the enlarged unit cell volume and increased FeM1 population in the materials prepared at low temperatures ( < 200 °C) in aqueous conditions, in the context of their possible anion off-stoichiometry due to a partial replacement of phosphate with hydroxyl groups. Such a hydrotriphylite substitution introduces drastic changes in the crystal structure, rendering it noncentrosymmetric due to the concerted Li displacements from the center of the channels and the ensuing shortening of the Li-O bonds. This increases the activation barriers for the Li diffusion and, together with the FeM1 substitution, negatively impacts the electrochemical performance. The hydrotriphylite substitution lowers the temperature of antiferromagnetic ordering that can be used as an indicator to detect this substitution in the hydrothermally prepared materials. The off-stoichiometry caused by this substitution critically depends on the overall precursor and reducing agent concentration in the hydrothermal solutions, placing it among the most important parameters to control the chemical composition and defect concentration of the LiFePO4-based cathodes.

In this work, hydrolysis precipitation-an effective method-has been utilized for the first time to prepare the supported bimetallic catalysts, and the prepared Cu x Zn y -SiO2 catalyst presented a predominant activity in the hydrogenation of MA to EtOH. The HP method realized the significant high dispersion of copper and zinc species and the formation of the strong interaction between Cu and ZnO. Compared with the CuZnO/Al2O3 catalyst (STY = 0.775 gEtOH gcat -1 h-1) prepared by traditional coprecipitation method, the Cu9Zn1-SiO2 catalyst achieved significant higher catalytic performance with a STY of about 1.024 gEtOH gcat -1 h-1 in the MA hydrogenation. It was also found that the introduction of ZnO inhibits the formation of copper phyllosilicate, which is the cause of the decrease of Cu+ specific surface area. Meanwhile, the linear relationship between TOF (Cu+) and Zn/Cu molar ratio indicated that the increase of Zn/Cu molar ratio could enhance the formation of Cu-ZnO x species, which benefits more the generation of highly active Cu+ sites than Cu-O-Si species. This work could also provide a concept for the synthesis of other kinds of bimetallic catalysts.

Graphene has been functionalized with amine-containing groups, and this functionalized graphene has been used to prepare nanohybrids with bone cement. Functionalization has been verified through FTIR and Raman spectroscopic measurement along with the changes in morphology. The mixing temperature has significantly been reduced to the body temperature in functionalized graphene composite, thereby avoiding any cell necrosis during the implantation of bone cement. The nature of the interaction between functionalized graphene and bone cement has been worked out through FTIR and UV-vis studies. The thermal stability has increased by 37 °C compared to pure bone cement. Both the stiffness and the toughness increase significantly for the nanohybrids vis-a-vis pure bone cement. The cell viability through MTT assay and cell adhesion has been greatly enhanced in nanohybrids in comparison to pure bone cement, which has further been confirmed through cell morphology and imaging. An amine-functionalized graphene nanohybrid is found to moderate the rate of polymerization and make this class of material suitable for implant. In vivo study has been performed with this material, and it is found to be an excellent healing agent for fractured bone, as is evident from the calcination in just 20 days against no healing in the control or against the use of the usual bone cement as grouting material in the same time frame.

The atomic structures of the Eu-doped NaAlSiO4 systems were fully optimized by periodic DFT by using the PBE functional with a Hubbard U parameter of 2.5 eV for the Eu 4f electrons , and the PAW approach, as implemented in the VASP code. , The electrons of Eu (5s25p64f76s2), Na (2p63s1), Al (3s23p1), Si (3s23p2), and O (2s22p4) were treated as valence electrons. The "stress-strain" method was employed to calculate the elastic constants, based on which the elastic moduli were derived with the Voigt-Reuss-Hill approximations. The Debye temperature ΘD was then determined with the quasiharmonic model, which has been demonstrated previously to be an accurate approximation. The geometry optimizations were performed until the total energies and the forces on the atoms converged to 10-6 eV and 0.01 eV Å-1, respectively. A 2 × 2 × 2 k-point grid was used for L-NASO:0.083Eu2+ and N-NASO:0.143Eu2+, while for L-NASO:0.333Eu2+, a 4 × 4 × 2 k-point grid was adopted. The cutoff energy for the plane wave basis was set to 530 eV.

In this study, we analyzed the formation pathways and mechanism of N2O over Cu-SSZ-13 during the SCR process and learned the effect of reactant concentration in the feeding gas on N2O formation. NSCR is the major pathway, and NSNO also contributes to N2O formation at high temperatures. The decomposition and disproportionation of NO to N2O barely take place. When NO2 was introduced into the reactor, a significant amount N2O forms and O2 is not necessary for this process, while O2 is necessary for standard SCR condition. Besides, N2O formation at low ( < 350 °C) and high temperature takes place via different mechanisms. At low temperature, N2O formation is contributed by the formation and decomposition of NH4NO3. NH4NO3 could form on Cu (OH)+ under both NH3 + NO2 and NH3 + NO + O2 conditions because Cu (OH)+ is active for oxidation, which can oxidize NO to NO2 and nitrites to nitrates. NH4NO3 may also occur on Cu2+ and Brønsted acid site under NH3 + NO2 because of the disproportionation of NO2, but the amount is relatively small. However, the N2O formation may result from NSNO and the Eley-Rideal mechanism at a higher temperature.

In addition, ANR, NO2/NOx, and O2 and H2O concentration all affect N2O formation. Higher ANR leads to more N2O formation because of more sufficient reactants. The increase of NO2/NOx leads to more NH4NO3 formation at low temperatures, but N2O formation is also determined by the NH4NO3 decomposition rate, when the temperature is high enough for NH4NO3 decomposition, higher NO2/NOx leads to more N2O formation. Increasing NO2/NOx also leads to more N2O formation at high temperatures, but the increasing tread is different from that at low temperatures. O2 is necessary for NH3-SCR and N2O formation under standard SCR condition. The increase of O2 level from 1 to 10% leads to a continual increase in N2O formation but no effect on SCR activity. The increasing trends are totally different at low and high temperatures. The introduction of H2O could not only increase the Brønsted acid sites but also inhibit the NH3-SCR and N2O formation at low temperature. Increasing H2O concentration from 0 to 2% led to N2O formation and NOx conversion increase, whereas further increasing H2O concentration led to the inhibition of both. However, at high temperature, the introduction of H2O could decline the side reaction during the NH3-SCR process and lead to NH3-SCR activity increase and the N2O formation decrease.

The synthesis of ionomeric poly (hexamethylene isophthalamide), containing various amounts of sulfonated groups randomly distributed along the polymeric chains, was optimized. The reaction, which uses the 5-sulfoisophthalic acid sodium salt (5-SIPA) as a comonomer, proceeds easily and rapidly. All the prepared polyamides resulted amorphous and characterized by high T g values, which increase with the increment of ionic group amount. This behavior has been attributed to the formation of intermolecular links that contribute to reduce the chain mobility in the glassy state. Accordingly, the OTR values at RH50 decrease by increasing the presence of SO3Na groups. Moreover, polyamides having 10 mol % or more of ionic groups are characterized by water-solubility, and compositions with 15 mol % of 5-SIPA proved to be suitable for preparing waterborne coatings and adhesive layers even very thin and capable to adhere toward various polar substrates. Therefore, the authors believe that the remarkable melt processability of most composition (up to 10% of 5-SIPA) allows to use them as barrier layer in blown or cast film manufacturing, but also, and most importantly, as adhesives in extrusion coating or extrusion lamination of aluminum foil or vacuum coated films (i.e.. AlOx, SiOx, aluminum coated films). Particularly convenient could be the use of these compositions as modifiers of PA6 either to improve adhesion to polar substrates or to facilitate dispersion of fillers. Therefore, PA6I-co-5-SIPA can be a class of materials with a unique set of properties and range of possible applications.

Analysis of the spectra of the CH3CONHOH/Ar matrices exposed to a 225 nm laser line or to the full output of Xe arc lamp indicated the existence of two simultaneous photochemical processes: rotamerization reaction of the 1Z AHA isomer into 1E one (1Z → 1E) and AHA photodissociation reaction. The high yield of the isomerization reaction enabled identification of most of the 1E AHA wavenumbers in accord with the MP2/aug-cc-pVTZ calculated spectrum.

The identified products of the AHA photolysis reaction evidence existence of four reaction channels leading to the formation of the CH3OH HNCO (), H2O CH3NCO (), H2O CH3CNO (), and CO CH3NHOH () molecular complexes. Small amounts of the monomers forming each complex are also observed. The spectral and theoretical data obtained in this work for AHA and literature data on photodissociation of simple amides and hydroxamic acids allow us to conclude that the first step in formation of the complexes (), (), and () and their corresponding monomers is the fission of the N-O bond. In turn, a first step in formation of the complex () and its corresponding monomers is the cleavage of the C-N bond. The possible full mechanisms of the formation of the four pairs of coproducts are proposed.

The structures of each of the four complexes formed during AHA photodissociation were optimized in two steps using the MP2 computational level with the 6-311++G (2d,2p) and aug-cc-pVTZ basis sets. The calculations resulted in three stable structures for the CH3OH HNCO complex, in two configurations for the H2O CH3NCO and H2O CH3CNO pairs and in four stable isomers for the CO CH3NHOH complex. The spectra evidenced that during AHA photodissociation the configurations corresponding to the global minimum as well as those due to the local minima are formed. The performed study demonstrate that photolysis of a proper precursor entrapped in a rare-gas matrix is a powerful method of producing molecular complexes that may be difficult to obtain in a traditional way.

In this work, the effects of TBPO on the separation of CO2 from a CO2/CH4 (67.0 mol %) gas mixture had been studied through experiments. The results showed that the content of methane in residual gas was higher when the gas/liquid volume ratio was decreased. The highest CH4 concentration in the residual gas phase was increased from 67.0% to 89.6%, obtained in 26 wt % TBPO aqueous solution with an initial gas/liquid volume ratio of 2.23 by one stage hydrate separation at 287 K and 2 MPa. The CH4 recovery was 0.91, and the CO2 separation factor was 17.01 by adding 5.0 wt % TBPO. By recovering the pressure after the hydrate formation began through the use of a hand pump, the residual gas in the vessel continued to form hydrates; then the CH4 concentration in the residual gas phase increased to the highest level of 93.3%.

Biomimetic proteoglycans with full glycosaminoglycan bristles (chondroitin sulfate) and a synthetic polymer core in bottlebrush architecture have been synthesized. These molecules mimic the three-dimensional structure and water uptake of natural proteoglycans and can be modulated to mimic the broader family of proteoglycans.

Our synthesis design enables fabrication of various biomimetic proteoglycans by varying the length of an enzymatically resistant, synthetic polymer core, GAG bristle density, and type of GAG chains (depending on its primary amine content). A "grafting-to" approach, where GAG chains are coupled onto a polymer core through the reaction of a primary amine on a GAG would allow to avoid additional functionalization of disaccharide units commonly used in current synthesis strategies, thus, maintaining GAG chemical structure.

Butanol loss was measured as a function of the movable injector position, that is, interaction time between the VOC and dust surface. In a typical experiment, a freshly coated tube was placed in the reactor and the injector was set to bypass the reactor, so that no surface was exposed to the gas flow (position 0). The flow of butanol was then established and its concentration monitored. When it was constant, lights were switched on. After 60 min, the uptake measurements started by moving the injector stepwise (steps of 2 cm), exposing the ATD surface for 10 min. The injector was then reset to position 0 for another 10 min. The procedure was repeated until the entire length of the coated tube was exposed, which is equivalent to 10 positions of 2 cm each.

The decay of gas phase butanol obeyed first-order kinetics according to 1 ln C ( 0 ) C ( t ) = k obs t C(0) and C(t) are the inlet and outlet concentrations of butanol after a reaction time (t), and k obs is the measured first order rate constant. The uptake coefficient can then be calculated according to 2 γ = 4 k obs ⟨ v ⟩ V S surf where V is the total volume of the reactor, S surf is the surface area exposed to the gas, and ⟨ν⟩ is average molecular velocity. For a cylindrical flow tube, the geometric uptake coefficient is given by 3 γ geo = 2 r ⟨ v ⟩ k obs where r is the radius (r tube = 0.55 cm).
It is worth noting that the uptake coefficients reported here are at steady state, reached after 10 min of exposure, and not the initial uptake coefficients usually reported in the literature.

The reductive desorption experiments of SAMs was conducted by cyclic voltammetry in a solution of 0.5 M NaOH, scanning from -0.2 to -1.2 V with a scan rate of 0.02 V s-1. The cyclic voltammograms on the SAMs surface were obtained using a charged redox center at specific pH, scanning from -0.3 to 0.6 V with a scan rate of 0.1 V s-1. The approaching curves toward the SAMs were obtained using charged redox center with an approaching rate of 3.3 μm s-1. The tip was biased with 0.4 V and the substrate was at open circle potential. The SECM images were recorded within an area of 50 × 50 μm at the center of the SAMs electrode. The tip-to-substrate distance was set as 0.5 d/a using approaching curves.
The concentrations of various organic contaminants were determined by high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC; Agilent 1200 Series) based on our previous study. -

In the U.S.. acceptable chemical analysis methods for compliance monitoring of effluents under the NPDES are listed in the Code of Federal Regulations, title 40, part 136, but a permitting authority may specify the use of alternative methods. Passive sampling may not be the first method of choice for this type of compliance monitoring, because discharge permits are defined as TMDLs (i.e.. concentrations in total effluent, multiplied by the daily effluent discharge volume). By contrast, method requirements for ambient water monitoring by the States are essentially unregulated by federal law, but instead result from the interaction between the U.S. EPA and a given State's department of environmental quality on how to assess water quality in relation to the WQC, using the best available practices. The Consolidated Assessment and Listing Methodology (CALM) aims to continuously improve the quality of ambient water monitoring, using chemical, biological, and toxicological data, among others.

OSPAR and EU prescribe a number of criteria for chemical analysis and sampling to ensure that valid and comparable data are generated within monitoring programs (Table ). , Methods have to be documented and validated, and a quality assurance and control system needs to be in place to monitor and control data quality. WFD related methods have to be in accordance with EN/ISO/IEC 17025. Reference materials should be used, and laboratories must participate in proficiency testing schemes for the analytes of interest. Legally binding minimum performance requirements for chemical methods used in WFD monitoring are that the measurement uncertainty be ≤50% at the level of the EQS, and the limit of quantification ≤30% of the EQS. OSPAR does not specify quantitative requirements for these parameters, but requires that background assessment concentrations (BACs) for the target analytes in the sampled matrix be available. These BACs are derived from the mean and variance of long-term (10-year) concentration data for remote areas, as reported by participating laboratories. Measured concentration values are considered to be above background unless there is statistical evidence showing that it is near background. ,

Method requirements for the application of PSDs in chemical monitoring of nonpolar compounds in a regulatory context are fulfilled to varying degrees (Table ). Detailed guidelines for the use of PSDs are available for silicone sheet samplers and semipermeable membrane devices. ,, ASTM International developed a standard method for SPME of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) in pore waters. Several interlaboratory studies that demonstrate method consistency are available, and are discussed below. A proficiency testing scheme organized by QUASIMEME is operational (www.quasimeme.org). Certified reference materials (CRMs) are presently not available, but CRM preparation for passive sampling could be easier than for batch water sampling. Data quality can be assessed from repeated analysis of CRMs (when available) or reference materials prepared by laboratories in-house, similar to current practice for the analysis of sediment and biota samples. Although Table is focused on passive sampling in water, it can be envisioned that similar requirements exist for passive sampling in sediments.

In the U.S. context, ambient WQC for the protection of aquatic life against nonpolar compounds are based on toxicity tests with low organic carbon concentrations in the test water, and hence are essentially based on C free, albeit implicitly. WQC for the protection of human health are derived from chemical uptake by consumption (drinking water, fish/shellfish). Concentrations in fish/shellfish that are considered to be sufficiently protective are converted to aqueous concentrations using (preferably field derived) BAFs that are based on C free. However, for use in WQC development, to be consistent with water quality monitoring data, these BAFs are converted back to values based on the total concentration. , Thus, human health WQC cannot be directly compared with passive sampling results. Consequently, while regulators in the U.S. recognize the importance of C free, the actual water quality monitoring regulations do not yet use this parameter. OSPAR also aims to define water standards on a C free basis. Quality standards in the EU are commonly defined as C total, but EU regulations allow the use of standards for other matrices if these offer an equal level of protection. Generic suspended particulate matter (SPM) contents of 15 mg L-1 (fresh waters) and 3 mg L-1 (marine waters) are recommended to convert between C free, C total and concentrations in SPM. ,, An ISO standard for the deployment, retrieval, and analysis of passive samplers is available, but guidance that is specific to particular sampler types and contaminant groups (e.g.. polychlorinated biphenyls - PCBs, PAHs, polychlorinated dibenzo-p-dioxins/furans - PCDD/Fs) may have to be added in the future. This ISO standard also includes quality control measures to assess recoveries, precision, and method detection limits. Guidance for the selection, validation (QA/QC) and deployment of PSDs for contaminated sediments is also available.

Differences in the monitoring approaches between the U.S. and OSPAR on one hand, and the EU on the other, will likely affect the further application of passive sampling in a regulatory context. In the U.S. context, States, U.S. EPA, and the research community cooperate in the CALM approach, to generate monitoring data that are best fit for a given purpose. Also OSPAR promotes the use of new technologies to amend existing methods for chemical monitoring. By contrast, monitoring in the EU is strongly regulated in legally binding directives that define EU-wide EQSs and specify method requirements for compliance checking with these EQSs.

To promote adoption of passive sampling into the implementation of compliance monitoring regulations, there is a critical need to get beyond passive sampling as a purely scientific endeavor and begin to standardize PSD type selection, deployment, chemical analysis, and data reporting. For example, in the United States, the lack of standardized methods has impeded greater acceptance of passive sampling in regulations. The following discussion reviews the progress made with passive sampling with regard to use in water, sediments, and biota. The discussion also emphasizes the areas in which passive sampling needs more work before standardizing can be successfully initiated.

2-Hydroxydodecyl starch ethers were synthesized by reaction of 1,2-epoxydodecane with potato starch in aqueous alkaline medium. A careful attention has been given to the purification steps and, more precisely, to the identification and the quantification of the coproducts. In addition to classically observed 1,2-dodecanediol, bis (2-hydroxydodecyl) oxide was extracted from the crude. This dimer issued from the reaction of the diol on the epoxide has never been described during the synthesis of 2-hydroxyalkyl starch ethers. The purification by Soxhlet extraction compared to the process by grinding required fewer steps but a longer time. The values of the MS were always around 1.1 in the used conditions, but the recovery yields were higher for the treatment by grinding compared to Soxhlet (85 vs 63%). Finally, in term of industrial development, the recycling of the washing solvents is possible in the both cases. Nevertheless, the technologies available at industrial scale are more in line with the transposition of the grinding process that can provide better productivity through the use of existing and scalable equipment to handle both grinding of the crude product and extraction of soluble byproducts in relevant solvent.

Ketonization of the single component of the biomass pyrolysis vapor was carried out over CeO2. The optimum temperature range of each component was obtained, and its crossing point was 420 °C. The synergistic effect of acids, aldehydes, and furfurals in the ketonization process was studied. Acid was beneficial for the ketonization of the linear aldehyde by providing water (the conversion raised by 50%), while furfural inhibited the ketonization of acid (the yield of acetone reduced by 20%) because of the coverage of active sites by the active furfural. This study is helpful for the efficient utilization of biomass for ketonic platform compounds by designing the pyrolysis process.

Laminated magnetic (M/MoS2)/rGO has been successfully synthesized from a facile route, avoiding the problem of aggregation and incomplete reaction, meanwhile improving the efficiency of absorbing materials. The results show that (M/MoS2)/rGO composites have significant electromagnetic properties of the as-prepared magnetic (M/MoS2)/rGO composites. The dimensions of rGO and MoS2 interlayer spacing range from several nanometers to >0.816 nm. The dielectric Cole-Cole semicircle suggests that there are Debye relaxation processes in the laminated magnetic (M/MoS2)/rGO, which is beneficial for the enhancement of dielectric loss and the impedance matching level for electromagnetic-wave-absorbing materials. MoS2 and rGO could have the advantages of MoS2 and rGO, which could be defined as an electromagnetic complementary effect. When the (M/MoS2)/rGO content is 18 wt %, (M/MoS2)/rGO-wax composites exhibited good absorption properties. With a maximum reflection loss (RL) of -49.7 dB, (M/MoS2)/rGO-wax composites exhibited an effective EVA bandwidth of 5.81 GHz at a thickness of 2.5 mm. The strong absorption capability of (M/MoS2) and rGO could be used as promising materials for RWA and have broad absorption properties. The experimental results indicate that the enhanced absorbing performance of composites is attributed to the compensatory properties of (M/MoS2) and rGO. (M/MoS2)/rGO composites have a great potential in the development of lightweight and high-efficiency RWA materials.

In the main experiments, using some control devices led to an increase in the level of styrene and detection of new VOCs. To better understand VOC emission from the control devices, additional experiments were performed. First, a filter conditioning experiment was carried out. The air purifier with a freshly opened filter 1 or filter 2 was conditioned in a 3 m3 stainless steel chamber (self-built, Fraunhofer WKI; fulfills ISO 16000-9) at an air exchange rate of 0.5 h-1. The air purifier operated for 8 h per day at medium flow rate, for 4 days. The VOCs in the chamber were measured every day before and during the operation of the air purifier. A similar conditioning test for the filter cover was conducted. Details can be found in part S3 of the Supporting Information. Second, to evaluate whether conditioning the filters could minimize the VOC emissions, five additional 3D printing emission control tests were performed in the 30 m3 chamber (Weiss Umwelttechnik), using the same procedure that was used for the main emission control experiments. For details, see part S4 of the Supporting Information. Lastly, a filter heating experiment was conducted to investigate whether the adsorbed VOCs will be emitted upon heating. Filter 2 from the air purifier, the HEPA filter and the active carbon filter from the filter cover, which have been used in the additional 3D printing emission control experiments, were heated in the 3 m3 stainless steel chamber to ~62 °C. VOCs in the chamber during the heating process were measured. Details are provided in part S5 of the Supporting Information.

We emphasize here that redox proteins offer a number of potentially important mechanisms for achieving the catalytic effect, alongside with the traditional mechanism of reaching the activation barrier through collective polarization fluctuations of the polarizable medium. Nonergodic sampling and penetration of water to the protein's core are the mechanisms specific to proteins. The difference in polarizabilities of Ox and Red states is a more general mechanism applicable to all electron-transfer reactions, which gains importance depending on the magnitude of the polarizability change between the oxidation states.

Cytochrome c is an important case of a protein for which nonergodic sampling found in simulations of many other proteins was not reproduced. To explain reorganization energies reported by electrochemistry, polarizability of the active site was included. It results in a depression of the activation barrier similar to the effect of nonergodicity, as indeed confirmed by calculations based on the empirical valence-bond method. These results were recently challenged in ref , which could not confirm our previous reports. In an attempt to test different simulation/calculation protocols, a direct formalism for calculating the reorganization parameters from anisotropic linear polarizability and electrostatics produced by simulations is introduced here. Our present calculations confirm that polarizability of the active site couples to high-magnitude fluctuations of electrostatic fields and potentials from the protein-water interface to produce a significant depression of the electron-transfer activation barrier. This simplified model qualitatively supports previous findings involving full diagonalization of the active-site Hamiltonian and points to the deficiencies of the analysis attempted in ref . More importantly, it provides a transparent and physically appealing approach to study protein electron transfer involving polarizable active sites.

We find a curious match between the anisotropies of the polarizability difference tensor and the tensor of the electric field produced by the protein-water thermal bath. It appears that the design of cytochrome's active site allows large electric fields, originating from the contact between the heme and water, along the heme's plane where the active site is most polarizable. There are a number of instances found in previous simulations where partial penetration of water into the active site is significant for the electron-transfer kinetics , and for other protein function. ,- The general design principle in all such cases is the creation of strong interfacial heterogeneity and related strong interfacial electric fields. Here, we find that such fields, induced by the protein-water interface, combine with anisotropic polarizability of the active site to allow the depression of the activation barrier.

In this study, we constructed gentamicin-loaded silk fibroin coatings on 3D-printed porous CoCrMo bone substitutes by using EPD technique. Through optimization, relatively intact, continuous, homogeneous, and conformal coatings with average thickness of 2.30 ± 0.58 μm were deposited around the struts with few pores blocked. The porous metal substitutes showed no obvious loss in mechanical properties after the EPD process. The initial osteoblastic response on coated substrates was better than that on metal surface, and the SFGM coatings had significant antibacterial effect within 1 week. This work would be beneficial for exploiting the beneficial properties of silk fibroin EPD coatings to improve the biological functionality of porous structures made of medical metals.

First we describe the typical results of pressure-induced Raman spectral changes in the C-H stretching vibrational modes of the imidazolium cation, which are commonly used as an indicator of crystallization (Figure ). We found that the pressure-induced crystallizations of [C n mim] [BF4] did not occur, whereas [C2mim] [BF4] and [C8mim] [BF4] were found to crystallize during the decompression process from the superpressed state. The results for [C2mim] [BF4] are in an agreement with ref , where [C2mim] [BF4] shows crystal polymorphism at approximately 2.0 (phase II) and 1.0 GPa (phase I) upon decompression. Unfortunately, because the pressure range is beyond the coverage of direct thermodynamic measurements, such as DSC/DTA, in a fashion similar to previous studies, , we used the line broadening of the sharp ruby R 1 fluorescence line to distinguish high-pressure vitrification from crystallization. As an example of the results, we provide the spectral change of [C6mim] [BF4] in Figure . Figure shows the variations in the full width at half-maximum (fwhm) of the ruby R 1 line relative to the 0.1 MPa line on [C n mim] [BF4] for 2 ≤ n ≤ 8 during the compression process. The pressure where the line broadening begins is defined as the glass transition pressure p g. We can see that the increase of Δfwhm with increased pressure drastically increases above the initiation point p g. Thus, all the [C n mim] [BF4] homologues for n = 2-8 can be superpressed into a metastable (glassy) state without crystallizing. The effect of altering the alkyl chain length on the transition behavior is seen to be continuous.

Remarkably, when the superpressed liquid was further compressed above p g, another change in the Δfwhm occurred in the 4-6 GPa range, as shown in Figure . Here, we tentatively call the pressure where this change occurs p 1. We note that for n ≥ 5 one more kink appears to materialize in the Δfwhm, which we call p 2, though we experienced that the kinks in Δfwhm for p 1 and p 2 were sometimes shallow and difficult to define precisely. These results can be interpreted to indicate that other structural changes may be generated in [C n mim] [BF4], with other (densified) structures being induced by higher pressures. In this regard, it is interesting to note that the multiple glass transition behavior related to nanophase separation in poly (n-alkyl methacrylate) homopolymers was reported by Beiner et al.. who observed three qualitatively different glass transitions at 0.1 MPa. In an effort to explain this unusual glass transition behavior, two empirical mechanisms were suggested: a static nanophase separation between main and side chains and a dynamic heterogeneity with two intrinsic length scales.

Observed p g, p 1, p 2 values are plotted in Figure A, including their experimental uncertainties based on several runs. The variations in p g and p 1 against pressure yield a sigmoid-like curve. We find that solid and dotted lines in panel A can be fitted with the equations of state (n > 2) as below. 1 p g = [ a / 1 + e - { ( n - 3.825 ) / b } ] + 2.133 ± 0.04619 ; ⁣ a = 0.6574 ± 0.01132 and b = - 0.4029 ± 0.2617 2 p 1 = [ a / 1 + e - { ( n - 4.853 ) / b } ] + 3.753 ± 0.07036 ; ⁣ a = 2.032 ± 0.1147 and b = - 0.2114 ± 0.1817

As the alkyl chain length increases from n = 2 to 8, p g shifts from 2.8 GPa to lower pressures of ~2 GPa. In other words, the [C n mim] [BF4] with longer alkyl chains tend to solidify at rather low pressures. In addition, a drastic decrease in p 1 is observable at n ≥ 5, but p 2 is almost constant for n = 5-8. Since the ruby R 1 line reflects the non-hydrostatic condition, the shear and uniaxial stresses in [C n mim] [BF4] for n ≥ 5 are assumed to be non-negligible, despite being in the glassy solid state. We speculate that the differences in the extents of the line broadening for different values of n correlate with the divergence of the hierarchy structure. It appears that n = 5 is the crossover point, above which the applied pressure affects the inherent structure in [C n mim] [BF4] to a different degree. As mentioned above, we sometimes experienced that longer alkyl chains correspond to a less defined kink in the Δfwhm of p 1 and/or p 2. This results in difficulties in obtaining well-defined p 1 (and p 2) values at higher pressures. We suspect that this is due to the dynamic heterogeneity with the intrinsic hierarchy structure relaxing on different time scales. Interestingly, Faria et al. proposed that the Raman spectrum of crystallized [C3H7NH3] [NO3] shows microheterogeneity resulting from different local structures under high pressures; this means that different parts of the same sample exhibit different Raman profiles. Structural rearrangements take place in both the nonpolar and polar domains, which can be independent of each other.

Here we need to consider the interactions of ions due to strong Coulomb forces and of the alkyl chains due to weak van der Waals forces, which involves the compact packing of the alkyl chains with increasing pressure. Tokuda et al. proposed ionicity as a useful parameter to characterize the properties of ILs. Changes in the alkyl chain length cause changes in the interactive forces, which result in decreased electrostatic attraction between the cation and anion. On the other hand, the increase in the number of hydrocarbon units enhances the van der Waals interactions. Therefore, the balance between these two opposite factors is altered depending on the extent of applied pressure, besides the alkyl chain length.

The present remaining ambiguities include the change in the nanostructure domains of [C n mim] [BF4] with applied pressure. One idea is to perform SAXS experiments. As a first report on the SAXS mearements for the imidazolium-based ILs at ambient pressure, Triolo et al. showed that a characteristic peak at the low-Q region (2-4 nm-1) appeared. They proposed that this characteristic prepeak is direct evidence of the structural heterogeneity (nanophase separation) of ILs and the value of Bragg spacing D is the measure of an average size of the domain (the alkyl tail domain size + the thickness of the surrounding charged shell). However, there have been some debates on the molecular origin of the low-Q peak, and the relationship between liquid structure and the low-Q peak. For example, it was suggested that the position of the prepeak corresponds to a spatial correlation length, such as the distance between neighboring shells in the liquid structure and/or intermolecular correlations between anion pairs, adjacent tails, and cation tail/anion pairs. Hardacre et al. proposed that the low-Q peak arises from spatial correlations between imidazolium rings at the second coordination shell separated through the alkyl groups.

Figure shows a pressure dependence of SAXS intensities for [C8mim] [BF4] at room temperature. As far as the authors know, this is the first report on pressure-induced changes in the low-Q peak for ILs. An intense peak around 4 nm-1 is identified as Kapton films for X-ray windows. The observed intensities were normalized by the Kapton peak. At ambient pressure, the position of the prepeak for [C8mim] [BF4] was almost the same as the one reported by Triolo et al. With increasing pressure, the prepeak position shifted gradually to higher Q and the peak intensity decreased. A significant finding is that the prepeak almost disappeared above ~2 GPa, at which [C8mim] [BF4] falls into superpressed state shown by the Raman results. It should be noted that the peak intensity reverts back when we retrieve the sample at 0.1 MPa. The molecular origins of prepeak remain somewhat controversial, and thus we do not go much further. But, in view of the SAXS results, the causes for the structural changes at p g and p 1 are probably different from each other.

Then, we consider how the local structure changes under high pressure from other factors such as a conformational change of [C8mim]+ cation. The [C n mim]+ cation has conformational equilibria between the trans and gauche conformers for the main long alkyl chain. The ~625 and ~600 cm-1 peaks in the CH2 rocking mode are assigned to the trans and gauche conformers, respectively. , We determined the intensity fractions (f) of gauche and trans conformers by curve fitting spectra in the CH2 rocking mode (Figure A).

The f value of each conformer is given by 3 f gauche = I gauche I gauche + I trans , ⁣ f trans = I trans I gauche + I trans where I gauche and I trans indicate the relative Raman intensity of gauche and trans conformers of [C8mim]+ cation, respectively. The results are shown in Figure B.

Figure B shows that the [C8mim]+ cation prefers the gauche conformer in the liquid state at 0.1 MPa. The population of gauche (trans) conformer increases (decreases) by ~15% upon compression up to when the system falls into the glassy sate. After the p g point the gauche fraction becomes constant against pressure and then starts to decrease after p 1. After p 2, the slope of f gauche seems to change again. These results indicate that the local structure around the [C8mim]+ cation is changing with p g → p 1 → p 2. Interestingly, we can see that the behavior of the f against pressure is basically concordant with the ruby R 1 Δfwhm change in Figure . Taken together, a plausible interpretation is that p 1 (and p 2) is the result of the smaller dynamic heterogeneity of the main chains with two intrinsic length scales, i.e.. n = 2-4 and the longer alkyl chain segments.

In this study, we found that all [C n mim] [BF4] homologues for n = 2-8 exhibit glass transition behaviors at 0.1 MPa, and that with n = 2 exhibits cold crystallization, where a similar phenomenon is observable in the relaxation from the glassy sample of polymers upon heating at 0.1 MPa. , The frozen state at low temperatures is understood to be relaxed upon heating, thereby causing the crystalline phase, which is energetically favorable at these higher temperatures, to appear. The summarized glass transition temperature T g is plotted in Figure B, which shows that the T g increases as the chain length n increases. This is simply due to the higher viscosity coupled with the elongation of the alkyl chains for glass formation upon cooling. It is interesting to point out that Hamaguchi et al. reported the increment of the population of trans conformers with larger n values of [C n mim] [BF4] at 0.1 MPa and 298 K. The results in Figure B indicate that, the larger the population of trans conformers in the initial liquid phase, the higher the T g of [C n mim] [BF4] where the crystallization phenomenon is bypassed by supercooling.

We find that the solid line in Figure B can be fitted with the equation of state (n > 2) as below. 4 T g = a n 2 + b n + 167.4 ± 1.391 ; ⁣ a = - 0.1595 ± 0.06051 ⁣ and ⁣ b = 4.563 ± 0.6141 We also found that [C n mim] [BF4], which crystallizes upon decompression, tends to crystallize by thermal treatment at ambient pressure, although the two are not perfectly matched. Comparing the high-pressure (p g) and the low-temperature (T g) phase diagrams reveals a kind of mirror image in the behavior, suggesting that the high-pressure phase behavior of ILs can be anticipated from the results of the low-temperature phase behavior during crystallization or glass formation to some extent. We infer that the movement of a moiety of the alkyl chain is likely key to the phase transition behavior and triggers crystallization.

As we mentioned in our earlier reports, , the conformational behaviors of low-temperature (quick-cooled) and high-pressure glasses are completely different, although whether the two glassy phases are thermodynamically distinct remains an open question. Hence, it is important to note that, recently, Ribeiro et al. proposed the equations of state for ILs estimating molar volume under pressures on the order of GPa and showed the relationship between two states' p g values at 295 K and T g values at 0.1 MPa, introducing a scaling parameter γ. The present results may be valuable for testing this assumption.

In summary, based on the present study, we have provided a high-pressure phase diagram for [C n mim] [BF4] homologues with different alkyl chain lengths for 2 ≤ n ≤ 8. We have found that [C n mim] [BF4] homologues for 2 ≤ n ≤ 8 fall into the glassy state with applied pressures of 2-3 GPa. There is an implication of multiple phase or structural transitions to ~7 GPa. These p g values are lower than those of commonly used pressure media, such as a 4:1 mixture of methanol and ethanol (9.8 GPa) and 2-propanol (4.2 GPa), but are slightly higher than or comparable to those of glycerol (1.4 GPa) and silicone oil (0.9 GPa). If we consider the result of [C4mim] [PF6], which crystallizes upon compression, the results of [C n mim]-based ILs can be separated into, at least, three distinct groups on the basis of their behavior: (1) pressure-induced crystallization upon compression due to the reduction of lattice energies through disruption of packing efficiencies, (2) superpressurization upon compression, and (3) decompression-induced crystallization from the superpressurized glass. More advanced experiments, however, are required to present a thorough discussion.

In this publication, using Rayleigh-Schrodinger perturbation theory within a (time-dependent) density functional theory framework, we derived and studied three reactivity descriptors related to the responses of a molecular system to an electrostatic (point-charge) perturbation. We here focused on the calculation of δρ(r), the first-order reorganization of electron density, δN, the total number of shifted electrons under perturbation at first order, and E (2), the second-order correction to energy. Through identification of these descriptors to quantities deriving from the linear response function, a well-known conceptual-DFT descriptor, and physical interpretation of the equations, we could show the proposed descriptors should convey information on reactivity and selectivity, both at a qualitative and at quantitative level. Application of these descriptors on different systems whose chemical properties are known indeed proved their strong predictive potential. In all cases δρ(r) is able to provide qualitative information about the fate of the studied system, indicating the expected electron flows and hinting about the subsequent nuclei motions. δN and E (2), however, allow a more quantitative insight on reactivity, allowing us, for instance, to characterize numerically which site in a molecule is most prone to react.

Interestingly, as we could show in the last two examples, the proposed formalism also allows us to obtain insights on reactivity without the need for the user to implement his/her own chemical knowledge. Indeed, perturbation on nuclei still induces an electronic response relying on the "valence shell". In turn, this allows a full automation of the reactivity characterization of a given system, through a systematic evaluation of the descriptors after perturbation on each nucleus to be conceived. We feel this offers an interesting perspective to develop in the close future. The bridge with conceptual DFT also offers interesting perspectives; noticeably, what could be the equivalent of our descriptors within the grand-canonical ensemble?

On a different viewpoint, we could also use our approach to evaluate reactivity in confined systems, for instance, within enzymatic cavities or within a solid catalyst. At a first level of modeling, the confining entities could indeed be simply modeled by a collection of point charges, inducing an electrostatic potential on the chemical reagents they embed. One may then wonder how this embedding potential affects reactivity: could this electrostatic perturbation play a significant (if not preponderant) role in the observed catalyzes?

A nitrate-dependent iron oxidizer Pseudogulbenkiania strain 2002 was chosen as the Fe oxidizing microorganism. Nontronite, an Fe (III)-rich smectite, was selected as a model Fe-bearing clay mineral. Oxalate (OXA) and NTA were chosen as two representative ligands to study their effects on NDFO (Section S1). OXA is exudated by plants and fungi, and its typical concentration in the environment ranges from 25 μM to 1 mM. Synthetic NTA is used in daily products and radioactive waste decontamination projects, where its concentration can reach 5-10 mM. Nontronite (NAu-2), purchased from the Clay Minerals Society, has a formula of M0.72(Si7.55Al0.45) (Fe3.83Mg0.05) O20(OH)4, where M represents interlayer cations. The Fe content is 24%, of which 92% is in octahedral site and 8% in tetrahedral site. Bulk NAu-2 sample was size-fractionated to obtain 0.02-0.5 μm fraction. NAu-2 was prereduced by Shewanella putrefaciens CN32 and pasteurized (23% extent of reduction, Section S2). Anoxic and sterile NTA and OXA (Sigma, ACS grade) stock solutions were prepared (Section S2).

Strain 2002 is an anaerobic betaproteobacterium capable of either heterotrophic or lithoautotrophic growth, and cell stock was prepared in a heterotrophic growth medium (Section S3). , To rule out the two ligands as growth substrate or toxic compounds, preliminary experiments were performed (Section S4). OXA and NTA (5 mM concentration) neither served as growth substrates nor had any toxic effect to strain 2002 (Figure S1). A previous study also did not show toxic effect of NTA at 5 mM concentration. Thus, NTA and OXA were used for subsequent NDFO experiment.

Balch tubes (25 mL total volume) containing bicarbonate buffer were purged with N2/CO2 (80:20), sealed, and autoclaved. In an anaerobic chamber, sterilized rNAu-2 stock was added as the sole electron donor [final conc. 5 g/L, equivalent to 5 mM Fe (II)], amended with anoxic and sterilized sodium nitrate as the sole electron acceptor ( ~ 10 mM final conc.). Vitamins and trace minerals were omitted to maintain a nongrowth condition. NTA or OXA stock solution was added to achieve a final concentration of 5 mM. Cell stock suspension was added to achieve a final cell concentration of ~3 × 108 cell/mL. Two biotic experimental groups were set up: Fe (II) + Cells + NO3 - + NTA and Fe (II) + Cells + NO3 - + OXA. No-ligand control was identical to biotic experimental treatments but without ligand. Abiotic and heat-killed controls were also set up. Heat-killed (HK) cells were prepared by heating ~3 × 108 cell/mL at 121 °C for 30 min. For N2 (a product of nitrate reduction) gas measurement, separate experiments were set up, where the headspace of each tube was purged with He for 15 min. Because NO3 - was added in all control and experimental groups, in later descriptions, NO3 - was omitted for simplicity. The total volume of each reactor was ~10 mL. All groups were in duplicate and incubated in an anaerobic chamber at 30 °C in the dark. The pH was recorded in all groups and remained at 6.8-7.0 throughout the experiment.

As a comparison, a supplementary experiment was performed, where ligand-complexed aqueous Fe (II) replaced structural Fe (II) in rNAu-2 under otherwise identical condition (Section S5). To test the possibility of abiotic Fe (II) oxidation by nitrite (a product of nitrate reduction), another supplementary experiment was set up (Section S6). Because we observed more dissolution of rNAu-2 (by NTA and OXA) in abiotic groups (e.g.. rNAu-2) than in cell-amended groups (e.g.. oxidized NAu-2), we hypothesized that rNAu-2 was more soluble than oxidized NAu-2. To test this hypothesis, a third supplementary experiment was performed, where unreduced NAu-2 was mixed with 5 mM OXA or NTA under otherwise identical conditions (Section S7). NAu-2 dissolution was determined by measuring aqueous concentrations of major elements using inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectroscopy (ICP-OES).

In this work, we demonstrate for the first time the use of an amorphous polymeric matrix, in combination with an ionic liquid, to control the oxygen reduction chemistry across multiple electrodes in a Li-O2 cell. In the presence of Li cations, a 2 mol e-/O2 process is observed, but when Li+ are absent, and ionic liquid cations are present, the ionic liquid becomes the active cationic specie, leading to a 1 mol e-/O2 process and the formation of solid ionic liquid-superoxide complexes.

The ability to obtain a 1 mol e-/O2 chemistry through a gel polymer electrolyte, without the addition of expensive catalysts, can allow for remediation of the sluggish kinetics, significant reactivity, high charging overpotentials, and poor capacity retention typically attributed to the 2 mol e-/O2 process in Li-O2 batteries. Furthermore, this approach reduces the stringency of requiring high lithium-ion conductivity in electrolytes (any bulky cationic source can be used), and could be explored in other metal-air batteries, and metal-sulfur systems where the limitation of intermediate polysulfide solubility is vital. Further optimization of this system, development of more stable ionic liquids, an investigation of a broader set of stable polymer systems with differing glass transition, ionic liquid compatibility, and molecular transport properties can allow for higher ionic liquid utilization, higher capacities, and longer cycle life.

To discuss the development of the IR absorption bands as a function of cluster size, Figure shows the n = 1-4 cluster IR depletion spectra in the 2600-4000 cm-1 hydride stretch region. The IR depletion spectra of 2PY (H2O) n , n = 1-3A were measured by detecting at the respective S0 → S1 electronic origin, using 2C-R2PI excitation/ionization; these are marked by red arrows in Figure . As the origin bands of n = 3B and n = 4A are less intense, their IR depletion spectra were measured by detecting at the 31 404 and 31 297 cm-1 bands, respectively. In Figure a-c one sees that the IR spectra of the n = 1, 2, and 3A clusters resemble each other, while those of isomer 3B and 4A differ strongly from the others, especially in the 3000-3750 cm-1 range.

Figure compares the IR spectrum of the n = 1 complex to the stick spectra calculated with the different DFT and correlated ab initio methods discussed above. All previous work ,,,, and the computational methods employed here agree that the H2O molecule of the n = 1 complex accepts an H-bond from the 2-pyridone NH group and acts as an H-donor to the O-C group; see Figure . The weak and narrow band at 3725 cm-1 in Figure a is assigned to the free (non-H-bonded) OH stretch, labeled OHf in the calculated IR spectra. On the basis of the calculations, the intense and broad band at 3346 cm-1 is assigned to the H-bonded OH stretch vibration, denoted OHb in the calculated spectra. The calculations agree that the intense and broad band at 3292 cm-1 should be assigned to the NH stretch of the 2PY moiety. The group of four narrow and weak bands between 3140 and 3240 cm-1 arise from the CH stretch fundamentals of 2PY. The weak band at 3040 cm-1 is not predicted by the calculations; we assign it as an overtone or combination band. The NH and OH stretch B97-D normal-mode eigenvectors for the n = 1 complex are shown in the Supporting Information, Figure S3.

Note that we are comparing harmonic wavenumbers to anharmonic experimental wavenumbers; no account for anharmonicity is made in the calculations. Thus, good mutual agreement of calculated and experimental wavenumbers should not be viewed a sign of success of the given DFT/basis set combination, because anharmonicity in OH and NH stretches is substantial. However, uniform scaling of the calculated wavenumbers cannot be employed, because the anharmonicity varies with coordination pattern.

In agreement with previous results ,, the computational methods employed here predict that the n = 2 cluster forms a water-wire bridging the NH and C-O groups of 2PY. In Figure we compare the n = 2 experimental IR spectrum to the five calculated IR spectra. The narrow and weak bands at 3719 and 3727 cm-1 are assigned to the free OH stretches, denoted OHf(1) and OHf(2). The broad and intense band at 3340 cm-1 is assigned as the OHb(2) stretch of the second water molecule, denoted DA(2) in Figure . Both this water molecule and DA(1) of the n = 1 complex are H-donors to the O-C group of 2PY (see Figure ), consistent with the observation that the wavenumbers of the n = 1 and 2 OHb bands practically coincide. The band at 3264 cm-1 is assigned to the OHb stretch of water DA(1), which is H-bonded to DA(2). The band at 3198 cm-1 is assigned to the NH stretch; it is the most intense band in the IR spectrum, and its wavenumber is lowered by 94 cm-1 relative to the NH stretch of n = 1. Both features imply an increase of the NH O hydrogen-bond strength relative to the n = 1 complex. The narrow bands in the 3000-3200 cm-1 range arise from the four CH stretch fundamentals of 2-pyridone. These may acquire additional intensity by intramolecular harmonic mixing with the NH stretch, which is shifted closer to the CH stretches, compared to the n = 1 complex. The other bands in the 3000-3200 cm-1 region arise from overtones and/or combination bands. The calculated wavenumbers and intensities are also given in Tables and . The NH and OH stretch B97-D normal-mode eigenvectors are shown in the Supporting Information, Figure S3.

Our interpretations agree with those of Matsuda et al. who assigned the FDIR bands of 2PY H2O and with those of Florio et al. who discussed the IR bands of the n = 1 and 2 clusters, supplemented with ab initio calculations.

This combined experimental and modeling study explores ways in which MW-activated hydrogen plasmas operating under conditions relevant to contemporary diamond CVD reactors, i.e. at a high gas temperature (T g ~ 3000 K) and moderate pressure (p ~ 150 Torr), are affected by additions of noble gas (R = Ar and Kr). The experiments provided spatially resolved optical emission spectra from the d and G excited states of H2, from the n = 3 level of atomic hydrogen and from various excited states of Ar and Kr, as functions of gas mixing ratio. The experimental data are compared and contrasted with the outputs of a self-consistent 2-D (r, z) model of the plasma-chemical, transport and electromagnetic processes prevailing in H2/Ar plasmas with different X 0(Ar). Such comparisons allow characterization of the dominant plasma (and plasma emission) generation mechanisms prevailing in MW-activated H2/Ar plasmas, and identification of the more important Ar-H, Ar-H2, and H-H2 coupling reactions. Noble gas addition causes a radial expansion of the plasma, and thus leads to more uniform [H] and T g profiles just above the substrate-a finding that should find use when planning diamond growth experiments involving larger area substrates and dilute C/H/(Ar) gas mixtures. Noble gas addition in the current experiments is also found to exacerbate (unwanted) sputtering of the copper section within the reactor base plate. The observed gas phase Cu* emission intensities correlate well with the calculated ArH+ (and KrH+) ion concentrations just above the substrate surface but appear insensitive to the (relatively more abundant) H3 + and H3O+ ion concentrations in this region.

In this paper, we worked out the mixed quantum/classical theory for the inelastic collision of two asymmetric-top rotors, which is the most general case of two-body scattering. In this method, the state-to-state transitions between the internal rotational (or ro-vibrational) states of molecules are treated quantum mechanically using the time-dependent Schrodinger equation, whereas their relative translational motion (responsible for scattering) is treated classically using the average trajectory (Ehrenfest) approach. Two versions of the formula for transition matrix elements were presented: a straightforward approach that uses numerical multidimensional quadrature over all internal degrees of freedom and a (more standard) analytic approach that uses an expansion of the PES over the basis set of spherical harmonics. Adaptation to the case of identical-molecule scattering was also presented.

This theory was then applied to the rotational excitation of two water molecules, H2O + H2O, using the PES from recent literature. Properties of the expansion coefficients of the PES, and of the state-to-state transition matrix elements, were analyzed to reveal the major features of this system, such as a long-range dipole-dipole interaction. Calculations of collisional excitation from the ground state of the system, 000000, into a number of low-lying excited rotational states were carried out in a broad range of energies, up to 10 000 cm-1. Analysis of computed opacity functions showed a rather unusual scattering regime, dominated by a strong anisotropic long-range interaction (dipole-dipole). Several most important dipole-driven transitions were identified and discussed in detail. The coupled-states approximation was tested and found to agree semiquantitatively (within a factor of 2) with the fully coupled version of the method. Differential cross sections for the elastic scattering were computed for several collision energies and found to have a very narrow forward scattering peak.

The computer program written for this work is now being packaged into a user-friendly suite and will be made available for the community as a part of a forthcoming publication: Semenov, A.; Babikov, D. "MQCT. II. User-Ready Program for Calculations of Inelastic Scattering of Two Molecules", which we announce here. It is being designed to have an interface similar to that of MOLSCAT, such as simple input files and the same way of feeding into the PES.

In summary, a MDW structure with high efficiency of coupled fluorescence emission was fabricated and used as the sample substrate for fluorescence microscopy. This MDW structure sustains several guided modes mainly distributed in the dielectric layer. By a focused radially polarized annular beam illumination, a virtual optical probe is formed in the dielectric layer. Fluorophores on top of the structure were excited by the virtual optical probe and then coupled into the optical modes inducing the directional and enhanced fluorescence emission, which is verified by fluorescence BFP image. By scanning the sample with the virtual optical probe, confocal fluorescence images assisted by PSs on the substrate is achieved. In contrast to the structure used for SPCE, MDW substrate provides highly enhanced fluorescence image. Also, due to minimized metal quenching effects in the MDW substrate, the fluorophores from the MDW structure are more stable, over 10× longer, than that from the SP structure. This simple MDW design can be readily modified for different resonant wavelengths by changing the thickness of the dielectric layer. The multilayer format offers new opportunities for high efficiency fluorescence imaging.

In this paper, we have explored the hole polaron formation in Fe-doped BaZrO3 and Y-doped BaZrO3 in both the dilute limit and at increased dopant concentrations. We have established that doping of BaZrO3 with Fe and Y, respectively, leads to completely different polaron configurations, in which the polaron is centered on the dopant when BaZrO3 is Fe-doped and on an oxygen ion when BaZrO3 is Y-doped. The polaron is also more delocalized in Fe-doped BaZrO3 than in Y-doped BaZrO3. These differences are attributed to the difference in covalency between Fe-O and Y-O bonds, with the former having a much more covalent character. Moreover, in Fe-doped BaZrO3, there are two polaron configurations where the polaron charge density is delocalized over either four or two neighboring oxygens. Our results are fully consistent with the recent XAS data, but we show that the correct interpretation is that in Fe-doped BaZrO3 the polaron is centered on the Fe ion, not confined to the oxygen ion as claimed in ref .

In the dilute limit, the polaron is strongly associated with the Fe dopant with a trapping energy of about 0.6 eV compared with a free polaron, a self-trapped hole. This implies a hole mobility with an activated temperature dependence. In the case of an Y dopant, the corresponding trapping energy is much smaller, about 0.1 eV.

With increasing Fe dopant concentration, the acceptor level is smeared out and downshifted, and finally, the electronic band gap is nearly closed. This results in higher electronic mobility and higher hole concentration and a more metallic-like conductivity. Our data support that this dramatic increase of the conductivity occurs around the dopant concentration 25% and our results are consistent with the percolation conduction mechanism seen experimentally. We show that the electronic structure is sensitive to the ordering of the dopants. To obtain the percolating behavior, we identify that the critical configuration is two polaron configurations delocalized in the same plane and where the distance between the polaron configurations is two lattice spacings and parallel to a B-O bond direction (Fe-O-Zr-O-Fe). We find that small lattice distortions may lower the energy and open up a small electronic band gap, again emphasizing the sensitivity of the electronic structure on the details of the ordering of the dopants. We also discuss the effect of the oxygen vacancies in the material, but a more detailed study of the vacancy-hole interaction is beyond the scope of the present work. In contrast to the Fe-doped system, we find no indication of a transition to a percolation conduction mechanism in the Y-doped system.

In conclusion, our results contribute to the atomistic understanding of the percolation conduction mechanism seen experimentally in Fe-doped BaZrO3 and to the understanding of the connection between the chemical nature of various dopants and how they impact the overall electronic properties of acceptor-doped BaZrO3.

Density functional theory was utilized to confirm the bond energy and products. The stationary and transition-state structures of all reaction pathways in the S0 state were optimized at the B3LYP/6-311++g (d,p) level. Vibrational frequencies were calculated at the same level to characterize the imaginary frequency status. The stationary structures were confirmed by all real frequencies and transition structures in the presence of lone imaginary frequency.

In the current study, we have analyzed the structures and energetics of the coexistence of multiple noncovalent interactions. 4-Amino-2-iodophenol as a model system has been chosen to understand cooperativity among the nine different kinds of noncovalent interactions, viz.. cation-π (CP) hydrogen bond (HB) through O (OHB), HB through N (NHB), halogen bond (XB), π-π (PP), metal ion-lone pair (ML) through O (OML), ML through N (NML), charge assisted hydrogen bond (CHB) through O (OCHB) and CHB through N (NCHB). Through all possible combinations of these noncovalent interactions, based on energy, geometry, charge, and AIM analysis, we have systematically analyzed the cooperativity among 40 ternary systems and 105 quaternary systems. We have found that CP-HB, CP-PP, HB-HB, HB-XB, and HB-PP interactions are cooperative in nature, as shown in earlier studies. - ,- We have explicitly observed that CP-XB, HB-ML, HB-CHB, XB-PP, XB-ML, XB-CHB, PP-ML, and PP-OCHB can also form cooperative ternary systems. While studying the quaternary systems, we have observed that HB, XB, and PP work together by enhancing each others' strength. While analysizing our results, we have found that ∑ρ - ∑ρ (binary) (and/or ∑∇2ρ - ∑∇2ρ (binary)) may be considered as a signature of cooperativity for the system. It is interesting to observe that HB-HB, HB-PP, or HB-HB-PP interactions are cooperative, which are primarily responsible for forming the helical structure of DNA. In our study, we have found that CP-HB, CP-PP, HB-ML, HB-CHB, PP-ML, PP-CHB, CP-HB-HB, HB-HB-CHB, HB-HB-ML, HB-PP-ML, and HB-PP-CHB are also cooperative. These findings indicate that the positively charged species can play a crucial role in biological systems. From this study, we have observed that the positively charged species enhances HB-HB and HB-PP interactions and forms cooperative HB-HB-CHB, HB-HB-ML, HB-PP-ML, and HB-PP-CHB systems. Surprisingly, OHB-OML-NML, OHB-OML-OCHB, OHB-OML-NCHB, OHB-NML-OCHB, NHB-OML-NML, NHB-OML-NCHB, and NHB-NML-OCHB are also cooperative in nature despite the electrostatic repulsion between two positive charge species. The current study explains the coexistence of cooperative and anticooperative effects and highlights that a fine balance between these two aspects results in imparting stability to macromolecular assemblies.

The method for modifying and optimizing tips and substrates in this approach is effective and useful. All measured forces of molecular pairs were consistent and within the ranges reported in the literature. Estimation of molecular interaction forces in force-distance curves for bioapplication is still challenging. There are many potential bioapplications with further investigations. Providing additional screening reference for microsensing applications is just one example. This method could provide references regarding intermolecular forces for various interactions of immunocomplexes and ligand-receptors in bioapplications. This method is also useful for studying the structures and properties of molecular, cellular, and bacterial surfaces.

We have presented a detailed analysis, at both the classical and quantum levels, of the temperature dependence of isomeric equilibria and vibrational spectra of M+(H2O) n clusters, with n = 1-3 and M+ = Li+, Na+, K+, Rb+, and Cs+, calculated with the MB-nrg PEFs introduced in ref . Nuclear quantum effects are found to play a negligible role in determining the relative stability of different isomers of clusters containing the lighter ions, Li+ and Na+, with one structure of each M+(H2O) n cluster effectively dominating the isomeric equilibria over the temperature range between 0 and 200 K. Although the small number of water molecules considered in this study is not sufficient to fully complete the first solvation shell around Li+ and Na+, the most stable structures of Li+(H2O) n and Na+(H2O) n clusters tend to resemble those found in solution, with the ion at the center of the cluster. At the classical level, competing effects between ion-water and water-water interactions become more pronounced for the heavier ions, which results in a larger number of low-lying isomers, some of which appear to serve as initial seeds for extended hydrogen-bonded networks. Within this picture, K+ holds a special place since, at the classical level, the relative stability of its clusters with water follows a trend similar to that of the lighter ions at low temperature and the heavier ions at high temperature.

When nuclear quantum effects are explicitly taken into account within the path-integral formalism, the relative stability of K+(H2O) n clusters is largely modified by zero-point energy contributions which shift the isomeric equilibria toward structures with no hydrogen-bonded water molecules, such as those predicted for Li+(H2O) n and Na+(H2O) n clusters. A similar trend is followed by Rb+(H2O) n clusters, which exhibit increasing stability for isomers containing hydrogen-bonded water molecules. Water clusters containing Cs+ are the first ones for which the most stable structures correspond to isomers where the ion is interacting with a network of two and three hydrogen-bonded water molecules.

For all clusters, good agreement is found between anharmonic vibrational spectra calculated within the local monomer approximation and the available experimental data. ,- Besides providing further support for the accuracy of the MB-nrg PEFs, this level of agreement emphasizes the importance of properly taking into account the anharmonic and quantum effects in computer simulations for a correct description of M+(H2O) n clusters. Importantly, the possibility to directly connect experimental measurements with computer simulations at the molecular level provides hope for the development of a consistent picture of ion hydration from the gas to the condensed phase.

Using MD simulations, we have presented a systematic study of structural and material properties of various lipid nanodiscs differing in size and lipid composition. The computational analysis tool we have recently developed was used here to extract the spatially resolved elastic moduli from MD trajectories of finite-size nanodisc structures. The analysis revealed that for a given lipid type all the measured properties (i.e.. area per lipid, bilayer thickness, bending rigidity, and tilt modulus) varied within each nanodisc and between nanodiscs of different sizes. Moreover, the nanodiscs are significantly stiffer than their corresponding unconstrained (periodic) membranes. The results indicate strong correlation between the locally extracted bending rigidity and area per lipid (or bilayer thickness) that obey a common scaling law. Our findings may have implications as to how proteins embedded in nanodiscs can be structurally and functionally influenced by properties of the surrounding lipid environment.

The shear viscosity of four alkylaminoethanol-based CO2 absorbents is determined as the function of temperature and CO2 loading. A modified version of the VFT equation is proposed to correlate the viscosity as the functions of these two parameters simultaneously. Compared at the same volume concentration of CO2, the shear viscosity of the solution increases with increasing the alkyl chain length, and the effect of the chain length becomes stronger with CO2 loading. The SAXS profiles of these absorbents before and after the CO2 absorption are measured. A prepeak representing the mesoscopic domain structure is observed when the alkyl chain is long, and the prepeak is enhanced by CO2 absorption. It is thus considered that the mesoscopic domain structure works to increase the shear viscosity of the CO2-loaded amine solutions, although the detailed microscopic mechanisms are to be clarified yet.

We demonstrated four types of photo-TE effects: the n-type normal effect of H y WO3, the p-type normal effect of PTO on SiO2, the n-type anomalous effect of PTO (50 nm)/H y WO3, and the p-type anomalous effect of PTO (90, 200, 250 nm)/H y WO3 and PTO (50 nm)/WO3. The anomalous photo-TE effect, i.e.. the increase in both S and σ under light irradiation, is important because it fulfills the conditions for high TE performance. In particular, we achieved both n-type and p-type anomalous photo-TE effects using the same components, PTO and WO3 (H y WO3), by controlling the thickness of PTO, with and without applying the chromic reaction to WO3. We need to enhance the photo-TE properties as well as the transparency before the PC reaction and the spectral change before and after the reaction. Such studies are now underway in our laboratory. However, on the basis of the fact that the TE devices are composed of n- and p-type materials, the present findings would be expected to lead to a functional material for use as a component of photochromic smart windows, which are anticipated to provide shade from sunlight while simultaneously generating electric power.

Sediment cores were collected at 32 sites from 2010 to 2013 throughout the nGoM (Figure , Table ) using an Ocean Instruments MC-800 multicoring system, which collects eight cores (diameter: 10 cm; length: up to 70 cm) simultaneously, one of which was used from each site for short-lived radioisotope analysis.
